======================================================================
ARTICLE: Biochar
WIKIPEDIA REVISION TEXT
======================================================================

{{short description|Lightweight black residue, made of carbon and ashes, after pyrolysis of biomass}}
{{About|charcoal which goes into soil|more general information|Charcoal}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=September 2026}}
[[File:Biochar pile.jpg|alt=A large pile of biochar|thumb|A pile of biochar]]
[[File:Biochar ready for application.jpg|thumb|alt=Biochar mixture ready for soil application|Biochar mixture ready for soil application]]
'''Biochar''' is a form of [[charcoal]], sometimes modified, that is intended for organic use, as in soil. It is the lightweight black remnants remaining after the [[pyrolysis]] of [[biomass]], consisting of [[carbon]] and [[Ash (analytical chemistry)|ashes]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Khedulkar |first1=Akhil Pradiprao |last2=Dang |first2=Van Dien |last3=Thamilselvan |first3=Annadurai |last4=Doong |first4=Ruey-an |last5=Pandit |first5=Bidhan |date=2024-01-30 |title=Sustainable high-energy supercapacitors: Metal oxide-agricultural waste biochar composites paving the way for a greener future |journal=Journal of Energy Storage |volume=77 |article-number=109723 |doi=10.1016/j.est.2023.109723 |issn=2352-152X |doi-access=free|bibcode=2024JEnSt..7709723K }}</ref> Despite its name, biochar is sterile immediately after production and only gains biological life following assisted or incidental exposure to biota. Biochar is defined by the International Biochar Initiative as the "solid material obtained from the [[thermochemical]] conversion of biomass in an [[Reducing atmosphere|oxygen-limited]] environment".<ref name="auto2">{{cite web |date=23 November 2015 |title=Standardized production definition and product testing guidelines for biochar that is used in soil |url=https://www.biochar-international.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/04/IBI_Biochar_Standards_V2.1_Final.pdf |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190225044804/https://www.biochar-international.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/04/IBI_Biochar_Standards_V2.1_Final.pdf |archive-date=25 February 2019 |website=International Biochar Initiative}}</ref>

Biochar is mainly used in soils to increase soil aeration, reduce soil emissions of greenhouse gases,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Wang |first1=Yuchen |last2=Gu |first2=Jiayu |last3=Ni |first3=Junjun |date=2023-12-01 |title=Influence of biochar on soil air permeability and greenhouse gas emissions in vegetated soil: A review |journal=Biogeotechnics |volume=1 |issue=4 |article-number=100040 |doi=10.1016/j.bgtech.2023.100040 |issn=2949-9291 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2023Biogt...100040W}}</ref> improve soil fertility,<ref>Ding, Y., Liu, Y., Liu, S. ''et al.'' Biochar to improve soil fertility. A review. ''Agron. Sustain. Dev.'' '''36''', 36 (2016). <nowiki>https://doi-org.ezproxy.rice.edu/10.1007/s13593-016-0372-z</nowiki></ref> reduce nutrient leaching, reduce [[soil acidity]],<ref name=":5" /> and potentially increase the water content of coarse soils.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Razzaghi |first1=Fatemeh |last2=Obour |first2=Peter Bilson |last3=Arthur |first3=Emmanuel |date=2020-03-01 |title=Does biochar improve soil water retention? A systematic review and meta-analysis |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0016706119322153 |journal=Geoderma |volume=361 |article-number=114055 |doi=10.1016/j.geoderma.2019.114055 |bibcode=2020Geode.36114055R |issn=0016-7061|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Biochar application may increase [[soil fertility]] and [[agricultural productivity]].<ref name=":5">{{Cite journal |last1=Dai |first1=Zhongmin |last2=Zhang |first2=Xiaojie |last3=Tang |first3=C. |last4=Muhammad |first4=Niaz |last5=Wu |first5=Jianjun |last6=Brookes |first6=Philip C. |last7=Xu |first7=Jianming |date=2017-03-01 |title=Potential role of biochars in decreasing soil acidification - A critical review |journal=The Science of the Total Environment |volume=581-582 |pages=601–611 |doi=10.1016/j.scitotenv.2016.12.169 |issn=1879-1026 |pmid=28063658|bibcode=2017ScTEn.581..601D }}</ref> However, when applied excessively or made from [[feedstock]] unsuitable for the soil type, biochar soil amendments also have the potential for negative effects, including harming soil biota, reducing available water content, altering soil pH, and increasing salinity.<ref name=":4">{{Cite journal |last1=Brtnicky |first1=Martin |last2=Datta |first2=Rahul |last3=Holatko |first3=Jiri |last4=Bielska |first4=Lucie |last5=Gusiatin |first5=Zygmunt M. |last6=Kucerik |first6=Jiri |last7=Hammerschmiedt |first7=Tereza |last8=Danish |first8=Subhan |last9=Radziemska |first9=Maja |last10=Mravcova |first10=Ludmila |last11=Fahad |first11=Shah |last12=Kintl |first12=Antonin |last13=Sudoma |first13=Marek |last14=Ahmed |first14=Niaz |last15=Pecina |first15=Vaclav |date=2021-11-20 |title=A critical review of the possible adverse effects of biochar in the soil environment |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0048969721038286 |journal=Science of the Total Environment |volume=796 |article-number=148756 |doi=10.1016/j.scitotenv.2021.148756 |pmid=34273836 |bibcode=2021ScTEn.79648756B |issn=0048-9697|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Beyond soil application, biochar can be used for [[slash-and-char]] farming, for [[Water retention curve|water retention]] in soil, and as an additive for [[Fodder|animal fodder]]. There is an increasing focus on the potential role of biochar application in global climate change mitigation. Due to its [[refractory]] stability, biochar can stay in soils or other environments for thousands of years.<ref name="indep1">{{cite news |last=Lean |first=Geoffrey |date=7 December 2008 |title=Ancient skills 'could reverse global warming' |url=https://www.independent.co.uk/environment/climate-change/ancient-skills-could-reverse-global-warming-1055700.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110913052413/http://www.independent.co.uk/environment/climate-change/ancient-skills-could-reverse-global-warming-1055700.html |archive-date=13 September 2011 |access-date=1 October 2011 |work=The Independent}}</ref> This has given rise to the concept of [[biochar carbon removal]], a process of [[carbon sequestration]] in the form of biochar.<ref name="indep1" /> Carbon removal can be achieved when high-quality biochar is applied to soils, or added as a substitute material to construction materials such as concrete and tar.

== Etymology ==
The word "biochar" is a late-20th century English [[neologism]] derived from the Greek word '{{lang|grc|[[wikt:βίος|βίος]]}}' (''bios'', '[[life]]') and '[[Char (chemistry)|char]]' ([[charcoal]] produced by [[carbonization]] of biomass).<ref>{{Cite OED | biochar }}</ref> It is recognized as charcoal that participates in biological processes found in soil, aquatic habitats, and animal digestive systems.{{Citation needed|date=May 2024}}

== History ==
[[Pre-Columbian era|Pre-Columbian]] [[Amazon rainforest|Amazonian]]s produced biochar by [[smolder]]ing agricultural waste (i.e., covering burning biomass with soil)<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Solomon|first1=Dawit|last2=Lehmann|first2=Johannes|last3=Thies|first3=Janice|last4=Schäfer|first4=Thorsten|last5=Liang|first5=Biqing|last6=Kinyangi|first6=James|last7=Neves|first7=Eduardo|last8=Petersen|first8=James|last9=Luizão|first9=Flavio|last10=Skjemstad|first10=Jan|date=May 2007|title=Molecular signature and sources of biochemical recalcitrance of organic C in Amazonian Dark Earths|journal=Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta|volume=71|issue=9|pages=2285–2298|doi=10.1016/j.gca.2007.02.014|bibcode=2007GeCoA..71.2285S|issn=0016-7037|quote=Amazonian Dark Earths (ADE) are a unique type of soils apparently developed between 500 and 9000 years B.P. through intense anthropogenic activities such as biomass-burning and high-intensity nutrient depositions on pre-Columbian Amerindian settlements that transformed the original soils into Fimic Anthrosols throughout the Brazilian Amazon Basin.}}</ref> in pits or trenches.<ref name="ReferenceA">{{harvnb|Lehmann|2007a|pp=381–387}}: "Similar soils are found, more scarcely, elsewhere in the world.  To date, scientists have been unable to completely reproduce the beneficial growth properties of ''terra preta''. It is hypothesized that part of the alleged benefits of ''terra preta'' require the biochar to be aged so that it increases the cation exchange capacity of the soil, among other possible effects. In fact, there is no evidence natives made biochar for soil treatment, but rather for transportable fuel charcoal; there is little evidence for any hypothesis accounting for the frequency and location of terra preta patches in Amazonia. Abandoned or forgotten charcoal pits left for centuries were eventually reclaimed by the forest. In that time, the initially harsh negative effects of the char (high pH, extreme ash content, salinity) wore off and turned positive as the forest soil ecosystem saturated the charcoals with nutrients." (internal citations omitted){{br}}
----''supra'' note 2 at p. 386: "Only aged biochar shows high cation retention, as in Amazonian Dark Earths. At high temperatures (30–70&nbsp;°C), cation retention occurs within a few months. The production method that would attain high CEC in soil in cold climates is not currently known."</ref> It is not known if they intentionally used biochar to enhance soil productivity.<ref name="ReferenceA"/> European settlers called it ''[[Terra preta|terra preta de Indio]]''.<ref>{{harvnb|Glaser|Lehmann|Zech|2002|pp=219–220}}: "These so-called Terra Preta do Indio (Terra Preta) characterize the settlements of pre-Columbian Indios. In Terra Preta soils large amounts of black C indicate a high and prolonged input of carbonized organic matter probably due to the production of charcoal in hearths, whereas only low amounts of charcoal are added to soils as a result of forest fires and slash-and-burn techniques." (internal citations omitted)</ref> Following observations and experiments, one research team working in [[French Guiana]] hypothesized that the Amazonian earthworm ''[[Pontoscolex corethrurus]]'' was the main agent of fine powdering and incorporation of charcoal debris in the mineral soil.<ref>{{cite journal |author1=Jean-François Ponge |author2=Stéphanie Topoliantz |author3=Sylvain Ballof |author4=Jean-Pierre Rossi |author5=Patrick Lavelle |author6=Jean-Marie Betsch |author7=Philippe Gaucher |year=2006 |title=Ingestion of charcoal by the Amazonian earthworm ''Pontoscolex corethrurus'': a potential for tropical soil fertility |journal=Soil Biology and Biochemistry |volume=38 |issue=7 |pages=2008–2009 |doi=10.1016/j.soilbio.2005.12.024 |bibcode=2006SBiBi..38.2008P |url=https://hal.archives-ouvertes.fr/hal-00495398/file/Article_SBB.pdf |access-date=24 January 2016 }}</ref>

== Production ==
[[File:Kontiki kiln.jpg|thumb|alt=Artisanal biochar production in a Kontiki-Kiln|Artisanal biochar production in a Kon-tiki kiln]]
Biochar is a high-carbon, fine-grained residue that is produced via [[pyrolysis]]. It is the direct [[thermal decomposition]] of biomass in the absence of [[oxygen]], which prevents [[combustion]], and produces a mixture of solids (biochar), liquid ([[Pyrolysis oil|bio-oil]]), and gas ([[syngas]]) products.<ref name="auto">{{cite web |year=2015 |title=Standardized production definition and product testing guidelines for biochar that is used in soil |url=https://www.biochar-international.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/04/IBI_Biochar_Standards_V2.1_Final.pdf |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190225044804/https://www.biochar-international.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/04/IBI_Biochar_Standards_V2.1_Final.pdf |archive-date=25 February 2019 |access-date=23 November 2015}}</ref>

=== Gasification ===
[[Gasification|Gasifiers]] produce most of the biochar sold in the United States.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Integrated biochar research: A roadmap|first1=James E|last1=Amonette|first2=Humberto|last2=Blanco-Canqui|first3=Chuck|last3=Hassebrook|first4=David A|last4=Laird|first5=Rattan|last5=Lal|author5-link=Rattan Lal|first6=Johannes|last6=Lehmann|first7=Deborah|last7=Page-Dumroese|journal=[[Journal of Soil and Water Conservation]]|date=January 2021|volume=76|issue=1|pages= 24A–29A|doi=10.2489/jswc.2021.1115A|s2cid=231588371 |quote=Large-scale wood gasifiers used to generate bioenergy, however, are relatively common and currently provide the majority of the biochar sold in the United States. Consequently, one of these full-scale facilities would be used to produce a standard wood biochar made from the same feedstock to help calibrate results across the regional sites.|doi-access=free|bibcode=2021JSWC...761115AA |osti=1783242 |url=https://www.osti.gov/biblio/1783242}}</ref> The gasification process consists of four main stages: oxidation, drying, [[pyrolysis]], and [[reducing atmosphere|reduction]].<ref>{{cite journal|title=A Combined Overview of Combustion, Pyrolysis, and Gasification of Biomass|journal=Energy Fuels|date=5 July 2018|doi=10.1021/acs.energyfuels.8b01678|first1=Ali|last1=Akhtar|first2=Vladimir|last2=Krepl
|first3=Tatiana|last3=Ivanova|volume=32|issue=7|pages=7294–7318|bibcode=2018EnFue..32.7294A |s2cid=105089787 }}</ref> Temperature during pyrolysis in gasifiers is {{convert|250|-|550|C|K}}, {{convert|600|-|800|C|K}} in the reduction zone, and {{convert|800|-|1000|C|K}} in the combustion zone.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Gasification reactor engineering approach to understanding the formation of biochar properties|journal=Proceedings of the Royal Society
|first=Andrew N|last=Rollinson|date=1 August 2016|doi=10.1098/rspa.2015.0841|volume=472
|issue=2192|pmid=27616911
|pmc=5014096
|bibcode=2016RSPSA.47250841R
|quote=Figure 1. Schematic of downdraft gasifier reactor used for char production showing (temperatures) energy transfer mechanisms and thermal stratification. (and) Many authors define highest treatment temperature (HTT) during pyrolysis as an important parameter for char characterization.}}</ref>

The specific yield from pyrolysis (the step of gasification that produces biochar) is dependent on process conditions such as temperature, heating rate, and [[residence time]].<ref>{{cite journal
| first1= Manoj|last1= Tripathi|first2= J.N.|last2= Sabu|first3= P.|last3= Ganesan|title= Effect of process parameters on production of biochar from biomass waste through pyrolysis: A review|journal= Renewable and Sustainable Energy Reviews|volume= 55|date= 21 November 2015|pages= 467–481|issn=1364-0321|doi= 10.1016/j.rser.2015.10.122}}</ref> These parameters can be tuned to produce either more energy or more biochar.<ref>{{harvnb|Gaunt|Lehmann|2008|pp=4152, 4155}}: "Assuming that the energy in syngas is converted to electricity with an efficiency of 35%, the recovery in the life cycle energy balance ranges from 92 to 274&nbsp;kg {{CO2}} MWn<sup>−1</sup> of electricity generated where the pyrolysis process is optimized for energy and 120 to 360&nbsp;kg {{CO2}} MWn<sup>−1</sup> where biochar is applied to land. This compares to emissions of 600–900&nbsp;kg {{CO2}} MWh<sup>−1</sup> for fossil-fuel-based technologies."</ref> Temperatures of {{convert|400|-|500|C|K}} produce more [[Char (chemistry)|char]], whereas temperatures above {{convert|700|C|K}} favor the yield of liquid and gas fuel components.<ref name="Winsley1">{{cite journal
| last=Winsley |first=Peter |title=Biochar and bioenergy production for climate change mitigation |volume=64
| journal=[[New Zealand Science Review]]|year=2007}} (See Table 1 for differences in output for Fast, Intermediate, Slow, and Gasification).</ref> Pyrolysis occurs more quickly at higher temperatures, typically requiring seconds rather than hours. The increasing heating rate leads to a decrease in biochar yield, while the temperature is in the range of {{convert|350|-|600|C|K}}.<ref>{{cite journal| first1= Tevfik|last1= Aysu|first2= M. Maşuk|last2= Küçük|title= Biomass pyrolysis in a fixed-bed reactor: Effects of pyrolysis parameters on product yields and characterization of products|journal= Energy|volume= 64|issue =1|date= 16 December 2013|pages= 1002–1025|issn=0360-5442|doi= 10.1016/j.energy.2013.11.053}}</ref> Typical yields are 60% bio-oil, 20% biochar, and 20% syngas. By comparison, slow pyrolysis can produce substantially more char (≈35%);<ref name=Winsley1/> this contributes to soil fertility. Once initialized, both processes produce net energy. For typical inputs, the energy required to run a "fast" pyrolyzer is approximately 15% of the energy that it outputs.<ref>{{harvnb|Laird|2008|pp=100, 178–181}}: "The energy required to operate a fast pyrolyzer is ≈15% of the total energy that can be derived from the dry biomass. Modern systems are designed to use the syngas generated by the pyrolyzer to provide all the energy needs of the pyrolyzer."</ref> Pyrolysis plants can use the syngas output and yield 3–9 times the amount of energy required to run.<ref name=ReferenceA/>

The Amazonian pit/trench method,<ref name="ReferenceA" /> in contrast, harvests neither bio-oil nor syngas, and releases {{CO2}}, [[black carbon]], and other [[greenhouse gas]]es (GHGs) (and potentially, [[toxicant]]s) into the air, though less greenhouse gasses than captured during the growth of the biomass.{{Citation needed|date=May 2024}} Commercial-scale systems process agricultural waste, paper byproducts, and even municipal waste and typically eliminate these side effects by capturing and using the liquid and gas products.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bora |first1=Raaj R. |last2=Tao |first2=Yanqiu |last3=Lehmann |first3=Johannes |last4=Tester |first4=Jefferson W. |last5=Richardson |first5=Ruth E. |last6=You |first6=Fengqi |date=2020-04-13 |title=Techno-Economic Feasibility and Spatial Analysis of Thermochemical Conversion Pathways for Regional Poultry Waste Valorization |journal=ACS Sustainable Chemistry & Engineering |volume=8 |issue=14 |pages=5763–5775 |doi=10.1021/acssuschemeng.0c01229 |bibcode=2020ASCE....8.5763B |s2cid=216504323}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bora |first1=Raaj R. |last2=Lei |first2=Musuizi |last3=Tester |first3=Jefferson W. |last4=Lehmann |first4=Johannes |last5=You |first5=Fengqi |date=2020-06-08 |title=Life Cycle Assessment and Technoeconomic Analysis of Thermochemical Conversion Technologies Applied to Poultry Litter with Energy and Nutrient Recovery |journal=ACS Sustainable Chemistry & Engineering |volume=8 |issue=22 |pages=8436–8447 |doi=10.1021/acssuschemeng.0c02860 |bibcode=2020ASCE....8.8436B |s2cid=219485692}}</ref> The 2018 winner of the [[X Prize Foundation]] for [[atmospheric water generator]]s harvests potable water from the drying stage of the gasification process.<ref>{{cite web |date=24 October 2018 |title=XPrize-winning team sources fresh water from the air |url=https://www.kcrw.com/news-culture/shows/design-and-architecture/xprize-winning-team-sources-fresh-water-from-the-air |access-date=26 October 2018 |website=KCRW Design and Architecture Podcast |publisher=KCRW}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |date=8 December 2018 |title=We Won - All Power Labs |url=https://www.allpowerlabs.com/news/we-won.html |access-date=30 October 2022 |website=All Power Labs |archive-date=7 November 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221107095522/https://www.allpowerlabs.com/news/we-won.html }}</ref> The production of biochar as an output is not a priority in most cases.{{Citation needed|date=May 2024}}

=== Small-scale methods ===
[[File:Smallholder biochar production.jpg|thumb|Smallholder biochar production with fruit-orchard prunings]]
Smallholder farmers in developing countries easily produce their own biochar without special equipment. They make piles of crop waste (e.g., maize stalks, rice straw, or wheat straw), light the piles on the top, and quench the embers with dirt or water to make biochar. This method greatly reduces smoke compared to traditional methods of burning crop waste. This method is known as the top-down burn or conservation burn.<ref>{{Citation |title=Top Down Burn of Maize Stalks - Less Smoke - Make Biochar | date=13 September 2022 |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5M4ntJi_JmY |language=en |access-date=2022-12-17}}</ref><ref>{{Citation |title=STOP BURNING BRUSH!, Make Easy Biochar, Every Pile is an Opportunity! | date=10 April 2017 |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ixtxNfU9Rb8 |language=en |access-date=2022-12-17}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Top-Down Burn with Maize Stalks - Trials in Malawi.docx |url=https://docs.google.com/document/d/15ANxl15r8RM5fi27TcLKO7kXeLJsuUSA/edit?usp=sharing&ouid=112234683056230543280&rtpof=true&sd=true&usp=embed_facebook |access-date=2022-12-17 |website=Google Docs |language=en}}</ref>

Alternatively, more industrial methods can be used on small scales. While in a centralized system, unused biomass is brought to a central plant for processing into biochar,<ref name="renewableenergyworld.com">{{Cite web |last=Crowe |first=Robert |date=2011-10-31 |title=Could Biomass Technology Help Commercialize Biochar? |url=https://www.renewableenergyworld.com/storage/could-biomass-technology-help-commercialize-biochar/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210424235817/https://www.renewableenergyworld.com/storage/could-biomass-technology-help-commercialize-biochar/ |archive-date=24 April 2021 |access-date=2021-08-16 |website=Renewable Energy World |language=en-US}}</ref> it is also possible for each farmer or group of farmers to operate a [[kiln]].{{Citation needed|date=May 2024}} In this scenario, a truck equipped with a pyrolyzer moves from place to place to pyrolyze biomass. Vehicle power comes from the syngas stream, while the biochar remains on the farm. The [[biofuel]] is sent to a refinery or storage site. Factors that influence the choice of system type include the cost of transportation of the liquid and solid byproducts, the amount of material to be processed, and the ability to supply the power grid.{{Citation needed|date=May 2024}}

Various companies in North America, Australia, and England also sell biochar or biochar production units. In Sweden, the 'Stockholm Solution' is an urban tree planting system that uses 30% biochar to support urban forest growth.<ref>{{cite news|last1=O'Sullivan|first1=Feargus|date=20 December 2016|title=Stockholm's Ingenious Plan to Recycle Yard Waste|website=Citylab|url=https://www.citylab.com/solutions/2016/12/stockholm-throw-out-old-christmas-trees-biochar-environment/511196/|access-date=15 March 2018|archive-date=16 March 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180316084824/https://www.citylab.com/solutions/2016/12/stockholm-throw-out-old-christmas-trees-biochar-environment/511196/|url-status=live}}</ref> At the 2009 International Biochar Conference, a mobile pyrolysis unit with a specified intake of {{convert|1000|lb}} was introduced for agricultural applications.<ref name="biomassmag.com/article_id=3091">{{cite news|last=Austin|first=Anna|date=October 2009|title=A New Climate Change Mitigation Tool|work=Biomass Magazine|publisher=BBI International|url=http://www.biomassmagazine.com/article.jsp?article_id=3091&q=&page=all|access-date=30 October 2009|archive-date=3 January 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100103070928/http://biomassmagazine.com/article.jsp?article_id=3091&q=&page=all|url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Crops used ===
Common crops used for making biochar include various tree species, as well as various [[energy crop]]s. Some of these energy crops (i.e. [[Pennisetum purpureum|Napier grass]]) can store much more carbon on a shorter timespan than trees do.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Menezes |first1=Bruna Rafaela da Silva |last2=Daher |first2=Rogério Figueiredo |last3=Gravina |first3=Geraldo de Amaral |last4=Pereira |first4=Antônio Vander |last5=Pereira |first5=Messias Gonzaga |last6=Tardin |first6=Flávio Dessaune |date=2016-09-20 |title=Combining ability in elephant grass (Pennisetum purpureum Schum.) for energy biomass production |url=http://www.cropj.com/meneze_10_9_2016_1297_1305.pdf |url-status=live |journal=Australian Journal of Crop Science |volume=10 |issue=9 |pages=1297–1305 |doi=10.21475/ajcs.2016.10.09.p7747  |doi-access=free|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180602194900/http://www.cropj.com/meneze_10_9_2016_1297_1305.pdf |archive-date=2 June 2018 |access-date=3 May 2019}}</ref>

For crops that are not exclusively for biochar production, the [[residue-to-product ratio]] (RPR) and the collection factor (CF), the percent of the residue not used for other things, measure the approximate amount of feedstock that can be obtained. For instance, Brazil harvests approximately 460 million tons (MT) of [[sugarcane]] annually,<ref>{{cite web |year=2006 |title=Production Quantity Of Sugar Cane In Brazil In 2006 |url=http://faostat.fao.org/site/567/DesktopDefault.aspx?PageID=567 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150906230329/http://faostat.fao.org/site/567/DesktopDefault.aspx?PageID=567 |archive-date=6 September 2015 |access-date=1 July 2008 |publisher=FAOSTAT }}</ref> with an RPR of 0.30, and a CF of 0.70 for the sugarcane tops, which normally are burned in the field.<ref>{{Cite journal |date=March 2006 |title=06/00891 Assessment of sustainable energy potential of non-plantation biomass resources in Sri Lanka |journal=Fuel and Energy Abstracts |volume=47 |issue=2 |page=131 |doi=10.1016/s0140-6701(06)80893-3 |issn=0140-6701 }} (showing RPRs for numerous plants, describing method for determining available agricultural waste for energy and char production).</ref> This translates into approximately 100 MT of residue annually, which could be pyrolyzed to create energy and soil additives. Adding in the [[bagasse]] (sugarcane waste) (RPR=0.29, CF=1.0), which is otherwise burned (inefficiently) in boilers, raises the total to 230 MT of pyrolysis feedstock. Some plant residue, however, must remain on the soil to avoid increased costs and emissions from nitrogen fertilizers.<ref>{{harvnb|Laird|2008|p=179}}: "Much of the current scientific debate on the harvesting of biomass for bioenergy is focused on how much can be harvested without doing too much damage."</ref>

=== Hydrochar ===
Besides pyrolysis, [[torrefaction]] and [[hydrothermal carbonization]] processes can also thermally decompose biomass to the solid material. However, these products cannot be strictly defined as biochar. The carbon product from the torrefaction process contains some [[Volatile organic compound|volatile organic components]]; thus its properties are between that of biomass feedstock and biochar.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kambo |first1=Harpreet Singh |last2=Dutta |first2=Animesh |date=14 February 2015 |title=A comparative review of biochar and hydrochar in terms of production, physicochemical properties and applications |journal=Renewable and Sustainable Energy Reviews |volume=45 |pages=359–378 |doi=10.1016/j.rser.2015.01.050 |bibcode=2015RSERv..45..359K |issn=1364-0321}}</ref> And although hydrothermal carbonization can produce a carbon-rich solid product, the process is evidently different from the conventional thermal conversion process,<ref>{{cite book |last1=Lee |first1=Jechan |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/book/9780128117293/biochar-from-biomass-and-waste |title=Biochar from biomass and waste - Fundamentals and applications |last2=Sarmah |first2=Ajit K. |last3=Kwon |first3=Eilhann E. |publisher=Elsevier |year=2019 |isbn=978-0-12-811729-3 |pages=1–462 |doi=10.1016/C2016-0-01974-5 |hdl=10344/443 |access-date=23 March 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190323203606/https://www.sciencedirect.com/book/9780128117293/biochar-from-biomass-and-waste |archive-date=23 March 2019 |url-status=live |s2cid=229299016}}</ref> so the product is therefore defined as "hydrochar" rather than "biochar".

=== Thermo-catalytic depolymerization ===
Thermo-catalytic depolymerization is another method to produce biochar, which utilizes [[Dielectric heating|microwave]]s. It has been used to efficiently convert organic matter to biochar on an industrial scale, producing about 50% char.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Karagöz |first1=Selhan |last2=Bhaskar |first2=Thallada |last3=Muto |first3=Akinori |last4=Sakata |first4=Yusaku |last5=Oshiki |first5=Toshiyuki |last6=Kishimoto |first6=Tamiya |date=1 April 2005 |title=Low-temperature catalytic hydrothermal treatment of wood biomass: analysis of liquid products |journal=Chemical Engineering Journal |volume=108 |issue=1–2 |pages=127–137 |bibcode=2005ChEnJ.108..127K |doi=10.1016/j.cej.2005.01.007 |issn=1385-8947}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last=Jha |first=Alok |date=13 March 2009 |title='Biochar' goes industrial with giant microwaves to lock carbon in charcoal |url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2009/mar/13/charcoal-carbon |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131219064330/http://www.theguardian.com/environment/2009/mar/13/charcoal-carbon |archive-date=19 December 2013 |access-date=23 September 2011 |newspaper=The Guardian}}</ref>

==Properties==
[[File:Biochar sample size.jpg|alt=Small pellets of biochar|thumb|Smaller pellets of biochar]]
[[File:Biochar.jpg|thumb|alt=A hand holding a piece of biochar with a bucket of it in the background|Biochar produced from residual wood]]

The physical and chemical properties of biochars as determined by feedstocks and technologies are crucial. Characterization data explain their performance in a specific use. For example, guidelines published by the International Biochar Initiative provide standardized evaluation methods.<ref name="auto" /> Properties can be categorized in several respects, including the [[Energy value of coal#Chemical composition|proximate]] and elemental composition, pH value, and porosity. The [[atomic ratio]]s of biochar, including [[Hydrogen|H]]/[[Carbon|C]] and [[Oxygen|O]]/C, correlate with the properties that are relevant to organic content, such as [[Chemical polarity|polarity]] and [[aromaticity]].<ref>{{cite journal|first1=Kyle|last1=Crombie|first2=Ondřej|last2=Mašek|first3=Saran P.|last3=Sohi|first4=Peter|last4=Brownsort|first5=Andrew|last5=Cross|s2cid=54693411|title=The effect of pyrolysis conditions on biochar stability as determined by three methods|journal=Global Change Biology Bioenergy|volume=5|issue=2|date=21 December 2012|pages=122–131|issn=1757-1707|doi=10.1111/gcbb.12030|url=https://www.pure.ed.ac.uk/ws/files/14931650/Crombie_et_al_2013_Author_copy.pdf|doi-access=free|access-date=1 September 2020|archive-date=6 July 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210706024220/https://www.pure.ed.ac.uk/ws/files/14931650/Crombie_et_al_2013_Author_copy.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref> A [[Van Krevelen diagram|van-Krevelen diagram]] can show the evolution of biochar atomic ratios in the production process.<ref>{{cite journal|first1=van|last1=Krevelen D.|title=Graphical-statistical method for the study of structure and reaction processes of coal|journal=Fuel|date=1950|volume=29|pages=269–284|url=https://ci.nii.ac.jp/naid/10027945730/en/|access-date=24 February 2019|archive-date=25 February 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190225102956/https://ci.nii.ac.jp/naid/10027945730/en/|url-status=live}}</ref> In the carbonization process, both the H/C and O/C atomic ratios decrease due to the release of functional groups that contain hydrogen and oxygen.<ref>{{cite journal|first1=Kathrin|last1=Weber|first2=Peter|last2=Quicker|title=Properties of biochar|journal=Fuel|volume=217|date=1 April 2018|pages=240–261|issn=0016-2361|doi=10.1016/j.fuel.2017.12.054|bibcode=2018Fuel..217..240W }}</ref>
[[File:High magnification view of Pine Biochar.jpg|thumb|Scanning electron image of biochar shows detailed morphology]]
Production temperatures influence biochar properties in several ways. The molecular carbon structure of the solid biochar matrix is particularly affected. Initial pyrolysis at 450&ndash;550&nbsp;°C leaves an [[amorphous carbon]] structure. Temperatures above this range will result in the progressive thermochemical conversion of amorphous carbon into turbostratic [[graphene]] sheets. Biochar [[electrical resistivity and conductivity|conductivity]] also increases with production temperature.<ref>{{cite journal |quote=(observed five) orders of magnitude decrease in the electrical resistivity of charcoal with increasing HTT from 650 to 1050&nbsp;°C | doi=10.1021/ie030358e | url = https://pubs.acs.org/doi/abs/10.1021/ie030358e | title = Electrical and Physical Properties of Carbonized Charcoals| year=2003 | last1=Mochidzuki | first1=Kazuhiro | last2=Soutric | first2=Florence | last3=Tadokoro | first3=Katsuaki | last4=Antal | first4=Michael Jerry | last5=Tóth | first5=Mária | last6=Zelei | first6=Borbála | last7=Várhegyi | first7=Gábor | journal=Industrial & Engineering Chemistry Research | volume=42 | issue=21 | pages=5140–5151 | url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | quote = When carbonized under 500&nbsp;°C, wood charcoal can be used as electric insulation | doi = 10.1016/j.compositesb.2012.10.012 | url = https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S135983681200666X | title = Effect of carbonization temperature on electrical resistivity and physical properties of wood and wood-based composites
| year = 2013 | last1 = Kwon | first1 = Jin Heon | last2 = Park | first2 = Sang Bum | last3 = Ayrilmis | first3 = Nadir | last4 = Oh | first4 = Seung Won | last5 = Kim | first5 = Nam Hun | journal = Composites Part B: Engineering | volume = 46 | pages = 102–107 | url-access = subscription }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | quote = The conductivity of all biochar increases with increase in heating temperature, due to increasing degree of carbonization and degree of graphitization | url =  https://tspace.library.utoronto.ca/bitstream/1807/110772/1/Gabhi_Randeep_Singh_202203_MAS_thesis.pdf | title = Electrical Conductivity of Wood-derived Nanoporous Monolithic Biochar }}</ref> Important to carbon capture, aromaticity and intrinsic recalcitrance increases with temperature.<ref>{{cite journal | title = Biochar persistence, priming and microbial responses to pyrolysis temperature series | year = 2016 | doi = 10.1007/s00374-016-1116-6 | quote = ...biochars produced at higher temperatures contain more aromatic structures, which confer intrinsic recalcitrance...| last1 = Budai | first1 = Alice | last2 = Rasse | first2 = Daniel P. | last3 = Lagomarsino | first3 = Alessandra | last4 = Lerch | first4 = Thomas Z. | last5 = Paruch | first5 = Lisa | journal = Biology and Fertility of Soils | volume = 52 | issue = 6 | pages = 749–761 | s2cid = 6136045 | doi-access = free | bibcode = 2016BioFS..52..749B | hdl = 11250/2499741 | hdl-access = free }}</ref>

== Applications ==

=== Carbon sink ===
{{further|Biochar carbon removal}}

The [[refractory]] stability of biochar leads to the concept of [[biochar carbon removal]], a process of [[carbon sequestration]] in the form of biochar.<ref>Constanze Werner, Hans-Peter Schmidt, Dieter Gerten, Wolfgang Lucht und Claudia Kammann (2018). Biogeochemical potential of biomass pyrolysis systems for limiting global warming to 1.5&nbsp;°C. [[Environmental Research Letters]], 13(4), 044036. doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/aabb0e</ref><ref name="indep1"/> It may be a means to [[Climate change mitigation|mitigate climate change]] due to its potential of sequestering carbon with minimal effort.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Yousaf |first1=Balal |last2=Liu |first2=Guijian |last3=Wang |first3=Ruwei |last4=Abbas |first4=Qumber |last5=Imtiaz |first5=Muhammad |last6=Liu |first6=Ruijia |year=2016 |title=Investigating the biochar effects on C-mineralization and sequestration of carbon in soil compared with conventional amendments using stable isotope (δ13C) approach |journal=Global Change Biology Bioenergy |volume=9 |issue=6 |pages=1085–1099 |doi=10.1111/gcbb.12401 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name="RoyalSociety">{{cite web |year=2009 |title=Geoengineering the climate: science, governance and uncertainty |url=http://royalsociety.org/Geoengineering-the-climate/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110908221216/http://royalsociety.org/Geoengineering-the-climate/ |archive-date=8 September 2011 |access-date=22 August 2010 |publisher=[[The Royal Society]]}}</ref><ref name="DOI10.1038/ncomms1053">
{{cite journal |author=Dominic Woolf |author2=James E. Amonette |author3=F. Alayne Street-Perrott |author-link3=Alayne Street-Perrott|author4=Johannes Lehmann |author5=Stephen Joseph |date=August 2010 |title=Sustainable biochar to mitigate global climate change |journal=Nature Communications |volume=1 |issue=5 |page=56 |bibcode=2010NatCo...1...56W |doi=10.1038/ncomms1053  |doi-access=free|issn=2041-1723 |pmc=2964457 |pmid=20975722}}
</ref> Biomass burning and natural decomposition releases large amounts of [[Carbon dioxide in Earth's atmosphere|carbon dioxide]] and [[methane]] to the Earth's atmosphere. The biochar production process also releases {{CO2}} (up to 50% of the biomass); however, the remaining carbon content becomes indefinitely stable.<ref name="DOI10.1038/ncomms1053"/> Biochar carbon remains in the ground for centuries, slowing the growth in atmospheric [[greenhouse gas]] levels. Simultaneously, its presence in the earth can improve [[water quality]], increase [[soil fertility]], raise [[agricultural productivity]], and reduce pressure on [[old-growth forest]]s.<ref>{{harvnb|Laird|2008|pp=100, 178–181}}</ref>

Biochar can sequester carbon in the soil for hundreds to thousands of years, like [[coal]].<ref name="Terra Preta de Indio">{{cite journal
| url=https://www.css.cornell.edu/faculty/lehmann/research/terra%20preta/terrapretamain.html
| title=Terra Preta de Indio
| last=Lehmann
| first=Johannes
| journal=Soil Biochemistry (Internal Citations Omitted)
| access-date=15 September 2009
| archive-date=24 April 2013
| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130424061552/http://www.css.cornell.edu/faculty/lehmann/research/terra%20preta/terrapretamain.html
| url-status=live
}} Not only do biochar-enriched soils contain more carbon - 150gC/kg compared to 20-30gC/kg in surrounding soils - but biochar-enriched soils are, on average, more than twice as deep as surrounding soils.{{Citation needed|date=August 2011}}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Lehmann|2007b|p=143}}: "this sequestration can be taken a step further by heating the plant biomass without oxygen (a process known as low-temperature pyrolysis)."</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Lehmann|2007a|pp=381, 385}}: "pyrolysis produces 3–9 times more energy than is invested in generating the energy. At the same time, about half of the carbon can be sequestered in soil. The total carbon stored in these soils can be one order of magnitude higher than adjacent soils."</ref><ref>{{cite journal
 |journal      = [[New Zealand Science Review]]
 |url          = http://www.biochar-international.org/images/NZSR64_1_Winsley.pdf

 }}</ref><ref>{{Citation|last1=Kern|first1=DC|chapter=Terra Preta Nova: The Dream of Wim Sombroek|date=2009|title=Amazonian Dark Earths: Wim Sombroek's World Bank, "biochar retains between 10 percent and 70 percent (on average about 50 percent) of the carbon present in the original biomass and slows down the rate of carbon decomposition by one or two orders of magnitude, that is, in the scale of centuries or millennia".<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Scholz |first1=Sebastian B. |url=http://elibrary.worldbank.org/doi/book/10.1596/978-0-8213-9525-7 |title=Biochar Systems for Smallholders in Developing Countries: Leveraging Current Knowledge and Exploring Future Potential for Climate-Smart Agriculture |last2=Sembres |first2=Thomas |last3=Roberts |first3=Kelli |last4=Whitman |first4=Thea |last5=Wilson |first5=Kelpie |last6=Lehmann |first6=Johannes |date=2014-06-23 |publisher=The World Bank |isbn=978-0-8213-9525-7 |language=en |doi=10.1596/978-0-8213-9525-7 |hdl=10986/18781 }}{{Dead link|date=February 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref> Early works proposing the use of biochar for [[carbon dioxide removal]] to create a long-term stable [[carbon sink]] were published in the early 2000s.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Ogawa|first1=Makoto|last2=Okimori|first2=Yasuyuki|last3=Takahashi|first3=Fumio|date=2006-03-01|title=Carbon Sequestration by Carbonization of Biomass and Forestation: Three Case Studies|journal=Mitigation and Adaptation Strategies for Global Change|language=en|volume=11|issue=2|pages=429–444|doi=10.1007/s11027-005-9007-4|bibcode=2006MASGC..11..429O |s2cid=153604030|issn=1573-1596}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Lehmann|first1=Johannes|last2=Gaunt|first2=John|last3=Rondon|first3=Marco|date=2006-03-01|title=Bio-char Sequestration in Terrestrial Ecosystems – A Review|journal=Mitigation and Adaptation Strategies for Global Change|language=en|volume=11|issue=2|pages=403–427|doi=10.1007/s11027-005-9006-5|bibcode=2006MASGC..11..403L |s2cid=4696862|issn=1573-1596}}</ref><ref>{{Citation |last1=Möllersten |first1=K. |chapter=Negative emission biomass technologies in an uncertain climate future |date=2006 |chapter-url=https://kth.diva-portal.org/smash/record.jsf?pid=diva2%3A1813115&dswid=-8586 |title=Progress in biomass and bioenergy research |editor-last=Warnmer |editor-first=S. F. |access-date=2023-11-23 |place=NY |publisher=Nova Science Publishers |isbn=978-1-60021-328-1 |last2=Chladna |first2=Z. |last3=Chladny |first3=M. |last4=Obersteiner |first4=M.}}</ref> This technique is advocated by scientists including [[James Hansen]]<ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.thestar.com/sciencetech/article/654444 | location=Toronto | work=The Star | title=Sole option is to adapt, climate author says | first=Tyler | last=Hamilton | date=22 June 2009 | access-date=24 August 2017 | archive-date=20 October 2012 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121020205803/http://www.thestar.com/sciencetech/article/654444 | url-status=live }}</ref> and [[James Lovelock]].<ref>{{harvnb|Vince|2009}}</ref>

A 2010 report estimated that sustainable use of biochar could reduce the global net emissions of carbon dioxide ({{chem|CO|2}}), [[methane]], and [[nitrous oxide]] by up to 1.8 billion tonnes [[carbon dioxide equivalent]] ({{chem|CO|2}}e) per year (compared to the about 50 billion tonnes emitted in 2021), without endangering [[food security]], [[habitat]]s, or [[soil conservation]].<ref name="DOI10.1038/ncomms1053"/> However a 2018 study doubted enough biomass would be available to achieve significant carbon sequestration.<ref name=":0" /> A 2021 review estimated potential {{CO2}} removal from 1.6 to 3.2 billion tonnes per year,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Lehmann|first1=Johannes|last2=Cowie|first2=Annette|last3=Masiello|first3=Caroline A.|author3-link=Caroline A. Masiello|last4=Kammann|first4=Claudia|last5=Woolf|first5=Dominic|last6=Amonette|first6=James E.|last7=Cayuela|first7=Maria L.|last8=Camps-Arbestain|first8=Marta|last9=Whitman|first9=Thea|date=December 2021|title=Biochar in climate change mitigation|url=https://www.nature.com/articles/s41561-021-00852-8|journal=Nature Geoscience|language=en|volume=14|issue=12|pages=883–892|doi=10.1038/s41561-021-00852-8|bibcode=2021NatGe..14..883L|s2cid=244803479|issn=1752-0908|url-access=subscription}}</ref> and by 2023 it had become a lucrative business renovated by carbon credits.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/ancient-farming-practice-draws-cash-from-carbon-credits-a803aee1|title=Ancient Farming Practice Draws Cash From Carbon Credits|first=Amrith Ramkumar &#124; Photographs by Alexandra Hootnick for The Wall Street|last=Journal|newspaper=The Wall Street Journal|date=25 February 2023 }}</ref>

As of 2023, the significance of biochar's potential as a carbon sink is widely accepted. Biochar was found to have the technical potential to sequester 7% of carbon dioxide on average across all countries, with twelve nations able to sequester over 20% of their greenhouse gas emissions—Bhutan leads this proportion (68%), followed by India (53%).<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Karan |first1=Shivesh Kishore |last2=Woolf |first2=Dominic |last3=Azzi |first3=Elias Sebastian |last4=Sundberg |first4=Cecilia |last5=Wood |first5=Stephen A. |date=December 2023 |title=Potential for biochar carbon sequestration from crop residues: A global spatially explicit assessment |journal=GCB Bioenergy |language=en |volume=15 |issue=12 |pages=1424–1436 |doi=10.1111/gcbb.13102 |bibcode=2023GCBBi..15.1424K |issn=1757-1693|doi-access=free }}</ref>

In 2021 the cost of biochar ranged around European carbon prices,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Fawzy|first1=Samer|last2=Osman|first2=Ahmed I.|last3=Yang|first3=Haiping|last4=Doran|first4=John|last5=Rooney|first5=David W.|date=2021-08-01|title=Industrial biochar systems for atmospheric carbon removal: a review|journal=Environmental Chemistry Letters|language=en|volume=19|issue=4|pages=3023–3055|doi=10.1007/s10311-021-01210-1|s2cid=232202598|issn=1610-3661|doi-access=free|bibcode=2021EnvCL..19.3023F }}</ref> but was not yet included in the EU or [[UK Emissions Trading Scheme]].<ref name=":3">{{Cite web|title=Greenhouse Gas Removals: Summary of Responses to the Call for Evidence|url=https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/government/uploads/system/uploads/attachment_data/file/1026494/ggr-cfe-summary-of-responses.pdf|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211020132909/https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/government/uploads/system/uploads/attachment_data/file/1026494/ggr-cfe-summary-of-responses.pdf |archive-date=20 October 2021 }}</ref>

Biochar adsorption of {{chem|CO|2}} can be limited by the surface area of the material, which can be improved by using resonant acoustic mixing.<ref>{{Cite web |title=XXXI International Mineral Processing Congress 2024 Proceedings page 289 |url=https://store.smenet.org/22ocik7/313 |access-date=2024-12-30 |website=store.smenet.org }}{{Dead link|date=February 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref>

In developing countries, biochar derived from [[improved cookstove]]s for home-use can reduce carbon emissions (when the traditional cookstove is discontinued), as well as achieve other benefits for sustainable development.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Sundberg|first1=Cecilia|last2=Karltun|first2=Erik|last3=Gitau|first3=James K.|last4=Kätterer|first4=Thomas|last5=Kimutai|first5=Geoffrey M.|last6=Mahmoud|first6=Yahia|last7=Njenga|first7=Mary|last8=Nyberg|first8=Gert|last9=Roing de Nowina|first9=Kristina|last10=Roobroeck|first10=Dries|last11=Sieber|first11=Petra|date=2020-08-01|title=Biochar from cookstoves reduces greenhouse gas emissions from smallholder farms in Africa|journal=Mitigation and Adaptation Strategies for Global Change|language=en|volume=25|issue=6|pages=953–967|doi=10.1007/s11027-020-09920-7|s2cid=219947550|issn=1573-1596|doi-access=free|bibcode=2020MASGC..25..953S |hdl=10568/113484|hdl-access=free}}</ref>

Biochar has been proposed as a negative emissions technology with substantial long term climate mitigation potential. While early scenario studies focused on technical maxima and suggested that several gigatonnes of CO<sub>2</sub> equivalent could be avoided annually, more recent work emphasizes that economically feasible deployment is likely to be smaller, with global removal potentials of roughly 0.3–1.8 Gt CO<sub>2</sub> per year under carbon prices below US$100 per tonne.<ref>International Biochar Initiative. FY24 Impact Snapshot (2024).</ref> Real world implementation remains at an early stage: global biochar production is estimated to be on the order of a few hundred thousand tonnes per year, delivering well under 1 Mt CO<sub>2</sub> per year of certified removal, though voluntary carbon market deliveries and installed capacity have grown quickly in recent years. Because feedstock availability, logistics and co product use strongly influence costs, some applications are currently viable only where biochar provides additional agronomic or environmental benefits or can access carbon removal credits. The rapid expansion of publications on biochar has led to concerns in the literature that expectations for its climate role could trigger a 'boom and bust' cycle if projected benefits are not realized at scale.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://observer.land/post/805618839684513792/biochar-at-the-edge-of-its-own-story|title=Biochar at the edge of its own story |website=Observer.land|access-date=24 May 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |author=L. Gristina |author2=R. Scalenghe |date=2026 |journal=Nature Sustainability |volume=8 |doi=10.1038/s41893-025-01748-w |title= Biochar boom-and-bust cycle}}</ref>

=== Soil health ===
[[File:Biochar pile in tarp.jpg|thumb|alt=Biochar in a white tarp|Biochar in preparation as a soil amendment]]
Biochar offers multiple [[soil health]] benefits in degraded tropical soils but is less beneficial in temperate regions.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Vijay|first1=Vandit|last2=Shreedhar|first2=Sowmya|last3=Adlak|first3=Komalkant|last4=Payyanad|first4=Sachin|last5=Sreedharan|first5=Vandana|last6=Gopi|first6=Girigan|last7=Sophia van der Voort|first7=Tessa|last8=Malarvizhi|first8=P|last9=Yi|first9=Susan|last10=Gebert|first10=Julia|last11=Aravind|first11=PV|date=2021|title=Review of Large-Scale Biochar Field-Trials for Soil Amendment and the Observed Influences on Crop Yield Variations|journal=Frontiers in Energy Research|volume=9|page=499|article-number=710766 |doi=10.3389/fenrg.2021.710766|issn=2296-598X|doi-access=free|bibcode=2021FrER....910766V |url=https://research.rug.nl/en/publications/72828309-04e5-4af9-84bf-683e3a48d637|hdl=11370/72828309-04e5-4af9-84bf-683e3a48d637|hdl-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Slash and Char |url=http://www.biochar.org/joomla/index2.php?option=com_content&do_pdf=1&id=24 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140717181754/http://www.biochar.org/joomla/index2.php?option=com_content&do_pdf=1&id=24 |archive-date=17 July 2014 |access-date=19 September 2014}}</ref> Its porous nature is effective at retaining both water and water-soluble nutrients. Soil biologist [[Elaine Ingham]] highlighted its suitability as a habitat for beneficial soil [[soil biology|microorganisms]]. She pointed out that when pre-charged with these beneficial organisms, biochar promotes good soil and plant health.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2015-02-17|title=Interview with Dr Elaine Ingham - NEEDFIRE|url=http://www.needfire.info/home/interview-with-dr-elaine-ingham|access-date=2021-08-16|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150217052426/http://www.needfire.info/home/interview-with-dr-elaine-ingham|archive-date=17 February 2015}}</ref>

Biochar reduces leaching of ''[[Escherichia coli|''E. coli'']]'' through sandy soils depending on application rate, feedstock, pyrolysis temperature, [[soil moisture]] content, [[soil texture]], and surface properties of the bacteria.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Bolster | first1 = C.H. | last2 = Abit | first2 = S.M. | s2cid = 1689197 | year = 2012 | title = Biochar pyrolyzed at two temperatures affects Escherichia coli transport through a sandy soil | journal = Journal of Environmental Quality | volume = 41 | issue = 1| pages = 124–133 | doi=10.2134/jeq2011.0207| pmid = 22218181 | bibcode = 2012JEnvQ..41..124B }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Abit | first1 = S.M. | last2 = Bolster | first2 = C.H. | last3 = Cai | first3 = P. | last4 = Walker | first4 = S.L. | year = 2012 | title = Influence of feedstock and pyrolysis temperature of biochar amendments on transport of Escherichia coli in saturated and unsaturated soil | journal =  Environmental Science & Technology| volume = 46 | issue = 15| pages = 8097–8105 | doi=10.1021/es300797z| pmid = 22738035 | bibcode = 2012EnST...46.8097A }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Abit | first1 = S.M. | last2 = Bolster | first2 = C.H. | last3 = Cantrell | first3 = K.B. | last4 = Flores | first4 = J.Q. | last5 = Walker | first5 = S.L. | year = 2014 | title = Transport of Escherichia coli, Salmonella typhimurium, and microspheres in biochar-amended soils with different textures | journal = Journal of Environmental Quality | volume = 43 | issue = 1| pages = 371–378 | doi=10.2134/jeq2013.06.0236| pmid = 25602571 | bibcode = 2014JEnvQ..43..371A }}</ref>

For plants that require high [[potash]] and elevated [[pH]],<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Lehmann|first1=Johannes|last2=Pereira da Silva|first2=Jose|last3=Steiner|first3=Christoph|last4=Nehls|first4=Thomas|last5=Zech|first5=Wolfgang|last6=Glaser|first6=Bruno|date=2003-02-01|title=Nutrient availability and leaching in an archaeological Anthrosol and a Ferralsol of the Central Amazon basin: fertilizer, manure and charcoal amendments|journal=Plant and Soil|language=en|volume=249|issue=2|pages=343–357|doi=10.1023/A:1022833116184|bibcode=2003PlSoi.249..343L |s2cid=2420708|issn=1573-5036}}</ref> biochar can improve yield.<ref name="Tenic, E. 2020">{{cite journal | last1 = Tenic | first1 = E. | last2 = Ghogare | first2 = R. | last3 = Dhingra | first3 = A. | year = 2020 | title = Biochar—A Panacea for Agriculture or Just Carbon? | journal = Horticulturae | volume = 6 | issue = 3 | page = 37 | doi=10.3390/horticulturae6030037| doi-access = free | bibcode = 2020Hort....6...37T }}</ref>

Biochar can improve water quality, reduce soil emissions of [[greenhouse gases]], reduce [[leaching (agriculture)|nutrient leaching]], reduce [[soil acidity]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Joseph |first1=Stephen |last2=Cowie |first2=Annette L. |last3=Zwieten |first3=Lukas Van |last4=Bolan |first4=Nanthi |last5=Budai |first5=Alice |last6=Buss |first6=Wolfram |last7=Cayuela |first7=Maria Luz |last8=Graber |first8=Ellen R. |last9=Ippolito |first9=James A. |last10=Kuzyakov |first10=Yakov |author-link10=Yakov Kuzyakov |last11=Luo |first11=Yu |date=2021 |title=How biochar works, and when it doesn't: A review of mechanisms controlling soil and plant responses to biochar |journal=GCB Bioenergy |language=en |volume=13 |issue=11 |pages=1731–1764 |doi=10.1111/gcbb.12885 |issn=1757-1707 |s2cid=237725246 |doi-access=free|bibcode=2021GCBBi..13.1731J |hdl=1885/294216 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> and reduce [[irrigation]] and [[fertilizer]] requirements.<ref>{{Cite journal|date=March |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/323446392 |title=Biochar, Activated Biochar & Its Applications |date=February 2018 |via=Amazon}}</ref> Due to its porosity, the small holes in biochar can keep water and dissolved minerals in the upper layers of soil, assisting plant growth and reducing the need for and expense of fertilizer.<ref name=":7" /> Under certain circumstances biochar induces plant systemic responses to [[Leaf|foliar]] fungal diseases and improves plant responses to diseases caused by soilborne pathogens.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Elad | first1 = Y. | last2 = Rav David Biochar's impacts are dependent on its properties<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Silber | first1 = A. | last2 = Levkovitch | first2 = I. | last3 = Graber | first3 = E. R. | year = 2010 | title = pH-dependent mineral release and surface properties of corn straw biochar: Agronomic implications | url = https://figshare.com/articles/pH_Dependent_Mineral_Release_and_Surface_Properties_of_Cornstraw_Biochar_Agronomic_Implications/2704741| journal = Environmental Science & Technology| volume = 44 | issue = 24| pages = 9318–9323 | doi=10.1021/es101283d| pmid = 21090742 | bibcode = 2010EnST...44.9318S | url-access = subscription }}</ref> as well as the amount applied,<ref name="Jaiswal, A.K. 2014"/> although knowledge about the important mechanisms and properties is limited.<ref>{{harvnb|Glaser|Lehmann|Zech|2002|p=224|loc=note 7}}: "Three main factors influence the properties of charcoal: (1) the type of organic matter used for charring, (2) the charring environment (e.g. temperature, air), and (3) additions during the charring process. The source of charcoal material strongly influences the direct effects of charcoal amendments on nutrient contents and availability."</ref> Biochar impact may depend on regional conditions including soil type, soil condition (depleted or healthy), temperature, and humidity.<ref>Dr. Wardle points out that improved plant growth has been observed in tropical (depleted) soils by referencing Lehmann, but that in the boreal (high native [[soil organic matter]] content) forest this experiment was run in, it accelerated the native soil organic matter loss. Wardle, ''supra'' note 18. ("Although several studies have recognized the potential of black C for enhancing ecosystem carbon sequestration, our results show that these effects can be partially offset by its capacity to stimulate loss of native soil C, at least for boreal forests.") (internal citations omitted) (emphasis added).</ref> Modest additions of biochar reduce [[nitrous oxide]] ({{chem|N|2|O}})<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://sior.ub.edu/jspui/cris/socialimpact/socialimpact00542|title=Biochar decreased N2O emissions from soils. <!--Unrelated to the next passage, unless rewritten it with the addition of conjunction: Pollutants, such as metals and [[pesticide]]s, seep into soil and contaminate food supplies, reducing the amount of land suitable for agricultural production. -->Studies reported positive effects from biochar on crop production in degraded and nutrient–poor soils.<ref>{{cite web|url= http://www.csiro.au/resources/Biochar-Factsheet.html|title= Biochar fact sheet|publisher= csiro.au|access-date= 2 September 2016|archive-date= 22 January 2017|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20170122100232/http://www.csiro.au/resources/Biochar-Factsheet.html}}</ref> The application of [[compost]] and biochar under [[Framework Programmes for Research and Technological Development|FP7]] project FERTIPLUS had positive effects on soil humidity, crop productivity and quality in multiple countries.<ref name="socialimpact00544">{{Cite web |title=Improvement of soil quality. Social Impact Open Repository}}</ref> Biochar can be adapted with specific qualities to target distinct soil properties.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ars.usda.gov/research/publications/publication/?seqNo115=238024|access-date=2021-08-16|website=ars.usda.gov|last=Novak|first=Jeff|title=Development of Designer Biochar to Remediate Specific Chemical and Physical Aspects of Degraded Soils. Proc. of North American Biochar Conference 2009|archive-date=16 August 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210816015841/https://www.ars.usda.gov/research/publications/publication/?seqNo115=238024|url-status=live}}</ref> In Colombian savanna soil, biochar reduced leaching of critical nutrients, created a higher nutrient uptake, and provided greater nutrient availability.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Major|first1=Julie|last2=Rondon|first2=Marco|last3=Molina|first3=Diego|last4=Riha|first4=Susan J.|last5=Lehmann|first5=Johannes|date=July 2012|title=Nutrient Leaching in a Colombian Savanna Oxisol Amended with Biochar|journal=Journal of Environmental Quality|volume=41|issue=4|pages=1076–1086|doi=10.2134/jeq2011.0128|pmid=22751049|bibcode=2012JEnvQ..41.1076M |issn=0047-2425}}</ref> At 10% levels, biochar reduced contaminant levels in plants by up to 80%, while reducing [[chlordane]] and [[DDX (chemistry)|DDX]] content in the plants by 68 and 79%, respectively.<ref>Elmer, Wade, Jason C. White, and Joseph J. Pignatello. Impact of Biochar Addition to Soil on the Bioavailability of Chemicals Important in Agriculture. Rep. New Haven: University of Connecticut, 2009. Print.</ref> However, because of its high adsorption capacity, biochar may reduce pesticide efficacy.<ref name="Graber, E.R. 2011">{{Cite journal|last1=Graber|first1=E. R.|last2=Tsechansky|first2=L.|last3=Gerstl|first3=Z.|last4=Lew|first4=B.|date=2011-10-15|title=High surface area biochar negatively impacts herbicide efficacy|journal=Plant and Soil|volume=353|issue=1–2|pages=95–106|doi=10.1007/s11104-011-1012-7|s2cid=14875062|issn=0032-079X}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Graber|first1=E. R.|last2=Tsechansky|first2=L.|last3=Khanukov|first3=J.|last4=Oka|first4=Y.|date=July 2011|title=Sorption, Volatilization, and Efficacy of the Fumigant 1,3-Dichloropropene in a Biochar-Amended Soil|journal=Soil Science Society of America Journal|volume=75|issue=4|pages=1365–1373|doi=10.2136/sssaj2010.0435|bibcode=2011SSASJ..75.1365G|issn=0361-5995}}</ref> High-surface-area biochars may be particularly problematic.<ref name="Graber, E.R. 2011"/>

Biochar may be plowed into soils in crop fields or added to gardens to enhance their fertility and stability<ref>{{Cite web |last=Buck |first=Jordan James |date=2024-02-09 |title=7 Tips For Using Biochar in Your Soil |url=https://northernhomesteading.com/7-tips-for-using-biochar-in-your-soil/ |access-date=2025-02-10 |website=Northern Homesteading |language=en-us}}</ref> and for medium- to long-term carbon sequestration in these soils. It even shows good results when top-dressed. It has shown positive effects in increasing soil fertility and improving disease resistance in West European soils.<ref name="socialimpact00544" /> Gardeners taking [[individual action on climate change]] add biochar to soil,<ref>{{cite web |title=Biochar Market Report by Feedstock Type (Woody Biomass, Agricultural Waste, Animal Manure, and Others), Technology Type (Slow Pyrolysis, Fast Pyrolysis, Gasification, Hydrothermal Carbonization, and Others), Product Form (Coarse and Fine Chips, Fine Powder, Pellets, Granules, and Prills, Liquid Suspension), Application (Farming, Gardening, Livestock Feed, Soil, Water and Air Treatment, and Others), and Region 2023-2028 |url=https://www.imarcgroup.com/biochar-market |website=imarc Impactful Insights |publisher=IMARC Services Private Limited |access-date=29 September 2023}}</ref> increasing plant yield and thereby drawing down more carbon.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Allohverdi |first1=Tara |last2=Kumar Mohanty |first2=Amar |last3=Roy |first3=Poritosh |last4=Misra |first4=Manjusri |title=A Review on Current Status of Biochar Uses in Agriculture |journal=  Molecules|date=14 September 2021 |volume=26 |issue=18 |page=5584 |doi=10.3390/molecules26185584 |pmid=34577054 |pmc=8470807 |doi-access=free }}</ref> The use of biochar as a feed additive is a way to apply biochar to pastures and to reduce methane emissions.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Schmidt|first1=Hans-Peter|last2=Hagemann|first2=Nikolas|last3=Draper|first3=Kathleen|last4=Kammann|first4=Claudia|date=2019-07-31|title=The use of biochar in animal feeding|journal=PeerJ|volume=7|article-number=e7373|doi=10.7717/peerj.7373|issn=2167-8359|pmc=6679646|pmid=31396445 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2019PeerJ...7e7373S }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|last=Cusack|first=Mikki|date=2020-02-07|title=Can charcoal make beef better for the environment?|url=https://www.bbc.com/future/article/20200206-can-charcoal-cut-cows-methane-to-fight-climate-change|url-status=live|access-date=2021-11-22|publisher=BBC|language=en|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200207234343/https://www.bbc.com/future/article/20200206-can-charcoal-cut-cows-methane-to-fight-climate-change |archive-date=7 February 2020 }}</ref>

Application rates of {{convert|2.5|-|20|tonne/ha}} appear required to improve plant yields significantly. Biochar costs in developed countries vary from $300–$7,000/tonne, which is generally impractical for the farmer/horticulturalist and prohibitive for low-input field crops. In developing countries, constraints on agricultural biochar relate more to biomass availability and production time. A compromise is to use small amounts of biochar in lower-cost biochar-fertilizer complexes.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Joseph|first1=S|last2=Graber|first2=ER|last3=Chia|first3=C|last4=Munroe|first4=P|last5=Donne|first5=S|last6=Thomas|first6=T|last7=Nielsen|first7=S|last8=Marjo|first8=C|last9=Rutlidge|first9=H|last10=Pan|first10=GX|last11=Li|first11=L|date=June 2013|title=Shifting paradigms: development of high-efficiency biochar fertilizers based on nano-structures and soluble components|journal=Carbon Management|volume=4|issue=3|pages=323–343|doi=10.4155/cmt.13.23|bibcode=2013CarM....4..323J|s2cid=51741928|issn=1758-3004|hdl=1959.4/unsworks_35633|hdl-access=free}}</ref>

Biochar soil amendments, when applied at excessive rates or with unsuitable soil type and biochar feedstock combinations, also have the potential for negative effects, including harming soil biota, reducing available water content, altering soil pH, and increasing salinity.<ref name=":4" />

=== Slash-and-char ===

Suggested as an alternative to ''[[slash-and-burn]]'' , ''[[slash-and-char]]'' farming techniques in tropical regions can decrease both deforestation and [[Greenhouse gas emissions|carbon dioxide emission]], as well as increase crop yields. Slash-and-burn leaves only 3% of the carbon from the organic material in the soil<ref>{{harvnb|Glaser|Lehmann|Zech|2002|p=225|loc=note 7}}: "The published data average at about 3% charcoal formation of the original biomass C."</ref> whereas slash-and-char can retain up to 50%.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Lehmann|first1=Johannes|last2=Gaunt|first2=John|last3=Rondon|first3=Marco|date=March 2006|title=Bio-char Sequestration in Terrestrial Ecosystems – A Review|journal=Mitigation and Adaptation Strategies for Global Change|volume=11|issue=2|pages=403–427|doi=10.1007/s11027-005-9006-5|bibcode=2006MASGC..11..403L |s2cid=4696862|issn=1381-2386|quote= ''supra'' note 11 at p. 407: "If this woody above-ground biomass were converted into biochar by means of simple kiln techniques and applied to soil, more than 50% of this carbon would be sequestered in a highly stable form.}}</ref> The global potential for carbon sequestration by shifting from slash-and-burn to slash-and-char farming techniques has been estimated to between 0.22 and 0.42 Gt C/yr.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Sirén |first=Anders Henrik |date=2024-10-02 |title=The global potential for carbon removal through biochar in shifting cultivation systems |journal=Mitigation and Adaptation Strategies for Global Change |language=en |volume=29 |issue=7 |article-number=75 |doi=10.1007/s11027-024-10170-0 |bibcode=2024MASGC..29...75S |issn=1573-1596}}</ref> Biochar reduces the need for nitrogen fertilizers, thereby reducing cost and emissions from fertilizer production and transport.<ref>{{harvnb|Gaunt|Lehmann|2008|p=4152 |loc=note 3}}: "This results in increased crop yields in low-input agriculture and increased crop yield per unit of fertilizer applied (fertilizer efficiency) in [[Intensive farming|high-input agriculture]] as well as reductions in off-site effects such as runoff, erosion, and gaseous losses."</ref> Additionally, by improving soil's till-ability, fertility, and productivity, biochar-enhanced soils can indefinitely sustain agricultural production. This is unlike slash-and-burn soils, which quickly become depleted of nutrients, forcing farmers to abandon fields, producing a continuous slash-and-burn cycle. Using pyrolysis to produce bio-energy does not require infrastructure changes the way, for example, processing biomass for [[cellulosic ethanol]] does. Additionally, biochar can be applied by the widely used machinery.<ref>{{harvnb|Lehmann|2007b|p=143 |loc=note 9}}: "It can be mixed with manures or fertilizers and included in no-tillage methods, without the need for additional equipment."</ref>

=== Water retention ===

Biochar is [[hygroscopic]] due to its [[porosity|porous structure]] and high [[specific surface area]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Ricigliano|first=Kristin|date=2011|title=Terra Pretas: Charcoal Amendments Influence on Relict Soils and Modern Agriculture|journal=Journal of Natural Resources and Life Sciences Education|volume=40|issue=1|pages=69–72|doi=10.4195/jnrlse.2011.0001se|bibcode=2011NScEd..40...69R |issn=1059-9053}}</ref> As a result, fertilizer and other nutrients are retained for plants' benefit.

=== Stock fodder ===
[[File:Chicken feeding on crushed biochar in Namibia.png|thumb|alt=Domestic chicken feeding on biochar in Namibia|Domestic chicken feeding on biochar in Namibia]]
Biochar has been used in animal feed for centuries.<ref>{{cite journal | title = The use of biochar in animal feeding | year = 2019| pmc = 6679646|quote = (During the 19th century and early 20th century) in the USA, charcoal was considered a superior feed additive for increasing butterfat content of milk.| last1 = Schmidt| first1 = H. P.| last2 = Hagemann| first2 = N.| last3 = Draper| first3 = K.| last4 = Kammann| first4 = C.| journal = PeerJ| volume = 7| article-number = e7373| doi = 10.7717/peerj.7373| pmid = 31396445| doi-access = free| bibcode = 2019PeerJ...7e7373S}}</ref>

Doug Pow, a [[Western Australia]]n farmer, explored the use of biochar mixed with [[molasses]] as stock [[fodder]]. He asserted that in [[ruminant]]s, biochar can assist digestion and reduce [[Methane#Ruminants|methane production]]. He also used [[dung beetle]]s to work the resulting biochar-infused dung into the soil without using machinery. The nitrogen and carbon in the dung were both incorporated into the soil rather than staying on the soil surface, reducing the production of [[Nitrous oxide#Greenhouse effect|nitrous oxide]] and [[Carbon dioxide#In Earth's atmosphere|carbon dioxide]]. The nitrogen and carbon added to soil fertility. On-farm evidence indicates that the fodder led to improvements of liveweight gain in [[Aberdeen Angus|Angus-cross cattle]].<ref name="abc.net.au-2019-10-18-beetles-charcoal">{{cite news
 | url =https://www.abc.net.au/news/rural/2019-10-18/wa-farmer-uses-beetles-and-charcoal-to-combat-climate-change/11613846

=== Concrete additive ===
Ordinary [[Portland cement]] (OPC), an essential component of concrete mix, is energy- and emissions-intensive to produce; cement production accounts for around 8% of global CO<sub>2</sub> emissions.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2018-06-13 |title=Making Concrete Change: Innovation in Low-carbon Cement and Concrete |url=https://www.chathamhouse.org/2018/06/making-concrete-change-innovation-low-carbon-cement-and-concrete |access-date=2023-02-21 |website=Chatham House – International Affairs Think Tank |language=en}}</ref> The concrete industry has increasingly shifted to using supplementary cementitious materials (SCMs), additives that reduce the volume of OPC in a mix while maintaining or improving concrete properties.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Arvaniti |first1=Eleni C. |last2=Juenger |first2=Maria C. G. |last3=Bernal |first3=Susan A. |last4=Duchesne |first4=Josée |last5=Courard |first5=Luc |last6=Leroy |first6=Sophie |last7=Provis |first7=John L. |last8=Klemm |first8=Agnieszka |last9=De Belie |first9=Nele |date=November 2015 |title=Physical characterization methods for supplementary cementitious materials |url=https://orbi.uliege.be/bitstream/2268/172919/1/SCM_1.pdf |journal=Materials and Structures |language=en |volume=48 |issue=11 |pages=3675–3686 |doi=10.1617/s11527-014-0430-4 |hdl=1854/LU-7095955 |s2cid=255308209 |issn=1359-5997|hdl-access=free }}</ref> Biochar has been shown to be an effective SCM, reducing concrete production emissions while maintaining required strength and ductility properties.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last1=Gupta |first1=Souradeep |last2=Kua |first2=Harn Wei |last3=Koh |first3=Hui Jun |date=2018-04-01 |title=Application of biochar from food and wood waste as green admixture for cement mortar |url=http://scholarbank.nus.edu.sg/handle/10635/139301 |journal=Science of the Total Environment |language=en |volume=619-620 |pages=419–435 |doi=10.1016/j.scitotenv.2017.11.044 |pmid=29156263 |bibcode=2018ScTEn.619..419G |issn=0048-9697|url-access= }}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last1=Suarez-Riera |first1=D. |last2=Restuccia |first2=L. |last3=Ferro |first3=G. A. |date=2020-01-01 |title=The use of Biochar to reduce the carbon footprint of cement-based materials |journal=Procedia Structural Integrity |series=1st Mediterranean Conference on Fracture and Structural Integrity, MedFract1 |language=en |volume=26 |pages=199–210 |doi=10.1016/j.prostr.2020.06.023 |s2cid=226528390 |issn=2452-3216|doi-access=free }}</ref>

Studies have found that a 1–2% weight concentration of biochar is optimal for use in concrete mixes, from both a cost and strength standpoint.<ref name=":1" /> A 2 wt.% biochar solution has been shown to increase concrete flexural strength by 15% in a three-point bending test conducted after 7 days, compared to traditional OPC concrete.<ref name=":2" /> Biochar concrete also shows promise in high-temperature resistance and permeability reduction.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Gupta |first1=Souradeep |last2=Kua |first2=Harn Wei |last3=Pang |first3=Sze Dai |date=2020-02-20 |title=Effect of biochar on mechanical and permeability properties of concrete exposed to elevated temperature |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0950061819327904 |journal=Construction and Building Materials |language=en |volume=234 |article-number=117338 |doi=10.1016/j.conbuildmat.2019.117338 |bibcode=2020CBMat.23417338G |s2cid=210233275 |issn=0950-0618|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

A cradle-to-gate [[Life-cycle assessment|life cycle assessment]] of biochar concrete showed decreased production emissions with higher concentrations of biochar, which tracks with a reduction in OPC.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Campos |first1=J. |last2=Fajilan |first2=S. |last3=Lualhati |first3=J. |last4=Mandap |first4=N. |last5=Clemente |first5=S. |date=2020-06-01 |title=Life Cycle Assessment of Biochar as a Partial Replacement to Portland Cement |journal=IOP Conference Series: Earth and Environmental Science |volume=479 |issue=1 |article-number=012025 |doi=10.1088/1755-1315/479/1/012025 |bibcode=2020E&ES..479a2025C |s2cid=225645864 |issn=1755-1307|doi-access=free }}</ref> Compared to other SCMs from industrial waste streams (such as [[fly ash]] and [[silica fume]]), biochar also showed decreased toxicity.{{Citation needed|date=November 2024}}

=== Fuel slurry ===
Biochar mixed with liquid media such as water or organic liquids (such as ethanol) is an emerging fuel type known as ''biochar-based slurry''.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Cueva Zepeda |first1=Lolita |last2=Griffin |first2=Gregory |last3=Shah |first3=Kalpit |last4=Al-Waili |first4=Ibrahim |last5=Parthasarathy |first5=Rajarathinam |date=2023-05-01 |title=Energy potential, flow characteristics and stability of water and alcohol-based rice-straw biochar slurry fuel |journal=Renewable Energy |volume=207 |pages=60–72 |doi=10.1016/j.renene.2023.02.104 |issn=0960-1481|doi-access=free |bibcode=2023REne..207...60C }}</ref> Adapting slow pyrolysis in large biomass fields and installations enables the generation of biochar slurries with unique characteristics. These slurries are becoming promising fuels in countries with regional areas where biomass is abundant, and power supply relies heavily on diesel generators.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Liu |first1=Pengfei |last2=Zhu |first2=Mingming |last3=Zhang |first3=Zhezi |last4=Leong |first4=Yee-Kwong |last5=Zhang |first5=Yang |last6=Zhang |first6=Dongke |date=2017-02-01 |title=Rheological behaviour and stability characteristics of biochar-water slurry fuels: Effect of biochar particle size and size distribution |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S037838201630621X |journal=Fuel Processing Technology |volume=156 |pages=27–32 |doi=10.1016/j.fuproc.2016.09.030 |bibcode=2017FuPrT.156...27L |issn=0378-3820|url-access=subscription }}</ref> This type of fuel resembles a [[coal slurry]], but with the advantage that it can be derived from biochar from renewable resources.

=== Water treatment ===
Biochar also has applications in water treatment.<ref>{{cite journal |title=Use of biomass-derived biochar in wastewater treatment and power production: A promising solution for a sustainable environment |journal=Science of the Total Environment |date=15 June 2022 |volume=825 |issue=153892 |doi=10.1016/j.scitotenv.2022.153892 |last1=Gupta |first1=Meenal |last2=Savla |first2=Nishit |last3=Pandit |first3=Chetan |last4=Pandit |first4=Soumya |last5=Gupta |first5=Piyush Kumar |last6=Pant |first6=Manu |last7=Khilari |first7=Santimoy |last8=Kumar |first8=Yogesh |last9=Agarwal |first9=Daksh |last10=Nair |first10=Remya R. |last11=Thomas |first11=Dessy |last12=Thakur |first12=Vijay Kumar |article-number=153892 |pmid=35181360 |bibcode=2022ScTEn.82553892G }}</ref> Its properties, porosity in particular, can be modified using different methods to increase the efficiency of contaminant removal.<ref>{{cite journal |title=Production of highly porous biochar via microwave physiochemical activation for dechlorination in water treatment |journal=Chemosphere |date=December 2022 |volume=309 |issue=136624 |bibcode=2022Chmsp.30936624S }}</ref> Biochar is reported to remove contaminants such as heavy metals, dyes, organic pollutants.<ref name=":6">{{cite journal |title=Removal of heavy metals from soil with biochar composite: A critical review of the mechanism |journal=Journal of Environmental Chemical Engineering |date=October 2021 |volume=9 |issue=5 |doi=10.1016/j.jece.2021.105830 |journal=Chemosphere |date=May 2020 |volume=246 |issue=125734 |doi=10.1016/j.chemosphere.2019.125734 |last1=Wu |first1=Jia |last2=Yang |first2=Jianwei |last3=Feng |first3=Pu |last4=Huang Research is also ongoing on the application of biochar to coarse soils in semi-arid and degraded ecosystems. In [[Namibia]], biochar is under exploration as a [[climate change adaptation]] effort, strengthening local communities' drought resilience and [[food security]] through the local production and application of biochar from abundant [[Woody plant encroachment|encroacher biomass]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Trendafilova |first=Petya |date=2024-04-04 |title=Planboo And Omiti Biochar Launch 'From Bush |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-10-31 |title=PyroNam Targets 50 Biochar Plants in Namibia by 2030 to Tackle Carbon and Soil Health |url=https://biochartoday.com/2024/10/31/pyronam-targets-50-biochar-plants-in-namibia-by-2030-to-tackle-carbon-and-soil-health/ |access-date=2024-11-05 |website=Biochar Today |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=De-bushing Advisory Service Namibia |date=2020-09-23 |title=Kick-start for Biochar Value Chain: Practical Guidelines for Producers Now Published |publisher=De-bushing Advisory Service}}</ref> Similar solutions for rangeland affected by woody plant encroachment have been explored in Australia.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Simmons |first1=Aaron T. |last2=Cowie |first2=Annette L. |last3=Waters |first3=Cathy M. |date=2021-05-20 |title=Pyrolysis of invasive woody vegetation for energy and biochar has climate change mitigation potential |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0048969721003442 |journal=Science of the Total Environment |volume=770 |article-number=145278 |doi=10.1016/j.scitotenv.2021.145278 |pmid=33736413 |bibcode=2021ScTEn.77045278S |issn=0048-9697|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

In recent years, biochar has attracted interest as a wastewater filtration medium as well as for its adsorbing capacity for wastewater pollutants, such as pharmaceuticals, [[personal care products]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Mukarunyana |first1=Brigitte |last2=Boman |first2=Christoffer |last3=Kabera |first3=Telesphore |last4=Lindgren |first4=Robert |last5=Fick |first5=Jerker |last1=Dalahmeh |first1=Sahar |last2=Ahrens |first2=Lutz |last3=Gros |first3=Meritxell |last4=Wiberg |first4=Karin |last5=Pell |first5=Mikael |date=2018-01-15 |title=Potential of biochar filters for
