{{Short description|Substance added to soil to enhance plant growth}}
{{Redirect|Plant food|the drug term|Bath salts (drug)|other uses|Plant food (disambiguation)}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=October 2021}}
{{Use American English|date=September 2025}}
[[File:Manure spreading Hlokozi 2007 11 29.jpg|thumb|upright=1.35|A [[farmer]] spreading [[manure]] to improve [[soil fertility]]]]
{{owidslider
|start        = 2023
|list         = Template:OWID/Fertilizer use in kg per hectare of arable land#gallery
|location      = commons
|caption      =
|title        =
|language     =
|file         = [[File:Fertilizer use in kg per hectare of arable land, World, 2023 (cropped).svg|link=|thumb|upright=1.6|right|Fertilizer use in kg per hectare of arable land]]
|startingView = World
}}
A '''fertilizer''' or '''fertiliser''' is any material of natural or synthetic origin that is applied to [[soil]] or to [[plant tissue]]s to supply [[plant nutrition|plant nutrients]]. Fertilizers may be distinct from [[Liming (soil)|liming materials]] or other non-nutrient [[soil amendments]]. Many sources of fertilizer exist, both natural and [[Agrochemical|industrially]] produced.<ref name="Scherer2009">{{cite book |doi=10.1002/14356007.a10_323.pub3 |chapter=Fertilizers, 1. General |date=15 July 2009 |last1=Scherer |first1=Heinrich W. |last2=Mengel |first2=Konrad |last3=Kluge |first3=Günter |last4=Severin |first4=Karl |title=[[Ullmann's Encyclopedia of Industrial Chemistry]] |volume=14 |isbn=978-3-527-30673-2 |pages=171–97 |chapter-url=https://z-library.ec/book/09QgD6k4Xp |access-date=17 April 2026 }}{{Dead link|date=June 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref> For most modern [[agricultural practice]]s, fertilization focuses on three main [[macronutrient]]s: [[nitrogen]] (N), [[phosphorus]] (P), and [[potassium]] (K) with occasional addition of supplements like [[rock flour]] for [[micronutrient]]s. Farmers apply these fertilizers in a variety of ways: through dry or [[pelletized]] or liquid application processes, using large [[agricultural equipment]], or [[Hand tool|hand-tool]] methods.

Historically, fertilization came from natural or organic sources: [[compost]], [[Manure|animal manure]], [[Human waste|human manure]], harvested [[mineral]]s, [[crop rotation]]s, and byproducts of human-nature industries (e.g. [[Fish meal|fish processing waste]], or [[Blood meal|bloodmeal]] from [[animal slaughter]]).<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Güldner |first1=Dino |last2=Larsen |first2=Laura |last3=Cunfer |first3=Geoff |date=20 August 2021 |title=Soil fertility transitions in the context of industrialization, 1750–2000 |journal=[[Social Science History]] |volume=45 |issue=Special Issue 4 |pages=785–811 |doi=10.1017/ssh.2021.26 |url=https://www.academia.edu/65291943 |access-date=13 April 2026 |language=en }}</ref> However, starting in the 19th century, after innovations in [[plant nutrition]] following [[Justus von Liebig]]'s discoveries, an [[Industrial agriculture|agricultural industry]] developed around synthetically created [[Agrochemical|agrochemical fertilizers]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Russell |first1=Darrell A. |last2=Williams |first2=Gerald G. |date=March–April 1970 |title=History of chemical fertilizer development |journal=[[Soil Science Society of America Journal]] |volume=41 |issue=2 |pages=260–5 |doi=10.2136/sssaj1977.03615995004100020020x |url=https://z-library.ec/book/09QgpZdWXp |access-date=17 April 2026 |language=en }}{{Dead link|date=June 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref> This transition was important in transforming the [[Food system|global food system]] towards larger-scale [[Intensive farming|industrial agriculture]] with large crop yields in [[monoculture]]s.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Tilman |first1=David |last2=Cassman |first2=Kenneth G. |last3=Matson |first3=Pamela A. |last4=Naylor |first4=Rosamond |last5=Polasky |first5=Stephen |date=8 August 2002 |title=Agricultural sustainability and intensive production practices |journal=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]] |volume=418 |issue=6898 |pages=671–7 |doi=10.1038/nature01014 |pmid=12167873 |bibcode=2002Natur.418..671T |url=https://www.academia.edu/2279116 |access-date=13 April 2026 |language=en }}</ref>
[[File:Fertilization (JOKAMT2Pe14-1).tif|thumb|A farmer broadcasting solid fertilizer into his field in [[Janakkala|Janakkala, Finland]] in 1960]]
The invention of [[Haber process]] for producing [[ammonia]] for nitrogen in the 20th century combined with amplified [[Productive capacity|chemical production capacity]] created during [[World War II]] led to a boom in using [[nitrogen fertilizer]]s.<ref>{{cite web |date=1 June 2016 |title=Fritz Haber |url=https://www.sciencehistory.org/historical-profile/fritz-haber |access-date=13 April 2026 |website=[[Science History Institute]] |language=en }}</ref> In the latter half of the 20th century, increased use of nitrogen fertilizers (800% increase between 1961 and 2019) has been a crucial component of the increased productivity of [[conventional food systems]] as part of the so-called "[[Green Revolution]]".<ref name="Mbow2019"/>

Fertilizers, especially when applied excessively, can have environmental consequences such as [[water pollution]]<ref>{{cite book |last=McIsaac |first=Gregory |title=Encyclopedia of water Science |year=2003 |publisher=[[CRC Press]] |editor-last1=Steward |editor-first1=Bertram A. |editor-last2=Howell |editor-first2=Terry A. |edition=1st |location=Boca Raton, Florida |pages=950–5 |chapter=Surface water pollution by nitrogen fertilizers |doi=10.1201/NOE0849396274 |isbn=978-1-351-24982-9 |access-date=13 April 2026 |chapter-url=https://www.academia.edu/88573588 }}</ref> and [[eutrophication]]<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Huang |first1=Jing |last2=Xu |first2=Chang-chun |last3=Ridoutt |first3=Bradley G. |last4=Wang |first4=Xue-chun |last5=Ren |first5=Pin-an |date=15 August 2017 |title=Nitrogen and phosphorus losses and eutrophication potential associated with fertilizer application to cropland in China |journal=[[Journal of Cleaner Production]] |volume=159 |pages=171–9 |doi=10.1016/j.jclepro.2017.05.008 |bibcode=2017JCPro.159..171H |url=https://www.academia.edu/109493106 |access-date=13 April 2026 |language=en }}</ref> due to nutrient [[Runoff (hydrology)|runoff]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Harmel |first1=R. Daren |last2=Pampell |first2=Rehanon A. |last3=Leytem |first3=April B. |last4=Smith |first4=D. R. |last5=Haney |first5=Rick L. |date=1 January 2018 |title=Assessing edge-of-field nutrient runoff from agricultural lands in the United States: how clean is clean enough? |journal=[[Journal of Soil and Water Conservation]] |volume=73 |issue=1 |pages=9–23 |doi=10.2489/jswc.73.1.9 |bibcode=2018JSWC...73....9H |url=https://z-library.ec/book/B9EYqrNo95 |access-date=13 April 2026 |language=en }}{{Dead link|date=June 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref> Additionally, the chemical process for creating the fertilizers results in byproducts, including [[Carbon emissions|carbon]] and other emissions.<ref>{{cite web |date=October 2016 |title=Carbon footprint analysis of mineral fertilizer production in Europe and other world regions |last1=Brentrup |first1=Frank |last2=Hoxha |first2=Antoine |last3=Christensen |first3=Bjarne |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/312553933 |access-date=13 April 2026 |website=LCA Food 2016 |language=en }}</ref> In some cases [[Soil contamination|contamination and pollution of soil]] result by accumulation of [[heavy metals]] contained in some fertilizers collected through mining.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Zwolak |first1=Aneta |last2=Sarzyńska |first2=Magdalena |last3=Szpyrka |first3=Ewa |last4=Stawarczyk |first4=Kinga |date=6 July 2019 |title=Sources of soil pollution by heavy metals and their accumulation in vegetables: a review |journal=[[Water, Air, and Soil Pollution]] |volume=230 |issue=7 |article-number=164 |doi=10.1007/s11270-019-4221-y |doi-access=free |bibcode=2019WASP..230..164Z |language=en }}</ref> [[sustainable agriculture|Sustainable agricultural]] practices, such as [[reduced tillage]] and planting [[buffer strip]]s, can minimize these adverse environmental effects.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Muhie |first=Seid Hussen |date=December 2022 |title=Novel approaches and practices to sustainable agriculture |journal=Journal of Agriculture and Food Research |volume=10 |article-number=100446 |doi=10.1016/j.jafr.2022.100446 |doi-access=free |language=en }}</ref>

== History ==
{{Main|History of fertilizer}}
[[File:Total fertilizer production by nutrient, OWID.svg|thumb|upright=1.6|Total fertilizer production by type.<ref>{{cite web |title=Fertilizer use per capita, World, 1961 to 2022 |url=https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/fertilizer-per-capita?time=1961..2022&tab=stacked-area |website=[[Our World in Data]] |access-date=13 April 2026 }}</ref>]]
[[File:World population supported by synthetic nitrogen fertilizers, OWID.svg|thumb|upright=1.6|World population supported with and without synthetic nitrogen fertilizers.<ref>{{cite web |title=World population with and without synthetic nitrogen fertilizers |url=https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/world-population-with-and-without-fertilizer |website=[[Our World in Data]] |access-date=13 April 2026 }}</ref>]]
[[File:Instalaciones MIRAT S.A. Salamanca.JPG|thumb|Founded in 1812, [[Mirat]], producer of [[manure]]s and fertilizers, is claimed to be the oldest industrial business in [[Salamanca]] (Spain).]]
[[File:Cropland nitrogen balance by component and region.svg|thumb|Cropland nitrogen balance by component and region<ref name="FAO2025">{{cite book |last=[[Food and Agriculture Organization|FAO]] |title=World Food and Agriculture – Statistical Yearbook 2025 |year=2025 |publisher=[[Food and Agriculture Organization|FAO]] |location=Rome, Italy |isbn=978-92-5-140174-3 |language=en |doi=10.4060/cd4313en |doi-access=free }}</ref>]]
Management of [[soil fertility]] has preoccupied farmers since the beginning of agriculture. [[Middle East]]ern,<ref>{{cite journal |last=Zeder |first=Melinda A. |date=October 2011 |title=The origins of agriculture in the Near East |journal=[[Current Anthropology]] |volume=52 |issue=S4 |pages=221–35 |doi=10.1086/659307 |doi-access=free |language=en }}</ref> [[China|Chin]]ese,<ref>{{cite journal |last=Cohen |first=David Joel |date=October 2011 |title=The beginnings of agriculture in China: a multiregional view |journal=[[Current Anthropology]] |volume=52 |issue=S4 |pages=273–93 |doi=10.1086/659965 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2011CurrA..52S.273C |language=en }}</ref> [[Mesoamerica]]n,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Zizumbo-Villarreal |first1=Daniel |last2=Colunga-GarcíaMarín |first2=Patricia |date=2 February 2010 |title=Origin of agriculture and plant domestication in West Mesoamerica |journal=Genetic Resources and Crop Evolution |volume=57 |issue=6 |pages=813–25 |doi=10.1007/s10722-009-9521-4 |bibcode=2010GRCEv..57..813Z |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/225361062 |access-date=14 April 2026 |language=en }}</ref> and [[Andean civilizations|cultures of the Central Andes]]<ref>{{cite book |last=Pearsall |first=Deborah M. |title=Handbook of South American archaeology |year=2008 |publisher=[[Springer Science+Business Media]] |location=New York, New York |editor-last1=Silverman |editor-first1=Helaine |editor-last2=Isbell |editor-first2=William H. |edition=1st |pages=105–20 |chapter=Plant domestication and the shift to agriculture in the Andes |doi=10.1007/978-0-387-74907-5_7 |isbn=978-0-387-74907-5 |access-date=17 April 2026 |chapter-url=https://z-library.ec/book/YyVgvvqBXp }}{{Dead link|date=June 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref> were all early adopters of agriculture. This is thought to have led to their cultures growing faster in population which allowed an exportation of culture to neighboring hunter-gatherer groups.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Spielmann |first1=Katherine A. |last2=Eder |first2=James F. |year=1994 |title=Hunters and farmers: then and now |journal=[[Annual Review of Anthropology]] |volume=23 |pages=303–23 |doi=10.1146/annurev.an.23.100194.001511 |url=https://z-library.ec/book/D9PzDPvZXm |access-date=17 April 2026 |language=en }}{{Dead link|date=June 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref> Fertilizer use along with agriculture allowed some of these early societies a critical advantage over their neighbors, leading them to become dominant cultures in their respective regions.<ref>{{cite book |last=Bellwood |first=Peter |url=https://z-library.sk/book/MyRa37K2vQ |title=First farmers: the origins of agricultural societies |year=2004 |publisher=[[Wiley-Blackwell]] |location=Hoboken, New Jersey |isbn=978-0-631-20566-1 |language=en |access-date=14 April 2026 }}{{Dead link|date=June 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Liu |first1=Min |last2=Zhong |first2=Taiyang |last3=Lyu |first3=Xiao |date=22 January 2024 |title=Spatial spillover effects of "New Farmers" on diffusion of sustainable agricultural practices: evidence from China |journal=Land |language=en |volume=13 |issue=1 |article-number=119 |doi=10.3390/land13010119 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2024Land...13..119L |issn=2073-445X }}</ref> [[Egyptians]], [[Roman people|Romans]], [[Babylonia]]ns, and early [[Germans]] are all recorded as using [[mineral]]s or [[manure]] to enhance the [[productivity]] of their farms.<ref name="Scherer2009"/> The scientific research of [[plant nutrition]] started well before the work of German chemist [[Justus von Liebig]] although his name is most mentioned as the "father of the fertilizer industry".<ref>{{cite web |url=http://scihi.org/justus-von-liebig-agricultural-revolution/ |title=Justus von Liebig and the agricultural revolution |date=12 May 2020 |archive-date=12 July 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240712172042/http://scihi.org/justus-von-liebig-agricultural-revolution/ |url-status=dead }}</ref> [[Nicolas Théodore de Saussure]] and scientific colleagues at the time were quick to disprove the simplifications of von Liebig.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Werner |first1=Petra |last2=Holmes |first2=Frederic L. |date=September 2002 |title=Justus Liebig and the plant physiologists |journal=[[Journal of the History of Biology]] |volume=35 |issue=3 |pages=421–41 |doi=10.1023/A:1021182316792 |url=https://z-library.ec/book/PLKRWbwYXB |access-date=17 April 2026 |language=en }}{{Dead link|date=June 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref> Prominent scientists whom von Liebig drew were [[Carl Ludwig Sprenger]] and [[Hermann Hellriegel]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Böhm |first1=Wolfgang |last2=Wissemeier |first2=Alexander H. |date=August 2025 |title=Contribution to the hiStory series in plant nutrition: nitrogen issues in the 19th century. II. What is special about legumes in terms of their nitrogen nutrition? |journal=Journal of Plant Nutrition and Soil Science |volume=188 |issue=4 |pages=585–92 |doi=10.1002/jpln.12019 |doi-access=free |language=en }}</ref> In this field, a 'knowledge erosion' took place,<ref>{{cite book |last=Uekötter |first=Frank |title=Die Wahrheit ist auf dem Feld: eine Wissensgeschichte der deutschen Landwirtschaft |publisher=[[Vandenhoeck & Ruprecht]] |location=Göttingen, Germany |year=2010 |isbn=978-3-5253-1705-1 |language=German |edition=3rd }}</ref> partly driven by an intermingling of economics and research.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Uekötter |first=Frank |date=1 January 2014 |title=Why panaceas work: recasting science, knowledge, and fertilizer interests in German agriculture |journal=[[Agricultural History (journal)|Agricultural History]] |volume=88 |issue=1 |pages=68–86 |doi=10.3098/ah.2014.88.1.68 |jstor=10.3098/ah.2014.88.1.68 |issn=0002-1482 |url=https://z-library.ec/book/vydJmezmLV |access-date=14 April 2026 }}{{Dead link|date=June 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref> [[John Bennet Lawes]], an English [[entrepreneur]], began experimenting on the effects of various [[manure]]s on plants growing in pots in 1837, and a year or two later the experiments were extended to crops in the field. One immediate consequence was that in 1842 he patented a manure formed by treating [[phosphate]]s with [[sulfuric acid]], and thus was the first to create the artificial manure industry. In the succeeding year, he enlisted the services of [[Joseph Henry Gilbert]]; together they performed crop experiments at the [[Rothamsted Research|Institute of Arable Crops Research]].<ref>{{cite journal |last=Warington |first=Robert |date=13 September 1900 |title=Sir John Bennet Lawes, Bart., F.R.S. |journal=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]] |volume=62 |issue=1611 |pages=467–8 |doi=10.1038/062467a0 |bibcode=1900Natur..62..467W |url=https://z-library.ec/book/MXlpJ7lMX6 |access-date=17 April 2026 }}{{Dead link|date=June 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref>

The [[Birkeland–Eyde process]] was one of the competing industrial processes at the beginning of nitrogen-based fertilizer production.<ref>{{cite book |title=The development of modern chemistry |last=Ihde |first=Aaron John |publisher=[[Harper & Row]] |location=New York |url=https://archive.org/details/developmentofmod00ihde/page/678/mode/2up |year=1964 |page=678 |access-date=14 April 2026 }}</ref> This process was used to fix atmospheric [[nitrogen]] (N<sub>2</sub>) into [[nitric acid]] (HNO<sub>3</sub>), one of several chemical processes called [[nitrogen fixation]]. The resultant nitric acid was then used as a source of [[nitrate]] (NO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>). A factory based on the process was built in [[Rjukan]] and [[Notodden (town)|Notodden]] in Norway and large [[hydroelectric power]] facilities were built.<ref>{{cite book |title=The world's greatest fix: a history of nitrogen and agriculture |last=Leigh |first=G. Jeffery |publisher=[[Oxford University Press]] |location=Oxford, United Kingdom |date=9 September 2004 |isbn=978-0-19-516582-1 |pages=134–9 |url=https://z-library.ec/book/5JLZ6N5nL8 |access-date=17 April 2026 }}{{Dead link|date=June 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref>

The 1910s and 1920s witnessed the rise of the [[Haber process]] and the [[Ostwald process]]. The Haber process produces [[ammonia]] (NH<sub>3</sub>) from [[methane]] (CH<sub>4</sub>) ([[natural gas]]) and [[molecular nitrogen]] (N<sub>2</sub>) from the air. The ammonia from the Haber process is then partially converted into [[nitric acid]] (HNO<sub>3</sub>) in the [[Ostwald process]].<ref>{{cite book |title=A short history of twentieth-century technology c. 1900-c. 1950 |last1=Williams |first1=Trevor Illtyd |last2=Thomas Kingston |first2=Derry |publisher=[[Oxford University Press]] |location=Oxfors, United Kingdom |date=7 October 1982 |isbn=978-0-19-858159-8 |pages=134–5 |url=https://archive.org/details/B-001-000-137/page/n157/mode/2up |access-date=14 April 2026 }}</ref> It is estimated that a third of annual global food production uses ammonia from the [[Haber–Bosch process]] and that this supports nearly half the world's population.<ref>{{cite book |first=Vaclav |last=Smil |year=2004 |title=Enriching the Earth: Fritz Haber, Carl Bosch, and the transformation of world food production |location=Cambridge, Massachusetts |publisher=[[MIT Press]] |isbn=978-0-262-69313-4 |page=156 |doi=10.7551/mitpress/2767.001.0001 |url=https://z-library.ec/book/EaXjwkkALY |access-date=14 April 2026 }}{{Dead link|date=June 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |first=Claudia |last=Flavell-While |title=Fritz Haber and Carl Bosch: feed the world |url=https://www.thechemicalengineer.com/features/cewctw-fritz-haber-and-carl-bosch-feed-the-world/ |access-date=14 April 2026 |website=www.thechemicalengineer.com |archive-date=19 June 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210619021457/https://www.thechemicalengineer.com/features/cewctw-fritz-haber-and-carl-bosch-feed-the-world/ |url-status=live }}</ref> After [[World War II]], nitrogen production plants that had ramped up for wartime bomb manufacturing were pivoted towards agricultural uses.<ref>{{cite web |last=Philpott |first=Tom |title=A brief history of our deadly addiction to nitrogen fertilizer |url=https://www.motherjones.com/food/2013/04/history-nitrogen-fertilizer-ammonium-nitrate/ |date=19 April 2013 |website=[[Mother Jones (magazine)|Mother Jones]] |language=en |access-date=14 April 2026 }}</ref> The use of synthetic nitrogen fertilizers has increased steadily over the last 50 years of the 20th century, rising almost 20-fold to a rate of 100 million [[tonnes]] of nitrogen per year in 2003.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Glass |first=Anthony |date=September 2003 |title=Nitrogen use efficiency of crop plants: physiological constraints upon nitrogen absorption |journal=Critical Reviews in Plant Sciences |volume=22 |issue=5 |doi=10.1080/713989757 |pages=453–70 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/279933619 |access-date=14 April 2026 }}</ref>

The development of synthetic nitrogen fertilizers has significantly supported global [[population growth]]. It has been estimated that almost half the people on the Earth are currently fed due to synthetic nitrogen fertilizer use.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Erisman |first1=Jan Willem |first2=Mark A. |last2=Sutton |first3=James |last3=Galloway |first4=Zbigniew |last4=Klimont |first5=Wilfried |last5=Winiwarter |s2cid-access=free |title=How a century of ammonia synthesis changed the world |journal=[[Nature Geoscience]] |pages=636–9 |date=28 September 2008 |volume=1 |doi=10.1038/ngeo325 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/248828433 |access-date=14 April 2026 |issue=10 |bibcode=2008NatGe...1..636E |s2cid=94880859 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100723223052/http://www.physics.ohio-state.edu/~wilkins/energy/Resources/Essays/ngeo325.pdf.xpdf |archive-date=23 July 2010 |url-status=live }}</ref> The use of phosphate fertilizers has also increased from 9 million tonnes per year in 1960 to 40 million tonnes per year in 2000, but future phosphorus fertilizer availability is now a critical issue.<ref name="Blackwell2019">{{cite journal |last1=Blackwell |first1=Martin |last2=Darch |first2=Tegan |last3=Haslam |first3=Richard |title=Phosphorus use efficiency and fertilizers: future opportunities for improvements |journal=Frontiers of Agricultural Science and Engineering |pages=332–40 |year=2019 |volume=6 |doi=10.15302/J-FASE-2019274 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/345394914 |issue=4 |access-date=14 April 2026 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

Agricultural use of inorganic fertilizers in 2021 was 195 million tonnes of nutrients, of which 56% was nitrogen.<ref name="FAO2023">{{cite book |last=[[Food and Agriculture Organization|FAO]] |title=World Food and Agriculture – Statistical Yearbook 2023 |year=2023 |publisher=[[Food and Agriculture Organization|FAO]] |location=Rome, Italy |isbn=978-92-5-138262-2 |language=en |doi=10.4060/cc8166en |doi-access=free }}</ref> Asia represented 53% of the world's total agricultural use of inorganic fertilizers in 2021, followed by the Americas (29%), Europe (12%), Africa (4%) and Oceania (2%). This ranking of the regions is the same for all nutrients. The main users of inorganic fertilizers are, in descending order, China, India, Brazil, and the United States of America (see Table 15), with China the largest user of each nutrient.<ref name="FAO2023"/> Agricultural use of inorganic fertilizers in 2023 was 190 million tonnes of nutrients, of which 112 million tonnes (58%) was nitrogen.<ref>{{cite book |last=[[Food and Agriculture Organization|FAO]] |url=https://openknowledge.fao.org/handle/20.500.14283/cd4313en |title=World Food and Agriculture – Statistical Yearbook 2025 |year=2025 |publisher=[[Food and Agriculture Organization|FAO]] |isbn=978-92-5-140174-3 |language=en |doi=10.4060/cd4313en |access-date=20 April 2026 }}</ref>

A [[maize]] crop yielding 6–9 tonnes of grain per [[hectare]] ({{cvt|1|ha|acre |1|disp=out}}) requires {{convert|31|–|50|kg}} of [[phosphate]] fertilizer to be applied; [[soybean]] crops require about half, 20–25&nbsp;kg per hectare.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Vance |first1=Carroll P. |last2=Uhde-Stone |first2=Claudia |last3=Allan |first3=Deborah L. |date=March 2003 |title=Phosphorus acquisition and use: critical adaptations by plants for securing a non renewable resource |journal=[[New Phytologist]] |volume=157 |issue=3 |pages=423–47 |jstor=1514050 |s2cid=53490640 |doi=10.1046/j.1469-8137.2003.00695.x |pmid=33873400 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2003NewPh.157..423V }}</ref> [[Yara International]] is the world's largest producer of nitrogen-based fertilizers.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.economist.com/business/2010/02/18/a-growth-business |title=A growth business: feeding the world has become a mouth-watering opportunity |date=18 February 2010 |newspaper=[[The Economist]] |access-date=14 April 2026 }}</ref>

== Mechanism ==
[[File:Reuse of urine demonstration - fertilised and not fertilised tomato plant experiment (3617543234).jpg|thumb|upright=1.4|Six tomato plants grown with and without nitrate fertilizer on nutrient-poor sand/clay soil. One of the plants in the nutrient-poor soil has died.]]
[[File:Inorganic fertilizer use by region-.svg|thumb|Inorganic fertilizer use by region<ref name="FAO2025"/>]]
Fertilizers enhance the growth of plants. This goal is met in two ways, the traditional one being additives that provide [[nutrient]]s. The second mode by which some fertilizers act is to enhance the effectiveness of the soil by modifying its water-holding capacity and aeration.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Naveed |first1=Muhammad |last2=Moldrup |first2=Per |last3=Vogel |first3=Hans-Jörg |last4=Lamandé |first4=Mathieu |last5=Wildenschild |first5=Dorthe |last6=Tuller |first6=Markus |last7=De Jonge |first7=Lis Wollesen |date=April 2014 |title=Impact of long-term fertilization practice on soil structure evolution |journal=Geoderma |volume=217–218  |pages=181–9 |doi=10.1016/j.geoderma.2013.12.001 |bibcode=2014Geode.217..181N |url=https://www.academia.edu/48626941 |access-date=14 April 2026 }}</ref> This article, like many on fertilizers, emphasizes the nutritional aspect.

Fertilizers typically provide, in varying [[Proportionality (mathematics)|proportions]]:<ref name="Dittmar2009">{{cite book |doi=10.1002/14356007.n10_n01 |chapter=Fertilizers, 2. Types |date=15 July 2009 |last1=Dittmar |first1=Heinrich |last2=Drach |first2=Manfred |last3=Vosskamp |first3=Ralf |last4=Trenkel |first4=Martin E. |last5=Gutser |first5=Reinhold |last6=Steffens |first6=Günter |title=[[Ullmann's Encyclopedia of Industrial Chemistry|Ullmann's Encyclopedia of Industrial Chemistry, volume 14]] |isbn=978-3-527-30673-2 |pages=199–246 |chapter-url=https://z-library.ec/book/DLnWvMxo96 |access-date=17 April 2026 }}{{Dead link|date=June 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref>
*[[Labeling of fertilizer|Three main macronutrients (NPK)]]:
** [[Nitrogen]] (N): leaf growth and stems;<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Pearman |first1=I. |last2=Thomas |first2=Susan M. |last3=Thorne |first3=Gillian N. |date=January 1977 |title=Effects of nitrogen fertilizer on growth and yield of spring wheat |journal=[[Annals of Botany]] |volume=41 |issue=1 |pages=93–108 |doi=10.1093/oxfordjournals.aob.a085289 |url=https://z-library.ec/book/D92k6qJDyZ |access-date=17 April 2026 }}{{Dead link|date=June 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref>
** [[Phosphorus]] (P): development of roots, flowers, seeds and fruit;<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Majeed |first1=Muhammad Atif |last2=Ahmad |first2=Rashid |last3=Tahir |first3=Muhammad |last4=Tanveer |first4=Asif |last5=Ahmad |first5=Muhammad |date=January–March 2014 |title=Effect of phosphorus fertilizer sources and rates on growth and yield of wheat (''Triticum aestivum'' L.) |journal=Asian Journal of Agriculture and Biology |volume=2 |issue=1 |pages=14–9 |url=https://www.asianjab.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/05/3-MS-No.-40.pdf |access-date=14 April 2026 }}</ref>
** [[Potassium]] (K): strong stem growth, movement of water in plants, promotion of [[flowering]] and [[fruiting]];<ref>{{cite journal |last=Pettigrew |first=William T. |date=August 2008 |title=Potassium influences on yield and quality production for maize, wheat, soybean and cotton |journal=[[Physiologia Plantarum]] |volume=133 |issue=4 |pages=670–81 |doi=10.1111/j.1399-3054.2008.01073.x |pmid=18331406 |bibcode=2008PPlan.133..670P |url=https://z-library.ec/book/mLBel1QNXz |access-date=17 April 2026 }}{{Dead link|date=June 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref>
* Micronutrients: [[copper]] (Cu), [[Iron fertilisation|iron]] (Fe), [[manganese]] (Mn), [[molybdenum]] (Mo), [[zinc]] (Zn), and [[boron]] (B).<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Saquee |first1=Francess Sia |last2=Diakite |first2=Simbo |last3=Kavhiza |first3=Nyasha John |last4=Pakina |first4=Elena |last5=Zargar |first5=Meisam |date=16 February 2023 |title=The efficacy of micronutrient fertilizers on the yield formulation and quality of wheat grains |journal=[[Agronomy (journal)|Agronomy]] |volume=13 |issue=2 |article-number=566 |doi=10.3390/agronomy13020566 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2023Agron..13..566S }}</ref> Of occasional significance are [[silicon]] (Si), [[cobalt]] (Co), and [[vanadium]] (V).<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kaur |first1=Simranjeet |last2=Kaur |first2=Navneet |last3=Siddique |first3=Kadambot H. M. |last4=Nayyar |first4=Harsh |date=27 October 2015 |title=Beneficial elements for agricultural crops and their functional relevance in defence against stresses |journal=Archives of Agronomy and Soil Science |volume=62 |issue=7 |pages=905–20 |doi=10.1080/03650340.2015.1101070 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/282430748 |access-date=14 April 2026 }}</ref>

Although calcium uptake by plant roots has long-time been considered as luxury consumption,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Loneragan |first1=Jack F. |last2=Snowball |first2=K. |date=1 June 1969 |title=Calcium requirements of plants |journal=[[Australian Journal of Agricultural Research]] |volume=20 |issue=3 |pages=465–78 |doi=10.1071/AR9690465 |url=https://z-library.ec/book/4yN2mBxRyw |access-date=17 April 2026 }}{{Dead link|date=June 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref> it is now considered as an essential element for its various roles in the maintenance of the integrity of plant [[cell wall]]s and [[cell membrane]]s.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=White |first1=Philip J. |last2=Broadley |first2=Martin R. |date=October 2003 |title=Calcium in plants |journal=[[Annals of Botany]] |volume=92 |issue=4 |pages=487–511 |doi=10.1093/aob/mcg164 |pmid=12933363 |pmc=4243668 |url=https://z-library.ec/book/4yNwGaovXw |access-date=17 April 2026 }}{{Dead link|date=June 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref> [[Liming (soil)|Liming]] has also a decisive and positive influence on [[crop yield]]s by couteracting [[soil acidification]],<ref name="soil_acidification_and">{{cite journal |last=Goulding |first=Keith W. T. |date=September 2016 |title=Soil acidification and the importance of liming agricultural soils with particular reference to the United Kingdom |journal=Soil Use and Management |volume=32 |issue=3 |pages=390–9 |doi=10.1111/sum.12270 |doi-access=free |pmid=27708478 |pmc=5032897 |bibcode=2016SUMan..32..390G }}</ref> a side-effect of [[plant growth]]<ref>{{cite journal |last=Haynes |first=Richard J. |date=March 1983 |title=Soil acidification induced by leguminous crops |journal=Grass and Forage Science |volume=38 |issue=1 |pages=1–11 |doi=10.1111/j.1365-2494.1983.tb01614.x |bibcode=1983GForS..38....1H |url=https://z-library.ec/book/w9JWQ4RlyD |access-date=17 April 2026 }}{{Dead link|date=June 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref> and nutrient export by crops,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Burle |first1=Marilia L. |last2=Mielniczuk |first2=João |last3=Focchi |first3=Sandro |date=March 1997 |title=Effect of cropping systems on soil chemical characteristics, with emphasis on soil acidification |journal=[[Plant and Soil]] |volume=190 |issue=2 |pages=309–16 |doi=10.1023/A:1004266831343 |url=https://www.academia.edu/19984729 |access-date=14 April 2026 }}</ref> improving [[soil structure]], and thus [[soil aeration]],<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Schack-Kirchner |first1=Helmer |last2=Hildebrand |first2=Ernst E. |date=February 1998 |title=Changes in soil structure and aeration due to liming and acid irrigation |journal=[[Plant and Soil]] |volume=199 |issue=1 |pages=167–76 |doi=10.1023/A:1004290226402 |bibcode=1998PlSoi.199..167S |url=https://z-library.ec/book/aXjexdM4yY |access-date=17 April 2026 }}{{Dead link|date=June 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref> and increasing soil biological activity, thereby [[soil fertility]], in particular through increased [[nitrification]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Fuentes |first1=Juan P. |last2=Bezdicek |first2=David F. |last3=Flury |first3=Markus |last4=Albrecht |first4=Stefan |last5=Smith |first5=Jeffrey L. |date=July 2006 |title=Microbial activity affected by lime in a long-term no-till soil |journal=Soil and Tillage Research |volume=88 |issue=1–2 |pages=123–31 |url=https://www.academia.edu/5088782 |doi=10.1016/j.still.2005.05.001 |bibcode=2006STilR..88..123F |access-date=14 April 2026 }}</ref>

The [[nutrient]]s required for healthy plant life are classified according to the [[Chemical element|elements]], but the elements are not used as fertilizers. Instead, [[chemical compound|compounds]] containing these elements are the basis of fertilizers. Macro-nutrients are present in plant tissue in quantities from 0.15% to 6.0% on a [[dry matter]] (DM) (0% moisture) basis but they are sometimes consumed in larger quantities than required (luxury consumption), in particular when fertilizers are used in excess of plant requirements ([[Over fertilization|overfertilization]]).<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Van Wesenbeeck |first1=Cornelia F. A. |last2=Keyzer |first2=Michiel A. |last3=Van Veen |first3=Wim C. M. |last4=Qiu |first4=Huanguang |date=May 2021 |title=Can China's overuse of fertilizer be reduced without threatening food security and farm incomes? |journal=Agricultural Systems |volume=190 |article-number=103093 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/349184262 |doi=10.1016/j.agsy.2021.103093 |bibcode=2021AgSys.19003093V |access-date=14 April 2026 |hdl=1871.1/bb647d6a-eb28-4b09-a669-fc63877c68b9 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> Plants are made up of four main elements: [[hydrogen]], [[oxygen]], [[carbon]], and [[nitrogen]]. Carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen are widely available respectively in [[carbon dioxide]] and in [[water]]. Although nitrogen makes up most of the [[atmosphere]], it is in a form that is unavailable to plants. Nitrogen is the most important fertilizer since nitrogen is present in [[protein]]s ([[amide bond]]s between [[amino-acid|amino acid]]s), [[DNA]] ([[purine|puric]] and [[pyrimidine|pyrimidic]]{{typo help inline|reason=pyrimidinic?|date=May 2026}} bases), and other components (e.g., [[porphyrin|tetrapyrrolic]] [[heme]] in [[chlorophyll]]). It is common tenet that nitrogen is absent from the [[parent rock]] and thus cannot be obtained from [[mineral weathering]], although recent studies point to the equal importance of the atmosphere and bedrock as nitrogen sources.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Houlton |first1=Benjamin Z. |last2=Morford |first2=Scott L. |last3=Dahlgren |first3=Randy A. |date=6 April 2018 |title=Convergent evidence for widespread rock nitrogen sources in Earth's surface environment |journal=[[Science (journal)|Science]] |volume=360 |issue=6384 |pages=58–62 |url=https://z-library.ec/book/BXbDajpg97 |doi=10.1126/science.aan4399 |pmid=29622648 |bibcode=2018Sci...360...58H |access-date=17 April 2026 }}{{Dead link|date=June 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref> Nitrogen is made available to plants through [[weathering]] of nitrogen-containing [[parent rock]]s<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Morford |first1=Scott L. |last2=Houlton |first2=Benjamin Z. |last3=Dahlgren |first3=Randy A. |date=January 2016 |title=Direct quantification of long-term rock nitrogen inputs to temperate forest ecosystems |journal=[[Ecology (journal)|Ecology]] |volume=97 |issue=1 |pages=54–64 |url=https://z-library.ec/book/nLAJzB0g9z |doi=10.1890/15-0501.1 |pmid=27008775 |bibcode=2016Ecol...97...54M |access-date=17 April 2026 }}{{Dead link|date=June 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref> and [[nitrogen fixation]]. Only some free-living (e.g. ''[[Clostridium]]'') and [[symbiotic bacteria]] living in root systems of [[host plant]]s (notably [[legume]]s) can fix atmospheric nitrogen ({{chem2|N2}}) by converting it to [[ammonia]] ({{chem2|NH3}}) and [[amino acid]]s which are available to plants.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Day |first1=David Alexander |last2=Poole |first2=Philip S. |last3=Tyerman |first3=Stephen D. |last4=Rosendahl |first4=Lis |date=January 2001 |title=Ammonia and amino acid transport across symbiotic membranes in nitrogen-fixing legume nodules |journal=[[Cellular and Molecular Life Sciences]] |volume=58 |issue=1 |pages=61–71 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/12101562 |doi=10.1007/PL00000778 |pmid=11229817 |pmc=11146490 |access-date=14 April 2026 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Smercina |first1=Darian N. |last2=Evans |first2=Sarah E. |last3=Friesen |first3=Maren L. |last4=Tiemann |first4=Lisa K. |date=6 March 2019 |title=To fix or not to fix: controls on free-living nitrogen fixation in the rhizosphere |journal=[[Applied and Environmental Microbiology]] |volume=85 |issue=6 |article-number=e02546-18 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/330483677 |doi=10.1128/AEM.02546-18 |pmid=30658971 |pmc=6414387 |bibcode=2019ApEnM..85E2546S |access-date=14 April 2026 }}</ref> [[Phosphate]] ({{chem2|PO4(3-)}}) is required for the production of [[Deoxyribonucleic acid|DNA]] ([[genetic code]]) and [[Adenosine triphosphate|ATP]], the main energy carrier in [[Cell (biology)|cells]], as well as certain [[lipid]]s ([[phospholipid]]s, the main components of the [[liposome|lipidic double layer]] of the [[cell membrane]]s).<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Poirier |first1=Yves |last2=Jaskolowski |first2=Aime |last3=Clúa |first3=Joaquín |date=20 June 2022 |title=Phosphate acquisition and metabolism in plants |journal=[[Current Biology]] |volume=32 |issue=12 |pages=R623–R629 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/330483677 |doi=10.1016/j.cub.2022.03.073 |pmid=35728542 |bibcode=2022CBio...32.R623P |access-date=15 April 2026 }}</ref>

=== Microbiological considerations ===

Two sets of [[enzymatic reaction]]s are highly relevant to the efficiency of nitrogen-based fertilizers. 
;Urease
The first is the [[hydrolysis]] (reaction with water) of [[urea]] ({{chem2|CO(NH2)2}}). Many [[soil]] [[bacteria]] possess the enzyme [[urease]], which [[catalysis|catalyzes]] the conversion of urea to [[ammonium]] ion ({{chem2|NH4+}}) and [[bicarbonate]] [[ion]] ({{chem2|HCO3-}}).<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lloyd |first1=A. B. |last2=Sheffe |first2=M. Jane |date=August 1973 |title=Urease activity in soils |journal=[[Plant and Soil]] |volume=39 |issue=1 |pages=71–80 |url=https://z-library.ec/book/BXbEb8qgy7 |doi=10.1007/BF00018046 |bibcode=1973PlSoi..39...71L |access-date=17 April 2026 }}{{Dead link|date=June 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref>
;Ammonia oxidation
[[Ammonia-oxidizing bacteria]] (AOB), such as species of ''[[Nitrosomonas]]'', [[Redox|oxidize]] ammonia ({{chem2|NH3}}) to [[nitrite]] ({{chem2|NO2-}}), a process termed [[nitrification]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Marsh |first1=K. L. |last2=Sims |first2=Gerald K. |last3=Mulvaney |first3=Richard L. |date=28 June 2005 |title=Availability of urea to autotrophic ammonia-oxidizing bacteria as related to the fate of <sup>14</sup>C- and <sup>15</sup>N-labeled urea added to soil |journal=Biology and Fertility of Soils |volume=42 |issue=2 |pages=137–45 |url=https://www.academia.edu/20293146 |doi=10.1007/S00374-005-0004-2 |bibcode=2005BioFS..42..137M |access-date=15 April 2026 }}</ref> [[Nitrite-oxidizing bacteria]], especially ''[[Nitrobacter]]'', oxidize [[nitrite]] ({{chem2|NO2-}}) to [[nitrate]] ({{chem2|NO3-}}), which is extremely [[solubility|soluble]] and mobile, being [[Leaching (agriculture)|leached]] easily to [[groundwater]] then to rivers then to the sea, and is a major cause of [[eutrophication]]<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Smolders |first1=Alfons J. P. |last2=Lucassen |first2=Esther C. H. E. T. |last3=Bobbink |first3=Roland |last4=Roelofs |first4=Jan G. M. |last5=Lamers |first5=Leon P. M. |date=5 November 2009 |title=How nitrate leaching from agricultural lands provokes phosphate eutrophication in groundwater fed wetlands: the sulphur bridge |journal=Biogeochemistry |volume=98 |issue=1 |pages=1–7 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/225619718 |doi=10.1007/s10533-009-9387-8 |access-date=15 April 2026 |doi-access=free }}</ref> and [[algal bloom]]s in rivers, lakes and sea shores.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Wurtsbaugh |first1=Wayne A. |last2=Paerl |first2=Hans W. |last3=Dodds |first3=Walter K. |date=September–October 2019 |title=Nutrients, eutrophication and harmful algal blooms along the freshwater to marine continuum |journal=[[Wiley Interdisciplinary Reviews. Water|Wiley Interdisciplinary Reviews Water]] |volume=6 |issue=5 |article-number=e1373 |url=https://www.academia.edu/81075704 |doi=10.1002/WAT2.1373 |bibcode=2019WIRWa...6E1373W |access-date=15 April 2026 }}</ref>

== Classification ==

Fertilizers are classified in several ways. They are classified according to whether they provide a single nutrient (e.g., K, P, or N), in which case they are classified as ''straight fertilizers''. ''Multinutrient fertilizers'' (or ''complex fertilizers'') provide two or more nutrients, for example, N and P combined. Fertilizers are also sometimes classified as inorganic (the topic of most of this article) versus organic. Inorganic fertilizers exclude carbon-containing materials except [[urea]]. Organic fertilizers are usually (recycled) plant- or animal-derived matter (e.g. [[compost]], [[manure]], respectively). Inorganic are sometimes called synthetic fertilizers since various chemical treatments are required for their manufacture.<ref>{{cite book |doi=10.1201/b11577 |chapter=Inorganic chemical fertilizers and their properties |year=2012 |last=Jones |first=J. Benton Jr |title=Plant nutrition and soil fertility manual |edition=2nd |isbn=978-0-429-13081-6 |pages=157–67 |chapter-url=https://z-library.ec/book/jL56n0xV9g |access-date=17 April 2026 }}{{Dead link|date=June 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref>

=== Single nutrient ("straight") fertilizers ===

The main nitrogen-based straight fertilizer is [[ammonia]] (NH<sub>3</sub>), [[ionized]] in solution as [[ammonium]] (NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>), applied in the form of [[Salt (chemistry)|salt]]s or [[Derivative (chemistry)|derivative]]s, including:
* [[Ammonium nitrate]] (NH<sub>4</sub>NO<sub>3</sub>) with 34-35% nitrogen is widely used.
* [[Urea]] (CO(NH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>2</sub>), with 45-46% nitrogen, another popular source of nitrogen, having the advantage that it is solid and non-explosive, unlike ammonia and ammonium nitrate.
* [[Calcium ammonium nitrate]] Is a blend of 20-30% [[limestone]] CaCO<sub>3</sub> or [[Dolomite (mineral)|dolomite]] CaMg(CO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> and 70-80% [[ammonium nitrate]] with 24-28% nitrogen.
*[[Calcium nitrate]] with 15.5% nitrogen and 19% calcium, reportedly holding a small share of the nitrogen fertilizer market (4% in 2007).<ref name="Smil2004">{{cite book |doi=10.7551/mitpress/2767.003.0009 |chapter=Synthetic fertilizers |year=2004 |last=Smil |first=Vaclav |title=Enriching the Earth: Fritz Haber, Carl Bosch, and the transformation of world food production |isbn=978-0-262-28385-4 |pages=153–64 |url=https://z-library.ec/book/EaXjwkkALY |publisher=[[MIT Press]] |location=Cambridge, Massachusetts |access-date=17 April 2026 }}{{Dead link|date=June 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref>

The main straight phosphate fertilizers are the [[superphosphate]]s:
* [[Single superphosphate]] (SSP) consisting of 14–18% P<sub>2</sub>O<sub>5</sub>, again in the form of Ca(H<sub>2</sub>PO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>, but also [[phosphogypsum]] ({{chem2|Ca[[SO4]] * 2 H2O}}).
* [[Triple superphosphate]] (TSP) typically consists of 44–48% of P<sub>2</sub>O<sub>5</sub> and no gypsum.

A mixture of single superphosphate and triple superphosphate is called double superphosphate. More than 90% of a typical superphosphate fertilizer is water-soluble.

The main potassium-based straight fertilizer is [[muriate of potash]] (MOP, 95–99% KCl). It is typically available as 0-0-60 or 0-0-62 fertilizer.

=== Multinutrient fertilizers ===

These fertilizers are common. They consist of two or more nutrient components.

;Binary (NP, NK, PK) fertilizers
Major two-component fertilizers provide both nitrogen and phosphorus to the plants. These are called NP fertilizers. The main NP fertilizers are 
*[[monoammonium phosphate]] (MAP) NH<sub>4</sub>H<sub>2</sub>PO<sub>4</sub>. With 11% nitrogen and 48% P<sub>2</sub>O<sub>5</sub>.
*[[diammonium phosphate]] (DAP). (NH<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>HPO<sub>4</sub>. With 18% nitrogen and 46% P<sub>2</sub>O<sub>5</sub>

About 85% of MAP and DAP fertilizers are soluble in water.

;NPK fertilizers
{{Main|Labeling of fertilizer}}

{{multiple image
 | width = 200
 | footer = 
 | image1 = Compound fertiliser.jpg
 | alt1 = Compound fertilizer
 | caption1 = Compound fertilizer
 | image2 = Bulk-blend fertiliser.jpg
 | alt2 = Bulk-blend fertilizer
 | caption2 = Bulk-blend fertilizer
}}
NPK fertilizers are three-component fertilizers providing nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium. There exist two types of NPK fertilizers: compound and blends. Compound NPK fertilizers contain chemically bound ingredients, while blended NPK fertilizers are physical mixtures of single nutrient components.

[[NPK rating]] is a rating system describing the amount of nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium in a fertilizer. NPK ratings consist of three numbers separated by dashes (e.g., 10-10-10 or 16–4–8) describing the chemical content of fertilizers.<ref>{{cite web |title=Label requirements of specialty and other bagged fertilizers |url=https://www.michigan.gov/en/mdard/plant-pest/fertilizer/fertilizerinfo/label-requirements-of-specialty-and-other-bagged-fertilizers |publisher=[[Michigan Department of Agriculture and Rural Development]] |location=Lansing, Michigan |access-date=15 April 2026 }}</ref> The first number represents the percentage of nitrogen in the product; the second number, P<sub>2</sub>O<sub>5</sub>; the third, K<sub>2</sub>O. Fertilizers do not actually contain P<sub>2</sub>O<sub>5</sub> or K<sub>2</sub>O, but the system is a conventional shorthand for the amount of phosphorus (P) or potassium (K) in a fertilizer. A {{convert|50|lb|adj=on}} bag of fertilizer labeled 16-4-8 contains {{cvt|8|lb}} of nitrogen (16% of the 50 pounds), an amount of phosphorus equivalent to that in 2 pounds of P<sub>2</sub>O<sub>5</sub> (4% of 50 pounds), and 4 pounds of K<sub>2</sub>O (8% of 50 pounds). Most fertilizers are labeled according to this N-P-K convention, although Australian convention, following an N-P-K-S system, adds a fourth number for sulfur, and uses elemental values for all values including P and K.<ref>{{cite web |title=National code of practice for fertilizer description and labelling |date=October 2024 |url=https://fertilizer.org.au/Portals/0/Documents/COPs/National%20Code%20of%20Practice%20for%20Fertilizer%20Description%20and%20Labelling.pdf |website=Australian Government [[Department of Agriculture and Water Resources]] |access-date=15 April 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150228200433/http://www.fertilizer.org.au/files/pdf/regulation/National%20Code%20of%20Practice%20for%20Fertilizer%20Description%20%26%20Labelling%20March%2011%202011.pdf |archive-date=28 February 2015 |url-status=live }}</ref>

=== Micronutrients ===

[[Micronutrients]] are consumed in smaller quantities and are present in plant tissue on the order of [[Parts-per notation|parts-per-million]] (ppm), ranging from 0.15 to 400 ppm or less than 0.04% dry matter.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://aesl.ces.uga.edu/publications/plant/Nutrient.html |title=Nutrient content of plants |website=[[University of Georgia]], Agricultural & Environmental Services Laboratories |location=Athens, Georgia |access-date=15 April 2026 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Bryson |first1=Gretchen M. |last2=Mills |first2=Harry A. |year=2014 |title=Plant analysis handbook IV |publisher=Micro-Macro Publishing |location=Athens, Greece |isbn=978-1-878148-03-2 |url=https://storwukenticomedia.blob.core.windows.net/media/wfu/media/images/plant-analysis-handbook-iv_2.pdf |access-date=15 April 2026 }}</ref> These elements are often required as [[co-enzymes]] for [[enzyme]]s essential to the plant's [[metabolism]]. Because these elements enable [[Catalysis|catalyst]]s (enzymes), their impact far exceeds their [[concentration]]. Typical micronutrients are [[boron]], [[zinc]], [[molybdenum]], [[iron]], and [[manganese]].<ref name="Dittmar2009"/> These elements are provided as water-soluble salts. Iron presents special problems because it converts from soluble ([[ferrous]]) to insoluble bio-unavailable ([[ferric]]) compounds at moderate soil pH and phosphate concentrations.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Mitra |first1=Ashim K. |last2=Matthews |first2=Michael L. |date=February 1985 |title=Effects of pH and phosphate on the oxidation of iron in aqueous solution |journal=[[International Journal of Pharmaceutics]] |volume=23 |issue=2 |pages=185–93 |url=https://z-library.ec/book/lXWj6wqwyq |doi=10.1016/0378-5173(85)90008-0 |access-date=15 April 2026 }}{{Dead link|date=June 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref> For this reason, iron is often administered as a [[Chelation|chelate complex]], e.g., the [[Ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid|EDTA]] or [[EDDHA]] derivatives. The micronutrient needs depend on the plant and the environment. For example, [[sugar beet]]s appear to require [[boron]], and [[legume]]s require [[cobalt]],<ref name="Scherer2009"/> while environmental conditions such as heat or drought make boron less available for plants, causing [[Boron deficiency (plant disorder)|boron deficiency]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=García-Sánchez |first1=Francisco |last2=Simón-Grao |first2=Silvia |last3=Martínez-Nicolás |first3=Juan J. |last4=Alfosea-Simón |first4=Marina |last5=Liu |first5=Chunguang |last6=Chatzissavvidis |first6=Christos |last7=Pérez-Pérez |first7=Juan G. |last8=Cámara-Zapata |first8=José M. |date=5 October 2020 |title=Multiple stresses occurring with boron toxicity and deficiency in plants |journal=[[Journal of Hazardous Materials]] |volume=397 |article-number=122713 |doi=10.1016/j.jhazmat.2020.122713 |pmid=32402955 |bibcode=2020JHzM..39722713G |hdl=20.500.11939/6476 |url=https://www.academia.edu/99551270 |access-date=15 April 2026 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

== Production ==

The production of synthetic, or inorganic, fertilizers require prepared chemicals,<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/335233580 |title=Fertilizer production process |last=Rajani |first=Ashokkumar V. |year=2019 |doi=10.13140/RG.2.2.32689.53604 |access-date=15 April 2026 }}</ref> whereas organic fertilizers are derived from the [[biological process]]ing of plant and animal remains or [[excreta]] (e.g. [[urine]], [[feces]]).<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/378265096 |title=Advanced strategies in organic fertilizer production: comprehensive guide to sustainable practices and techniques |last=Hossain |first=Md. Mikail |access-date=15 April 2026 }}</ref>

=== Nitrogen fertilizers ===

[[File:Nitrogen fertilizer consumption, OWID.svg|thumb|left|Total nitrogenous fertilizer consumption per region, measured in tonnes of total nutrient per year.]]
Nitrogen fertilizers are made from [[ammonia]] (NH<sub>3</sub>) [[ammonia production|produced]] by the [[Haber process|Haber–Bosch process]].<ref name="Smil2004"/> In this [[energy-intensive]] process, [[natural gas]] (CH<sub>4</sub>) [[Hydrogen production|usually]] [[Steam reforming|supplies the hydrogen]], and the nitrogen (N<sub>2</sub>) is [[Nitrogen#Production|derived from the air]]. This ammonia is used as a [[feedstock]] for all other nitrogen fertilizers, such as [[ammonium nitrate|anhydrous ammonium nitrate]] (NH<sub>4</sub>NO<sub>3</sub>) and [[urea]] (CO(NH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>2</sub>).

Deposits of [[sodium nitrate]] (NaNO<sub>3</sub>) ([[Chilean saltpeter]]) are also found in the [[Atacama Desert]] in [[Chile]] and were one of the original (1830) nitrogen-rich fertilizers used.<ref>{{cite web |title=Supplemental technical report for sodium nitrate (crops) |url=https://www.ams.usda.gov/sites/default/files/media/Sodium%20Nitrate%20TR%202011.pdf |website=ams.usda.gov |access-date=15 April 2026 |archive-date=14 July 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140714165048/http://www.ams.usda.gov/AMSv1.0/getfile?dDocName=STELPRDC5090064 |url-status=live }}</ref> It is still mined for fertilizer use.<ref>{{cite web |title=Caliche ore |url=http://www.sqm.com/ACERCADESQM/RecursosNaturales/Caliche.aspx |website=sqm.com |access-date=6 July 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140714152959/http://www.sqm.com/ACERCADESQM/RecursosNaturales/Caliche.aspx |archive-date=14 July 2014 |url-status=dead }}</ref> Nitrates are also produced from ammonia by the [[Ostwald Process|Ostwald process]].

=== Phosphate fertilizers ===
{{owidslider
|start        = 2023
|list         = Template:OWID/Phosphate application per hectare of cropland#gallery
|location      = commons
|caption      =
|title        =
|language     =
|file         = [[File:Phosphate application per hectare of cropland, World, 2023 (cropped).svg|link=|thumb|upright=1.6|right|Phosphate application per hectare of cropland]]
|startingView = World
}}

[[File:Siilinjärvi Särkijärvi pit.jpg|thumb|left|An apatite mine for phosphates in [[Siilinjärvi carbonatite|Siilinjärvi]], Finland]]
Phosphate fertilizers are obtained by extraction from [[phosphate rock]], which contains two principal phosphorus-containing minerals, [[fluorapatite]] Ca<sub>5</sub>(PO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>3</sub>F (CFA) and [[hydroxyapatite]] Ca<sub>5</sub>(PO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>3</sub>OH. Billions of kg of phosphate rock are mined annually, but the size and quality of the remaining ore is decreasing.<ref name="Blackwell2019"/> These minerals are converted into water-soluble phosphate salts by treatment with [[acid]]s.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1016/j.gloenvcha.2008.10.009 |title=The story of phosphorus: global food security and food for thought |date=May 2009 |last1=Cordell |first1=Dana |last2=Drangert |first2=Jan-Olof |last3=White |first3=Stuart |journal=[[Global Environmental Change]] |volume=19 |issue=2 |pages=292–305 |bibcode=2009GEC....19..292C |s2cid=1450932 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/222545474 |access-date=15 April 2026 }}</ref> The large production of [[sulfuric acid]] is primarily motivated by this application.<ref>{{cite book |doi=10.1016/C2009-0-30414-6 |year=1997 |last1=Greenwood |first1=Norman Neill |last2=Earnshaw |first2=Alan |title=Chemistry of the elements |isbn=978-0-7506-3365-9 |edition=2nd |url=https://z-library.ec/book/7lXeMQ7KXg |access-date=17 April 2026 |publisher=[[Butterworth-Heinemann]] |location=Oxford, United Kingdom }}{{Dead link|date=June 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref> In the [[nitrophosphate process]] or Odda process (invented in 1927), [[phosphate rock]] with up to a 20% phosphorus (P) content is dissolved with [[nitric acid]] (HNO<sub>3</sub>) to produce a mixture of [[phosphoric acid]] (H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub>) and [[calcium nitrate]] (Ca(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>). This mixture can be combined with a potassium fertilizer to produce a ''compound fertilizer'' with the three macronutrients N, P and K in easily dissolved form.<ref>{{cite web |last=EFMA |title=Production of NPK fertilizers by the nitrophosphate route |url=http://productstewardship.eu/fileadmin/user_upload/user_upload_prodstew/documents/Booklet_nr_7_Production_of_NPK_Compound_Fertilizers_by_Nitrophosphate_route.pdf |website=fertilizerseurope.com |publisher=European Fertilizer Manufacturers' Association |location=Brussels, Belgium |access-date=15 April 2026 |year=2000 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140729004328/http://www.fertilizerseurope.com/fileadmin/user_upload/publications/tecnical_publications/guidence_techn_documentation/EFMABATNPKN.pdf |archive-date=29 July 2014 |url-status=live }}</ref>

=== Potassium fertilizers ===
{{owidslider
|start        = 2023
|list         = Template:OWID/Potash fertilizer application per hectare of cropland#gallery
|location      = commons
|caption      =
|title        =
|language     =
|file         = [[File:Potash fertilizer application per hectare of cropland, World, 2023 (cropped).svg|link=|thumb|upright=1.6|right|Potash fertilizer application per hectare of cropland]]
|startingView = World
}}

[[Potash]] is a mixture of potassium minerals used to make potassium (chemical symbol: K) fertilizers. Potash is soluble in water, so the main effort in producing this nutrient from the ore involves some purification steps, e.g., to remove [[sodium chloride]] (NaCl) (common [[salt]]).<ref>{{cite web |last=Myrenfors |first=Peter |date=August 1992 |title=Potassium chloride |url=https://www.inchem.org/documents/pims/pharm/potasscl.htm |access-date=15 April 2026 |website=www.inchem.org }}</ref> Sometimes potash is referred to as K<sub>2</sub>O, as a matter of convenience to those describing the potassium content. In fact, potash fertilizers are usually [[potassium chloride]], [[potassium sulfate]], [[potassium carbonate]], or [[potassium nitrate]].<ref name="Gowariker2009">{{cite book |doi=10.1002/9780470431771 |year=2009 |last1=Gowariker |first1=Vasant |last2=Krishnamurthy |first2=V. N. |last3=Gowariker |first3=Sudha |last4=Dhanorkar |first4=Manik |last5=Paranjape |first5=Kalyani |title=The fertilizer encyclopedia |isbn=978-0-470-43177-1 |url=https://z-library.ec/book/MjL5mlx2Lg |access-date=17 April 2026 }}{{Dead link|date=June 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref>

=== NPK fertilizers ===
{{main|NPK fertilizer}}

[[File:NPK 19-19-19 Fertilizer in 1 KG Commercial Packing (2).jpg|thumb|NPK 19-19-19 Fertilizer in 1&nbsp;kg Commercial Packing]]
[[File:NPK 19-19-19 Fertilizer (4).jpg|thumb|NPK 19-19-19 Fertilizer]]
There are three major routes for [[manufacturing]] NPK fertilizers (named for their main ingredients: nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), and potassium (K)):

* Bulk blending. The individual fertilizers are combined in the desired nutrient ratio. 
{| class="wikitable"
|+ Bulk blending. Ingredient kg/ton
|-

|}

* The wet process is based on chemical reactions between liquid raw materials [[phosphoric acid]], [[sulfuric acid]], [[ammonia]]) and solid raw materials (such as [[potassium chloride]]).
* The nitrophosphate process.
Step 1. Nitrophosphates are made by acidiculating [[phosphate rock]] with [[nitric acid]].

** Nitric acid + Phosphate rock → [[Phosphoric acid]] + [[Calcium sulfate|Calcium sulphate]] + [[hexafluorosilicic acid]].
** Ca<sub>5</sub>F(PO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>3</sub> + 10 HNO<sub>3</sub> →6 H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub> + 5 Ca(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> + HF      
** 6 HF + SiO<sub>2</sub> →H<sub>2</sub>SiF<sub>6</sub> + 2 H<sub>2</sub>O

Step 2. Removal of Calcium Nitrate. It is important to remove the [[calcium nitrate]] because calcium nitrate is extremely [[Hygroscopy|hygroscopic]].

** Method 1.(Odda process) Calcium nitrate crystals are removed by centrifugation. 
** Method 2. Sulfonitric Process Ca(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + 2NH<sub>3</sub> → CaSO<sub>4</sub> + 2NH<sub>4</sub>NO<sub>3</sub>
** Method 3.Phosphonitric Process Ca(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub> + 2NH<sub>3</sub> → CaHPO<sub>4</sub> + 2NH<sub>4</sub>NO<sub>3</sub>
** Method 4.Carbonitric Process Ca(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> + CO<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O + 2NH<sub>3</sub> → CaCO<sub>3</sub> + 2NH<sub>4</sub>NO<sub>3</sub>

=== Organic fertilizers ===
{{Main|Organic fertilizer}}

[[File:HomeComposting Roubaix Fr59.JPG|thumb|Compost bin for small-scale production of organic fertilizer]]
[[File:Krechty kompostarna.jpg|thumb|A large commercial compost operation]]
''Organic fertilizers'' can describe those fertilizers with a biological origin, i.e. derived from living or formerly living materials. ''Organic fertilizers'' can also describe commercially available and frequently packaged products that strive to follow the expectations and restrictions adopted by [[organic farming]] and [[environmentally friendly]] gardening, i.e. related systems of food and plant production that significantly limit or strictly avoid the use of synthetic fertilizers and [[pesticide]]s. The ''organic fertilizer products'' typically contain both some organic materials as well as acceptable additives such as nutritive rock powders, ground [[seashell]]s ([[crab]], [[oyster]], etc.), other prepared products such as seaweed meal or [[kelp]], and cultivated [[microorganism]]s and derivatives.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Bergstrand |first=Karl-Johan |date=15 March 2022 |title=Organic fertilizers in greenhouse production systems: a review |journal=Scientia Horticulturae |volume=295 |article-number=110855 |doi=10.1016/j.scienta.2021.110855 |bibcode=2022ScHor.29510855B |url=https://pub.epsilon.slu.se/27475/1/bergstrand-k-j-et-al-220329.pdf |access-date=15 April 2026 }}</ref>

Fertilizers of an organic origin (the first definition) include [[manure|animal wastes]], plant wastes from agriculture, [[Seaweed fertilizer|seaweed]], [[compost]], and treated [[sewage sludge]] ([[biosolid]]s). Beyond manures, animal sources can include products from [[animal slaughter]]s: [[bloodmeal]], [[bone meal]], [[feather meal]], [[Hide (skin)|hides]], [[hoof]]s, and [[Horn (anatomy)|horns]] all are typical components.<ref name="Dittmar2009"/> Organically derived materials available to industry such as [[sewage sludge]] may not be acceptable components of [[organic farming]] and [[organic horticulture|gardening]], because of factors ranging from residual contaminants<ref>{{cite journal |last=Smith |first=Stephen R. |date=13 October 2009 |title=Organic contaminants in sewage sludge (biosolids) and their significance for agricultural recycling |journal=[[Philosophical Transactions A]] |volume=367 |issue=1904 |pages=4005–41 |doi=10.1098/rsta.2009.0154 |pmid=19736232 |bibcode=2009RSPTA.367.4005S |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/26795123 |access-date=15 April 2026 }}</ref> to public perception.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.3389/fsufs.2021.647780 |title=Resources and risks: perceptions on the application of sewage sludge on agricultural land in Sweden, a case study |date=19 April 2021 |last1=Ekane |first1=Nelson |last2=Barquet |first2=Karina |last3=Rosemarin |first3=Arno |journal=[[Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems]] |volume=5 |article-number=647780 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2021FrSFS...547780E }}</ref> No matter the definition nor composition, most of these products contain less-concentrated nutrients, and the nutrients are not as easily quantified.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1080/03650340.2014.978763 |title=Chemical characterization of commercial organic fertilizers |date=14 November 2014 |last1=Möller |first1=Kurt |last2=Schultheiß |first2=Ute |journal=Archives of Agronomy and Soil Science |volume=61 |issue=7 |pages=989–1012 |url=https://z-library.ec/book/lXWaa1Ax9q |access-date=15 April 2026 }}{{Dead link|date=June 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref> They can offer soil-building advantages as well as be appealing to those who are trying to farm or garden more naturally.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Haynes |first1=Richard J. |last2=Naidu |first2=Ravi |date=June 1998 |title=Influence of lime, fertilizer and manure applications on soil organic matter content and soil physical conditions: a review |journal=Nutrient Cycling in Agroecosystems |volume=51 |issue=2 |pages=123–37 |doi=10.1023/A:1009738307837 |bibcode=1998NCyAg..51..123H |s2cid=20113235 |url=https://www.academia.edu/12537819 |access-date=15 April 2026 }}</ref>

In terms of volume, [[peat]] is the most widely used packaged organic [[soil amendment]]. It is an immature form of [[coal]] which improves [[soil aeration]] and [[soil moisture|moisture]] and thus soil biological activity but confers no direct [[nutritional value]] to the plants. It is therefore not a fertilizer as defined in the beginning of the article, but rather an [[Soil conditioner|amendment]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Vepsäläinen |first1=Milja |last2=Erkomaa |first2=Kirsti |last3=Kukkonen |first3=Sanna |last4=Vestberg |first4=Mauritz |last5=Wallenius |first5=Kaisa |last6=Niemi |first6=R. Maarit |date=July 2004 |title=The impact of crop plant cultivation and peat amendment on soil microbial activity and structure |journal=[[Plant and Soil]] |volume=264 |issue=1–2 |pages=273–86 |doi=10.1023/B:PLSO.0000047763.46795.cb |bibcode=2004PlSoi.264..273V |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/225239908 |access-date=15 April 2026 }}</ref> However, peat is avoided by many gardeners because its extraction destroys habitats, releases carbon dioxide, and increases flood risk.<ref>{{cite web |title=Peat-free gardening |url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/advice/peat |publisher=Royal Horticultural Society |access-date=16 September 2026}}</ref> [[Coir]] (derived from [[coconut]] [[husk]]s), [[Bark (botany)|bark]], and [[sawdust]] are mainly applied as [[mulch]] and protects the soil from [[desiccation]]<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Zhang |first1=Jiayi |last2=Fu |first2=Guohua |last3=Jin |first3=Zhiyang |last4=Chi |first4=Lihang |last5=Xu |first5=Guocheng |last6=Yue |first6=Daran |date=4 December 2021 |title=Optimization of organic mulches thickness improves soil moisture retention under controlled conditions |journal=Phyton |volume=91 |issue=4 |pages=841–57 |doi=10.32604/phyton.2022.017938 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/380035723 |access-date=15 April 2026 |doi-access=free }}</ref> while preventing the development of [[weed]]s<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Khamare |first1=Yuvraj |last2=Marble |first2=S. Christopher |date=12 December 2023 |title=Mulching as a weed management tool in container plant production: review |journal=[[Frontiers in Agronomy]] |volume=5 |article-number=1235196 |doi=10.3389/fagro.2023.1235196 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2023FrAgr...535196K }}</ref> and improving soil structure,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Mulumba |first1=Lukman Nagaya |last2=Lal |first2=Rattan |date=January 2008 |title=Mulching effects on selected soil physical properties |journal=Soil and Tillage Research |volume=98 |issue=1 |pages=106–11 |doi=10.1016/j.still.2007.10.011 |bibcode=2008STilR..98..106M |url=https://www.academia.edu/59816076 |access-date=15 April 2026 }}</ref> but do not confer any [[nutritional value]] to the soil. Some organic additives can even have a reverse effect on nutrients. Fresh [[sawdust]] can consume soil nutrients as it breaks down and is colonized by [[Wood-decay fungus|wood-decay fungi]], causing [[nitrogen deficiency]] (nitrogen drawdown) in the absence of nutrient addition.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Sharman |first1=K. V. |last2=Whitehouse |first2=Michael |date=April 1993 |title=Nitrogen drawdown index as a predictor of nitrogen requirements for ''Nephrolepis'' in sawdust media |journal=Scientia Horticulturae |volume=54 |issue=1 |pages=23–33 |doi=10.1016/0304-4238(93)90080-A |bibcode=1993ScHor..54...23S |url=https://z-library.ec/book/jL5KMJK2yg |access-date=15 April 2026 }}{{Dead link|date=June 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref> However, this property can be used to capture excess mineral nitrogen.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Clocchiatti |first1=Anna |last2=Hannula |first2=S. Emilia |last3=Hundscheid |first3=Maria P. J. |last4=Gunnewiek |first4=
Paulien J.A. klein |last5=De Boer |first5=Wietse |date=January 2023 |title=Utilizing woody materials for fungal-based management of soil nitrogen pools |journal=Applied Soil Ecology |volume=181 |article-number=104663 |doi=10.1016/j.apsoil.2022.104663 |bibcode=2023AppSE.18104663C |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/363650466 |access-date=15 April 2026 |hdl=1887/3631601 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> These same organic soil texturizers (as well as compost, etc.) may increase the availability of nutrients through improved [[cation-exchange capacity]],<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Simsek |first1=Ugur |last2=Erdel |first2=Erhan |last3=Barik |first3=Kenan |date=December 2017 |title=Effect of mulching on soil moisture and some soil characteristics |journal=Fresenius Environmental Bulletin |volume=26 |issue=12 |pages=7437–43 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/322661363 |access-date=15 April 2026 }}</ref> or through increased growth of microorganisms that in turn increase availability of certain plant nutrients.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Tu |first1=Cong |last2=Ristaino |first2=Jean B. |last3=Hu |first3=Shuijin |date=February 2006 |title=Soil microbial biomass and activity in organic tomato farming systems: effects of organic inputs and straw mulching |journal=[[Soil Biology and Biochemistry]] |volume=38 |issue=2 |pages=247–55 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/223742815 |doi=10.1016/j.soilbio.2005.05.002 |bibcode=2006SBiBi..38..247T |access-date=15 April 2026 }}</ref> True organic fertilizers such as [[compost]]s and [[manure]]s may be distributed locally without going into industry production, making actual consumption more difficult to quantify.
