[[File:Inorganic fertilizer use per cropland area by nutrient and region.svg|thumb|Inorganic fertilizer use per cropland area by nutrient and region]]
[[File:Variation in the use of fertilizers in cropland, 1964–2023.svg|thumb|Variation in the use of fertilizers in cropland by continent, 1964–2023.]]
China has become the largest producer and consumer of nitrogen fertilizers<ref>{{cite book |last=Smil |first=Vaclav |title=Making the modern world: materials and dematerialization |publisher=[[John Wiley & Sons]] |location=Hoboken, New Jersey |date=December 2013 |isbn=978-1-119-94253-5 |url=https://z-library.ec/book/jPXzmQAAy6 |access-date=17 April 2026 }}{{Dead link|date=June 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref> while Africa has little reliance on nitrogen fertilizers.<ref>{{cite book |last=Smil |first=Vaclav |title=Harvesting the biosphere: what we have taken from Nature |publisher=[[MIT Press]] |location=Cambridge, Massachusetts |year=2012 |isbn=978-0-262-01856-2 |doi=10.7551/mitpress/8990.001.0001 |url=https://z-library.ec/book/D9PJBZZPXm |access-date=15 April 2026 }}{{Dead link|date=June 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref> Agricultural and chemical minerals are very important in industrial use of fertilizers, which is valued at approximately $200 billion.<ref name="Kesler2015">{{cite book |last1=Kesler |first1=Stephen E. |last2=Simon |first2=Adam C. |title=Mineral resources, economics and the environment |edition=2nd |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]] |location=Cambridge, United Kingdom |year=2015 |isbn=978-1-107-07491-0 |url=https://archive.org/details/mineralresources0000kesl/mode/2up |access-date=15 April 2026 }}</ref> Nitrogen has a significant impact in the global mineral use, followed by potash and phosphate. The production of nitrogen has drastically increased since the 1960s. Phosphate and potash have increased in price since the 1960s, which is larger than the consumer price index.<ref name="Kesler2015"/> Potash is produced in [[Canada]], [[Russia]] and [[Belarus]], together making up over half of the world production.<ref name="Kesler2015"/> Potash production in Canada rose in 2017 and 2018 by 18.6%.<ref>{{cite news |title=Industry stats – Fertilizer Canada |language=en-US |work=Fertilizer Canada |url=https://fertilizercanada.ca/about-fertilizer-canada/resources/industry-resources/industry-stats/ |access-date=28 March 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180404202635/https://fertilizercanada.ca/about-fertilizer-canada/resources/industry-resources/industry-stats/ |archive-date=4 April 2018 |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Canadian fertilizer production, by product type and fertilizer year, cumulative data (x 1,000) |date=3 March 2026 |website=[[Statistics Canada]] |url=https://www150.statcan.gc.ca/t1/tbl1/en/tv.action?pid=3210003701 |access-date=15 April 2026 }}</ref> Conservative estimates report 30 to 50% of crop yields are attributed to natural or synthetic commercial fertilizers.<ref name="Gowariker2009"/><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Stewart |first1=W. M. |last2=Dibb |first2=David W. |last3=Johnston |first3=Adrian E. |last4=Smyth |first4=T. J. |date=January 2005 |title=The contribution of commercial fertilizer nutrients to food production |journal=[[Agronomy Journal]] |volume=97 |issue=1 |pages=1–6 |doi=10.2134/agronj2005.0001 |bibcode=2005AgrJ...97....1S |url=https://scispace.com/pdf/the-contribution-of-commercial-fertilizer-nutrients-to-food-1s8rr2meq2.pdf |access-date=15 April 2026 |archive-date=21 May 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250521161620/https://scispace.com/pdf/the-contribution-of-commercial-fertilizer-nutrients-to-food-1s8rr2meq2.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref> Fertilizer consumption has surpassed the amount of farmland in the United States.<ref name="Kesler2015"/>

Data on the fertilizer consumption per hectare [[arable land]] in 2012 are published by [[The World Bank]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Fertilizer consumption (kilograms per hectare of arable land) |url=https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/AG.CON.FERT.ZS |access-date=15 April 2026 }}</ref> The diagram below shows fertilizer consumption by the [[European Union]] (EU) countries as kilograms per hectare (pounds per acre). The total consumption of fertilizer in the EU reached a peak of 11.6 million tons in 2017 but decreased steadily since that time, down to 9.3 million tons in 2023<ref>{{cite web |title=Agri-environmental indicator: mineral fertiliser consumption |url=https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Agri-environmental_indicator_-_mineral_fertiliser_consumption |access-date=15 April 2026 |website=[[Eurostat]] }}</ref> for 157 million hectares arable land area in 2020, 1.5 million hectares less than in 2010.<ref>{{cite web |title=Agri-environmental indicator: cropping patterns |url=https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Agri-environmental_indicator_-_cropping_patterns |access-date=15 April 2026 |website=[[Eurostat]] }}</ref> This figure equates to 70&nbsp;kg of fertilizers consumed per ha arable land on average by the EU countries in 2020.

Total agricultural use of inorganic fertilizers, expressed as the sum of the three nutrients nitrogen (N), phosphorus (expressed as P2 O5 ) and potassium (expressed as K2 O), was 190 million tonnes in 2023, up 1% compared with 2022. 112 million tonnes of nitrogen (58% of the total), 41 million tonnes of phosphorus (21% ) and 38 million tonnes of potassium (20% ). Overall fertilizer use in 2023 was 55 million tonnes (41%) higher than in 2000 (38% higher for nitrogen, 26% higher for phosphorus and 73% higher for potassium). Asia represented 56% of world total agricultural use of inorganic fertilizers in 2023, followed by the Americas (27% ), Europe (11%), Africa (4%) and Oceania (2%).<ref name="FAO2025" />

== Application ==
[[File:Farm fertilizer.jpg|thumb|Fertilizer [[sprayer]]]]
[[File:Drone crop fertilizer.jpg|thumb|[[Agricultural drone|Drone crop fertilizer]]]]
[[File:7252 Hand top-dressing of super phosphate on Banks Peninsula.jpg|thumb|Applying [[superphosphate]] fertilizer by hand, New Zealand, 1938]]
Fertilizers are commonly used for growing all crops, with application rates depending on [[soil fertility]], usually as measured by a [[soil test]] and according to the particular crop. [[Legume]]s, for example, [[Nitrogen fixation|fix nitrogen]] from the atmosphere and generally do not require nitrogen fertilizer, hence their promising use for ensuring agriculture [[sustainability]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Stagnari |first1=Fabio |last2=Maggio |first2=Albino |last3=Galieni |first3=Angelica |last4=Pisante |first4=Michele |date=2 February 2017 |title=Multiple benefits of legumes for agriculture sustainability: an overview |journal=Chemical and Biological Technologies in Agriculture |volume=4 |issue=1 |article-number=2 |doi=10.1186/s40538-016-0085-1 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2017CBTA....4....2S }}</ref>

=== Timing and amount of application ===

The timing of application of fertilizers (here only mineral fertilizers will be considered) is a function of crop requirements, [[weather]] condition and [[Market economy|market]] opportunities. It varies in nature and amount according to the type of agriculture (e.g. [[intensive farming]] versus [[conservation agriculture]], [[grassland]] versus [[arable land]]), and the presence or absence of signs of [[nutrient deficiencies]]. Timing fertilization with peak nutrient uptake demand is essential for optimizing both yield and quality. In general, nutrient uptake rates are highest from early to midgrowing season, which is why fertilization near the time of seeding is generally very effective. With fall-planted grains (e.g. [[winter wheat]]), fall N fertilization followed by spring [[topdressing]] is likely the best combination of fertilization practices to optimize yield.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Jones |first1=Clain |last2=Jacobsen |first2=Jeff |date=May 2009 |title=Fertilizer placement and timing |website=[[Montana State University]] |url=https://wwwtest.certifiedcropadviser.org/files/certifications/certified/education/self-study/exam-pdfs/41.pdf |access-date=15 April 2026 }}{{Dead link|date=August 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref> The application of a soluble mineral fertilizer (e.g. [[ammonium nitrate]]) is avoided during [[Heavy rain (meteorology)|heavy rain]]fall because most of it would be lost for the crop<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Guo |first1=Jiangying |last2=Chen |first2=Jiwei |date=29 November 2022 |title=The impact of heavy rainfall variability on fertilizer application rates: evidence from maize farmers in China |journal=[[International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health]] |volume=19 |issue=23 |article-number=15906 |doi=10.3390/ijerph192315906 |doi-access=free |pmid=36497975 |pmc=9740578 }}</ref> and would rapidly pollute the [[aquifer]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Singh |first1=Bijay |last2=Craswell |first2=Eric |date=31 March 2021 |title=Fertilizers and nitrate pollution of surface and ground water: an increasingly pervasive global problem |journal=[[SN Applied Sciences]] |volume=3 |issue=4 |article-number=518 |doi=10.1007/s42452-021-04521-8 |doi-access=free |hdl=1885/267455 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> In [[conservation agriculture]] (including [[no-till farming]], [[permaculture]]) as well as other non-organic alternatives to [[intensive farming]] (e.g. [[smallholding]] agriculture) the application of mineral fertilizers is reduced to the strict requirements of the cultivated plants and sometimes is quite unnecessary.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Dumanski |first1=Julian |last2=Peiretti |first2=Roberto |last3=Benites |first3=José R. |last4=McGarry |first4=Diane |last5=Pieri |first5=Christian |date=31 August 2006 |title=The paradigm of conservation agriculture |website=World Association of Soil and Water Conservation (WASWAC) |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/284061910 |access-date=15 April 2026 }}</ref>

After harvest of a main crop (e.g. [[wheat]], [[maize]], [[potato]]es) a [[catch crop]] can be sown, using plant species with a rapid growth rate and high demand of nitrogen (e.g. [[white mustard]]).<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Żuk-Gołaszewska |first1=Krystyna |last2=Wanic |first2=Maria |last3=Orzech |first3=Krzysztof |date=29 January 2019 |title=The role of catch crops in field plant production: a review |journal=Journal of Elementology |volume=24 |issue=2 |pages=575–87 |doi=10.5601/jelem.2018.23.3.1662 |doi-access=free }}</ref> This allows excess nitrogen, in particular the very mobile [[nitrate]] anion, to be taken up and transformed in plant [[protein]]s<ref>{{cite journal |last=Tischner |first=Rudolf |date=October 2000 |title=Nitrate uptake and reduction in higher and lower plants |journal=[[Plant, Cell & Environment]] |volume=23 |issue=10 |pages=1005–24 |doi=10.1046/j.1365-3040.2000.00595.x |doi-access=free |bibcode=2000PCEnv..23.1005T }}</ref> before contaminating the [[groundwater]], and the associated [[Geochemistry|geochemical]] processes, which would rapidly occur in the absence of plant cover.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Menció |first1=Anna |last2=Mas-Pla |first2=Josep |last3=Otero |first3=Neus |last4=Regàs |first4=Oriol |last5=Boy-Roura |first5=Mercè |last6=Puig |first6=Roger |last7=Bach |first7=Joan |last8=Domènech |first8=Cristina |last9=Zamorano |first9=Manel |last10=Brusi |first10=David |last11=Folch |first11=Albert |date=1 January 2016 |title=Nitrate pollution of groundwater: all right…, but nothing else? |journal=[[Science of the Total Environment]] |volume=539 |pages=241–51 |doi=10.1016/j.scitotenv.2015.08.151 |pmid=26363397 |bibcode=2016ScTEn.539..241M |hdl=2445/127799 |url=https://www.academia.edu/77866252 |access-date=15 April 2026 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> The catch crop is further buried, allowing its transformation in [[humus]] in which nitrogen is fixed according to various stable [[chemical bond]]s.<ref>{{cite book |doi=10.2136/1990.humicsubstances.c5 |chapter=Nitrogen in humic substances as related to soil fertility |date=1 January 1990 |last1=Stevenson |first1=Frank J. |last2=He |first2=Xin-Tao |editor-last1=MacCarthy |editor-first1=Patrick |editor-last2=Clapp |editor-first2=C. Edward |editor-last3=Malcolm |editor-first3=Ronald L. |editor-last4=Bloom |editor-first4=Paul R. |title=Humic substances in soil and crop sciences: selected readings |isbn=978-0-89118-104-0 |pages=91–109 |chapter-url=https://z-library.ec/book/w9J1Rq8aLD |access-date=15 April 2026 }}{{Dead link|date=June 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref>

=== Liquid vs solid ===

Fertilizers are applied to crops both as solids and as liquid. About 90% of fertilizers are applied as solids. The most widely used solid inorganic fertilizers are [[urea]], [[diammonium phosphate]] and [[potassium chloride]].<ref>{{cite web |title=About fertilizers: nutrients for crops and humans |url=https://www.fertilizer.org/En/Knowledge_Resources/About_Fertilizers/About_Fertilizers_Home_Page.aspx? |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140330225212/http://www.fertilizer.org/En/Knowledge_Resources/About_Fertilizers/About_Fertilizers_Home_Page.aspx |archive-date=30 March 2014 |website=fertilizer.org |publisher=[[International Fertilizer Association]] |access-date=19 December 2017 |url-status=dead }}</ref> Solid fertilizer is typically granulated or powdered. Often solids are available as [[prill]]s, a solid globule. Liquid fertilizers comprise aqueous solutions of [[Ammonia solution|ammonia]], aqueous solutions of [[ammonium nitrate]] or [[urea]]. These concentrated products may be diluted with water to form a concentrated liquid fertilizer (e.g., [[UAN]]). Advantages of liquid fertilizer are its more rapid effect and easier coverage.<ref name="Dittmar2009"/> The addition of fertilizer to irrigation water is called ''[[fertigation]]''.<ref name="Gowariker2009"/> Granulated fertilizers are more economical to ship and store, not to mention easier to apply.<ref>{{cite book |doi=10.1002/14356007.n10_n03.pub2 |chapter=Fertilizers, 4. Granulation |date=15 July 2009 |last1=Kiiski |first1=Harri |last2=Dittmar |first2=Heinrich |title=[[Ullmann's Encyclopedia of Industrial Chemistry]] |volume=14 |isbn=978-3-527-30673-2 |pages=1–32 |chapter-url=https://z-library.ec/book/B9EwgOGVX5 |access-date=17 April 2026 }}{{Dead link|date=June 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |date=19 August 2025 |title=Fertilizer granulation plant: a practical guide to high-quality NPK, DAP & custom blends |url=https://ceylanport.com/fertilizer-granulation-plant/ |website=Ceylan Machine & Process |access-date=15 April 2026 }}</ref>

=== Slow- and controlled-release fertilizers ===
{{Main|Controlled-release fertiliser}}

A '''[[controlled-release fertiliser]]''' ('''CRF''') is a [[granulated]] [[fertiliser]] that releases [[nutrient]]s gradually into the [[soil]] (i.e., with a [[controlled release]] period).<ref>{{cite book |title=Soil and environmental science dictionary |last1=Gregorich |first1=Edward G. |last2=Turchenek |first2=Larry W. |last3=Carter |first3=Michael R. |last4=Angers |first4=Denis A. |year=2001 |publisher=[[CRC Press]] |location=Boca Raton, Florida |isbn=978-0-8493-3115-2 |page=132 |url=https://z-library.ec/book/E4yNnj2kyw |lccn=2001025292 |access-date=15 April 2026 }}{{Dead link|date=June 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref> Controlled-release fertilizer is also known as ''controlled-availability fertilizer'', ''delayed-release fertilizer'', ''metered-release fertilizer'', or ''slow-acting fertilizer''. Usually slow- and controlled-release fertilizers refer to nitrogen-based fertilizers, e.g. [[ureaform]], needing degradation by a wide spectrum of [[soil organisms]] before nitrogen could be liberated as nitrate.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Alexander |first1=Alvin |last2=Helm |first2=Hans-Ulrich |year=1990 |title=Ureaform as a slow release fertilizer: a review |journal=Zeitschrift für Pflanzenernährung und Bodenkunde |volume=153 |issue=4 |pages=249–55 |doi=10.1002/jpln.19901530410 |bibcode=1990ZPflD.153..249A |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/229466112 |access-date=15 April 2026 }}</ref> Slow-release fertilizers (SRF) and controlled-release fertilizers (CRF) offer various benefits over conventional ones, ensuring [[sustainability]] in fertilizing practice.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Priya |first1=E. |last2=Sarkar |first2=Sudipta |last3=Maji |first3=Pradip K. |date=August 2024 |title=A review on slow-release fertilizer: nutrient release mechanism and agricultural sustainability |journal=Journal of Environmental Chemical Engineering |volume=12 |issue=4 |article-number=113211 |doi=10.1016/j.jece.2024.113211 |url=https://archive.org/details/priya-et-al.-2024 |access-date=15 April 2026 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Vejan |first1=Pravin |last2=Khadiran |first2=Tumirah |last3=Abdullah |first3=Rozaslin |last4=Ahmad |first4=Noraini |date=10 November 2021 |title=Controlled release fertilizer: a review on developments, applications and potential in agriculture |journal=[[Journal of Controlled Release]] |volume=339 |pages=321–34 |doi=10.1016/j.jconrel.2021.10.003 |pmid=34626724 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/355197772 |access-date=15 April 2026 }}</ref>

=== Foliar application ===
{{Main|Foliar feeding}}

[[Foliar feeding|Foliar fertilizers]] are applied directly to leaves. They can reduce the total amounts of fertilizer applied and achieve high fertilizer efficiency.<ref name="Niu2020">{{cite journal |last1=Niu |first1=Junhao |last2=Liu |first2=Chang |last3=Huang |first3=Mingli |last4=Liu |first4=Kezhong |last5=Yan |first5=Dongyun |date=9 October 2020 |title=Effects of foliar fertilization: a review of current status and future perspectives |journal=Journal of Soil Science and Plant Nutrition |volume=21 |issue=1 |pages=104–118 |doi=10.1007/s42729-020-00346-3 |url=https://z-library.ec/book/zXOzmVBRyb |access-date=17 April 2026 }}{{Dead link|date=June 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref> This method is almost invariably used to apply water-soluble straight nitrogen fertilizers and used especially for high-value crops such as fruits. Urea is the most common foliar fertilizer.<ref name="Dittmar2009"/> However, [[chelation]] of the foliar-applied nutrient is recommended for improving absorption and migration of the targeted nutrient and thereby avoiding loss to the soil and the groundwater.<ref name="Niu2020"/>

=== Chemicals that affect nitrogen uptake ===
[[File:N-butylthiophosphoryltriamide.svg|thumb|left|N-Butylthiophosphoryltriamide, an enhanced efficiency fertilizer]]
Various chemicals are used to enhance the efficiency of nitrogen-based fertilizers. In this way farmers can limit the [[nitrogen pollution|polluting effects of nitrogen run-off]]. [[Nitrification]] inhibitors (also known as nitrogen stabilizers) suppress the conversion of [[ammonia]] into [[nitrate]], an anion that is more prone to leaching. 1-Carbamoyl-3-methylpyrazole (CMP), [[dicyandiamide]], [[nitrapyrin]] (2-chloro-6-trichloromethylpyridine) and 3,4-dimethylpyrazole phosphate (DMPP) are popular.<ref name="YangFang2016">{{cite journal |last1=Yang |first1=Ming |last2=Fang |first2=Yunting |last3=Sun |first3=Di |last4=Shi |first4=Yuanliang |title=Efficiency of two nitrification inhibitors (dicyandiamide and 3, 4-dimethypyrazole phosphate) on soil nitrogen transformations and plant productivity: a meta-analysis |journal=[[Scientific Reports]] |volume=6 |issue=1 |article-number=22075 |date=23 February 2016 |issn=2045-2322 |doi=10.1038/srep22075 |pmid=26902689 |bibcode=2016NatSR...622075Y |pmc=4763264 |doi-access=free }}</ref> [[Urease inhibitor]]s are used to slow the hydrolytic conversion of urea into ammonia catalyzed by [[urease]]s, ammonia being prone to evaporation<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Hayashi |first1=Kentaro |last2=Nishimura |first2=Seiichi |last3=Yagi |first3=Kazuyuki |title=Ammonia volatilization from a paddy field following applications of urea: rice plants are both an absorber and an emitter for atmospheric ammonia |journal=[[Science of the Total Environment]] |volume=390 |issue=2–3 |pages=485–94 |date=15 February 2008 |doi=10.1016/j.scitotenv.2007.10.037 |pmid=18054067 |bibcode=2008ScTEn.390..485H |url=https://z-library.ec/book/PXznnwJYX6 |access-date=17 April 2026 }}{{Dead link|date=June 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref> as well as nitrification.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Wendeborn |first=Sebastian |title=The chemistry, biology, and modulation of ammonium nitrification in soil |journal=[[Angewandte Chemie]] |volume=59 |issue=6 |pages=2182–202 |date=3 February 2020 |doi=10.1002/anie.201903014 |pmid=31116902 |bibcode=2020ACIE...59.2182W |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/333299514 |access-date=15 April 2026 }}</ref> A popular inhibitor of ureases is ''N''-(''n''-butyl)thiophosphoric triamide ([[NBPT]]).

=== Overfertilization ===
[[File:Fertilizer-Burn.jpg|upright|thumb|Fertilizer burn]]
Careful use of fertilization technologies is important because excess nutrients can be detrimental to the cultivated plant.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://hubcap.clemson.edu/~blpprt/nitrofer.html |title=Nitrogen fertilization |publisher=Hubcap.clemson.edu |access-date=17 June 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120629000817/http://hubcap.clemson.edu/~blpprt/nitrofer.html |archive-date=29 June 2012 |url-status=dead }}</ref> [[Fertilizer burn]] can occur when too much fertilizer is applied, resulting in damage or even death of the plant. Fertilizers vary in their tendency to burn roughly in accordance with their [[Fertilizer burn#Salt index and effects|salt index]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Garrett |first=Howard |title=Organic lawn care: growing grass the natural way |year=2014 |publisher=[[University of Texas Press]] |location=Austin, Texas |isbn=978-0-292-72849-3 |pages=55–6 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=UEHTAwAAQBAJ&pg=PA55 |access-date=16 April 2026 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last=Laboski |first=Carrie |url=https://extension.soils.wisc.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/68/2016/07/Laboski_salt2008ppt.pdf |title=Understanding salt index of fertilizers |access-date=22 July 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130528143421/http://www.soils.wisc.edu/extension/wcmc/2008/ppt/Laboski1.pdf |archive-date=28 May 2013 |url-status=live }}</ref>

[[soil loss]].<ref>{{cite journal |last=Montgomery |first=David R. |date=14 August 2007 |title=Soil erosion and agricultural sustainability |journal=[[Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America]] |language=en |volume=104 |issue=33 |pages=13268–72 |doi=10.1073/pnas.0611508104 |doi-access=free |pmid=17686990 |pmc=1948917 |bibcode=2007PNAS..10413268M }}</ref>

In order to mitigate [[environmental concerns|environmental]] and [[food security]] concerns, the [[international community]] has included [[food system]]s in [[Sustainable Development Goal 2]] which focuses on creating a [[Effects of climate change on agriculture|climate-friendly]] and [[sustainable food system|sustainable food production system]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Resolution adopted by the General Assembly on 6 July 2017 |url=https://ggim.un.org/documents/a_res_71_313.pdf |date=10 July 2017 |website=[[United Nations]] |access-date=16 April 2026 }}</ref> Most [[policy]] and regulatory approaches to address these issues focus on pivoting [[agricultural practice]]s towards [[Sustainable agriculture|sustainable]] or [[Regenerative agriculture|regenerative agricultural]] practices: these use less [[synthetic fertilizer]]s (for example [[sustainable agriculture]]), better [[soil management]] (for example [[No-till farming|no-till agriculture]]) and more [[organic fertilizer]]s (for example [[organic farming]], [[conservation agriculture]], [[biodynamic agriculture]]).

[[File:GypStack.JPG|thumb|Large pile of [[phosphogypsum]] waste near [[Fort Meade, Florida]]]]
For each ton of [[phosphoric acid]] produced by the processing of [[phosphate rock]], five tons of [[waste]] are generated. This waste takes the form of impure, useless, radioactive solid called [[phosphogypsum]]. Estimates range from 100,000,000 and 280,000,000 tons of phosphogypsum waste produced annually worldwide.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1016/j.jenvman.2009.03.007 |pmid=19406560 |title=Environmental impact and management of phosphogypsum |journal=[[Journal of Environmental Management]] |volume=90 |issue=8 |pages=2377–86 |date=June 2009 |last1=Tayibi |first1= Hanan |last2=Choura |first2=Mohamed |last3=López |first3=Félix A. |last4=Alguacil |first4=Francisco J. |last5=López-Delgado |first5=Aurora |bibcode=2009JEnvM..90.2377T |hdl=10261/45241 |s2cid=24111765 |url=https://www.academia.edu/6272018 |access-date=16 April 2026 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

=== Water ===
{{Main|Eutrophication}}

[[File:Aquatic Dead Zones.jpg|thumb|Red circles show the location and size of many [[Dead zone (ecology)|dead zones]]]]
Phosphorus and nitrogen fertilizers can affect soil, surface water, and [[groundwater]]<ref name="Kesler2015"/> due to the dispersion of minerals into [[waterway]]s under high rainfall,<ref name="Fletcher2021">{{cite journal |last1=Fletcher |first1=Daniel Marcus McKay |last2=Ruiz |first2=Siul A. |last3=Dias |first3=Tiago |last4=Chadwick |first4=Dave R. |last5=Jones |first5=Davey L. |last6=Roose |first6=Tiina |date=20 February 2021 |title=Precipitation-optimised targeting of nitrogen fertilisers in a model maize cropping system |url=https://archive.org/details/fletcher-et-al.-2021 |journal=[[Science of the Total Environment]] |language=en |volume=756 |article-number=144051 |doi=10.1016/j.scitotenv.2020.144051 |pmid=33280884 |bibcode=2021ScTEn.75644051M |s2cid=227522409 |issn=0048-9697 |access-date=16 April 2026 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Watson |first1=Catherine J. |last2=Foy |first2=Robert H. |date=June 2001 |title=Environmental impacts of nitrogen and phosphorus cycling in grassland systems |url=https://www.academia.edu/110101616 |journal=Outlook on Agriculture |language=en |volume=30 |issue=2 |pages=117–27 |doi=10.5367/000000001101293562 |bibcode=2001OutAg..30..117W |access-date=16 April 2026 }}</ref> snowmelt and can [[Leaching (agriculture)|leach]] into [[groundwater]] over time.<ref>{{cite web |title=Sources and solutions: agriculture |url=https://www.epa.gov/nutrientpollution/sources-and-solutions-agriculture |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230405023648/https://www.epa.gov/nutrientpollution/sources-and-solutions-agriculture |archive-date=5 April 2023 |access-date=16 April 2026 |website=[[United States Environmental Protection Agency]] |date=26 February 2026 |language=en |url-status=live }}</ref> Agricultural [[Runoff (hydrology)|run-off]] is a major contributor to the [[eutrophication]] of [[Fresh water|freshwater]] bodies. For example, in the [[United States|US]], about half of all the lakes surveyed by the [[United States Environmental Protection Agency]] (US EPA) were [[eutrophic]] in 2007 with a further alarming increase to 80 per cent in 2012.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Stoddard |first1=John L. |last2=Van Sickle |first2=John |last3=Herlihy |first3=Alan T. |last4=Brahney |first4=Janice |last5=Paulsen |first5=Steven |last6=Peck |first6=David V. |last7=Mitchell |first7=Richard |last8=Pollard |first8=Amina I. |date=25 February 2016 |title=Continental-scale increase in lake and stream phosphorus: are oligotrophic systems disappearing in the United States? |journal=[[Environmental Science & Technology]] |language=en |volume=50 |issue=7 |pages=3409–15 |doi=10.1021/acs.est.5b05950 |doi-access=free |pmid=26914108 |bibcode=2016EnST...50.3409S }}</ref> The main contributor to eutrophication is [[phosphate]], which is normally a [[limiting nutrient]], besides nitrogen; high P concentrations promote the growth of [[cyanobacteria]] and [[algae]], the [[demise]] of which consumes oxygen.<ref name="Werner2002">{{cite book |doi=10.1002/14356007.n10_n05 |chapter=Fertilizers, 6. Environmental aspects |date=15 July 2009 |last=Werner |first=Wilfried |title=[[Ullmann's Encyclopedia of Industrial Chemistry]] |volume=14 |isbn=978-3-527-30673-2 |pages=295–314 |chapter-url=https://z-library.ec/book/vydPDnp2yV |access-date=16 April 2026 }}{{Dead link|date=June 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref> [[Cyanobacteria]] blooms ('[[algal blooms]]') can also produce harmful [[Eutrophication#Toxicity|toxins]] that can accumulate in the [[food chain]], and can be harmful to humans.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.circleofblue.org/2014/world/toledo-issues-emergency-warning-residents-drink-water/ |title=Toledo issues emergency 'Do not drink water' warning to residents |last=Kozacek |first=Codi |date=2 August 2014 |access-date=16 April 2026 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |pmc=3709275 |doi=10.3390/toxins5050992 | pmid=23676698 |volume=5 |issue=5 |title=Variations in the microcystin content of different fish species collected from a eutrophic lake |date=15 May 2013 |journal=[[Toxins (journal)|Toxins]] |pages=992–1009 |last1=Schmidt |first1=Justine R. |last2=Shaskus |first2=Mylynda |last3=Estenik |first3=John F. |last4=Oesch |first4=Carl |last5=Khidekel |first5=Roman |last6=Boyer |first6=Gregory L. |doi-access=free |bibcode=2013Toxin...5..992S }}</ref> Fertilizer run-off can be reduced by using weather-optimized fertilization strategies.<ref name="Fletcher2021"/>

The nitrogen-rich compounds found in [[fertilizer runoff]] are the primary cause of serious [[oxygen depletion]] in many parts of [[ocean]]s, especially in coastal zones, [[lake]]s and [[river]]s.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kostenko |first1=Viktor |last2=Tavrel |first2=Maryna |last3=Bohomaz |first3=Olha |last4=Kostenko |first4=Tetiana |last5=Kostyrka |first5=Olesia |last6=
Zemlianskyi |first6=Oleh |year=2023 |title=Studying the effect of mineral fertilizers on the development of the eutrophication process in the water bodies |journal=Ecological Engineering and Environmental Technology |language=en |volume=24 |issue=4 |pages=79–87 |doi=10.12912/27197050/161950 |doi-access=free }}</ref> The resulting lack of dissolved oxygen greatly reduces the ability of these areas to sustain oceanic [[fauna]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Ocean dead zones: the growing crisis beneath the waves |url=https://www.oceans-research.com/ocean-dead-zones-causes-solutions/ |last=Gennari |first=Enrico |date=15 May 2025 |website=Oceans Research News |access-date=16 April 2026 }}</ref> The number of oceanic [[Dead zone (ecology)|dead zones]] near inhabited coastlines is increasing.<ref>{{cite web |last=Heilprin |first=John |url=http://dsc.discovery.com/news/2006/10/20/deadzone_pla.html |title=Ocean 'dead zones' growing |website=[[Discovery Channel]] |access-date=25 August 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100618192917/http://dsc.discovery.com/news/2006/10/20/deadzone_pla.html |archive-date=18 June 2010 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

As of 2006, the application of nitrogen fertilizer is being increasingly controlled in northwestern Europe<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Van Grinsven |first1=Hans J. M. |last2=Ten Berge |first2=Hein F. M. |last3=Dalgaard |first3=Tommy |last4=Fraters |first4=B. |last5=Durand |first5=Patrick |last6=Hart |first6=Alwyn |last7=Hofman |first7=Georges |last8=Jabobsen |first8=Brian H. |last9=Lalor |first9=Stan T. J. |last10=Lesschen |first10=Jan Peter |last11=Osterburg |first11=Bernhard |last12=Richards |first12=Karl G. |last13=Techen |first13=Anja-Kristina |last14=Vertès |first14=Françoise |last15=Webb |first15=J. |last16=Willems |first16=W. Jaap |title=Management, regulation and environmental impacts of nitrogen fertilization in northwestern Europe under the Nitrates Directive: a benchmark study |journal=[[Biogeosciences]] |date=14 December 2012 |volume=9 |issue=12 |pages=5143–60 |doi=10.5194/bg-9-5143-2012 |bibcode = 2012BGeo....9.5143V |doi-access=free |hdl=1854/LU-3072131 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> and the United States.<ref>{{cite web |title=A farmer's guide to agriculture and water quality issues. 3. Environmental requirements and incentive programs for nutrient management |url=http://www.cals.ncsu.edu/wq/wqp/wqpollutants/nutrients/incentives.html |website=cals.ncsu.edu |access-date=3 July 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150923200107/http://www.cals.ncsu.edu/wq/wqp/wqpollutants/nutrients/incentives.html |archive-date=23 September 2015 |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last=State-EPA Nutrient Innovations Task Group |title=An urgent call to action: report of the State-EPA Nutrient Innovations Task Group |date=August 2009 |archive-date=9 October 2022 |url-status=dead |website=epa.gov |access-date=22 December 2025 }}</ref> In cases where [[eutrophication]] can be reversed, it may nevertheless take decades<ref>{{cite web |title=Study shows eutrophic lakes may not recover for a millennium |url=https://news.wisc.edu/study-shows-eutrophic-lakes-may-not-recover-for-a-millennium/ |access-date=17 April 2026 |website=news.wisc.edu |date=13 June 2005 }}</ref> and need significant soil management<ref>{{cite book |last=Wilkinson |first=Grace M. |chapter=Eutrophication of freshwater and coastal ecosystems |volume=4 |year=2017 |chapter-url=https://z-library.ec/book/BXbOOVolL7 |title=Encyclopedia of sustainable technologies |pages=145–52 |editor-last=Abraham |editor-first=Martin A. |location=Amsterdam, The Netherlands |publisher=Elsevier |language=en |doi=10.1016/b978-0-12-409548-9.10160-5 |isbn=978-0-12-804792-7 |access-date=17 April 2026 }}{{Dead link|date=June 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref> before the accumulated nitrates in [[groundwater]] can be broken down by natural [[denitrification]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Hiscock |first1=Kevin M. |last2=Lloyd |first2=Joshua W. |last3=Lerner |first3=David N. |date=September 1991 |title=Review of natural and artificial denitrification of groundwater |journal=Ecological Engineering and Environmental Technology |language=en |volume=24 |issue=4 |pages=79–87 |doi=10.12912/27197050/161950 |url=https://z-library.ec/book/JLZ85PPwy8 |access-date=17 April 2026 |doi-access=free }}{{Dead link|date=June 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref>

==== Nitrate pollution ====

Only a fraction of the nitrogen-based fertilizers is converted to plant matter. The remainder accumulates in the soil or is lost as run-off.<ref>{{cite book |doi=10.1007/978-94-007-7814-6_5 |pages=55–71 |year=2014 |last1=Callisto |first1=Marcos |last2=Molozzi |first2=Joseline |last3=Barbosa |first3=José Lucena Etham |title=Eutrophication: causes, consequences and control |volume=2 |editor-last1=Ansari |editor-first1=Abid A. |editor-last2=Gill |editor-first2=Sarvajeet Singh |chapter=Eutrophication of lakes |isbn=978-94-007-7813-9 |url=https://www.academia.edu/84339913 |access-date=17 April 2026 }}</ref> High application rates of nitrogen-containing fertilizers combined with the high [[water solubility]] of nitrate leads to increased [[Surface runoff#Agricultural issues|runoff]] into [[surface water]] as well as [[Leaching (agriculture)|leaching]] into [[groundwater]], thereby causing [[groundwater pollution]].<ref>{{cite web |last1=Rosen |first1=Carl J. |last2=Horgan |first2=Brian P. |url=https://conservancy.umn.edu/server/api/core/bitstreams/8c445d65-63ee-41de-871b-56623bfa5689/content?trackerId=0e7353bcaefb4142 |title=Preventing pollution problems from lawn and garden fertilizers |publisher=Extension.umn.edu |date=9 January 2009 |access-date=17 April 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140310024038/http://www.extension.umn.edu/garden/yard-garden/lawns/preventing-pollution-problems/ |archive-date=10 March 2014 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |title=Fertilizer-N use efficiency and nitrate pollution of groundwater in developing countries |journal=Journal of Contaminant Hydrology |doi=10.1016/0169-7722(95)00067-4 |volume=20 |issue=3–4 |pages=167–84 |bibcode=1995JCHyd..20..167S |date=December 1995 |last1=Bijay-Singh |last2=Yadvinder-Singh |last3=Sekhon |first3=G. S. |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/222010760 |access-date=17 April 2026 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last=Schonbeck |first=Mark |url=http://www.nofa.org/tnf/nitrogen.php |title=Ecologically sound nitrogen management: one researcher's educated guess |publisher=Nofa.org |date=25 February 2004 |access-date=25 August 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20040324090920/http://www.nofa.org/tnf/nitrogen.php |archive-date=24 March 2004 |url-status=dead }}</ref> The excessive use of nitrogen-containing fertilizers (be they synthetic or natural) is particularly damaging, as much of the nitrogen that is not taken up by plants is transformed into nitrate which is easily leached.<ref>{{cite journal |year=2008|title=Roots, nitrogen transformations, and ecosystem services |journal=[[Annual Review of Plant Biology]] |volume=59 |pages=341–63 |doi=10.1146/annurev.arplant.59.032607.092932 |pmid=18444903 |last1=Jackson |first1=Louise E. |last2=Burger |first2=Martin |last3=Cavagnaro |first3=Timothy R. |issue=1 |bibcode=2008AnRPB..59..341J |url=https://www.academia.edu/72027047 |access-date=17 April 2026 }}</ref>

Nitrate levels above 10&nbsp;mg/L (10 ppm) in groundwater can cause '[[blue baby syndrome]]' (acquired [[methemoglobinemia]]).<ref>{{cite journal |pmc=1638204 |title=Blue babies and nitrate-contaminated well water |pmid=10903623 |volume=108 |issue=7 |date=July 2000 |journal=[[Environmental Health Perspectives]] |pages=675–8 |last1=Knobeloch |first1=Lynda |last2=Salna |first2=Barbara |last3=Hogan |first3=Adam |last4=Postle |first4=Jeffrey |last5=Anderson |first5=Henry |doi=10.1289/ehp.00108675 |bibcode=2000EnvHP.108..675K |url=https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1638204/pdf/envhper00308-0137.pdf |access-date=17 April 2026 }}</ref> The nutrients, especially nitrates, in fertilizers can cause problems for natural habitats and for human health if they are washed off into [[watercourses]] or leached through the soil into [[groundwater]].<ref>{{cite web |last=Water Science School |url=https://www.usgs.gov/water-science-school/science/nitrogen-and-water |title=Nitrogen and water |website=[[United States Geological Survey]] |date=21 May 2018 |access-date=17 April 2026 }}</ref> Run-off can lead to fertilizing [[algal bloom]]s that use up all the oxygen and leave huge "dead zones" behind where other fish and aquatic life can not live.<ref>{{cite web |last=Biello |first=David |language=en |date=14 March 2008|title=Fertilizer runoff overwhelms streams and rivers, creating vast "dead zones" |url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/fertilizer-runoff-overwhelms-streams/ |website=[[Scientific American]] |access-date=17 April 2026 }}</ref>

=== Soil ===

==== Acidification ====
{{See also|Soil pH|Soil acidification}}
Soil acidification refers to the process by which the [[pH]] level of soil becomes more acidic over time. Soil pH is a measure of the soil's acidity or alkalinity and is determined on a scale from 0 to 14, with 7 being neutral. A pH value below 7 indicates [[acid]]ic soil, while a pH value above 7 indicates [[Alkali soil|alkaline]] or [[Base (chemistry)|basic]] soil. Soil acidification is a significant concern in agriculture and horticulture, leading to cation leaching, unstable soil aggregate structure, metal toxicity, decreased nutrient availability, and thus affecting soil biological properties and plant performances.<ref>{{cite book |doi=10.1007/978-981-15-4964-9_1 |pages=1–26 |year=2020 |last1=Yadav |first1=Durgesh Singh |last2=Jaiswal |first2=Bhavna |last3=Gautam |first3=Meenu |last4=Agrawal |first4=Madhoolika |title=Plant responses to soil pollution |editor-last1=Singh |editor-first1=Pratibha |editor-last2=Singh |editor-first2=Sunita Kumari |editor-last3=Prasad |editor-first3=Sheo Mohan |chapter=Soil acidification and its impact on plants |isbn=978-981-15-4964-9 |chapter-url=https://archive.org/details/yadav-et-al.-2020 |access-date=17 April 2026 |publisher=Springer Singapore |location=Singapore, Singapore }}</ref> 

Nitrogen-containing fertilizers release [[ammonium]] or [[nitrate]] ions, which can [[soil acidification|acidify the soil]] as they undergo [[biochemical]] reactions.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1080/00103624.2020.1845347 |volume=51 |issue=20 |title=Soil acidification and nitrogen release following application of nitrogen fertilizers |journal=Communications in Soil Science and Plant Analysis |pages=2551–8 |date=16 November 2020 |last1=Dal Molin |first1=Sulian Junkes |last2=Ernani |first2=Paulo Roberto |last3=Muniz Gerber |first3=Jaqueline |bibcode=2020CSSPA..51.2551D |url=https://z-library.ec/book/nLGl1PK49w |access-date=17 April 2026 }}{{Dead link|date=June 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref> When nitrogen-containing fertilizers, whether mineral or organic, are added to the soil, they increase the concentration of hydrogen ions (H+) in the soil solution, which lowers the pH of the soil.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1126/science.324_721b |pmid=19423798 |bibcode=2009Sci...324..721S |volume=324 |issue=5928 |title=Eutrophication: more nitrogen data needed |journal=[[Science (journal)|Science]] |pages=721–2 |date=8 May 2009 |last1=Schindler |first1=David W. |last2=Hecky |first2=Robert E. |url=https://z-library.ec/book/DLnpaJKMy6 |access-date=17 April 2026 }}{{Dead link|date=June 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.2136/sssaj2007.0071N |volume=72 |issue=1 |title=Phosphorus solubility in response to acidification of dairy manure amended soils |journal=[[Soil Science Society of America Journal]] |pages=238–43 |bibcode=2008SSASJ..72..238P |date=1 January 2008 |last1=Penn |first1=Chad J. |last2=Bryant |first2=Ray B. |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/43262980 |access-date=17 April 2026 }}</ref> This may lead to decrease in [[nutrient]] availability which may be offset by [[liming (soil)|liming]].<ref name="soil_acidification_and" />

Soil acidification occurs also through [[acid rain]], a man-induced [[global change|concern]] despite severe measures to suppress or mitigate industrial [[Greenhouse gas emissions|gas emissions]] since the 1970s.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1504/IJEE.2013.054703 |volume=5 |issue=3 |title=Acid rain: past, present, and future |journal=International Journal of Environmental Engineering |pages=229–72 |date=24 June 2013 |last1=Abbasi |first1=Tasneem |last2=Poornima |first2=P. |last3=Kannadasan |first3=T. |last4=Abbasi |first4=S. A. |url=https://z-library.ec/book/JLZ4pQM8y8 |access-date=17 April 2026 }}{{Dead link|date=June 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref> Among reported causes of acid rain, nitrogen fertilizers (whether mineral or organic), and the subsequent emissions of [[nitrous oxide|nitrous]] and [[nitric oxide]]s are prominent in regions of intensive agriculture.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1111/j.1475-2743.1997.tb00601.x |volume=13 |issue=S4 |title=Emissions of N2O and NO associated with nitrogen fertilization in intensive agriculture, and the potential for mitigation |journal=Soil Use and Management |pages=296–304 |date=December 1997 |last1=Smith |first1=K. A. |last2=McTaggart |first2=Iain P. |last3=Tsuruta |first3=Haruo |url=https://www.academia.edu/63390572 |access-date=17 April 2026 }}</ref> The mechanisms are complex, involving [[Ammonia volatilization from urea|ammonia volatilization]] from manure (whether stored or spread) or urea and direct redeposition followed by [[nitrification]] in the soil or previous oxidation to [[nitrogen oxide]]s in the atmosphere before redeposition as [[nitric acid]].<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1016/0004-6981(87)90154-5 |volume=21 |issue=9 |title=Ammonia emissions and their role in acid deposition |journal=[[Atmospheric Environment]] |pages=1939–46 |year=1987 |last1=ApSimon |first1=Helen M. |last2=Kruse |first2=Marc |last3=Bell |first3=John Nigel Berridge |bibcode=1987AtmEn..21.1939A |url=https://z-library.ec/book/D9P6GN28Xm |access-date=17 April 2026 }}{{Dead link|date=June 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref>

==== Accumulation of toxic elements ====

===== Cadmium =====

The concentration of [[cadmium]] in phosphorus-containing fertilizers varies considerably and can be problematic.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=McLaughlin |first1=Mike John |last2=Tiller |first2=K. G. |last3=Naidu |first3=Ravi |last4=Stevens |first4=Daryl P. |title=Review: the behaviour and environmental impact of contaminants in fertilizers |journal=[[Australian Journal of Soil Research]] |date=1 February 1996 |volume=34 |issue=1 |pages=1–54 |doi=10.1071/sr9960001 |bibcode=1996SoilR..34....1M |url=https://z-library.ec/book/eXqzOnGQLK |access-date=17 April 2026 }}{{Dead link|date=June 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref> For example, [[Monoammonium phosphate|mono-ammonium phosphate]] fertilizer may have a cadmium content of as low as 0.14&nbsp;mg/kg or as high as 50.9&nbsp;mg/kg.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lugon-Moulin |first1=Nicolas |last2=Ryan |first2=L. |last3=Donini |first3=Paolo |last4=Rossi |first4=Luca |title=Cadmium content of phosphate fertilizers used for tobacco production |journal=[[Agronomy for Sustainable Development]] |date=26 July 2006 |volume=26 |issue=3 |pages=151–5 |url=http://hal.archives-ouvertes.fr/docs/00/88/63/51/PDF/hal-00886351.pdf |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20221009/http://hal.archives-ouvertes.fr/docs/00/88/63/51/PDF/hal-00886351.pdf |archive-date=9 October 2022 |url-status=live |access-date=17 April 2026 |doi=10.1051/agro:2006010|s2cid=13996565 }}</ref> The [[phosphate rock]] used in their manufacture can contain as much as 188&nbsp;mg/kg cadmium<ref>{{cite web |last=Chien |first=S. H. |title=Secondary nutrients, micronutrients, liming effect and hazardous elements associated with phosphate rock use |url=https://www.fao.org/4/y5053e/y5053e0d.htm |website=fao.org |publisher=[[Food and Agriculture Organization|FAO]] |location=Rome, Italy |access-date=17 April 2026 |year=2004 }}</ref> Examples are deposits on [[Nauru]]<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Syers |first1=J. Keith |last2=Mackay |first2=Alec D. |last3=Brown |first3=Michael W. |last4=Currie |first4=Lance D. |title=Chemical and physical characteristics of phosphate rock materials of varying reactivity |journal=[[Journal of the Science of Food and Agriculture]] |date=November 1986 |volume=37 |issue=11 |pages=1057–64 |doi=10.1002/jsfa.2740371102 |bibcode=1986JSFA...37.1057S |url=https://z-library.ec/book/09QmvDde9p |access-date=17 April 2026 }}{{Dead link|date=June 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref> and the [[Christmas Island]]s.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Trueman |first=Norman Anthony |title=The phosphate, volcanic and carbonate rocks of Christmas Island (Indian Ocean) |journal=[[Journal of the Geological Society of Australia]] |year=1965 |volume=12 |issue=2 |pages=261–83 |doi=10.1080/00167616508728596 |bibcode=1965AuJES..12..261T |url=https://z-library.ec/book/PXox6BxBLV |access-date=17 April 2026 }}{{Dead link|date=June 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref> Continuous use of high-cadmium fertilizer can contaminate soils<ref>{{cite journal |last=Taylor |first=Matthhew D. |title=Accumulation of cadmium derived from fertilizers in New Zealand soils |journal=[[Science of the Total Environment]] |date=3 December 1997 |volume=208 |issue=1–2 |pages=123–6 |doi=10.1016/S0048-9697(97)00273-8 |bibcode=1997ScTEn.208..123T |pmid=9496656 |url=https://z-library.ec/book/zXOww8RvXb |access-date=17 April 2026 }}{{Dead link|date=June 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref> and [[Phytotoxicity|plants]].<ref name="Chaney2012">{{cite book |last1=Chaney |first1=Rufus L. |chapter=Food safety issues for mineral and organic fertilizers |title=Advances in agronomy |editor-last=Sparks |editor-first=Donald L. |date=2012 |volume=117 |pages=51–99 |publisher=[[Elsevier]] |location=Amsterdam, The Netherlands |doi=10.1016/b978-0-12-394278-4.00002-7 |isbn=978-0-12-394278-4 |chapter-url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/279959207 |access-date=17 April 2026 }}</ref> Limits to the cadmium content of phosphate fertilizers have been considered by the [[European Commission]].<ref>{{cite web |last1=Oosterhuis |first1=Frans H. |last2=Brouwer |first2=Floor M. |last3=Wijnants |first3=H. J. |title=A possible EU wide charge on cadmium in phosphate fertilisers: economic and environmental implications |url=https://research.vu.nl/ws/portalfiles/portal/1646586/E-00-02+Cadmiumheffing+rapport.pdf |website=[[Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam]] |location=Amsterdam, The Netherlands |access-date=17 April 2026 |year=2000 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Putting all the cards on the table |url=http://www.fertilizerseurope.com/fileadmin/user_upload/news_assets/FI-458-decadmiation__3_.pdf |date=January–February 2014 |website=Fertilizer International |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140808082824/http://www.fertilizerseurope.com/fileadmin/user_upload/news_assets/FI-458-decadmiation__3_.pdf |archive-date=8 August 2014 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Wates |first1=Jeremy |title=Revision of the EU fertilizer regulation and cadmium content of fertilisers |url=https://www.iatp.org/documents/revision-eu-fertilizer-regulation-and-cadmium-content-fertilisers |website=[[Institute for Agriculture and Trade Policy]] |access-date=17 April 2026 |date=2 June 2014 }}</ref> Producers of phosphorus-containing fertilizers now select phosphate rock based on the cadmium content.<ref name="Werner2002"/>

===== Fluoride =====

Phosphate rocks contain high levels of [[fluoride]] in the form of [[fluorapatite]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Ramteke |first1=Lokeshkumar P. |last2=Sahayam |first2=Athyala Christian |last3=Ghosh |first3=Arup |last4=Rambabu |first4=Urlagaddala |last5=Reddy |first5=Muppala R. P. |last6=Popat |first6=Kiritkumar Mangaldas |last7=Rebary |first7=Babulal |last8=Kubavat |first8=Denish |last9=Marathe |first9=Kumudini V. |last10=Ghosh |first10=Pushpito K. |title=Study of fluoride content in some commercial phosphate fertilizers |journal=Journal of Fluorine Chemistry |date=June 2018 |volume=210 |pages=149–55 |doi=10.1016/j.jfluchem.2018.03.018 |bibcode=2018JFluC.210..149R |url=https://www.academia.edu/114779123 |access-date=17 April 2026 }}</ref> Consequently, the widespread use of phosphate fertilizers has increased soil fluoride concentrations.<ref name="Chaney2012"/> It has been found that [[food contamination]] from fertilizer is of little concern as plants accumulate little fluoride from the soil; of greater concern is the possibility of fluoride toxicity to livestock that ingest contaminated soil.<ref name="Loganathan2008">{{cite book |last1=Loganathan |first1=Paripurnanda |last2=Hedley |first2=Mike J. |last3=Grace |first3=Neville D. |title=Reviews of environmental contamination and toxicology |chapter=Pasture soils contaminated with fertilizer-rerived cadmium and fluorine: livestock effects |year=2008 |volume=192 |pages=29–66 |doi=10.1007/978-0-387-71724-1_2 |pmid=18020303 |isbn=978-0-387-71723-4 |url=https://z-library.ec/book/lXeBDg4VLg |access-date=17 April 2026 }}{{Dead link|date=June 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref><ref name="Cronin2000">{{cite journal |last1=Cronin |first1=Shane J. |last2=Manoharan |first2=Veeragathipillai |last3=Hedley |first3=Mike J. |last4=Loganathan |first4=Paripurnanda |title=Fluoride: a review of its fate, bioavailability, and risks of fluorosis in grazed-pasture systems in New Zealand |journal=New Zealand Journal of Agricultural Research |year=2000 |volume=43 |issue=3 |pages=295–321 |doi=10.1080/00288233.2000.9513430 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2000NZJAR..43..295C }}</ref> Also of possible concern are the effects of fluoride on [[soil microorganism]]s.<ref name="Loganathan2008"/><ref name="Cronin2000"/><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Wilke |first1=Berndt-Michael |title=Fluoride-induced changes in chemical properties and microbial activity of mull, moder and mor soils |journal=Biology and Fertility of Soils |date=October 1987 |volume=5 |issue=1 |pages=49–55 |doi=10.1007/BF00264346|bibcode=1987BioFS...5...49W |s2cid=1225884 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/225974092 |access-date=17 April 2026 }}</ref>

===== Radioactive elements =====

The [[Radioactive decay|radioactive]] content of the fertilizers varies considerably and depends both on their concentrations in the parent mineral and on the fertilizer production process.<ref name="Chaney2012"/><ref>{{cite web |last1=Mortvedt |first1=John J. |last2=Beaton |first2=James D. |title=Heavy metal and radionuclide contaminants in phosphate fertilizers |url=http://www.scopenvironment.org/downloadpubs/scope54/6mortvedt.htm |access-date=16 July 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140726193234/http://www.scopenvironment.org/downloadpubs/scope54/6mortvedt.htm |archive-date=26 July 2014 |url-status=dead }}</ref> [[Uranium-238]] concentrations can range from 7 to 100 pCi/g ([[picocuries]] per gram) in phosphate rock<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.epa.gov/radiation/tenorm-fertilizer-and-fertilizer-production-wastes |title=TENORM: fertilizer and fertilizer production wastes |date=29 December 2025 |website=[[United States Environmental Protection Agency|US EPA]] |access-date=17 April 2026 }}</ref> and from 1 to 67 pCi/g in phosphate fertilizers.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Khater |first1=Ashraf E. M. |chapter=Uranium and heavy metals in phosphate fertilizers |chapter-url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/226094606 |title=Uranium, mining and hydrogeology |year=2008 |editor-last1=Merkel |editor-first1=Broder J. |editor-last2=Hasche-Berger |editor-first2=Andrea |isbn=978-3-540-87746-2 |pages=193–8 |doi=10.1007/978-3-540-87746-2_26 |publisher=[[Springer Science+Business Media|Springer]] |location=Berlin, Germany |access-date=17 April 2026 }}</ref><ref name="NCRP1987">{{cite book |last=NCRP |title=Radiation exposure of the U.S. population from consumer products and miscellaneous sources |date=30 December 1987 |publisher=[[National Council on Radiation Protection and Measurements]] |pages=29–32 |url=https://z-library.ec/book/j0yDp37wyP |access-date=17 April 2026 }}{{Dead link|date=June 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last=Hussein |first=Esam M. |title=Radioactivity of phosphate ore, superphosphate, and phosphogypsum in Abu-zaabal phosphate plant, Egypt |journal=[[Health Physics (journal)|Health Physics]] |date=September 1994 |volume=67 |issue=3 |pages=280–2 |doi=10.1097/00004032-199409000-00010 |pmid=8056596 |bibcode=1994HeaPh..67..280H |url=https://z-library.ec/book/nLAn2kpA9z |access-date=17 April 2026 }}{{Dead link|date=June 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref> Where high annual rates of phosphorus fertilizer are used, this can result in [[uranium-238]] concentrations in soils and [[Drainage system (geomorphology)|drainage water]]s that are several times greater than are normally present.<ref name="NCRP1987"/><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Barišić |first1=Delko |last2=Lulíc |first2=Stipe |last3=Miletić |first3=P. |title=Radium and uranium in phosphate fertilizers and their impact on the radioactivity of waters |journal=[[Water Research]] |date=May 1992 |volume=26 |issue=5 |pages=607–11 |doi=10.1016/0043-1354(92)90234-U |bibcode=1992WatRe..26..607B |url=https://z-library.ec/book/7y3lxzagXJ |access-date=17 April 2026 }}{{Dead link|date=June 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref> However, the impact of these increases on the [[Sievert#Dose examples|risk to human health]] from radionuclidic contamination of foods is very small (less than 0.05 m[[Sievert|Sv]]/y).<ref name="NCRP1987"/><ref>{{cite web |last=Hanlon |first=Edward A. |title=Naturally occurring radionuclides in agricultural products |url=https://journals.flvc.org/edis/article/download/114205/109516 |website=edis.ifas.ufl.edu |publisher=[[University of Florida]] |access-date=17 April 2026 |date=December 2004 |archive-date=25 July 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140725171240/http://edis.ifas.ufl.edu/ss441 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Sharpley |first1=Andrew N. |last2=Menzel |first2=Ronald G. |chapter=The impact of soil and fertilizer phosphorus on the environment |title=Advances in Agronomy |volume=41 |year=1987 |editor-last=Brady |editor-first=Nyle C. |pages=297–324 |doi=10.1016/s0065-2113(08)60807-x |isbn=978-0-12-000741-7 |s2cid=83005521 |chapter-url=https://z-library.ec/book/lXW6JMvNyq |access-date=17 April 2026 }}{{Dead link|date=June 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref>

===== Other metals =====

[[Steel industry]] wastes such as steel [[slag]] are often recycled as a [[soil amendment]] or for the production of fertilizers due to their high Ca and Mg content and various [[trace element]]s necessary for plant growth.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Tozsin |first1=Gulsen |last2=Oztas |first2=Taskin |title=Utilization of steel slag as a soil amendment and mineral fertilizer in agriculture: a review |journal=Journal of Agricultural Sciences |date=24 October 2023 |volume=29 |issue=4 |pages=906–13 |doi=10.15832/ankutbd.1197239 |doi-access=free }}</ref> However, they can also include [[Toxic heavy metal|toxic metals]].<ref name="Wilson1997">{{cite web |last=Wilson |first=Duff |title=Fear in the fields: how hazardous wastes become fertilizer. Spreading heavy metals on farmland is perfectly legal, but little research has been done to find out whether it's safe |url=https://archive.seattletimes.com/archive/19970703/2547772/fear-in-the-fields----how-hazardous-wastes-become-fertilizer----spreading-heavy-metals-on-farmland-is-perfectly-legal-but-little-research-has-been-done-to-find-out-whether-its-safe |website=The Seattle Times |date=3 July 1997 |access-date=17 April 2026 |archive-date=18 November 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101118013539/http://community.seattletimes.nwsource.com/archive/?date=19970703&slug=2547772 |url-status=live }}</ref> Among them are [[arsenic]],<ref name="He2020">{{cite journal |last1=He |first1=Huaidong |last2=Xiao |first2=Qingqing |last3=Yuan |first3=Ming |last4=Huang |first4=Run |last5=Sun |first5=Xianbin |last6=Wang |first6=Xiaomei |last7=Zhao |first7=Huaiqiong |title=Effects of steel slag amendments on accumulation of cadmium and arsenic by rice (''Oryza sativa'') in a historically contaminated paddy field |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/342857567 |access-date=17 April 2026 }}</ref> [[cadmium]],<ref name="He2020"/> [[chromium]],<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kong |first1=Fanyi |last2=Ying |first2=Yuqian |last3=Lu |first3=Shenggao |title=Heavy metal pollution risk of desulfurized steel slag as a soil amendment in cycling use of solid wastes |journal=Journal of Environmental Sciences |date=May 2023 |volume=127 |pages=349–60 |doi=10.1016/j.jes.2022.05.010 |pmid=36522067 |bibcode=2023JEnvS.127..349K |url=https://archive.org/details/kong-et-al.-2023 |access-date=17 April 2026 }}</ref> and [[nickel]],<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Wang |first1=Xiaobin |last2=Li |first2=Xiuying |last3=Yan |first3=Xiang |last4=Tu |first4=Cheng |last5=Yu |first5=Zhaoguo |title=Environmental risks for application of iron and steel slags in soils in China: a review |journal=Pedosphere |date=February 2021 |volume=31 |issue=1 |pages=28–42 |doi=10.1016/S1002-0160(20)60058-3 |bibcode=2021Pedos..31...28W |url=https://z-library.ec/book/8L74mMEk90 |access-date=17 April 2026 }}{{Dead link|date=June 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref> while steel slag amendment rather contribute to immobilize [[lead]] in the soil and thus to decrease its toxicity to the cultivated plant.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Pei |first1=Guangpeng |last2=Li |first2=Yuxin |last3=Zhu |first3=Yuen |last4=Shi |first4=Weiyu |last5=Li |first5=Hua |title=Immobilization of lead by application of soil amendment produced from vinegar residue, stainless steel slag, and weathered coal |journal=Environmental Science and Pollution Research |date=11 August 2017 |volume=24 |issue=28 |pages=22301–11 |doi=10.1007/s11356-017-9917-1 |pmid=28801796 |bibcode=2017ESPR...2422301P |url=https://z-library.ec/book/Wyro5P4EXJ |access-date=17 April 2026 }}{{Dead link|date=June 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref> The most common toxic elements in this type of fertilizer are [[Mercury (element)|mercury]], lead, and arsenic.<ref>{{cite web |last=Shaffer |first=Matthew |url=https://safefoodandfertilizer.com/w-aste-lands-the-threat-of-toxic-f-ertilizer/ |title=Waste lands: the threat of toxic fertilizer |publisher=Safe Food and Fertilizer |location=Berkeley, California |date=9 November 2025 |access-date=17 April 2026 |archive-date=26 November 2010 |url=http://www.mindfully.org/Farm/Toxic-Waste-Fertilizers.htm |title=Toxic wastes found in fertilizers |website=Mindfully.org |access-date=25 August 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20020111124358/http://www.mindfully.org/Farm/Toxic-Waste-Fertilizers.htm |archive-date=11 January 2002 |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Zapata |first1=F. |last2=Roy |first2=R.
