The incorporation of [[biochar]] to steel slag make even the mixture a good amendement for the ([[Passivation (chemistry)|passivation]]) of [[heavy metals]] in agricultural soil.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Wang |first1=An |last2=Liu |first2=Yifan |last3=Zhang |first3=Yin |last4=Ren |first4=Jie |last5=Zeng |first5=Yang |last6=Huang |first6=Zhanbin |title=Synthesis of biochar modified steel slag composites for passivation of multiple heavy metals in soil |journal=Journal of Environmental Chemical Engineering |date=October 2024 |volume=12 |issue=5 |article-number=114026 |doi=10.1016/j.jece.2024.114026 |url=https://archive.org/details/wang-et-al.-2024 |access-date=17 April 2026 |doi-access=free }}</ref> Highly pure fertilizers are widely available and perhaps best known as the highly water-soluble fertilizers containing blue dyes used around [[household]]s, such as [[Miracle-Gro]]. These highly water-soluble fertilizers are used in the [[plant nursery]] business and are available in larger packages at significantly less cost than [[retail]] quantities. Some inexpensive retail granular garden fertilizers are made with high purity ingredients.<ref>{{cite web |last=Scott |first=Mariam |title=Understanding granular fertilizers: how they work and best uses |url=https://growcycle.com/learn/understanding-granular-fertilizers-how-they-work-and-best-uses |website=growcycle.com |access-date=17 April 2026 |date=16 October 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260228150112/https://growcycle.com/learn/understanding-granular-fertilizers-how-they-work-and-best-uses |archive-date=28 February 2026 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==== Trace mineral depletion ====

Attention has been addressed to the decreasing concentrations of [[micronutrient]]s such as [[iron]], [[zinc]], [[copper]] and [[magnesium]] in many foods over the last 50–60 years.<ref name="Davis2004">{{cite journal |last1=Davis |first1=Donald R. |last2=Epp |first2=Melvin D. |last3=Riordan |first3=Hugh D. |title=Changes in USDA food composition data for 43 garden crops, 1950 to 1999 |journal=[[Journal of the American College of Nutrition]] |year=2004 |volume=23 |issue=6 |pages=669–682 |doi=10.1080/07315724.2004.10719409 |pmid=15637215 |s2cid=13595345 |url=https://z-library.ec/book/jL5bJjv29g |access-date=20 April 2026 }}{{Dead link|date=June 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref><ref name="Thomas2007">{{cite journal |last1=Thomas |first1=David |title=The mineral depletion of foods available to us as a nation (1940–2002): a review of the 6th edition of McCance and Widdowson |journal=[[Nutrition and Health]] |date=July 2007 |volume=19 |issue=1–2 |pages=21–55 |doi=10.1177/026010600701900205 |pmid=18309763 |s2cid=372456 |url=https://downloads.clinicaleducation.org/protected-seminars/plm-jan19/research-papers/5/20-slide-the-mineral-depletion-of-foods-available-to-us-as-a-nation-(1940-2002)a-review-of-the-6th-edition-of-mccance-and-widdowson..pdf |access-date=20 April 2026 }}</ref> [[Intensive farming]] practices, including the use of synthetic fertilizers, are frequently suggested as reasons for these declines and [[organic farming]] is often suggested as a solution.<ref name="Thomas2007"/> Although improved crop yields resulting from NPK fertilizers are known to dilute the concentrations of other nutrients in plants,<ref name="Davis2004"/><ref>{{cite book |last1=Jarrell |first1=Wesley M. |last2=Beverly |first2=R. B. |chapter=The dilution effect in plant nutrition studies |title=Advances in Agronomy |year=1981 |volume=34 |editor-last=Brady |editor-first=Nyle C. |pages=197–224 |doi=10.1016/s0065-2113(08)60887-1 |isbn=978-0-12-000734-9 |chapter-url=https://z-library.ec/book/mX4QnlbELx |access-date=20 April 2026 }}{{Dead link|date=June 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref> much of the measured decline can be attributed to the use of progressively higher-yielding crop varieties that produce foods with lower mineral concentrations than their less-productive ancestors.<ref name="Davis2004"/><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Fan |first1=Ming-Sheng |last2=Zhao |first2=Fang-Jie |last3=Fairweather-Tait |first3=Susan J. |last4=Poulton |first4=Paul R. |last5=Dunham |first5=Sarah J. |last6=McGrath |first6=Steve P. |title=Evidence of decreasing mineral density in wheat grain over the last 160 years |journal=[[Journal of Trace Elements in Medicine and Biology]] |date=November 2008 |volume=22 |issue=4 |pages=315–24 |doi=10.1016/j.jtemb.2008.07.002 |pmid=19013359|bibcode=2008JTEMB..22..315F |url=https://www.academia.edu/63423887 |access-date=20 April 2026 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Zhao |first1=Fang-Jie |last2=Su |first2=Yu H. |last3=Dunham |first3=Sarah J. |last4=Rakszegi |first4=Marianna |last5=Bedo |first5=Zoltan |last6=McGrath |first6=Steve P. |last7=Shewry |first7=Peter R. |title=Variation in mineral micronutrient concentrations in grain of wheat lines of diverse origin |journal=Journal of Cereal Science |date=March 2009 |volume=49 |issue=2 |pages=290–5 |doi=10.1016/j.jcs.2008.11.007 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/248588653 |access-date=20 April 2026 }}</ref> It is, therefore, unlikely that [[organic farming]] or reduced use of fertilizers (e.g. [[conservation agriculture]]) will solve the problem; foods with high nutrient density are posited to be achieved using older, lower-yielding varieties or the development of new high-yield, nutrient-dense varieties.<ref name="Davis2004"/><ref name=Saltzman2013>{{cite journal |last1=Saltzman |first1=Amy |last2=Birol |first2=Ekin |last3=Bouis |first3=Howarth E. |last4=Boy |first4=Erick |last5=De Moura |first5=Fabiana F. |last6=Islam |first6=Yassir |last7=Pfeiffer |first7=Wolfgang H. |title=Biofortification: progress toward a more nourishing future |journal=Global Food Security |date=March 2013 |volume=2 |issue=1 |pages=9–17 |doi=10.1016/j.gfs.2012.12.003 |bibcode=2013GlFS....2....9S |url=https://z-library.ec/book/p9mE65A09z |access-date=20 April 2026 }}{{Dead link|date=June 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref>

Fertilizers are, in fact, more likely to solve trace mineral deficiency problems than cause them: in Western Australia deficiencies of [[zinc]], [[copper]], [[manganese]], [[iron]] and [[molybdenum]] were identified as limiting the growth of [[Broadacre|broad-acre]] crops and pastures in the 1940s and 1950s.<ref name="Moore2001">{{cite book |last=Moore |first=Geoff |title=Soilguide (Soil guid): a handbook for understanding and managing agricultural soils |year=2001 |publisher=[[Department of Primary Industries and Regional Development (Western Australia)|Department of Primary Industries and Regional Development]] |location=Perth, Western Australia |isbn=978-0-7307-0057-9 |pages=161–207 |url=https://library.dpird.wa.gov.au/bulletins/2/ |access-date=20 April 2026 }}</ref> Soils in Western Australia are very old, highly weathered and deficient in many of the major nutrients and trace elements.<ref name="Moore2001"/> Since this time these trace elements are routinely added to fertilizers used in agriculture in this state.<ref name="Moore2001"/> Many other soils around the world are deficient in zinc, leading to deficiency in both plants and humans,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Hambidge |first1=K. Michael |last2=Krebs |first2=Nancy F. |title=Zinc deficiency: a special challenge |journal=[[Journal of Nutrition]] |date=April 2007 |volume=137 |issue=4 |pages=1101–5 |doi=10.1093/jn/137.4.1101 |pmid=17374687 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/6432084 |access-date=20 April 2026 }}</ref> and zinc fertilizers are widely used to solve this problem.<ref>{{cite web |last=Alloway |first=Brian J. |url=https://www.topsoils.co.nz/wp-content/uploads/2014/09/Zinc-in-Soils-and-Crop-Nutrition-Brian-J.-Alloway.pdf |title=Zinc in soils and crop nutrition |publisher=[[International Fertilizer Association|International Fertilizer Industry Association]] |location=Paris, France |year=2008 |access-date=20 April 2026 }}</ref>

==== Changes in soil biology ====
{{Further|soil biology}}
High levels of fertilizer may cause the breakdown of the [[Symbiosis|symbiotic]] relationships between plant roots and [[mycorrhiza]]l fungi,<ref>{{cite book |last1=Carroll |first1=Steven B. |last2=Salt |first2=Steven D. |title=Ecology for gardeners |year=2004 |publisher=[[Timber Press]] |location=Portland, Oregon |isbn=978-0-88192-611-8 |pages=230–2 |url=https://archive.org/details/ecologyforgarden0000carr/page/230/mode/2up |access-date=29 December 2025 }}</ref> in particular when in excess of plant requirements.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Grant |first1=Cynthia |last2=Bittman |first2=Shabtai |last3=Montreal |first3=Marcia |last4=Plenchette |first4=Christian |last5=Morel |first5=Christian |title=Soil and fertilizer phosphorus: effects on plant P supply and mycorrhizal development |journal=[[Canadian Journal of Plant Science]] |date=January 2005 |volume=85 |issue=1 |pages=3–14 |doi=10.4141/P03-182 |doi-access=free }}</ref> It is still debated whether and how fertilizers affect [[soil animals]]. Both organic and organic–mineral fertilizers increase the abundance of soil fauna whereas mineral fertilizers had no such effect, with [[Idiosyncrasy|idiosyncratic]] responses of soil animal groups masking overall effects.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Zhu |first1=Yan |last2=Bian |first2=Haixue |last3=Ju |first3=Chenghui |last4=Xu |first4=Chonghua |last5=Zhou |first5=Yan |last6=Zhang |first6=Huiguang |last7=Xu |first7=Xia |title=Fertilization alters the abundance but not the diversity of soil fauna: a meta-analysis |journal=[[Global Ecology and Biogeography]] |date=April 2023 |volume=32 |issue=4 |pages=482–94 |doi=10.1111/geb.13641 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2023GloEB..32..482Z }}</ref> Chemical fertilizers stimulates the growth of [[Microbial population biology|microbial population]]s but did not change their richness and diversity, while decreases in [[enzymatic activity]] have been registered.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Dincä |first1=Lucian Constantin |last2=Grenni |first2=Paola |last3=Onet |first3=Cristian |last4=Onet |first4=Aurelia |title=Fertilization and soil microbial community: a review |journal=[[Applied Sciences (journal)|Applied Sciences]] |date=24 January 2022 |volume=12 |issue=3 |article-number=1198 |doi=10.3390/app12031198 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

The combination of [[soil acidification]] and high nitrogen content was probably unknown to most soil organisms before the advent of [[industrial agriculture]]. More generally, soils are either acidic and nutrient-poor, or neutral to basic and nutrient-rich (nitrogen included), in relation to the pH-dependent capacity of [[clay mineral]]s to hold nutrients.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Sumner |first1=Malcolm E. |last2=Fey |first2=Martin V. |last3=Noble |first3=Andrew D. |title=Soil acidity |year=1991 |publisher=[[Springer Science+Business Media|Springer]] |editor-last1=Ulrich |editor-first1=Bernhard |editor-last2=Sumner |editor-first2=Malcolm E. |edition=1st |location=Berlin, Germany |pages=149–82 |chapter=Nutrient status and toxicity problems in acid soils |doi=10.1007/978-3-642-74442-6_7 |isbn=978-3-642-74442-6 |access-date=20 April 2026 |chapter-url=https://archive.org/details/sumner-et-al.-1991 }}</ref> This unexpected combination of excess nutrient availability and acid [[Stress (biology)|stress]] causes a depletion in the sustainability of animal and microbial communities by weakening the linkages between aboveground and belowground components of [[agroecosystem]]s.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Chen |first1=Dima |last2=Lan |first2=Zhichun |last3=Hu |first3=Shuijin |last4=Bai |first4=Yongfei |title=Effects of nitrogen enrichment on belowground communities in grassland: relative role of soil nitrogen availability vs. soil acidification |journal=[[Soil Biology and Biochemistry]] |date=October 2015 |volume=89 |pages=99–108 |doi=10.1016/j.soilbio.2015.06.028 |bibcode=2015SBiBi..89...99C |url=https://z-library.ec/book/OLw2bYK2Xe |access-date=20 April 2026 }}{{Dead link|date=June 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref> Other [[ecosystem]]s are also affected by nitrogen-enriched acid rains originationg from intensive agricultural practices. [[Sphagnum bog]]s are now shifting from [[carbon sink]]s (thanks to the accumulation of recalcitrant sphagnum litter and [[Anoxic waters|anoxic]] conditions) to carbon sources under the influence of nitrogen deposition and subsequent stimulation of [[decomposer]] activity.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bragazza |first1=Luca |last2=Buttler |first2=Alexandre |last3=Habermacher |first3=Jonathan |last4=Brancaleoni |first4=Lisa |last5=Gerdol |first5=Renato |last6=Fritze |first6=Hannu |last7=Hanajík |first7=Peter |last8=Laiho |first8=Raija |last9=Johnson |first9=David |title=High nitrogen deposition alters the decomposition of bog plant litter and reduces carbon accumulation |journal=[[Global Change Biology]] |date=March 2012 |volume=18 |issue=3 |pages=1163–72 |doi=10.1111/j.1365-2486.2011.02585.x |bibcode=2012GCBio..18.1163B |url=https://z-library.ec/book/0yDxOZBKyP |access-date=20 April 2026 }}{{Dead link|date=June 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref> Other nutrient-poor ecosystems are also strongly affected, such as [[heathland]]s, with a surprising combination of higher [[soil organic matter]] accumulation and higher [[soil enzyme]] activity.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Jones |first1=Alan G. |last2=Power |first2=Sally A. |title=Field-scale evaluation of effects of nitrogen deposition on the functioning of heathland ecosystems |journal=[[Journal of Ecology]] |date=March 2012 |volume=100 |issue=2 |pages=331–42 |doi=10.1111/j.1365-2745.2011.01911.x |doi-access=free |bibcode=2012JEcol.100..331J }}</ref>

=== Organic agriculture ===
{{Further|organic farming}}
Two types of agricultural management practices include [[organic farming]] and [[conventional agriculture]]. The former encourages [[soil fertility]] using local resources to maximize efficiency. Organic agriculture avoids synthetic agrochemicals. Conventional agriculture uses all the components that organic agriculture does not use.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Gomiero |first1=Tiziano |last2=Pimentel |first2=David |last3=Paoletti |first3=Maurizio G. |date=29 April 2011 |title=Environmental impact of different agricultural management practices: conventional vs. organic agriculture |journal=Critical Reviews in Plant Sciences |volume=30 |issue=1–2 |pages=95–124 |doi=10.1080/07352689.2011.554355 |bibcode=2011CRvPS..30...95G |s2cid=83736589 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/255978998 |access-date=20 April 2026 }}</ref>

The excess use of organic amendments (e.g. pig [[slurry]]) may have detrimental effects on [[water quality]] through contamination of the [[aquifer]] and subsequent [[eutrophication]] of the [[water bodies]] it feds.<ref>{{cite book |last=Kopp |first=Radovan |chapter=Water quality after application of pig slurry |title=Ecological water quality: water treatment and reuse |date=16 May 2012 |editor-last=Voudouris |editor-first=Kostas |pages=161–82 |doi=10.5772/29100 |isbn=978-953-51-6208-7 |chapter-url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/268187395 |access-date=20 April 2026 }}</ref> This is a societal concern in areas where [[pig farming]] conflicts with [[environmental protection]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Öhlund |first1=Erika |last2=Hammer |first2=Monica |last3=Björklund |first3=Johanna |date=13 November 2017 |title=Managing conflicting goals in pig farming: farmers' strategies and perspectives on sustainable pig farming in Sweden |journal=International Journal of Agricultural Sustainability |volume=15 |issue=6 |pages=693–707 |doi=10.1080/14735903.2017.1399514 |bibcode=2017IJAgS..15..693O |url=https://z-library.ec/book/lXebdw82Lg |access-date=20 April 2026 }}{{Dead link|date=June 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref>

=== Fossil fuel consumption and sustainability ===

Most synthetic fertilizer is fed from [[fossil fuel]], using fossil energy and [[methane]] for producing [[hydrogen]] used in the synthesis of ammonia by the [[Haber process]], as well as various [[chemical reaction]]s used in the synthesis of most fertilizers (e.g. [[urea]], [[ammonium nitrate]], [[superphosphate]]).<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Ramírez |first1=C. Andrea |last2=Worrell |first2=Ernst |date=January 2006 |title=Feeding fossil fuels to the soil: an analysis of energy embedded and technological learning in the fertilizer industry |journal=Resources, Conservation and Recycling |volume=46 |issue=1 |pages=75–93 |doi=10.1016/j.resconrec.2005.06.004 |bibcode=2006RCR....46...75R |url=https://www.academia.edu/29813508 |access-date=20 April 2026 }}</ref> Some alternatives have been proposed for the production of hydrogen, such as [[solar energy]],<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Abdallah |first1=Ramez |last2=Juaidi |first2=Adel |last3=Almomani |first3=Fares |last4=Abdelsalam |first4=Emad |last5=Albatayneh |first5=Aiman |last6=Azzam |first6=Ahmad |last7=Ayub |first7=Hafiz Muhammad Uzair |title=Assessing solar energy utilization for green hydrogen production: a techno-economic and environmental assessment |journal=[[International Journal of Hydrogen Energy]] |date=3 July 2025 |volume=144 |issue=5 |pages=522–35 |doi=10.1016/j.ijhydene.2025.04.438 |bibcode=2025IJHE..144..522A |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/391825306 |access-date=20 April 2026 |doi-access=free }}</ref> waste treatment,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Budhijanto |first1=Budhijanto |last2=Pancasakti |first2=Bima Prasetya |title=Evaluating the potential of hydrogen production from agricultural waste in Indonesia: a comparative techno-economic analysis |journal=International Journal of Energy Economics and Policy |date=15 March 2024 |volume=14 |issue=2 |pages=618–23 |doi=10.32479/ijeep.15481 |doi-access=free }}</ref> or [[electrolysis]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Babaei |first1=Reza |last2=King |first2=David S. K. |last3=Carriveau |first3=Rupp |title=Hydrogen pathways for green fertilizer production: a comparative techno-economic study of electrolysis and plasmalysis |journal=[[International Journal of Hydrogen Energy]] |date=13 October 2025 |volume=178 |article-number=151571 |doi=10.1016/j.ijhydene.2025.151571 |bibcode=2025IJHE..17851571B |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/395941946 |access-date=20 April 2026 |doi-access=free |hdl=20.500.14776/19057 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

=== Contribution to the greenhouse effect ===
{{See also|Greenhouse gas emissions from agriculture}}
[[File:AtmosphericMethane.png|thumb|Global [[methane]] concentrations (surface and atmospheric) for 2005; note distinct plumes]]
The amount of [[greenhouse gas]]es [[carbon dioxide]], [[methane]] and [[nitrous oxide]] produced during the [[Haber process|manufacture]] and use of nitrogen fertilizer is estimated as around 5% of [[anthropogenic greenhouse gas emissions]]. One third is produced during the production and two thirds during the use of fertilizers.<ref>{{cite web |title=Carbon emissions from fertilizers could be reduced by as much as 80% by 2050 |date=9 February 2023 |url=https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2023/02/230209114736.htm |website=[[ScienceDaily|Science Daily]] |publisher=[[University of Cambridge]] |access-date=20 April 2026 }}</ref> [[Nitrate]] is converted by [[Nitrous oxide#Soil|soil bacteria]] to [[nitrous oxide]], a [[greenhouse gas]].<ref>{{cite web |date=10 September 2020 |title=How fertilizer is making climate change worse |url=https://businessfocus.co.ug/how-fertilizer-is-making-climate-change-worse/ |access-date=20 April 2026 |website=businessfocus.co.ug |language=en }}</ref> Nitrous oxide emissions by humans, most of which are from fertilizer, between 2007 and 2016 were estimated at 700 million tons of CO<sub>2</sub> equivalent.<ref>{{cite web |date=7 October 2020 |title=Nitrogen fertiliser use could 'threaten global climate goals' |url=https://www.carbonbrief.org/nitrogen-fertiliser-use-could-threaten-global-climate-goals |access-date=20 April 2026 |website=[[Carbon Brief]] |language=en }}</ref>

Nitrogen fertilizer was used at a rate of about 110 million tons (of N) per year in 2012.<ref>{{cite book |last=[[Food and Agriculture Organization|FAO]] |title=Current world fertilizer trends and outlook to 2016 |year=2012 |publisher=[[Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations]] |location=Rome, Italy |page=13 |url=http://large.stanford.edu/courses/2014/ph240/yuan2/docs/cwfto16.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170518105637/ftp://ftp.fao.org/ag/agp/docs/cwfto16.pdf |archive-date=18 May 2017 |access-date=20 April 2026 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1038/nature06592 |bibcode=2008Natur.451..293G |volume=451 |issue=7176 |title=An Earth-system perspective of the global nitrogen cycle |journal=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]] |pages=293–6 |pmid=18202647 |last1=Gruber |first1=Nicolas |last2=Galloway |first2=James N. |date=16 January 2008 |url=https://www.academia.edu/102851294 |access-date=20 April 2026 }}</ref> [[Nitrous oxide]] (N<sub>2</sub>O) is the third most important [[greenhouse gas]] after [[carbon dioxide]] and [[methane]]. It has 296 times greater [[greenhouse effect]] per ton than  [[carbon dioxide]]. The 2025 emissions contributed the equivalent of 700 megatons of CO<sub>2</sub> to the atmosphere.<ref>{{cite web |title=Pricing fertilizer emissions cuts climate pollution without making food expensive |url=https://cleantechnica.com/2026/01/18/pricing-fertilizer-emissions-cuts-climate-pollution-without-making-food-expensive/ |website=[[CleanTechnica]] |date=19 January 2026 |access-date=20 April 2026 |language=en-US |first=Michael |last=Barnard }}</ref> It also contributes to [[Stratosphere|stratospheric]] [[ozone depletion]].<ref>{{cite web |last1=Galloway |first1=James |last2=Erisman |first2=Jan |last3=Townsend |first3=Alan |last4=Davidson |first4=Eric |last5=Bekunda |first5=Mateete |last6=Cai |first6=Zejiang |last7=Freney |first7=John |last8=Martinelli |first8=Luiz |last9=Seitzinger |first9=Sybil |last10=Sutton |first10=Mark |title=Human alteration of the nitrogen cycle: threats, benefits and opportunities |url=https://unesdoc.unesco.org/ark:/48223/pf0000150916 |website=[[UNESCO]] |access-date=20 April 2026 |date=April 2007 }}</ref> Altering processes and procedures could reduce these emissions.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Roy |first1=Rabindra N. |last2=Misra |first2=Ram V. |last3=Montanez |first3=Adriana |title=Decreasing reliance on mineral nitrogen, yet more food |journal=[[Ambio]] |date=1 March 2002 |volume=31 |issue=2 |pages=177–83 |doi=10.1579/0044-7447-31.2.177 |pmid=12078007 |bibcode=2002Ambio..31..177R |s2cid=905322 |url=https://www.academia.edu/105572856 |access-date=20 April 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150924074035/http://www.planta.cn/forum/files_planta/decreasing_reliance_on_mineral_nitrogenyet_more_food_364.pdf |archive-date=24 September 2015 |url-status=live }}</ref>

[[Methane emissions]] from crop fields (notably rice [[paddy field]]s) are increased by the application of ammonium-based fertilizers. These emissions contribute to global climate change as methane is a potent greenhouse gas.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bodelier |first1=Paul L. E. |last2=Roslev |first2=Peter |last3=Henckel |first3=Thilo |last4=Frenzel |first4=Peter |date=27 January 2000 |title=Stimulation by ammonium-based fertilizers of methane oxidation in soil around rice roots |journal=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]] |volume=403 |pages=421–4 |pmid=10667792 |issue=6768 |doi=10.1038/35000193 |bibcode=2000Natur.403..421B |s2cid=4351801 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/12647135 |access-date=20 April 2026 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Banger |first1=Kamaljit |last2=Tian |first2=Hanqin |last3=Lu |first3=Chaoqun |title=Do nitrogen fertilizers stimulate or inhibit methane emissions from rice fields? |journal=[[Global Change Biology]] |date=October 2012 |volume=18 |issue=10 |pages=3259–67 |doi=10.1111/j.1365-2486.2012.02762.x |pmid=28741830 |bibcode=2012GCBio..18.3259B |s2cid=31666406 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/230788712 |access-date=20 April 2026 }}</ref>

== Policy ==

=== Regulation ===

In Europe, problems with high nitrate concentrations in [[Runoff (hydrology)|runoff]] are being addressed by the European Union's Nitrates Directive.<ref>{{cite web |last=[[European Union]] |title=Nitrates: protecting waters against pollution caused by nitrates from agricultural sources |url=https://environment.ec.europa.eu/topics/water/nitrates_en |access-date=31 December 2025 }}</ref> Within [[Great Britain|Britain]], farmers are encouraged to manage their land more sustainably in '[[Catchment Sensitive Farming|catchment-sensitive farming]]'.<ref>{{cite web |last=Defra |title=Catchment-sensitive farming: a clear solution for farmers |work=[[Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs|Defra]] |url=http://www.defra.gov.uk/food-farm/land-manage/nitrates-watercourses/csf/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110630000845/http://www.defra.gov.uk/food-farm/land-manage/nitrates-watercourses/csf/ |archive-date=30 June 2011 |access-date=31 December 2025 }}</ref> In the [[United States|US]], high concentrations of nitrate and phosphorus in runoff and [[Storm drain|drainage]] water are classified as nonpoint source pollutants due to their diffuse origin; this pollution is regulated at the state level.<ref>{{cite web |title=Polluted runoff: nonpoint source (NPS) pollution |url=https://www.epa.gov/nps |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101119180721/http://water.epa.gov/polwaste/nps/ |archive-date=19 November 2010 |publisher=[[United States Environmental Protection Agency|EPA]] |access-date=31 December 2025 |url-status=live }}</ref> [[Oregon]] and [[Washington (state)|Washington]], both in the [[United States]], have fertilizer registration programs with on-line [[database]]s listing chemical analyses of fertilizers.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://agr.wa.gov/departments/pesticides-and-fertilizers/fertilizers/fertilizer-database |title=Fertilizer product database |website=[[Washington State Department of Agriculture]] |year=2025 |access-date=31 December 2025 |archive-date=30 October 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131030002056/http://agr.wa.gov/PestFert/Fertilizers/ProductDatabase.aspx |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.regulatory-info-sc.com/ |title=Metals content for fertilizer and soil amendment products |website=regulatory-info-sc.com |access-date=31 December 2025 }}</ref> [[Carbon emission trading]] and [[eco-tariff]]s affect the production and price of fertilizer.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Habib |first1=Mehvish |last2=Singh |first2=Sakshi |last3=Bist |first3=Yograj |last4=Kumar |first4=Yogesh |last5=Jan |first5=Kulsum |last6=Bashir |first6=Khalid |last7=Jan |first7=Shumaila |last8=Saxena |first8=Dharmesh Chandra |title=Carbon pricing and the food system: implications for sustainability and equity |journal=[[Trends in Food Science and Technology]] |volume=150 |date=August 2024 |doi=10.1016/j.tifs.2024.104577 |article-number=104577 |url=https://archive.org/details/habib-et-al.-2024 |access-date=31 December 2025 }}</ref>

=== Subsidies ===

In [[China]], [[regulation]]s have been implemented to control the use of N fertilizers in farming. In 2008, Chinese governments began to partially withdraw fertilizer [[subsidy|subsidies]], including subsidies to fertilizer transportation and to electricity and natural gas use in the industry. In consequence, the price of fertilizer has gone up and large-scale farms have begun to use less fertilizer. If large-scale farms keep reducing their use of fertilizer subsidies, they have no choice but to optimize the fertilizer they have which would therefore gain an increase in both grain yield and profit.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Ju |first1=Xiaotang |last2=Gu |first2=Baojing |last3=Wu |first3=Yiyun |last4=Galloway |first4=James N. |date=November 2016 |title=Reducing China's fertilizer use by increasing farm size |journal=[[Global Environmental Change]] |volume=41 |pages=26–32 |doi=10.1016/j.gloenvcha.2016.08.005 |bibcode=2016GEC....41...26J |url=https://z-library.ec/book/92179414/84dd6c |access-date=1 January 2026 }}{{Dead link|date=May 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref>

In March 2022, the [[United States Department of Agriculture]] announced a new $250M grant to promote American fertilizer production. Part of the [[Commodity Credit Corporation]], the grant program will support fertilizer production that is independent of dominant fertilizer suppliers, made in America, and utilizing innovative production techniques to jumpstart future competition.<ref>{{cite web |last=Andrew |first=Hannah |date=5 July 2022 |title=Addressing consolidation in agriculture: USDA's response to President Biden's directive to promote competition in the American economy |url=https://www.vermontlaw.edu/sites/default/files/2022-07/Addressing-Consolidation-in-Agriculture.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220720135110/https://www.vermontlaw.edu/sites/default/files/2022-07/Addressing-Consolidation-in-Agriculture.pdf |archive-date=20 July 2022 |url-status=live |access-date=1 January 2026 |website=Center for Agriculture and Food Systems, [[Vermont Law and Graduate School]] |page=7 }}</ref>

In the [[European Union]] The [[Russo-Ukrainian war]] and the subsequent strong increase in energy and mineral fertiliser prices highlighted the need for greater autonomy and efficiency in the production and use of fertilisers. The amended Temporary Crisis and Transition Framework for State Aid<ref>{{cite web |date=19 July 2024 |title=Temporary Crisis and Transition Framework |url=https://competition-policy.ec.europa.eu/state-aid/legislation/temporary-crisis-and-transition-framework_en |access-date=1 January 2026 |website=[[European Commission]] }}</ref> enabled EU countries to provide specific support to farmers and fertiliser producers. Funds generated by measures such as the cap on the market revenues of certain [[Electric generator|electricity generator]]s and the solidarity contribution can also be used, subject to the applicable conditions, for purposes of national support schemes.<ref>{{cite web |date=8 November 2022 |title=Ensuring availability and affordability of fertilisers: measures to maintain a sustainable European fertilisers' production, optimise use and reduce dependency on mineral fertilisers |url=https://agriculture.ec.europa.eu/common-agricultural-policy/agri-food-supply-chain/ensuring-availability-and-affordability-fertilisers_en |access-date=1 January 2026 |website=[[European Commission]] }}</ref>

======================================================================
ARTICLE: Harvest
WIKIPEDIA REVISION TEXT
======================================================================

{{short description|Process of gathering mature crops from fields}}
{{Other uses}}
{{Redirect|Reaping|other uses|Reaping (disambiguation)}}
{{More citations needed|date=May 2008}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=March 2026}}
[[File:Agriculture in Volgograd Oblast 002.JPG|thumb|Harvesting in [[Volgograd Oblast]], [[Sovkhoz|State farm]]]]
[[File:Harvest Straw Bales in Schleswig-Holstein.jpg|thumb|[[Straw]] in a field in [[Schleswig-Holstein]], [[Germany]].]]

'''Harvesting''' is the process of collecting plants, animals, or fish (as well as fungi) as food,<ref>{{Cite news |title=harvesting|url=https://dictionary.cambridge.org/dictionary/english/harvesting |access-date=17 August 2023 |website=[[Cambridge Advanced Learner's Dictionary|Cambridge Dictionary]]}}</ref> especially the process of gathering mature crops, and "the harvest" also refers to the collected crops. Reaping is the cutting of [[grain]] or [[pulse (legume)|pulses]] for harvest, typically using a [[scythe]], [[sickle]], or [[reaper]].<ref>{{cite book |title=American Heritage Dictionary |edition=4th |year=2000 |publisher=Houghton Mifflin Co |location=Boston |isbn=0-618-08230-1}}</ref> On smaller farms with minimal [[mechanization]], harvesting is the most [[manual labour|labor]]-intensive activity of the growing season. On large mechanized farms, harvesting uses [[farm machinery]], such as the [[combine harvester]]. Automation has increased the efficiency of both the seeding and harvesting processes. Specialized harvesting equipment, using [[conveyor belt]]s for gentle gripping and mass transport, replaces the manual task of removing each [[seedling]] by hand.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.beltcorp.com/seedling-harvesting-belts|title=Belts For Seedling Harvesting - Belt Corporation of America|date=18 April 2017|work=Belt Corporation of America|access-date=23 August 2017|language=en-US|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170824010112/https://www.beltcorp.com/seedling-harvesting-belts|archive-date=24 August 2017|url-status=dead}}</ref> The term "harvesting" in general usage may include immediate [[postharvest]] handling, including cleaning, sorting, packing, and cooling.

The completion of harvesting marks the end of the growing season, or the growing cycle for a particular crop, and the social importance of this event makes it the focus of seasonal celebrations such as [[harvest festival]]s, found in many cultures and religions.<ref>{{Cite web |date=7 December 2022 |title=Harvesting is the process of gathering a ripe crop from the fields. Reaping is the cutting of grain or pulse - Brainly.in |url=https://brainly.in/question/54502925 |access-date=27 February 2025 |website=brainly.in |language=en-IN}}</ref>

==Etymology==
"[[wikt:harvest#Noun|Harvest]]", a noun, came from the [[Old English]] word {{lang|ang|hærf-est}} (coined before the Angles moved from [[Angeln]] to Britain)<ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=XEYjMYf-AFUC&pg=PA207 Proceedings of the Philological Society], vol. 5, p. 207.</ref> meaning "[[autumn]]" (the season), "harvest-time", or "August". (It continues to mean "autumn" in British dialect, and "season of gathering crops" generally.) "The harvest" came to also mean the activity of reaping, gathering, and storing grain and other grown products during the autumn season, and also the grain and other grown products themselves. "Harvest" was also [[verbification|verbified]]: "To [[wikt:harvest#Verb|harvest]]" means to reap, gather, and store the harvest (or the crop). People who harvest and equipment that harvests are harvesters; while they do it, they are harvesting.

==Crop failure==
[[File:Total estimated agricultural production losses (1991–2023).svg|thumb|Total estimated agricultural production losses from disasters (1991–2023).]]
Crop failure (also known as harvest failure) is an absent or greatly diminished [[crop yield]] relative to expectation, caused by the plants being damaged, killed, or destroyed, or affected in some way that they fail to form edible fruit, seeds, or leaves in their expected abundance.<ref>{{Cite web |last=sreenath2001 |date=11 July 2020 |title=CROP FAILURE |url=https://internationaljournalofresearch.com/2020/07/11/crop-failure/ |access-date=27 February 2025 |website=International Journal of Research (IJR) |language=en}}</ref>

Crop failures can be caused by catastrophic events such as [[plant disease]] outbreaks (such as the [[Great Famine (Ireland)|Great Famine in Ireland]]), [[volcanic eruption]]s (such as the [[Year Without a Summer]]), heavy rainfall, [[storm]]s, [[flood]]s, or [[drought]], or by slow, cumulative effects of [[soil degradation]], too-high [[soil salinity]], [[erosion]], [[desertification]], usually as results of [[drainage]], [[overdrafting]] (for [[irrigation]]), [[overfertilization]], or [[overexploitation]].

In history, crop failures and subsequent [[famine]]s have triggered [[human migration]], [[rural exodus]], etc.

The proliferation of [[industrial farming|industrial]] [[monoculture]]s, with their reduction in [[crop diversity]] and dependence on heavy use of [[artificial fertilizer]]s and [[pesticide]]s, has led to overexploited soils that are nearly incapable of [[regeneration (ecology)|regeneration]]. Over the years, [[unsustainable]] farming of land degrades [[soil fertility]] and diminishes [[crop yield]]. With a steadily-increasing [[world population]] and local [[overpopulation]], even slightly diminishing yields are already the equivalent to a partial harvest failure.  Fertilizers obviate the need for [[soil regeneration]] in the first place, and [[international trade]] prevents local crop failures from developing into famines.

==Other uses==
[[File:A man and his donkey on the way back from the field in Aswan, Egypt (edited).jpg|thumb|Some people use their own animals for harvesting their crops]]
''Harvesting'' commonly refers to [[cereal|grain]] and produce, but also has other uses: [[fishing]] and [[logging]] are also referred to as harvesting. The term harvest is also used in reference to [[harvest (wine)|harvesting grapes]] for [[wine]]. ''Wild harvesting'' refers to the collection of plants and other edible supplies which have not been cultivated.<ref>[[Food and Agriculture Organization|Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations]], [https://www.fao.org/3/AA010E/AA010e10.htm Impact of Cultivation and Gathering of Medicinal Plants on Biodiversity: Global Trends and Issues: Appendix 1, Table 7], October 2002, accessed 29 January 2024</ref> Within the context of [[irrigation]], ''[[rainwater harvesting|water harvesting]]'' refers to the collection and storage of rainwater for agricultural or domestic uses. Instead of ''harvest'', the term ''exploit'' is also used, as in exploiting fisheries or water resources. ''[[Energy harvesting]]'' is the process of capturing and storing [[energy]] (such as [[solar power]], thermal energy, [[wind energy]], salinity gradients, and [[kinetic energy]]) that would otherwise go unexploited. ''Body harvesting'', or ''[[cadaver]] harvesting'', is the process of collecting and preparing cadavers for [[anatomy|anatomical]] study. In a similar sense, ''[[organ harvesting]]'' is the removal of tissues or organs from a donor for the purposes of transplanting.

In a non-agricultural sense, the word "harvesting" is an economic principle which is known as an exit event or [[liquidity event]]. For example, if a person or business was to cash out of an ownership position in a company or eliminate their investment in a product, it is known as a harvest strategy.<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.investopedia.com/terms/h/harvest-strategy.asp|title=Harvest Strategy|author=Investopedia Staff|date=9 January 2011|work=Investopedia|access-date=23 August 2017|language=en-US}}</ref>

===Canada===

''Harvesting'' or ''Domestic Harvesting'' in Canada refers to hunting, fishing, and plant gathering by [[First Nations in Canada|First Nations]], [[Métis in Canada|Métis]], and [[Inuit]] in discussions of [[Indigenous land claims in Canada|aboriginal or treaty rights]]. For example, in the [[Gwich'in]] [[Comprehensive Land Claim]] Agreement, "Harvesting means gathering, hunting, trapping or fishing{{Nbsp}}...".<ref>{{cite web |title=Gwich'in Comprehensive Land Claim Agreement |url=http://www.ainc-inac.gc.ca/pr/agr/gwich/gwic/index_e.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20040529182125/http://www.ainc-inac.gc.ca/pr/agr/gwich/gwic/index_e.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=29 May 2004 |publisher=Aboriginal Affairs and Northern Development Canada website }}</ref> Similarly, in the [[Tłı̨chǫ|Tlicho]] Land Claim and Self Government Agreement, {{" '}}Harvesting' means, in relation to wildlife, hunting, trapping or fishing and, in relation to plants or trees, gathering or cutting."<ref>{{cite web |title=Tlicho Agreement |url=http://www.aadnc-aandc.gc.ca/eng/1292948193972 |publisher=Aboriginal Affairs and Northern Development Canada website |access-date=19 March 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120714091947/http://www.aadnc-aandc.gc.ca/eng/1292948193972 |archive-date=14 July 2012 |url-status=dead }}</ref>
