======================================================================
ARTICLE: Pig farming
WIKIPEDIA REVISION TEXT
======================================================================

{{short description|Raising and breeding of domestic pigs}}
{{redirect|Pig farmer|other uses|Pig Farmer (disambiguation)}}
{{for|the town in Ghana|Pig Farm (Ghana)}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=October 2018}}
[[File:JEFO-Pigs.jpg|thumb|[[Large White pig|Large White]] piglets on a farm]]
[[File:Suckling pigs.JPG|thumb|A [[Large White pig|Large White]] sow suckling her piglets]]
[[File:NMA.0063325 Interiör från svinhus, Bjärka-Säby, Östergötland.jpg|thumb|Interior of pig farm at [[Bjärka-Säby Castle]], [[Sweden]], 1911]]

'''Pig farming''', '''pork farming''', '''pig production''' or '''hog farming''' is the raising and breeding of [[domestic pig]]s as [[livestock]], and is a branch of [[animal husbandry]]. Pigs are farmed principally for [[food]] (e.g. [[pork]]: [[bacon]], [[ham]], [[gammon (meat)|gammon]]) and [[leather#From other animals|skins]].

Pigs are amenable to many different styles of farming: [[Intensive pig farming|intensive commercial units]], commercial [[free range]] enterprises, or extensive farming (being allowed to wander around a village, town or city, or tethered in a simple shelter or kept in a pen outside the owner's house). Historically, farm pigs were kept in small numbers and were closely associated with the residence of the owner, or in the same village or town.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Flisser |first1=Ana |last2=Ganaba |first2=Rasmané |last3=Praet |first3=Nicolas |last4=Carabin |first4=Hélène |last5=Millogo |first5=Athanase |last6=Tarnagda |first6=Zékiba |last7=Dorny |first7=Pierre |last8=Hounton |first8=Sennen |last9=Sow |first9=Adama |last10=Nitiéma |first10=Pascal |last11=Cowan |first11=Linda D. |title=Factors Associated with the Prevalence of Circulating Antigens to Porcine Cysticercosis in Three Villages of Burkina Faso |journal=PLOS Neglected Tropical Diseases |volume=5 |issue=1 |pages=e927 |year=2011 |pmid=21245913 |pmc=3014946 |doi=10.1371/journal.pntd.0000927 |doi-access=free }}</ref> They were valued as a source of meat and fat, and for their ability to convert inedible food into meat and manure, and were often fed household [[food waste]] when kept on a homestead.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lander |first1=Brian |last2=Schneider |first2=Mindi |last3=Brunson |first3=Katherine |title=A History of Pigs in China: From Curious Omnivores to Industrial Pork |journal=The Journal of Asian Studies |date=2020 |volume=79 |issue=4 |pages=865–889|doi=10.1017/S0021911820000054 |s2cid=225700922 |url=https://library.wur.nl/WebQuery/wurpubs/567921 |url-access=subscription }}</ref> Pigs have been farmed to dispose of municipal [[food waste|garbage]] on a large scale.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://archive.org/stream/collectiondispos00morsrich/collectiondispos00morsrich_djvu.txt |title=Full text of "The collection and disposal of municipal waste" |publisher=New York, The Municipal Journal and Engineer |access-date=6 October 2018}}</ref>

All these forms of pig farm are in use today, though [[intensive pig farming|intensive farms]] are by far the most popular, due to their potential to raise a large amount of pigs in a very cost-efficient manner.<ref>{{cite web |title=Where have all the pig farmers gone |publisher=ABC Rural |date=5 May 2014 |url=http://www.abc.net.au/news/rural/2014-05-02/pig-farmer-decline/5426020}}</ref> In developed nations, commercial farms house thousands of pigs in climate-controlled buildings.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://extension.missouri.edu/programs/swine-extension|title=Swine Extension - Programs &#124; MU Extension|website=extension.missouri.edu}}</ref> Pigs are a popular form of [[livestock]], with more than one billion pigs butchered each year worldwide, 100 million in the [[United States]]. The majority of pigs are used for human food, but also supply skin, [[Lard|fat]] and other materials for use in clothing, ingredients for processed foods,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.motherearthnews.com/real-food/seasonal-recipes/cooking-with-lard-zmgz12djzkon |title=The Lost Art of Cooking With Lard |work=Mother Earth News |date=30 October 2012 |access-date=6 October 2018}}</ref> cosmetics,<ref>{{cite web |url=https://cosmeticsinfo.org/ingredient/lard |title=Ingredient: Lard |work=cosmeticsinfo.org |access-date=6 October 2018 |archive-date=26 December 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171226211746/http://www.cosmeticsinfo.org/ingredient/lard |url-status=dead }}</ref> and medical use.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.purdue.edu/uns/html4ever/0002.Badylak.SIS.html |title=Material from pig intestine is remedy for deep sores, incontinence |publisher=Purdue.edu |access-date=6 October 2018}}</ref>

==Production and trade==
{{Infobox agricultural production|animal=pig|year=2019|amount1=310.4|amount10=12.7|amount9=14.1|amount8=18.4|amount7=19.6|amount6=21.6|amount5=23.7|amount4=40.6|amount3=78.7|amount2=143.1|country1={{PRC}} (Mainland)|country10={{PHL}}|country9={{CAN}}|country8={{MEX}}|country7={{VNM}}|country6={{MMR}}|country5={{RUS}}|country4={{BRA}}|country3={{USA}}|country2={{EU}}|world=850.3}}
Pigs are farmed in many countries, though the countries  mainly consuming them are in Asia, meaning there is a significant international and even intercontinental trade in live and slaughtered pigs. Despite having the world's largest herd, China is a net importer of pigs as China consumes about 50% of global pork production.<ref>{{Cite web |title=China's plan to cut meat consumption by 50% cheered by climate campaigners {{!}} China {{!}} The Guardian |url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2016/jun/20/chinas-meat-consumption-climate-change |access-date=2023-03-23 |website=amp.theguardian.com}}</ref> The total amount of pork consumed in China is 57 million tons (as of 2021) and pork accounted for 60 percent of total meat consumption within the country.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=Five new trends in China's meat consumption {{!}} McKinsey |url=https://www.mckinsey.com/industries/consumer-packaged-goods/our-insights/for-love-of-meat-five-trends-in-china-that-meat-executives-must-grasp |access-date=2023-03-23 |website=www.mckinsey.com}}</ref> China has been increasing its imports during its economic development; many within China's population of 1.2 billion people prioritize eating pork as their main consumption of meat, unlike other countries where most people would prioritize having [[poultry]].<ref name=":2" /> In addition, since 2007, China possesses a strategic pork reserve with a government mandate to  "stabilize live hog prices, prevent excessive hog price drops, which damage the interests of farmers and to ease the negative effects of the cyclical nature of hog production and market prices." In China, the government actively intervened in the pork market during periods of instability by releasing pork reserves into the market whenever hogs get too expensive in China, in order to hold down prices for consumers. Conversely when prices of pork are deemed too low and unsustainable for farmers, the reserve buys up pigs to ensure farmers remain profitable.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Kemp |first=Ted |date=2013-06-06 |title=Hog Stock: Inside China's Strategic Pork Reserve |url=https://www.cnbc.com/2013/06/06/hog-stock-inside-chinas-strategic-pork-reserve.html |access-date=2023-03-23 |website=CNBC |language=en}}</ref>

The largest exporters of pigs are the United States, the European Union, and Canada. As an example, more than half of Canadian production (22.8 million pigs) in 2008 was exported, going to 143 countries.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.canadapork.com/en/industry-information/canadian-pork-exports |title=Canadian Pork Exports |work=Canadapork.com |access-date=6 October 2018 |archive-date=8 December 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171208024240/http://www.canadapork.com/en/industry-information/canadian-pork-exports |url-status=dead }}</ref>

Among animals raised for their meat, pigs have a lower [[feed conversion ratio]] than cattle, which can provide an advantage in lower [[unit price]] of meat because the cost of [[animal feed]] per kilogram or pound of resultant meat is lower. However, there are also many other economic variables in [[meat industry|meat production and distribution]], so the price differential of pork and beef at the point of retail sale does not always correspond closely to the differential in feed conversion ratios. Nonetheless, the favorable ratio often tends to make pork more affordable compared to beef.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Ciuraru |first=Ioana |date=2021-03-31 |title=Why Is Pork So Cheap ? 3 Reasons Pork Is Cheaper Than Beef And Any Other Meat |url=https://foodiosity.com/why-is-pork-so-cheap/ |access-date=2023-03-23 |website=Foodiosity |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-06-08 |title=Why Is Pork Cheaper Than Beef? (5 Main Reasons Explained) |url=https://carnivorestyle.com/why-is-pork-cheaper-than-beef/ |access-date=2023-03-23 |language=en-US}}</ref>

==Relationship between handlers and pigs==
The way in which a stockperson interacts with pigs affects animal welfare which in some circumstances can correlate with production measures. Many routine interactions can cause fear, which can result in stress and decreased production.

There are various methods of handling pigs which can be separated into those which lead to positive or negative reactions by the animals. These reactions are based on how the pigs interpret a handler's behavior.

===Negative interactions===
Many negative interactions with pigs arise from stock-people dealing with large numbers of pigs. Because of this, many handlers can become complacent about [[animal welfare]] and fail to ensure positive interactions with pigs. Negative interactions include overly heavy tactile interactions (slaps, punches, kicks, and bites), the use of [[cattle prod|electric]] goads and fast movements. It can also include killing them. These interactions can result in fear in the animals, which can develop into stress. Overly heavy tactile interactions from the human handlers can cause increased basal cortisol levels (a "stress" hormone).<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Hemsworth |first1=P.H |title=Human–animal interactions in livestock production |journal=Applied Animal Behaviour Science |volume=81 |issue=3 |year=2003 |pages=185–98 |doi=10.1016/S0168-1591(02)00280-0}}</ref> Negative interactions that cause fear mean the escape reactions of the pigs can be extremely vigorous, thereby risking injury to both stock and handlers. Stress can result in [[immunosuppression]],<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Hemsworth PH, Coleman GJ, Barnett JL, Borg S |title=Relationships between human-animal interactions and productivity of commercial dairy cows |journal=Journal of Animal Science |volume=78 |issue=11 |pages=2821–31 |year=2000 |pmid=11063304 |url=http://www.animalsciencepublications.org/publications/jas/articles/78/11/2821 |doi=10.2527/2000.78112821x |url-access=subscription |archive-date=10 August 2016 |access-date=15 May 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160810162021/https://www.animalsciencepublications.org/publications/jas/articles/78/11/2821 |url-status=dead }}</ref> leading to an increased susceptibility to disease. Studies have shown that these negative handling techniques result in an overall reduction in growth rates of pigs.

"In Canada the Federal government does not regulate the treatment on farms and most provinces have animal cruelty legislation but they typically contain expectations for general agricultural practices."  This lack of legislation perpetuates the cruel treatment of swine.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |date=2020-11-12 |title=Humane Society International/Canada demands pork industry quit stalling on phasing out cruel crates for mother pigs |url=https://www.hsi.org/news-media/hsi-demands-pork-industry-phase-out-cruel-crates-for-mother-pigs/ |access-date=2022-03-03 |website=Humane Society International |language=en-US}}</ref> "The NFACC codes of practice are developed by the industry and are not enforced with third party oversight."<ref name=":0" />

===Positive interactions===
Various interactions can be considered either positive or neutral. Neutral interactions are considered positive because, in conjunction with positive interactions, they contribute to an overall non-negative relationship between the pig handler and the animal livestock. Pigs are often fearful of fast movements. When entering a pen, it is good practice for the pig handler to enter with slow and deliberate movements. These minimize fear and therefore reduce stress. Pigs are very curious animals. Allowing the pigs to approach and smell whilst patting or resting a hand on the pig's back are examples of positive behavior. Pigs also respond positively to verbal interaction. Minimizing fear of humans allow handlers to perform husbandry practices in a safer and more efficient manner. By reducing stress, stock are made more comfortable to feed when near the pig handlers, resulting in increased productivity.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Hemsworth |first1=P.H. |last2=Price |first2=E.O. |last3=Borgwardt |first3=R. |title=Behavioural responses of domestic pigs and cattle to humans and novel stimuli |journal=Applied Animal Behaviour Science |volume=50 |issue=1 |year=1996 |pages=43–56 |doi=10.1016/0168-1591(96)01067-2}}</ref>

==Impacts on sow breeding==

Hogs raised in confinement systems tend to produce 23.5 piglets per year. Between 2013 and 2016, sow death rates nearly doubled in the United States, from 5.8 to 10.2 percent. 25 to 50 percent of deaths were caused by [[pelvic organ prolapse|prolapse]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2018/oct/01/death-rates-surge-female-pigs-us|title='We've bred them to their limit': death rates surge for female pigs in the US|last=Greenaway|first=Twilight|date=2018-10-01|website=the Guardian|language=en|access-date=2018-11-17}}</ref>

Other probable causes of death include vitamin deficiency, [[mycotoxin]]s in feed, high density diets or abdominal issues.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://bigthink.com/technology-innovation/pig-deaths-in-factory-farming-doubles?rebelltitem=4#rebelltitem4|title=Considering the porcine future|date=2018-10-02|work=Big Think|access-date=2018-11-17|language=en}}</ref> [[Iowa]]'s Pork Industry Center collects mortality data in collaboration with the [[National Pork Board]] to collect data from over 400,000 sows from 16 U.S. states. The farms range in size and facility types. Increasing death rates are a profit concern to the industry, so money is invested into research to find solutions.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.ipic.iastate.edu/news/SowMortalityProject2018.html|title=Iowa Pork Industry Center - Iowa State University|website=ipic.iastate.edu|language=en-us|access-date=2018-11-17|archive-date=15 December 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181215084335/https://www.ipic.iastate.edu/news/SowMortalityProject2018.html|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Genetic manipulation==
Pigs were originally bred to rapidly gain weight and backfat in the late 1980s. In a more fat-conscious modern day America, pigs are now being bred to have less back fat and produce more offspring, which pushes the sow's body too far and is deemed one of the causes of the current prolapse epidemic. Researchers and veterinarians are seeking ways to positively impact the health of the hogs and benefit the hog business without taking much from the economy.<ref name="Big Think">{{cite news|url=https://bigthink.com/technology-innovation/pig-deaths-in-factory-farming-doubles?rebelltitem=3#rebelltitem3|title=Genetic manipulation for more salable pork or more pigs|date=2018-10-02|work=Big Think|access-date=2018-11-17|language=en}}</ref>

==Terminology==
{{Redirect-distinguish|Shoat|Sheep–goat hybrid}}

Pigs are extensively farmed, and therefore the terminology is well developed:
*'''Pig''', '''hog''', or '''swine''', the species as a whole, or any member of it. The singular of "swine" is the same as the plural.
*'''Shoat''' (or shote), '''piglet''', or (where the species is called "hog") '''pig''', unweaned young pig, or any immature pig<ref>{{Cite web|url= https://teachingwiththemes.com/index.php/2018/10/15/pork-primary-sources/|title= What's a shoat?|last=Resor|first=Cynthia|date=October 2018|website=teachingwiththemes.com}}</ref>
*'''Sucker''', a pig between birth and weaning
*'''[[Weaner]]''', a young pig recently separated from the sow
*'''[[Runt]]''', an unusually small and weak piglet, often one in a litter
*'''Boar''' or '''hog''', male pig of breeding age
*'''Barrow''', male pig [[castration|castrated]] before puberty
*'''Stag''', male pig castrated later in life (castrated after maturity)
*'''Gilt''', young female not yet mated, or not yet farrowed, or after only one litter (depending on local usage).<ref name='ucdavis_swineguide'>[http://ucce.ucdavis.edu/files/filelibrary/1385/2027.PDF Swine Study Guide] {{webarchive|url= https://web.archive.org/web/20071202060724/http://ucce.ucdavis.edu/files/filelibrary/1385/2027.PDF |date=2 December 2007}} from [[UC Davis]]</ref>
*'''Sow''', breeding female, or female after first or second litter

===Pigs for slaughter===
[[File:NRCSAR83008 - Arkansas (279)(NRCS Photo Gallery).jpg|thumb|Finishing pigs on a farm]]
*'''[[Suckling pig]]''', a piglet slaughtered for its tender meat
*'''Feeder pig''', a weaned gilt or barrow weighing between {{convert|18|kg|lb|abbr=on}} and {{convert|37|kg|lb|abbr=on}} at 6 to 8 weeks of age that is sold to be finished for slaughter
*'''Porker''', market pig between {{convert|30|kg|lb|abbr=on}} and about {{convert|54|kg|lb|abbr=on}} dressed weight
*'''Baconer''', a market pig between {{convert|65|kg|lb|abbr=on}} and {{convert|80|kg|lb|abbr=on}} dressed weight. The maximum weight can vary between processors.
*'''Grower''', a pig between weaning and sale or transfer to the breeding herd, sold for slaughter or killed for rations.{{Clarify|date=June 2008}}<!-- What does "rations" mean? -->
*'''Finisher''', a grower pig over {{convert|70|kg|lb|abbr=on}} liveweight
*'''Butcher hog''', a pig of approximately {{convert|100|kg|lb|abbr=on}}, ready for the market. In some markets (Italy) the final weight of butcher pig is in the {{convert|180|kg|lb|abbr=on}} range. They tend to have hind legs suitable to produce cured ham
*'''Backfatter''', cull breeding pig sold for meat; usually refers specifically to a cull sow, but is sometimes used in reference to boars

===Groups===
*'''Herd''', a group of pigs, or all the pigs on a farm or in a region
*'''Sounder''', a small group of pigs (or [[wild boar]]) foraging in woodland

===Pig parts===
* [[Pig's trotters|'''Trotters''']], the hooves of pigs (they have four [[hoof]]ed toes on each foot, walking mainly on the larger central two)

===Biology===
*'''In pig''', pregnant
*'''Farrowing''', giving birth
*'''Hogging''', a sow when on heat (during [[estrus]])

===Housing===
[[File:Pig farm Vampula 9.jpg|thumb|Pig farm in [[Vampula]], [[Finland]]]]
*'''[[Sty]]''', a small pig-house, usually with an outdoor run or a pig confinement
*'''Pig-shed''', a larger pig-house
*'''Ark''', a low semi circular field-shelter for pigs
*'''Curtain-barn''', a long, open building with curtains on the long sides of the barn. This increases ventilation on hot, humid summer days

==Environmental and health impacts==
{{Main|Environmental impacts of pig farming}}

Feces and waste often spread to surrounding neighborhoods, polluting air and water with toxic waste particles.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Nicole |first=Wendee |date=21 April 2017 |title=CAFOs and Environmental Justice: The Case of North Carolina |journal=Environmental Health Perspectives |volume=121 |issue=6 |pages=a182–a189 |doi=10.1289/ehp.121-a182 |pmc=3672924 |pmid=23732659}}</ref> Waste from swine on these farms carry a host of pathogens and bacteria as well as [[Heavy metal (elements)|heavy metals]]. These toxins can leach down through the soil into groundwater, polluting local drinking water supplies. Pathogens can also become airborne, polluting the air and harming individuals when ingested.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Thorne|first=Peter S. |date=21 April 2017 |title=Environmental Health Impacts of Concentrated Animal Feeding Operations: Anticipating Hazards—Searching for Solutions |journal=Environmental Health Perspectives |volume=115 |issue=2 |pages=296–297 |doi=10.1289/ehp.8831 |pmc=1817701 |pmid=17384781}}</ref> Contents from waste have been shown to cause detrimental health implications, as well as harmful algal blooms in surrounding bodies of water.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://qz.com/244387/poisonous-algae-blooms-now-plague-20-states-around-the-us-not-just-ohio/ |title=It's not just Ohio—poisonous algae blooms now plague 20 US states |last=Guilford |first=Gwynn |work=Quartz|access-date=21 April 2017}}</ref> Due to [[Concentrated animal feeding operation|Concentrated Animal Feed Operations]] (CAFOs), those who live in the surrounding areas of pig farms tend to experience health complications. Symptoms included headaches, nausea, and weakness due to the fumes that are emitted from these farms.{{citation needed|date=November 2022}} Those who work directly inside these farms often experience these symptoms more intensely. Typically, workers of these farms experience respiratory issues such as wheezing, coughing, and tightness of the chest as well as eye and nasal irritation.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Crook|first1=B.|last2=Robertson|first2=J.F.|last3=Glass|first3=S.A. Travers|last4=Botheroyd|first4=E.M.|last5=Lacey|first5=J.|last6=Topping|first6=M.D.|date=1991-07-01|title=Airborne Dust, Ammonia, Microorganisms, and Antigens in Pig Confinement Houses and the Respiratory Health of Exposed Farm Workers|url=https://doi.org/10.1080/15298669191364721|journal=American Industrial Hygiene Association Journal|volume=52|issue=7|pages=271–279|doi=10.1080/15298669191364721|issn=0002-8894|pmid=1951065|url-access=subscription}}</ref> This is in part due to the air quality being poor because of the air particles being contaminated with hog feces.{{citation needed|date=November 2022}}

Little to no regulation has been written by the EPA and federal legislators surrounding CAFOs to protect the welfare of both the environment and humans from their impacts.<ref>{{Cite web|last=US EPA|first=OLEM|date=2017-09-05|title=CERCLA and EPCRA Reporting Requirements for Air Releases of Hazardous Substances from Animal Waste at Farms|url=https://www.epa.gov/epcra/cercla-and-epcra-reporting-requirements-air-releases-hazardous-substances-animal-waste-farms|access-date=2021-11-23|website=[[United States Environmental Protection Agency]]|language=en}}</ref> The only permit required by federal law on wastewater runoff by CAFOs is the National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) permit. NPDES are authorized under the Clean Water Act and aim to reduce dumping of pollutants in water systems.<ref>{{cite journal|journal = Harvard Environmental Law Review|volume=31|issue=2|ssrn=1555771|title=Generally Illegal: NPDES General Permits Under the Clean Water Act |date=25 March 2007 |last1=Gaba |first1=Jeffrey M.|url=https://heinonline.org/HOL/Page?handle=hein.journals/helr31&div=15&g_sent=1&casa_token=&collection=journals|access-date=2021-11-23}}</ref> However, one of the most detrimental waste management practices used at swine farms, manure lagoons, have little to no regulations surrounding waste management, as they are not connected to a moving water source and therefore is not seen as an imminent threat to human or environmental health.<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://doi.org/10.13031/2013.8827|access-date=2021-11-23|journal=Transactions of the ASAE|doi=10.13031/2013.8827 |language=en-us|title=Constructed Wetlands for Treatment of Swine Wastewater from an Anaerobic Lagoon |year=2002 |last1=p. g. Hunt |last2=a. a. Szögi |last3=f. j. Humenik |last4=j. m. Rice |last5=t. a. Matheny |last6=k. c. Stone |volume=45 |issue=3 |url-access=subscription }}</ref>

== Occupational hazards ==
Common occupational hazards faced by pig farmers include but are not limited to exposure to toxic gases and particulate matter.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Archibald |first=Joy |date=2015-07-21 |title=Upper Midwest Agricultural Safety and Health CenterOccupational Hazards in Pork Production Associated with Production Practices - Upper Midwest Agricultural Safety and Health Center |url=https://umash.umn.edu/portfolio/occupational-hazards-in-pork-production-associated-with-production-practices/ |access-date=2024-03-10 |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Board |first=National Pork |title=Noise |url=https://porkgateway.org/resource/noise/ |access-date=2024-03-10 |website=Pork Information Gateway}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=NASD - Ergonomics and Musculoskeletal Injuries in Agriculture |url=http://nasdonline.org/ |access-date=2024-03-10 |website=nasdonline.org}}</ref> The Occupational Safety and Health Administration or [[Occupational Safety and Health Administration|OSHA]] sets health and safety standards for hazardous substances in the workplace called [[permissible exposure limit]]s or PELs.<ref name=":02">{{Cite web |date=2022-12-14 |title=1988 OSHA PEL Project Documentation {{!}} NIOSH {{!}} CDC |url=https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/pel88/pelstart.html |access-date=2024-03-11 |website=www.cdc.gov |language=en-us}}</ref> Specific PELs exist for toxic gases and particulate matter and these standards are legally enforced by OSHA to ensure that the safety and health of workers are protected.<ref name=":02" />

===Toxic gas and particulate matter exposure===
[[File:GHS-pictogram-skull.svg|thumb|Toxic gases can accumulate to dangerous levels in pig barns]]
Toxic gases including [[hydrogen sulfide]], [[ammonia]], [[methane]] and [[carbon dioxide]] are produced as a result of the decomposition of pig waste and these gases become highly concentrated in enclosed spaces of pig barns which can be hazardous to health when inhaled.<ref name=":12">{{Cite web |title=Toxicities Caused by Gases {{!}} Iowa State University |url=https://vetmed.iastate.edu/vdpam/FSVD/swine/index-diseases/toxicities-gases |access-date=2024-03-11 |website=vetmed.iastate.edu}}</ref> [[Carbon monoxide]] is another commonly associated toxic gas that can accumulate in pig barns as a result of the trapping of combustion byproducts such as malfunctioning furnaces or gas heat sources in the absence of adequate ventilation.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Carbon Monoxide Toxicity {{!}} Iowa State University |url=https://vetmed.iastate.edu/vdpam/FSVD/swine/index-diseases/carbon-monoxide-toxicity |access-date=2024-03-11 |website=vetmed.iastate.edu}}</ref>

Hydrogen sulfide gas has a foul, "rotten eggs" smell at low concentrations but paralyzes the [[olfactory nerve]] at higher concentrations so that no smell is sensed.<ref name=":23">{{Cite web |title=Safety in Swine Production Systems – Hogs, Pigs, and Pork |url=https://swine.extension.org/safety-in-swine-production-systems/#Toxic_and_Asphyxiating_Gases |access-date=2024-03-11 |website=swine.extension.org}}</ref> Exposure to high levels, well beyond the OSHA [[Permissible exposure limit|PEL]], of hydrogen sulfide can cause fatal respiratory paralysis.<ref name=":12" /> The common source of hydrogen sulfide are covered manure pits below the pig barns that act as feces reservoirs.<ref name=":23"/> These manure pits require regular emptying and during this process, high levels of hydrogen sulfide is released and seeps into pig barns.<ref name=":12" /> Pig barns must be void of any human or animal inhabitants during this emptying process and require a several hour "waiting period" until occupants can safely reenter the barn.<ref name=":12" />

Ammonia gas has a strong odor that can be smelled at low levels, below the OSA PEL, but does not have any negative health effects.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |title=Ammonia Toxicity {{!}} Iowa State University |url=https://vetmed.iastate.edu/vdpam/FSVD/swine/index-diseases/ammonia-toxicity |access-date=2024-03-22 |website=vetmed.iastate.edu}}</ref> At higher levels, ammonia is irritating to the body's [[mucous membrane]]s such as the eyes, nose, mouth, throat and lungs.<ref name=":3" /> Particulate matter in pig barns often absorbs ammonia as it floats through the air.<ref name=":4">{{Cite journal |last1=Yang |first1=Xufei |last2=Haleem |first2=Noor |last3=Osabutey |first3=Augustina |last4=Cen |first4=Zhisheng |last5=Albert |first5=Karlee L. |last6=Autenrieth |first6=Daniel |date=March 2022 |title=Particulate Matter in Swine Barns: A Comprehensive Review |journal=Atmosphere |language=en |volume=13 |issue=3 |pages=490 |doi=10.3390/atmos13030490 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2022Atmos..13..490Y |issn=2073-4433}}</ref> These particles are then inhaled and increase the irritating effect of ammonia.<ref name=":4" />

Decomposition of pig waste produces methane and other combustible gases meaning that they can burn, catch fire or explode easily.<ref name=":5">{{Cite web |last1=Donham |first1=Kelley |last2=Aherin |first2=Robert |last3=Baker |first3=David |last4=Hetzel |first4=Glen |date=2006 |editor-last=Baker |editor-first=James |editor2-last=Bodman |editor2-first=Gerald |editor3-last=Kerig |editor3-first=Ken |editor4-last=Sweeten |editor4-first=John |title=Safety in Swine Production Systems |url=https://porkgateway.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/07/saftey-in-swine-production-systems1.pdf |access-date=March 22, 2024 |website=Fact Sheet: Pork Information Gateway}}</ref> some of these gases such as carbon dioxide and methane are also known as chemical [[Asphyxiant gas|asphyxiants]] and at high levels can cause suffocation by displacing oxygen from the air.<ref name=":5" />

[[Particulate matter]] is produced when small fragments of pig hair or skin, dried feces, or feed can detach and become suspended in the air in pig barns.<ref name=":4" /> The increased concentration of particulate matter in the air, especially in confined spaces, can lead to respiratory tract irritation and other health effects when inhaled.<ref name=":4" /> Bacteria and viruses, such as [[influenza]], can travel through the air on particulate matter and increase the risk of transmission of disease.<ref name=":4" />

OSHA requires that toxic gas and particulate matter be measured at least twice yearly preferably in the autumn months and again in the winter when natural ventilation is the most reduced.<ref name=":6">{{Cite web |last=Board |first=National Pork |title=Safety in Swine Production Systems |url=https://porkgateway.org/resource/safety-in-swine-production-systems/ |access-date=2024-03-24 |website=Pork Information Gateway}}</ref> Workers are also advised to wear [[N95 respirator|N-95 respirators]] and eye protection when inside of pig barns to prevent the inhalation of toxic gases and particulate matter as well as irritation to the eyes.<ref name=":23"/><ref name=":6" />

==Geopolitical issues==
As with other [[commodity|commodities]], pork presents challenges in the politics of [[international trade]] as national interests compete and seek economic [[modus vivendi]]. Changes to policy can upset the existing balances, prompting economic anxiety. For example, in 2020, the hog farming sector in Taiwan was upset by a decision to allow imports from the United States without labeling of [[ractopamine]] use.<ref name="Reuters-Wang-2020-12-15">{{cite news |last1=Wang |first1=Ann |title=In Taiwan pig country, U.S. pork decision rankles, divides families |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/taiwan-politics-pork/in-taiwan-pig-country-u-s-pork-decision-rankles-divides-families-idUSKBN28Q071 |access-date=2020-12-16 |work=Reuters.com |agency=Reuters wire service |date=2020-12-15}}</ref> Farmers' views varied on how negative the effects might be.<ref name="Reuters-Wang-2020-12-15"/> Issues of pride and degree of [[autarky]] also figure into such debates; people understandably wonder whether trade competition changes will deeply damage domestic production capability, while accurate quantitative answers are often difficult to find amid the mass of debate.<ref name="Reuters-Wang-2020-12-15"/>

==Drugs==
===Growth promoters===
====Ractopamine====
Most pigs in the US receive [[ractopamine]] which promotes muscle instead of fat, quicker weight gain,  and reduced costs and pollutants in the [[Environmental impacts of pig farming|environment]]. Such pigs consume less feed to reach finishing weight and produce less [[manure]]. Ractopamine has not been approved for use by the European Union, China, Russia, and several other countries.<ref>{{cite web|title=Ractopamine — a beta-agonist growth promotant; from google (pig drug accumulate fat) result 3| website= [[NPR]]| url= https://www.npr.org/sections/thesalt/2015/08/14/432102733/a-muscle-drug-for-pigs-comes-out-of-the-shadows}}</ref>

====Colistin====
[[China]] once used [[colistin]] (an antibiotic) as growth promoter ([[Antibiotic use in livestock#Growth stimulation|subtherapeutic antibiotic use]]) but discovered a colistin-resistant form of ''E. coli'' bacteria in a pig from a [[Shanghai]] farm in 2013. Investigations then led to the identification of "a gene called MCR-1 that allowed bacteria to survive colistin treatment in animals and humans."<ref name="china_colistin_1"/> In 2016, these findings led China to ban colistin as growth promoter.<ref name= "china_colistin_1">{{cite web| url= https://www.mrc.ac.uk/news/browse/uk-china-collaboration-informs-animal-feed-antibiotic-ban/|title=UK-China collaboration informs animal feed antibiotic ban |website=Medical Research Council |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20170327080933/https://www.mrc.ac.uk/news/browse/uk%2Dchina%2Dcollaboration%2Dinforms%2Danimal%2Dfeed%2Dantibiotic%2Dban/|archive-date=27 March 2017|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name= 'china_colistin_2'>{{cite web |last= McKenna |first=Maryn |title=Apocalypse Pig: The Last Antibiotic Begins to Fail |url=https://www.nationalgeographic.com/science/phenomena/2015/11/21/mcr-gene-colistin/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181007040042/https://www.nationalgeographic.com/science/phenomena/2015/11/21/mcr-gene-colistin/ |url-status=dead |archive-date=7 October 2018 |date=21 November 2015 |work=National Geographic}}</ref>

===Antibiotics===
A systematic review found that [[penicillin]]s and [[Tetracycline antibiotics|tetracyclines]] were the most commonly used antibiotics in pigs.<ref>{{Cite journal|date=2019-06-01|title=Patterns of antibiotic use in global pig production: A systematic review|journal=Veterinary and Animal Science|language=en|volume=7|article-number=100058|doi=10.1016/j.vas.2019.100058|issn=2451-943X|pmc=7386699|pmid=32734079|last1=Lekagul|first1=Angkana|last2=Tangcharoensathien|first2=Viroj|last3=Yeung|first3=Shunmay}}</ref>

==Parasites==
[[Toxoplasmosis]] is a constant pressure on pig farming. Worldwide, the percentage of pigs harboring viable ''[[Toxoplasma gondii]]'' parasites has been measured to be 3{{Nbsp}}% to 71.43{{Nbsp}}%.<ref name="Nissapatorn-et-al-2013">{{cite book | editor1-last=Lim | editor1-first=Yvonne Ai Lian | editor2-last=Vythilingam | editor2-first=Indra | last1=Nissapatorn | first1=Veeranoot | last2=Lau | first2=Yee-Ling | last3=Fong | first3=Mun-Yik | title=Parasites and their vectors | chapter=''Toxoplasma gondii'': The Parasite in Trend | publisher=[[Springer Vienna|Springer]] | publication-place=[[Vienna]] | year=2013 | isbn=978-3-7091-1553-4 | pages=155–175}}</ref> Surveys of seroprevalence (''T. gondii'' antibodies in blood) are more common, and such measurements are indicative of the high relative seroprevalence in pigs across the world.<ref name="Dubey-2016">{{cite book | last=Dubey | first=J. P. | title=Toxoplasmosis of animals and humans | publisher=[[CRC Press]] | publication-place=[[Boca Raton]] | year=2016 | isbn=978-1-4200-9236-3 | oclc=423572366 | pages=xvii+313}} {{isbn|9781420092363}}</ref>{{rp|145–151}} Neonatal [[piglet (animal)|piglet]]s have been found to suffer the entire range of severity, including progression to [[stillbirth]].<ref name="Dubey-2016"/>{{rp|153}}<ref name="Dubey-2009">{{cite journal | last=Dubey | first=J. P. | title=Toxoplasmosis in pigs—The last 20 years | journal=[[Veterinary Parasitology (journal)|Veterinary Parasitology]] | publisher=[[Elsevier]] | volume=164 | issue=2–4 | year=2009 | issn=0304-4017 | doi=10.1016/j.vetpar.2009.05.018 | pages=89–103| pmid=19559531 }}</ref>{{rp|95}} This was especially demonstrated in the foundational Thiptara et al. 2006, reporting a litter birth of three stillborns and six live in Thailand. This observation has been relevant not only to that country but to toxoplasmosis control in [[porciculture]] around the world.{{sfnp|Dubey|2016|p=154}}<ref name="Dubey-2009"/>{{rp|95}}<ref name="Nissapatorn-et-al-2013"/>

==Hygiene==
Excessively hygienic raising conditions were found to prevent proper [[gut microbiota]] development by Schmidt et al. 2011.<ref name="Yeoman-White-2014">{{cite journal | last1=Yeoman | first1=Carl J. | last2=White | first2=Bryan A. | title=Gastrointestinal Tract Microbiota and Probiotics in Production Animals | journal=[[Annual Review of Animal Biosciences]] | publisher=[[Annual Reviews (publisher)|Annual Reviews]] | volume=2 | issue=1 | date=2014-02-01 | issn=2165-8102 | doi=10.1146/annurev-animal-022513-114149 | pages=469–486| pmid=25384152 }}</ref> Moore et al. 1995 describes the pathology of ''[[Cryptosporidium]]'' infection, a common difficulty in piglet production.<ref name="Uzal-et-al-2016">{{cite book | last1=Uzal | first1=Francisco A. | last2=Plattner | first2=Brandon L. | last3=Hostetter | first3=Jesse M. | title=Jubb, Kennedy & Palmer's Pathology of Domestic Animals: Volume 2 | chapter=1 Alimentary System | publisher=[[Elsevier]] | year=2016 | isbn=978-0-7020-5318-4 | pages=1–257.e2}}</ref>

In an attempt to curb diseases such as [[African swine fever virus|African swine fever]],<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |date=2021-08-02 |title=China is using 13-storey 'hog hotels' to keep pigs safe from disease |url=https://www.independent.co.uk/asia/china/china-hog-hotels-african-swine-fever-b1894939.html |access-date=2022-11-18 |website=The Independent |language=en}}</ref> a number of Chinese companies have built condominium-style mega complexes multiple stories high to house thousands of pigs. The buildings have been dubbed "hog hotels" and come with strict protocols and advanced cleaning, veterinary, and disposal systems.<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=Hog heaven: China builds pig hotels for better biosecurity |url=https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2021/8/2/hog-heaven-china-builds-pig-hotels-for-better-biosecurity |access-date=2022-11-18 |website=www.aljazeera.com |language=en}}</ref> However, doubt has been raised by policy specialists and animal scientists over the facilities' efficacy in preventing outbreaks. The welfare of the animals has also been a source of concern, and it has been suggested that the poor welfare of the pigs may cause a decline in their immunity.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2020-09-18 |title=A 12-storey pig farm: has China found the way to tackle animal disease? |url=http://www.theguardian.com/environment/2020/sep/18/a-12-storey-pig-farm-has-china-found-a-way-to-stop-future-pandemics- |access-date=2022-11-18 |website=the Guardian |language=en}}</ref>

== Industry overview ==
As of 2024, [[Smithfield Foods]] is the largest pig producer in the world,<ref>{{Cite web |title=World's biggest pork producer Smithfield raises $522 million in IPO |url=https://www.nationalhogfarmer.com/market-news/world-s-biggest-pork-producer-smithfield-raises-522-million-in-ipo |access-date=2025-07-14 |website=www.nationalhogfarmer.com |language=en}}</ref> with a particularly large presence in the United States.<ref name="americanagnetwork.com">{{Cite web |title=Smithfield Foods Selling 150,000 Sows to Murphy Family Ventures |url=https://www.americanagnetwork.com/2024/12/03/smithfield-foods-selling-150000-sows-to-murphy-family-ventures/ |access-date=2025-07-07 |website=American Ag Network |language=en-US}}</ref>

Large corporations often contract out the farming to focus on processing, packaging, and marketing; in 2024, Smithfield Foods sold some pig farming operations to Murphy Farm Management, making Murphy one of the largest pig producers in the United States with the capacity to produce 3.2 million hogs per year.<ref>{{Cite web |last= |first= |title=Murphy Family to Return to Independent Pork Production Through Agreement with Smithfield |url=https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/murphy-family-to-return-to-independent-pork-production-through-agreement-with-smithfield-302320073.html |access-date=2025-07-07 |website=www.prnewswire.com |publisher=Smithfield Foods |language=en}}</ref><ref name="americanagnetwork.com"/>

[[File:Battery hens -Bastos, Sao Paulo, Brazil-31March2007.jpg|thumb|upright|Bank of cages for layer hens<ref name="Appleby et al. 1992">{{cite book |title=Poultry Production Systems: Behaviour, Management and Welfare |author1=Appleby, M.C. |author2=Hughes, B.O. |author3=Elson, H.A. |publisher=CAB International |year=1992}}</ref>]]{{farming}}
'''Poultry farming''' is the form of [[animal husbandry]] which breeds [[poultry|domesticated birds]] including [[chicken]]s, [[Domestic duck|ducks]], [[turkey (domesticated)|turkey]]s and [[domesticated goose|geese]] to produce [[chicken meat|meat]] or [[Egg as food|eggs]] for [[food]]. Poultry – mostly chickens – are farmed in great numbers.  More than 60 billion chickens are killed for consumption annually.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://faunalytics.org/global-animal-slaughter-statistics-and-charts/|title=Global Animal Slaughter Statistics And Charts|date=2018-10-10|website=[[Faunalytics]]|language=en-US|access-date=2019-11-05}}</ref><ref name="http">{{cite web |url= https://www.ciwf.org.uk/farm-animals/chickens/ |title= Compassion in World Farming – Poultry |publisher= Ciwf.org.uk |access-date= October 3, 2018 |quote= There are more chickens in the world than any other bird. In fact, more than 50 billion chickens are reared annually as a source of food, for both their meat and their eggs. |archive-date= April 26, 2017 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20170426063521/https://www.ciwf.org.uk/farm-animals/chickens/ |url-status= dead }}</ref> Chickens used for meat are known as [[broiler]]s, while chickens used for eggs are called layers — though they are usually also killed for their meat.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.ciwf.org.uk/farm-animals/chickens/ | title=Compassion in World Farming – Poultry | publisher=[[Compassion in World Farming]] | access-date=October 3, 2018 | quote=Chickens farmed for meat are called broiler chickens, whilst those farmed for eggs are called egg-laying hens. | archive-date=April 26, 2017 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170426063521/https://www.ciwf.org.uk/farm-animals/chickens/ | url-status=dead }}</ref>

In the United States, the national organization overseeing poultry production is the [[Food and Drug Administration (United States)|Food and Drug Administration]] (FDA). In the UK, the national organization is the [[Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs]] (DEFRA).
[[File:Poultry farm, South Africa.jpg|thumb|260px|Poultry farm in [[South Africa]], showing black terrain in foreground after [[controlled burn]] to stimulate new growth of nutritious grass]]

==Intensive and alternative==
{{Pie chart
 | caption = '''[[Biomass (ecology)|Biomass]] of [[bird]]s on [[Earth]]'''<ref>{{cite web |author=Damian Carrington |url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2018/may/21/human-race-just-001-of-all-life-but-has-destroyed-over-80-of-wild-mammals-study |title=Humans just 0.01% of all life but have destroyed 83% of wild mammals – study |website=www.theguardian.com |date=21 May 2018 |access-date=19 August 2018 |language=}}</ref>

 | label2  = [[Wildlife|Wild]] [[bird]]s 
 | value2  = 30 | color2 = green

According to the World Watch Institute, 74 percent of the world's poultry meat, and 68 percent of eggs are produced intensively.<ref name=WW2006>''State of the World 2006'' World Watch Institute, p. 26</ref> One alternative to intensive poultry farming is [[free range|free-range]] farming using lower stocking densities. Poultry producers routinely use nationally approved medications, such as antibiotics, in [[Poultry feed|feed]] or drinking water, to treat disease or to prevent [[poultry disease|disease]] outbreaks. Some FDA-approved medications are also approved for improved feed utilization.<ref>{{cite book | title=Food-Animal Production Practices and Drug Use | url=https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK232573/ | series=National Center for Biotechnical Information | year=1999 | publisher=National Academies Press (US) | access-date=February 28, 2016}}</ref>

== Chicken coop ==
A '''chicken coop''' or '''hen house''' is a structure where [[chicken]]s or other [[fowl]] are kept safe and secure. There may be nest boxes and perches in the house. There is a long-standing controversy over the basic need for a chicken coop. One philosophy, known as the "fresh air school", holds that chickens are mostly hardy but can be brought low by confinement, poor air quality and darkness, hence the need for a highly ventilated or open-sided coop with conditions more like the outdoors, even in winter.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.nortoncreekpress.com/fresh_air_poultry_houses.html |title=Fresh-Air Poultry Houses |last=Woods|first=Prince T. |date=October 2008 |publisher=Norton Creek Press |access-date=18 April 2012}}</ref>  However, others who keep chickens believe they are prone to illness in outdoor weather and need a controlled-environment coop. This has led to two housing designs for chickens: fresh-air houses with wide openings and nothing more than wire mesh between chickens and the weather (even in Northern winters), or closed houses with doors, windows and hatches which can shut off most ventilation.<ref>North and Bell, "Commercial Chicken Production Manual", 5th ed. Van Nostrand Reinhold, 1990, p 189.</ref>

==Egg-laying chickens ==
[[File:A Land Army girl holding a chicken, 1944. TR1568 (cropped).jpg|thumb|An agricultural worker holding an egg-laying hen, 1944]]
Commercial hens usually begin laying eggs at 16–21 weeks of age, although production gradually declines from approximately 25 weeks of age.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.hyline.com/Redbook/Performance/Gray_All.pdf |title=Performance Records of Hy-Line Grey |access-date=November 18, 2011}}{{dead link|date=March 2018 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> This means that in many countries, by approximately 72 weeks of age, flocks are considered economically unviable and are slaughtered after approximately 12 months of egg production,<ref name="autogenerated3">{{cite web |url=http://www.ciwf.org.uk/farm_animals/poultry/egg_laying_hens/default.aspx |title=Compassion in World Farming – Egg laying hens |publisher=Ciwf.org.uk |access-date=August 26, 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110928041331/http://www.ciwf.org.uk/farm_animals/poultry/egg_laying_hens/default.aspx |archive-date=September 28, 2011 }}</ref> although chickens will naturally live for 6 or more years. In some countries, hens are [[forced molting|force moult]]ed to re-invigorate egg-laying.

Environmental conditions are often automatically controlled in egg-laying systems. For example, the duration of the light phase is initially increased to prompt the beginning of egg-laying at 16–20 weeks of age and then mimics summer day length which stimulates the hens to continue laying eggs all year round; normally, egg production occurs only in the warmer months. Some commercial breeds of hen can produce over 300 eggs a year.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://homesteadchores.com/best-egg-laying-chickens/ |title=How to Select the Perfect Breed of Best Egg Laying Chickens |publisher=homesteadchores.com |access-date=October 5, 2017}}</ref>

===Free-range===
[[File:Baby Chicken in Ishawarganj, Mymensingh, Bangladesh.jpg|thumb|Baby free-range chicken in [[Ishwarganj Upazila]], [[Mymensingh]], Bangladesh]]
[[File:Free Range Hens - geograph.org.uk - 342791.jpg|thumb|Commercial free range hens in the Scottish Borders]]
[[File:freerangechickens.jpg|thumb|Free-range chickens being fed outdoors]]
[[File:Chicken coop situated in a compound house.jpg|thumb|Chicken coop in Ghana]]
{{main|Free range}}
Free-range poultry farming allows chickens to roam freely for a period of the day, although they are usually confined in sheds at night to protect them from predators or kept indoors if the weather is particularly bad. In the UK, the [[Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs]] (DEFRA) states that a free-range chicken must have day-time access to open-air runs during at least half of its life. Unlike in the United States, this definition also applies to free-range egg-laying hens, meaning they can still be confined in high stocking densities with limited outdoors access.{{Clarification needed|date=November 2024}} The [[European Union]] regulates marketing standards for egg farming, which specify a minimum condition for [[free-range eggs]], including that "hens have continuous daytime access to open air runs, except in the case of temporary restrictions imposed by veterinary authorities".<ref>{{cite web |url=https://eur-lex.europa.eu/LexUriServ/LexUriServ.do?uri=CONSLEG:1991R1274:20020101:EN:PDF |title=European Union Regulation for marketing standards for eggs – page 25 |access-date=August 26, 2011}}</ref> The [[RSPCA]] "Welfare standards for laying hens and pullets" indicates that the stocking rate must not exceed 1,000 birds per hectare (10 m<sup>2</sup> per hen) of range available and a minimum area of overhead shade/shelter of 8 m<sup>2</sup> per 1,000 hens must be provided.

Free-range farming of egg-laying hens is increasing its share of the market. DEFRA figures indicate that 45% of eggs produced in the UK throughout 2010 were free range, 5% were produced in barn systems and 50% from cages. This compares with 41% being free range in 2009.<ref>{{cite web |title=50% of UK eggs laid by free range hens |url=http://www.theranger.co.uk/news/50percent-of-UK-eggs-laid-by-free-range-hens_21575.html |work=The Ranger |access-date=November 18, 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160404072548/http://www.theranger.co.uk/news/50percent-of-uk-eggs-laid-by-free-range-hens_21575.html |archive-date=April 4, 2016 }}</ref>

Suitable land requires adequate drainage to minimise [[worm]]s and [[coccidia]]l oocysts, suitable protection from prevailing winds, good ventilation, access and protection from predators. Excess heat, cold or damp can have a harmful effect on the animals and their productivity.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Deeb|first1=N. |last2=Shlosberg|first2=A. |last3=Cahaner|first3=A. |title=Genotype-by-environment interaction with broiler genotypes differing in growth rate. 4. Association between responses to heat stress and to cold-induced ascites. |journal=Poultry Science |date=October 2002 |volume=81 |issue=10 |pages=1454–1462 |pmid=12412909 |doi=10.1093/ps/81.10.1454 |doi-access=free}}</ref> Free range farmers have less control than farmers using cages in what food their chickens eat, which can lead to unreliable productivity,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Mapiye|first1=C. |last2=Mwale|first2=M. |last3=Mupangwa|first3=J. F. |last4=Chimonyo|first4=M. |last5=Foti|first5=R. |last6=Mutenje|first6=M. J. |date=2008-11-03 |title=A Research Review of Village Chicken Production Constraints and Opportunities in Zimbabwe |journal=Asian-Australasian Journal of Animal Sciences |volume=21|issue=11|pages=1680–1688 |doi=10.5713/ajas.2008.r.07|issn=1011-2367 |doi-access=free}}</ref> though supplementary feeding reduces this uncertainty.

The benefits of free-range poultry farming for laying hens include opportunities for natural behaviours such as pecking, scratching, foraging and exercise outdoors.<ref name="ciwf.org.uk"/>  In some farms, the manure from free range poultry can be used to benefit crops.<ref>{{cite web |title=Chicken Feed: Grass-Fed Chickens & Pastured Poultry |url=http://www.lionsgrip.com/pastured.html |work=Lions Grip |access-date= July 6, 2007}}</ref>

Both intensive free-range poultry and "cage-free" farming with hens still being confined in close proximity due to high stocking densities have animal welfare concerns. [[Cannibalism (poultry)|Cannibalism]], [[feather pecking]] and [[vent pecking]] can be common, prompting some farmers to use [[debeaking|beak trimming]] as a preventative measure, although reducing stocking rates would eliminate these problems.<ref name="Sherwin et al.">{{cite journal |author1=Sherwin, C. |author2=Richards, G. |author3=Nicol, C. |year=2010 |title=A comparison of the welfare of layer hens in four housing systems used in the UK |journal=British Poultry Science |volume=51|issue=4 |pages=488–499|doi=10.1080/00071668.2010.502518 |pmid=20924842|s2cid=8968010}}</ref> Diseases can be common and the animals are vulnerable to predators.<ref name="Sherwin et al." /> Barn systems have been found to have the worst bird welfare.<ref name="Sherwin et al." /> In South-East Asia, a lack of disease control in free range farming has been associated with outbreaks of [[avian influenza]].<ref name=WSPA>WSPA International>{{cite web |url=http://wspa-international.org/publicfiles/Free_range_farming_and_avian_flu__3_.pdf |title="Free-range farming and avian flu in Asia" |website=wspa-international.org |date= |access-date=July 6, 2007 |language= |archive-date=June 25, 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080625192838/http://wspa-international.org/publicfiles/Free_range_farming_and_avian_flu__3_.pdf }}</ref>

====Free-run====
Instead of keeping them in cages, free-run laying hens roam freely within an enclosed barn. This type of housing also provides enrichment for the hens, including nesting boxes and perches that are often located along the floor of the barn. Many believe that this type of housing is better for the bird than any caging system, but it has its disadvantages, too. Due to the increase in activity of the birds, dust levels tend to elevate and the air quality decreases. When air quality drops, so does production as this compromises the health and welfare of both birds and their caretakers.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=David |display-authors=etal |first1=B |title=Air Quality in Alternative Housing Systems May Have an Impact on Laying Hen Welfare. Part I—Dust |journal=Animals |date=2015 |volume=3 |issue=5 |pages=495–511 |pmc=4598690 |pmid=26479370 |doi=10.3390/ani5030368|doi-access=free }}</ref>

====Organic====
In organic systems in the US, organic management starts with the selection of the livestock and should begin "no later than the second day of life".<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=Tipsheet: Organic Poultry Production for Meat and Eggs |url=https://www.ams.usda.gov/sites/default/files/media/Organic%20Poultry%20Production%20for%20Meat%20and%20Eggs_FINAL.pdf |website=United States Department of Agriculture}}</ref> Organic poultry production requires organic management in nutrition, preventative health care, living conditions, handling/processing, and record keeping.<ref name=":1" /> The [[Soil Association]] standards<ref name="scribd1">{{cite web |url=https://www.scribd.com/doc/26906267/Soil-Association-Organic-Standards-for-Producers-2009 |title=Soil Association Standards |access-date=December 5, 2011}}</ref> used to certify organic flocks in the UK indicate a maximum outdoors stocking density of 1,000 birds per hectare and a maximum of 2,000 hens in each poultry house. In the UK, organic laying hens are not routinely beak-trimmed.

===Yarding===
{{main|Yarding}}
[[File:Yarding poultry farm 02.jpg|thumb|right|[[Yarding]] poultry farm]]
While often confused with free range farming, yarding is actually a separate method by which a [[Hutch (animal cage)|hutch]] and fenced-off area outside are combined when farming poultry. The distinction is that free-range poultry are either totally unfenced, or the fence is so distant that it has little influence on their freedom of movement. Yarding is a common technique used by small farms in the Northeastern U.S.  The birds are released daily from hutches or coops.  The hens usually lay eggs either on the floor of the coop or in baskets if provided by the farmer. This husbandry technique can be complicated if used with roosters, mostly because of their aggressive behavior.

===Battery cage===
[[File:Poultry Farm in Namakkal, Tamil Nadu.jpg|thumb|Poultry farm using battery cages in India]]
{{main|Battery cage}}The majority of hens in many countries are housed in [[battery cage]]s, although the [[European Union Council Directive 1999/74/EC]]<ref name="eur-lex.europa.eu">{{cite web |url=https://eur-lex.europa.eu/LexUriServ/LexUriServ.do?uri=OJ:L:1999:203:0053:0057:EN:PDF |title=European Union Council Directive 1999/74/EC|access-date=November 15, 2011}}</ref> has banned the conventional battery cage in EU states from January 2012. As of April 1, 2017, no new battery cages are able to be installed in Canada.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Allison |first1=L |title=Canada's battery cage phase-out officially begins |url=https://www.cfhs.ca/canadas_battery_cage_phase_out_officially_begins |website=Canadian Federation of Humane Societies |access-date=April 11, 2018 |archive-date=April 12, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180412082117/https://www.cfhs.ca/canadas_battery_cage_phase_out_officially_begins |url-status=dead }}</ref> Farmers must move towards enriched housing or use a cage-free system. In 2016, the Egg Farmers of Canada announced that the country's egg farmers will be transitioning away from conventional hen housing systems (battery cages) and have no conventional caging left by 2036.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Lambert |first1=T |title=Why 20 years? The realities of transitioning an agriculture supply chain |url=http://www.eggfarmers.ca/2016/09/why-20-years-the-realities-of-transitioning-an-agriculture-supply-chain/ |website=eggfarmers.ca |date=September 19, 2016 |access-date=April 11, 2018 |archive-date=April 12, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180412001122/http://www.eggfarmers.ca/2016/09/why-20-years-the-realities-of-transitioning-an-agriculture-supply-chain/ |url-status=dead }}</ref> Batteries are small cages, usually made of metal in modern systems, housing 3 to 8 hens. The walls are made of either solid metal or mesh, and the floor is sloped wire mesh to allow the feces to drop through and eggs to roll onto an egg-collecting conveyor belt. Water is usually provided by overhead nipple systems, and food in a trough along the front of the cage replenished at regular intervals by a mechanical system.

Battery cages are arranged in long rows as multiple tiers, often with cages back-to-back (hence the term). Within a single barn, there may be several floors containing battery cages meaning that a single shed may contain many tens of thousands of hens. Light intensity is often kept low (e.g. 10 lux) to reduce feather pecking and vent pecking. Benefits of battery cages include easier care for the birds, floor-laid eggs (which are expensive to collect) are eliminated, eggs are cleaner, capture at the end of lay is expedited, generally less feed is required to produce eggs, [[broodiness]] is eliminated, more hens may be housed in a given house floor space, internal parasites are more easily treated, and labor requirements are generally much reduced.
 
In farms using cages for egg production, there are more birds per unit area; this allows for greater productivity and lower food costs.<ref name=VEGA>{{cite web |author=VEGA  |url=http://vegraaresearch.org/animal_poultry.asp |title="Laying hens, free range and bird flu" |date= |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220926230737/http://vegraaresearch.org/animal_poultry.asp |access-date=July 6, 2007|archive-date=September 26, 2022 }}</ref>  Floor space ranges upwards from 300&nbsp;cm<sup>2</sup> per hen. EU standards in 2003 called for at least 550&nbsp;cm<sup>2</sup> per hen.<ref>Chickens: Layer Housing, Michael C. Appleby, Encyclopedia of Animal Science. {{doi|10.1081/E-EAS-120019534}}</ref> In the US, the current recommendation by the United Egg Producers is 67 to 86 in<sup>2</sup> (430 to 560&nbsp;cm<sup>2</sup>) per bird.<ref>{{cite web |author= |url=http://www.uepcertified.com/program/guidelines/categories/housing-space-feed-water |title=Housing, space, feed and water |website=United Egg Producers www.uepcertified.com |access-date=November 30, 2011 |archive-date=February 24, 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120224093518/http://www.uepcertified.com/program/guidelines/categories/housing-space-feed-water }}</ref> The space available to battery hens has often been described as less than the size of a piece of A4 paper (623&nbsp;cm<sup>2</sup>).<ref name="washington post 2003">{{cite news |title = Animal Pragmatism: Compassion Over Killing Wants to Make the Anti-Meat Message a Little More Palatable |newspaper = Washington Post |date = September 3, 2003 |url = http://www.cok.net/feat/article-wp.php |access-date = July 30, 2009 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20121203235723/http://www.cok.net/feat/article-wp.php |archive-date = December 3, 2012 }}</ref> [[Animal welfare science|Animal welfare scientists]] have been critical of battery cages because they do not provide hens with sufficient space to stand, walk, flap their wings, perch, or make a nest, and it is widely considered that hens suffer through boredom and frustration through being unable to perform these behaviours.<ref>{{cite book |last=Appleby |first=M.C. |author2=J.A. Mench |author3=B.O. Hughes |year=2004 |title=Poultry Behaviour and Welfare |publisher=CABI Publishing |location= Wallingford and Cambridge MA |isbn=978-0-85199-667-7}}</ref>  This can lead to a wide range of [[abnormal behaviour of birds in captivity|abnormal behaviours]], some of which are injurious to the hens or their cagemates.

===Furnished cage===
{{main|Furnished cages}}
In 1999, the European Union Council Directive 1999/74/EC<ref name="eur-lex.europa.eu"/> banned conventional battery cages for laying hens throughout the [[European Union]] from January 1, 2012; they were banned previously in other countries including [[Switzerland]]. In response to these bans, development of prototype commercial furnished cage systems began in the 1980s.  Furnished cages, sometimes called 'enriched' or 'modified' cages, are cages for egg-laying hens which have been designed to allow the hens to perform their "natural behaviors" whilst retaining their economic and husbandry advantages, and also provide some of the welfare advantages of non-cage systems. Many design features of furnished cages have been incorporated because research in animal welfare science has shown them to be of benefit to the hens. In the UK, the DEFRA "Code for the Welfare of Laying Hens"<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.defra.gov.uk/publications/files/pb7274-laying-hens-020717.pdf |title=Defra Code For The Welfare Of Laying Hens |access-date=December 5, 2011}}</ref> states furnished cages should provide at least 750&nbsp;cm<sup>2</sup> of cage area per hen, 600&nbsp;cm<sup>2</sup> of which should be usable; the height of the cage other than that above the usable area should be at least 20&nbsp;cm at every point and no cage should have a total area that is less than 2000&nbsp;cm<sup>2</sup>.

In addition, furnished cages should provide a nest, litter such that pecking and scratching are possible, appropriate perches allowing at least 15&nbsp;cm per hen, a claw-shortening device, and a feed trough which may be used without restriction providing 12&nbsp;cm per hen. Furnished cages (Enriched) give the hens more space than the conventional battery cages, so that each bird may spread their wings without touching one another if desired. Enrichment such as nest boxes, perches, and dust baths are also provided so that the birds may carry out their natural behaviors such as nesting, roosting, and scratching as though they were outdoors.

Enrichment of laying hen cages ultimately results in better bone quality.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Tactacan |display-authors=etal |first1=G.B. |title=Performance and welfare of laying hens in conventional and enriched cages |journal=Poultry Science|date=April 2009 |volume=88 |issue=4 |pages=698–707 |doi=10.3382/ps.2008-00369|pmid=19276411 |doi-access=free }}</ref> This is a result of the increased activity in the hens from the additional space and enrichment provided in the furnished housing system.

Although the enriched housing system has advantages such as reduced aggression towards one another and cleaner eggs, modern egg-laying breeds often suffer from [[osteoporosis]], which results in weakened skeletal systems. During egg production, large amounts of calcium are transferred from bones to create egg-shell. Although dietary calcium levels are adequate, absorption of dietary calcium is not always sufficient, given the intensity of production, to fully replenish bone calcium.  This can lead to increases in bone breakages, particularly when the hens are being removed from cages at the end of laying. Osteoporosis may be prevented by free range and cage-free housing systems, as they have shown to have a beneficial impact on the skeletal system of the hens compared to those housed in caged systems.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Prafulla |first1=R |title=Influence of housing systems on bone properties of laying hens |journal=ProQuest Dissertations and Theses |date=2015}}</ref>

Countries such as Austria, Belgium and Germany are planning to ban furnished cages until 2025 additionally to the already banned conventional cages.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.theecologist.org/blogs_and_comments/commentators/other_comments/1046687/battery_egg_hens_still_face_hell_as_enriched_cages_phased_in.html |title=Ecologist, September 2011 |date=September 8, 2011 |access-date=January 22, 2012}}</ref>

===Urban chicken keeping===
{{main|Urban chicken keeping}}

Raising chickens in urban or suburban environments is experiencing a resurgence in popularity in many countries including the United States. Proponents of this practice cite benefits such as access to fresh eggs, natural pest control, educational opportunities, and a connection to sustainable food practices.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Elkhoraibi |first1=C. |last2=Blatchford |first2=R. A. |last3=Pitesky |first3=M. E. |last4=Mench |first4=J. A. |date=2014-11-01 |title=Backyard chickens in the United States: A survey of flock owners |journal=Poultry Science |language=en |volume=93 |issue=11 |pages=2920–2931 |doi=10.3382/ps.2014-04154 |pmid=25193256 |issn=0032-5791|doi-access=free }}</ref>

While commercial operations typically use [[leghorn chicken]]s, many other breeds such as the [[Bantam (poultry)|Bantam]] are well-suited for urban settings.<ref>{{Cite book|title=The Backyard Chicken Book: A Beginner's Guide|last=Schwanz|first=Lee|publisher=New York: Skyhorse Publishing, Inc. 2014|year=2014|isbn=978-1-60239-745-3|location=EBSCO}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|title=The Modern-Day Pioneer Simple Living in the 21st Century|last=Denholtz|first=Charlotte|publisher=Adams Media|year=2012|isbn=978-1-4405-5179-6}}</ref>

The practice faces legal and regulatory hurdles; many cities have specific ordinances regarding the number of chickens allowed, coop size, and potential noise and odor issues.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Brinkley |first1=Catherine |last2=Kingsley |first2=Jacqueline Scarlett |last3=Mench |first3=Joy |date=2018-08-01 |title=A Method for Guarding Animal Welfare and Public Health: Tracking the Rise of Backyard Poultry Ordinances |url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10900-017-0462-0 |journal=Journal of Community Health |language=en |volume=43 |issue=4 |pages=639–646 |doi=10.1007/s10900-017-0462-0 |pmid=29372351 |issn=1573-3610|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Concerns surrounding predation from wild carnivores<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Amador-Alcalá |first1=Saúl |last2=Naranjo |first2=Eduardo J. |last3=Jiménez-Ferrer |first3=Guillermo |date=April 2013 |title=Wildlife predation on livestock and poultry: implications for predator conservation in the rainforest of south-east Mexico |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/oryx/article/wildlife-predation-on-livestock-and-poultry-implications-for-predator-conservation-in-the-rainforest-of-southeast-mexico/E7B7824D09FA4696B911468E39E67C9F |journal=Oryx |language=en |volume=47 |issue=2 |pages=243–250 |doi=10.1017/S0030605311001359 |bibcode=2013Oryx...47..243A |issn=0030-6053}}</ref> such as raccoons,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kays |first1=Roland |last2=Parsons |first2=Arielle Waldstein |date=2014-09-01 |title=Mammals in and around suburban yards, and the attraction of chicken coops |url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11252-014-0347-2 |journal=Urban Ecosystems |language=en |volume=17 |issue=3 |pages=691–705 |doi=10.1007/s11252-014-0347-2 |bibcode=2014UrbEc..17..691K |issn=1573-1642|url-access=subscription }}</ref> heavy metal exposure,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Roegner |first1=Amber |last2=Giannitti |first2=Federico |last3=Woods |first3=Leslie W |last4=Mete |first4=Aslı |last5=Puschner |first5=Birgit |date=2013-04-03 |title=Public health implications of lead poisoning in backyard chickens and cattle: four cases |journal=Veterinary Medicine: Research and Reports |volume=4 |pages=11–20 |doi=10.2147/VMRR.S36083|doi-access=free |pmid=32670839 |pmc=7337163 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bautista |first1=Adrienne C. |last2=Puschner |first2=Birgit |last3=Poppenga |first3=Robert H. |date=September 2014 |title=Lead exposure from backyard chicken eggs: a public health risk? L. |last2=Stephen |first2=C. |last3=Skuridina |first3=N. |last4=Kosatsky |first4=T. |date=2012-06-01 |title=Raising Chickens in City Backyards: The Public Health Role
