Sheep have good hearing, and are sensitive to noise.{{sfn|Smith|Aseltine|Kennedy|1997|p=5}} Sheep have horizontal slit-shaped pupils, with excellent [[peripheral vision]]; with visual fields of about 270° to 320°, sheep can see behind themselves without turning their heads.<ref name="asi-care-guide">{{cite book |last=Shulaw |first=William P. |year=2006 |title=Sheep Care Guide |url=https://sheepusa.org/resources-publications-sheepcareguide |publisher=American Sheep Industry Association |access-date=8 September 2008 |archive-date=9 August 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190809185748/https://sheepusa.org/resources-publications-sheepcareguide |url-status=live }}</ref> Many breeds have only short hair on the face, and some have facial wool (if any) confined to the poll and or the area of the mandibular angle; the wide angles of peripheral vision apply to these breeds. A few breeds tend to have considerable wool on the face; for some individuals of these breeds, peripheral vision may be greatly reduced by "wool blindness", unless recently shorn about the face.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Terrill | first1 = C. E. | last2 = Hazel | first2 = L. N. | year = 1946 | title = Heritability of neck folds and face covering in range Rambouillet lambs as evaluated by scoring | url = https://archive.org/details/sim_journal-of-animal-science_1946-05_5_2/page/170 | journal = J. Anim. Sci. | volume = 5 | issue = 2| pages = 170–179 | doi = 10.2527/jas1946.52170x | pmid = 20985519 }}</ref> Sheep tend to balk at shadows on the ground, sharp contrasts between light and dark, and places they cannot see into, and move more readily into well-lit areas.<ref name="hanrahan-structures" />{{sfn|Wooster|2005|p=87}} Sheep also have an excellent sense of smell, and, like all species of their genus, have [[scent gland]]s just in front of the eyes, and interdigitally on the feet. The purpose of these glands is uncertain,{{sfn|Smith|Aseltine|Kennedy|1997|pp=3-4}} but those on the face may be used in breeding behaviors. The foot glands might also be related to reproduction, but alternative functions, such as secretion of a waste product or a scent marker to help lost sheep find their flock, have also been proposed.{{sfn|Smith|Aseltine|Kennedy|1997|pp=3-4}} <!-- This is a weak reference -->

===Comparison with goats===
Sheep and [[goat|goats]] are closely related: both are in the subfamily [[Caprinae]]. However, they are separate species, so [[Hybrid (biology)|hybrids]] rarely occur and are always infertile. A hybrid of a ewe and a buck (a male goat) is called a [[sheep-goat hybrid]], known as ''geep''.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Drost Project: The Visual Guide to Ovine Reproduction: Geep |url=https://visgar.vetmed.ufl.edu/en_ovirep/geep/geep.html |access-date=29 August 2026 |website=visgar.vetmed.ufl.edu}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Falker-Gieske |first1=Clemens |last2=Knorr |first2=Christoph |last3=Tetens |first3=Jens |date=25 November 2019 |title=Blood transcriptome analysis in a buck-ewe hybrid and its parents |journal=Scientific Reports |publisher=Nature Publishing Group |volume=9 |issue=1 |pages=17492 |doi=10.1038/s41598-019-53901-z |doi-access=free |pmid=31767945 |pmc=6877586 |bibcode=2019NatSR...917492F |issn=2045-2322}}</ref> Visual differences between sheep and goats include the beard of goats and divided upper lip ([[philtrum]]) of sheep. Sheep tails also hang down, even when short or [[Docking (animal)|docked]], while the short tails of goats are held upwards. Also, sheep breeds are often naturally [[Polled livestock|polled]] (either in both sexes or just in the female), while naturally polled goats are rare (though many are polled artificially). Males of the two species differ in that buck goats acquire a unique and strong odor during the [[Rut (mammalian reproduction)|rut]], whereas rams do not.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Small ruminant production and the small ruminant genetic resource in tropical Africa |url=https://www.fao.org/4/t0376e/T0376E05.htm |access-date=29 August 2026 |website=www.fao.org}}</ref>

===Breeds===
{{See also|List of sheep breeds}}
[[File:Synchronized Sheep Judging.jpg|thumb|upright=1.1|Sheep being judged for adherence to their [[breed standard]]]]
The domestic sheep is a multi-purpose animal.  More than 200 [[List of sheep breeds|breeds]] are recognized, created and bred to serve diverse purposes.{{sfn|Ensminger|2002|p=15}}<ref name="okstate-breeds">{{cite web |url=http://www.ansi.okstate.edu/breeds/sheep/ |title=Sheep (Ovis aries) |access-date=2 November 2007 |work=Breeds of Livestock |publisher=Oklahoma State University Dept. of Animal Science |archive-date=6 November 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071106035142/http://www.ansi.okstate.edu/breeds/sheep/ |url-status=live }}</ref> Some sources who use the term more freely give counts exceeding a thousand different breeds.<ref name="dwyer-welfare">{{cite book |editor-last=Dwyer |editor-first=Cathy M. |title=The Welfare of Sheep |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=KxlbW9to_1YC&pg=PA56 |access-date=15 October 2010 |date=2008 |publisher=Springer |isbn=978-1-4020-8552-9 |page=56 |archive-date=11 May 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130511031616/http://books.google.com/books?id=KxlbW9to_1YC&pg=PA56 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="Jensen2009">{{cite book|author=Per Jensen|title=The ethology of domestic animals: an introductory text|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=FuJKSEgccUEC&pg=PA162|access-date=15 October 2010|year=2009|publisher=CABI|isbn=978-1-84593-536-8|pages=162–|archive-date=11 May 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130511053444/http://books.google.com/books?id=FuJKSEgccUEC&pg=PA162|url-status=live}}</ref> although most sources do not recognize the marginal and sub-breeds included in larger counts.  The [[Food and Agriculture Organization|Food and Agriculture Organization of the UN]] (FAO) listed  1229 breeds as of 2006.<ref name="FAO 2007">FAO. 2007. State of the world's animal genetic resources for food and agriculture</ref>  Sheep are usually classified as being best suited to furnishing a certain product: wool, meat, milk, hides, or a combination. Other features used when classifying sheep include face color (generally white or black), tail length, presence or [[Polled livestock|lack of horns]], and the [[topography]] for which the breed has been developed. This last point is stressed in the UK, where breeds are described as either upland (hill or mountain) or lowland breeds.{{sfn|Brown|Meadowcroft|1989|pp=14–15}} A sheep may also be of a [[fat-tailed sheep|fat-tailed type]], with larger deposits of fat within and around its tail.{{sfn|Ryder|2007|pp=89-90, 222-225}}  In the wild, this fat tail could store nutrients, a useful trait in arid environments. In cultivation, they are generally dual-purpose sheep common in Africa and Asia.{{sfn|Ryder|2007|pp=89-90, 222-225}}

[[File:Barbados Blackbelly.JPG|thumb|left|upright=1.1|The [[Barbados Blackbelly]] is a hair sheep breed of Caribbean origin.]]
Breeds are often categorized by the type of their wool. Fine wool breeds are those that have wool of great crimp and density, which are preferred for textiles. Most of these were derived from [[Merino (sheep)|Merino]] sheep, and the breed continues to dominate the world sheep industry. Downs breeds have wool between the extremes, and are typically fast-growing meat and ram breeds with dark faces.<ref name="D'Arcy">D'Arcy, J.B., Sheep Management & Wool Technology, NSW University Press, 1986, {{ISBN|0-86840-106-4}}</ref> Some major medium wool breeds, such as the [[Corriedale sheep|Corriedale]], are dual-purpose crosses of long and fine-wooled breeds and were created for high-production commercial flocks. Long wool breeds are the largest of sheep, with long wool and a slow rate of growth. Long wool sheep are valued for crossbreeding and have been used to create new, merged sheep types. For example, the American [[Columbia (sheep)|Columbia]] breed was developed by crossing [[Lincoln (sheep)|Lincoln]] rams (a long wool breed) with fine-wooled [[American Rambouillet|Rambouillet]] ewes.{{sfn|Simmons|Ekarius|2019|at=2. Breeding and Breeds: Columbia}}

Coarse or carpet wool sheep are those with a medium to long length wool of characteristic coarseness. Breeds traditionally used for carpet wool show great variability, but the chief requirement is a wool that will not break down under heavy use (as would that of the finer breeds). During the late 20th century and 21st century, the price of coarse wool has steadily declined, partially a result of excess wool from meat-class sheep usually being coarse.  This has made raising sheep explicitly for coarse wool no longer profitable.

[[File:A flock of Australian White Sheep in Mudgegonga, Victoria, Australia. This is breed of hair sheep suited for the hot and varied Australian climate.jpg|thumb|upright=1.1|A flock of [[Australian White sheep|Australian White]] hair sheep in Mudgegonga, Victoria, Australia. This is a new breed of hair sheep suited for the hot and varied Australian climate.]]
One class of sheep are the dairy breeds, although they are much less common than [[dairy cattle|dairy cow]]s or [[dairy goat]]s.  There are a few breeds that are predominantly used for milking; there are also dual-purpose breeds that may primarily be meat or wool sheep can be used secondarily as milking animals. Dedicated dairy sheep breeds produce a higher quantity of milk and have slightly longer lactation curves.<ref>{{cite book |title=Dairy Sheep Nutrition |last=Pulina |first=Giuseppe |author2=Roberta Bencini |year=2004 |publisher=CABI Publishing |isbn=978-0-85199-595-3 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=rTdfR3UxWXQC&q=dairy+sheep+breeds |access-date=1 November 2020 |archive-date=15 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220315191248/https://books.google.com/books?id=rTdfR3UxWXQC&q=dairy+sheep+breeds |url-status=live }}</ref> In the quality of their milk, the fat and protein content percentages of dairy sheep vary from non-dairy breeds, but lactose content does not.<ref name="Pulina2">Pulina et al. p. 2.</ref>

Another group of sheep breeds is that of fur or hair sheep, which do not grow wool at all. Hair sheep are similar to the early domesticated sheep kept before woolly breeds were developed, and are raised for meat and pelts. Some modern breeds of hair sheep, such as the [[Dorper (sheep)|Dorper]], result from crosses between wool and hair breeds. For meat producers, hair sheep are cheaper to keep, as they do not need shearing. Hair sheep are also more resistant to parasites and hot weather.<!-- Needs a cite--> As the price of coarse wool has steadily declined, there has become more interest in these sheep varieties and crossbreeding with them; it often costs more to shear meat sheep than is earned from selling the wool.<ref name="wool-price-hair-sheep-nyt-2025">{{multiref2|{{cite news |date=13 February 2025 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2025/02/13/arts/design/sheep-exhibition-formafantasma-oltre-terra.html |title=11,000 Years of Designer Sheep |first=Nina |last=Siegal |newspaper=The New York Times}} | {{cite web |url=https://www.exlana.co.uk/breeding-the-wool-off-your-flock |title=Want to breed the wool off your sheep? |website=Exlana |publisher=Sheep Improved Genetics Ltd |first=Tim |last=White |date=2018 |access-date=24 October 2026 }} }}</ref>

The 20th and 21st century have seen the rise of corporate [[agribusiness]] and the decline of localized [[family farm]]s. Large sheep holders generally favor keeping just the "best" breeds for the land and pasture they have available, in particular favoring fast-growing and fertile breeds.  This has had the result that many breeds of sheep are in danger of extinction. The [[Rare Breeds Survival Trust]] estimated in 2008 that 22 breeds native to the United Kingdom as having 3,000 registered animals (each) or fewer, and [[The Livestock Conservancy]] listed 8 North American breeds as either "critical" or "threatened" in 2008.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.rbst.org.uk/watch-list/sheep.php |title=Sheep |access-date=7 September 2008 |author=[[Rare Breeds Survival Trust]] (UK) |date=January 2008 |work=Rare Breeds Watchlist | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20080622235527/http://www.rbst.org.uk/watch-list/sheep.php| archive-date = 22 June 2008}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.rbst.org.uk/watch-list/main.php|title=Watchlist |access-date=7 September 2008 |author=[[Rare Breeds Survival Trust]] (UK) | year=2008 |work=A numerical guide to the 2008 Watchlist categories | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20080731020600/http://www.rbst.org.uk/watch-list/main.php| archive-date = 31 July 2008}}</ref><ref>{{Citation|url = https://www.livestockconservancy.org/index.php/heritage/internal/conservation-priority-list#Sheep|title = Conservation Priority List|publisher = [[The Livestock Conservancy]]|access-date = 3 September 2013|work = livestockconservancy.org|archive-date = 25 October 2010|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20101025081314/http://albc-usa.org/cpl/wtchlist.html#Sheep|url-status = live}}</ref> Heritage or heirloom breeds have been pushed to the margins of the sheep industry.{{sfn|Wooster|2005|pp=17-21}}<!-- COuld use some non-Anglo sources here about the rest of the world.-->

== Diet ==

=== Herbivory ===

[[File:Rumen-sheep2.jpg|thumb|upright=1.1|Ruminant system of a sheep]]

Sheep are [[herbivorous]]. Most breeds prefer to graze on grass and other short [[roughage]], avoiding the taller woody parts of plants that goats readily consume. Both sheep and goats use their [[lip]]s and [[tongue]]s to select parts of the plant that are easier to digest or higher in nutrition. Sheep, however, graze well in [[monoculture]] pastures where most goats fare poorly.<ref name="rankins-pugh-feeding">{{cite book |last1=Rankins |first1=Darrell L. Jr. |last2=Pugh |first2=David G. |chapter=2. Feeding and Nutrition |editor1-last=Pugh |editor1-first=David G. |editor2-last=Baird |editor2-first=A. Nickie |title=Sheep and Goat Medicine |edition=2nd |date=2012 |publisher=Saunders |isbn=978-1-4377-2353-3 |page=18 }}</ref>

Like all ruminants, sheep have a complex [[digestive system]] composed of four chambers, allowing them to break down [[cellulose]] from stems, leaves, and seed hulls into simpler [[carbohydrate]]s. When sheep [[Grazing|graze]], vegetation is chewed into a mass called a [[Bolus (digestion)|bolus]], which is then passed into the [[rumen]], via the [[Reticulum (anatomy)|reticulum]]. The rumen is a 19- to 38-liter (5 to 10 gallon) organ in which feed is [[Fermentation (food)|fermented]].{{sfn|Simmons|Ekarius|2019|at=6. Feeds and Feeding: Digestion}} The fermenting organisms include bacteria, fungi, and protozoa.<ref>Van Soest, P. J. 1994.  Nutritional ecology of the ruminant. 2nd ed. Cornell Univ. Press. 476 pp.</ref> (Other important rumen organisms include some archaea, which produce methane from carbon dioxide.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Wright | first1 = A.-D. G. | display-authors = etal | year = 2004 | title = Molecular diversity of rumen methanogens from sheep in Western Australia | journal = Appl. Environ. Microbiol. | volume = 70 | issue = 3| pages = 1263–1270 | doi=10.1128/aem.70.3.1263-1270.2004| pmid = 15006742 | pmc = 368393| bibcode = 2004ApEnM..70.1263W }}</ref>) The bolus is periodically regurgitated back to the mouth as [[cud]] for additional chewing and [[salivation]].{{sfn|Simmons|Ekarius|2019|at=6. Feeds and Feeding: Digestion}} After fermentation in the rumen, feed passes into the [[Reticulum (anatomy)|reticulum]] and the [[omasum]].  Some feeds such as grains spend little time in the rumen and ferment rapidly.{{NoteTag|This has practical considerations in sheep husbandry.  Sheep at a feedlot are put on grain-heavy diets to fatten them up for slaughter, but if not properly acclimated, the rapid fermentation of the grain in the rumen can cause acidosis and illness.<ref name="jolly-cottle-feeding">{{cite book |last1=Jolly |first1=San |last2=Cottle |first2=David J. |chapter=14. Feeding |editor-last=Cottle |editor-first=David J. |title=International Sheep and Wool Handbook |date=2010 |publisher=Nottingham University Press |isbn=978-1-904761-86-0 |pages=351, 364 }}</ref>}} After the first three chambers, food moves into the [[abomasum]] for final digestion before processing by the [[intestine]]s. The abomasum is the chamber most analogous to a human stomach in operation, and is sometimes called the "true stomach".{{sfn|Simmons|Ekarius|2019|at=6. Feeds and Feeding: Digestion}}

Other than forage, the other staple feed for sheep is [[hay]], often during the winter months.{{sfn|Wooster|2005|pp=53-60}} The ability to thrive solely on pasture (even without hay) varies with breed, but all sheep can survive on this diet.<!-- ref? -->  Sheep also require minerals in their diet, either in a trace mix or from [[salt lick]]s.<ref name="cottle-digestion">{{cite book |last=Cottle |first=David J. |chapter=13. Digestion and Metabolism |editor-last=Cottle |editor-first=David J. |title=International Sheep and Wool Handbook |date=2010 |publisher=Nottingham University Press |isbn=978-1-904761-86-0 |pages=321–324 }}</ref> One complication with sheep husbandry is that sheep are substantially more vulnerable to [[copper toxicity]] than other livestock. [[Copper]], while needed in small quantities, becomes in large quantities a [[Bioaccumulation|cumulative poison]] to sheep that is excreted very slowly.  Sheep feeding on certain plants such as [[Heliotropium|heliotropes]] can cause stored copper in the liver to be discharged en masse, resulting in sudden death.  Careless farmers supplying to their flock mineral supplements designed for cattle, pigs, or horses that contain too much copper can cause sickness and death.<ref name="jolly-cottle-feeding" />{{sfn|Simmons|Ekarius|2019|at=6. Feeds and Feeding: Nutrients}}{{sfn|Wooster|2005|p=68}}

=== Grazing behavior ===

[[File:Grazing, rotational.svg|thumb|upright=1.3|[[Rotational grazing]] allows farmers to avoid [[overgrazing]]. ]]

Sheep follow a [[diurnality|diurnal]] pattern of activity, feeding from dawn to dusk, stopping sporadically to rest and chew their [[cud]]. Ideal pasture for sheep is not lawnlike grass, but an array of grasses, [[legume]]s and [[forb]]s.{{sfn|Simmons|Ekarius|2019|at=3. Pasture, Fences, and Facilities: Pasture}} Types of land where sheep are raised vary widely, from pastures that are seeded and improved intentionally to rough, native lands. Common plants toxic to sheep are present in most of the world, and include (but are not limited to) cherry, some oaks and acorns, tomato, [[Taxus|yew]], rhubarb, potato, and [[rhododendron]]. Just a few leaves of rhododendrons such as [[Azalea]]s can be lethal.{{sfn|Simmons|Ekarius|2019|at=6. Feeds and Feeding: Types of Feed}}

Sheep are largely [[grazing]] herbivores, unlike [[Browsing (predation)|browsing]] animals such as goats and deer that prefer taller foliage. With a much narrower face and a split upper lip, sheep crop plants very close to the ground and can [[overgraze]] a pasture much faster than cattle. For this reason, many shepherds use [[managed intensive rotational grazing]], where a flock is rotated through multiple pastures, giving plants time to recover.{{sfn|Brown|Meadowcroft|1989|pp=72–74}}<!-- NOTE: Needs a better ref, current ref does not cover sheep overgrazing faster than cattle. --> Sheep can both cause and solve the spread of [[invasive species|invasive plant species]]. By disturbing the natural state of pasture, sheep and other livestock can pave the way for invasive plants. However, sheep also prefer to eat invasives such as [[cheatgrass]], [[Euphorbia virgata|leafy spurge]], [[kudzu]] and [[spotted knapweed]] over native species such as [[sagebrush]], making grazing sheep effective for [[conservation grazing]].{{sfn|Simmons|Ekarius|2009|p=143}} <!--Not in 5th edition inexplicably, or at least not in the e-edition) --> Research conducted in [[Imperial County, California]] compared lamb grazing with [[herbicides]] for weed control in seedling [[alfalfa]] fields. Three trials demonstrated that grazing lambs were just as effective as herbicides in controlling winter weeds. [[Entomologist]]s also compared grazing lambs to [[insecticides]] for insect control in winter alfalfa. In this trial, lambs provided insect control as effectively as insecticides.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://ucanr.org/delivers/impactview.cfm?impactnum=176 |title=Sheep grazing reduces pesticide use in alfalfa |work=ucanr.org |publisher=University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources |access-date=11 May 2009 |archive-date=25 May 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100525075744/http://ucanr.org/delivers/impactview.cfm?impactnum=176 |url-status=live }}</ref> Sheep grazing labor has also been used to a limited extent for controlling hazardous species such as [[giant hogweed]].<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.invasivespecies.scot/sheep-grazing-management-guidance | title=Sheep Grazing as a Management Tool to Control Giant Hogweed {{!}} Scottish Invasive Species Initiative | access-date=6 February 2025 | archive-date=16 January 2025 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250116223244/https://www.invasivespecies.scot/sheep-grazing-management-guidance | url-status=dead }}</ref>

In the 21st century, sheep have been used in [[agrivoltaics]], grazing plants near solar power arrays.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Gasch |first1=Adam |last2=Lara |first2=Rafael |last3=Pearce |first3=Joshua M. |date=1 March 2025 |title=Financial analysis of agrivoltaic sheep: Breeding and auction lamb business models |journal=Applied Energy |volume=381 |bibcode=2025ApEn..38125057G |doi=10.1016/j.apenergy.2024.125057 |issn=0306-2619 |doi-access=free |article-number=125057}}</ref>

==Behavior==

===Flock behavior===
[[File:Border Collie sheepdog trial.jpg|thumb|upright=1.1|Sheep showing flocking behavior during a [[sheepdog trial]]]]
[[File:Herding sheep353 (edited).jpg|thumb|upright=1.1|Shepherd herding a flock in China]]
Sheep are [[Herd animal|flock]] animals and strongly [[gregarious]]; much sheep behavior can be understood on the basis of these tendencies. The [[dominance hierarchy]] of sheep and their natural inclination to follow a leader to new pastures were the pivotal factors in sheep being one of the first domesticated livestock species.{{sfn|Budiansky|1999|pp=65-67}} Furthermore, in contrast to the [[red deer]] and [[gazelle]] (two other ungulates of primary importance to meat production in prehistoric times), sheep do not defend [[Territory (animal)|territories]] although they do form [[home ranges]].<ref name="CluttonBrock, (1987)">Clutton-Brock, J., (1987). A Natural History of Domesticated Mammals. Cambridge University Press, Cambridge  pp.55</ref> All sheep have a tendency to congregate close to other members of a flock, although this behavior varies with breed;{{sfn|Smith|Aseltine|Kennedy|1997|p=5}} sheep can become stressed when separated from their flock members.{{sfn|Simmons|Ekarius|2019|at=1. Starting with Sheep: Emotions and Senses}}<!-- Weak ref--> During flocking, sheep have a strong tendency to follow, and a leader may simply be the first individual to move.  Relationships in flocks tend to be closest among related sheep: in mixed-breed flocks, subgroups of the same breed tend to form, and a ewe and her direct descendants often move as a unit within large flocks.{{sfn|Weaver|2005|p=17}} Sheep can become [[hefted]] to one particular local pasture (heft) so they do not roam freely in unfenced landscapes. Lambs learn the heft from ewes and if whole flocks are culled it must be retaught to the replacement animals.<ref>{{cite news| url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/uk_news/england/1634526.stm| work=BBC News| date=3 November 2001| title=Sheep taught to stay put| access-date=29 April 2006| archive-date=21 June 2006| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060621120854/http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/england/1634526.stm| url-status=live}}</ref>

Flock behavior in sheep is generally only exhibited in groups of four or more sheep; fewer sheep may not react as expected when alone or with few other sheep.{{sfn|Weaver|2005|pp=18, 50-51, 57}} Being a prey species, the primary defense mechanism of sheep is to flee from danger when their [[flight zone]] is entered. Cornered sheep may warn via any of hoof stamping, jumping, or adopting an aggressive posture.  They will charge and butt if they decide to fight, most notably for ewes protecting newborn lambs, and rams.  The English verb "[[:wikt|ram]]" directly comes from male sheep charging at targets of their ire, "ramming" them.{{sfn|Weaver|2005|pp=18, 50-51, 57}}

In regions where sheep have no natural predators, none of the native breeds of sheep exhibit a strong flocking behavior.

====Herding====
[[File:Round 'em up.jpg|thumb|right|upright=1.1|Escaped sheep being led back to pasture with the enticement of food. This method of moving sheep works best with smaller flocks.]]
Farmers exploit flocking behavior to keep sheep together on unfenced pastures such as in [[hill farming]], and to move them more easily. For this purpose shepherds often use [[herding dog]]s.  Humans can also herd sheep directly, most effectively with a promise of food, such as presenting a bucket of feed to them and carrying it in the desired direction.{{sfn|Wooster|2005|pp=73-75}}{{sfn|Weaver|2005|p=53}}  Association of humans with regular feeding results in sheep soliciting humans, essentially taking the behavior lambs have with their mothers and applying it to humans as well (e.g. bleating or pressing their noses for attention and food).{{sfn|Budiansky|1999|pp=97–102}}

===Dominance hierarchy===
Sheep establish a [[dominance hierarchy]] through fighting, threats and competitiveness. Dominant animals are inclined to be more aggressive with other sheep, and usually feed first at [[wikt:trough|troughs]].{{sfn|Simmons|Ekarius|2019|at=1. Starting with Sheep: Behavior}} Primarily among rams, horn size is a factor in the flock hierarchy. Rams with different size horns may be less inclined to fight to establish the dominance order, while rams with similarly sized horns are more so.{{sfn|Budiansky|1999|pp=78-79}} [[Merino]]s have an almost linear hierarchy whereas there is a less rigid structure in Border Leicesters when a competitive feeding situation arises.<ref name="Squires and Daws, (1975)">{{cite journal | last1 = Squires | first1 = V.R. | last2 = Daws | first2 = G.T. | year = 1975 | title = Leadership and dominance relationships in Merino and Border Leicester sheep | journal = Applied Animal Ethology | volume = 1 | issue = 3| pages = 263–274 | doi=10.1016/0304-3762(75)90019-x}}</ref>

In sheep, position in a moving flock is highly correlated with social dominance, but there is no definitive study to show consistent voluntary leadership by an individual sheep.<ref name="Squires and Daws, (1975)" />

In sheep husbandry, unfamiliar rams will often spar with each other to establish dominance; rams can potentially injure one another in such sparring.  It is usually recommended that rams be penned near each other while unable to harm the other for a day or two.  Rams may also butt their human handlers, especially if they are unwisely treated familiarly while lambs.{{sfn|Simmons|Ekarius|2019|at=9. Flock Management: The "Battering" Ram}}{{sfn|Wooster|2005|pp=108-110}}

===Intelligence and learning ability===
Sheep are frequently thought of as [[Animal cognition|unintelligent animals]].{{sfn|Smith|Aseltine|Kennedy|1997|pp=3-4}} The 18th-century naturalist [[Georges-Louis Leclerc, Comte de Buffon|Georges-Louis Leclerc]] wrote that the "weakness and stupidity of the sheep" was so extreme as that "without the assistance of man, the sheep could never have subsisted, or continued its species in a wild state," adding that they were "contemptible (...) and devoid of every mental quality."{{sfn|Armstrong|2016|pp=11-13}} In the 21st century, many sheep breeders are eager to share stories of particularly stupid ways a sheep in their flock got themselves killed, such as by getting their head stuck in a fence and breaking their neck in trying to escape.{{sfn|Armstrong|2016|pp=45-53}}

Despite these perceptions, there is evidence that sheep are not as dumb as traditionally portrayed. To begin with, cultures that prize independence tend to be more likely to depict sheep as unintelligent; cultures with a strong emphasis on collective security do not, seeing the flocking instincts of sheep as a wise survival strategy for the whole.{{sfn|Armstrong|2016|pp=45-53}} Another obvious aspect swaying perception of sheep as stupid is that commercially farmed sheep live in a very different situation than feral sheep; [[Thelma Rowell]] performed a study of feral sheep that observed inter-flock communication, long-term relationships, and techniques for leadership and reconciliation between clashing sheep. A [[University of Illinois system|University of Illinois]] monograph on sheep reported their intelligence to be just below that of pigs and on par with that of cattle.{{sfn|Weaver|2005|pp=14-15}} In a study published in ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]'' in 2001, Keith M. Kendrick and others reported: "Sheep recognize and are attracted to individual sheep and humans by their faces, as they possess similar specialized neural systems in the [[temporal lobe|temporal]] and [[frontal lobe]]s&nbsp;... individual sheep can remember 50 other different sheep faces for over 2 years".<ref name="nature-2001">{{cite journal |last1=Kendrick |first1=Keith M. |last2=da Costa |first2=Ana P. |last3=Leigh |first3=Andrea E. |last4=Hinton |first4=Michael R. |last5=Peirce |first5=Jon W. |date=November 2001 |title=Sheep don't forget a face |journal=Nature |volume=414 |issue=6860 |pages=165–166 |doi=10.1038/35102669 |pmid=11700543 |bibcode=2001Natur.414..165K |s2cid=4405566 }}</ref><ref name="morell-natgeo-2008">{{Cite journal |last=Morell |first=Virginia |date=March 2008 |title=Animal Minds |periodical=[[National Geographic Magazine]] |publisher=The [[National Geographic Society]] |volume=213 |issue=3 |page=47}}</ref> In addition to long-term facial recognition of individuals, sheep can also differentiate emotional states through facial characteristics.<ref name="tate-2006">{{cite journal |last1=Tate |first1=A. J. |last2=Fischer |first2=H. |last3=Leigh |first3=Andrea E. |last4=Kendrick |first4=Keith M. |date=2006 |title=Behavioural and neurophysiological evidence for face identity and face emotion processing in animals |journal=Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London. Series B, Biological Sciences |volume=361 |issue=1476 |pages=2155–2172 |doi=10.1098/rstb.2006.1937}}</ref><ref name="morell-natgeo-2008"/>{{sfn|Armstrong|2016|pp=45-53}} If worked with patiently, sheep may learn their names, and many sheep are trained to be led by [[halter]] for showing and other purposes.{{sfn|Weaver|2005|pp=56, 84}} Sheep have also responded well to [[clicker training]].{{sfn|Weaver|2005|p=138}} 

It has been reported that some sheep have apparently shown problem-solving abilities; a flock in [[West Yorkshire]], England, allegedly found a way to get over [[cattle grid]]s by rolling on their backs, although documentation of this has relied on anecdotal accounts.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/uk/2004/jul/30/sillyseason.ruralaffairs|title=Pennine spot where sheep won't be fenced in|last=Wainwright|first=Martin|date=30 July 2004|work=[[The Guardian]]|access-date=17 June 2008|archive-date=28 August 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130828034816/http://www.theguardian.com/uk/2004/jul/30/sillyseason.ruralaffairs|url-status=live}}</ref>{{sfn|Armstrong|2016|pp=45-53}} Merino sheep tested for their performance in [[maze]]s have shown the ability to learn from previous runs through a maze.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lee |first1=Caroline |last2=Colegate |first2=Steve |last3=Fisher |first3=Andrew D. |year=2006 |title=Development of a maze test and its application to assess spatial learning and memory in Merino sheep |journal=Applied Animal Behaviour Science |volume=96 |issue=1–2 |pages=43–51 |doi=10.1016/j.applanim.2005.06.001 }}</ref>{{sfn|Armstrong|2016|pp=45-53}}
<!-- Rarely, sufficiently large sheep have been used as pack animals, largely in Central Asia, such as by the [[Xiongnu]].  A few places in [[Tibet]] and [[Nepal]] continue this tradition.{{sfn|Weaver|2005|p=74}}-->

===Vocalizations===
{{anchor|Vocalisations}}
{{Redirect|Baa Baa|the nursery rhyme|Baa, Baa, Black Sheep}}
{{listen |filename=Sheep bleating.ogg |title=A sheep bleating|description=A sheep bleat}}
Sounds made by domestic sheep include bleats, grunts, rumbles and snorts. Bleating ("baaing") is used mostly for contact communication, especially between dam and lambs, but also at times between other flock members.<ref name=Lynch1992>Lynch, J.J., G. N Hinch and D. B. Adams. (1992). ''The Behaviour Of Sheep:  Biological Principles And Implications For Production.'' CABI, Wallingford. 237 pp.</ref> The bleats of individual sheep are distinctive, enabling the ewe and her lambs to recognize each other's vocalizations.<ref>Fraser, A. F. and D. M. Broom. (1997). ''Farm Animal Behaviour And Welfare.'' 3rd Ed. CABI, Wallingford, UK. 437 pp.</ref> Vocal communication between lambs and their dam declines to a very low level within several weeks after parturition.<ref name=Lynch1992/> A variety of bleats may be heard, depending on sheep age and circumstances. Apart from contact communication, bleating may signal distress, frustration or impatience; however, sheep are usually silent when in pain. Isolation commonly prompts bleating by sheep.<ref name="dwyer-welfare" /><!-- NOTE: Check page and verify --> Pregnant ewes may grunt when in labor.<ref>Vince, M. A., A. E. Billing, B. A. Baldwin, J. N. Toner and C. Weller. (1985). Maternal vocalizations and other sounds in the fetal lamb's sound environment. Early Human Development, 11: 179–190.</ref> Rumbling sounds are made by the ram during courting; somewhat similar rumbling sounds may be made by the ewe,<ref name=Lynch1992/> especially when with her neonate lambs. A snort (explosive exhalation through the nostrils) may signal aggression or a warning,<ref name=Lynch1992/><ref>Houpt, K. A. (2005). ''Domestic Animal Behavior For Veterinarians And Animal Scientists.'' Blackwell Publishers, Ames, Iowa. 506 pp.</ref> and is often elicited from startled sheep.<ref>Hurnik, J. F. (1995) ''Dictionary of Farm Animal Behavior'', quoted at [http://www.ansc.purdue.edu/USDA/viddic/viddics.htm Department of Animal Sciences, Purdue University] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160303223829/http://www.ansc.purdue.edu/USDA/viddic/viddics.htm |date=3 March 2016 }}</ref>

===Senses===
[[File:A curious Welsh Mountain sheep (Ovis aries).jpg|thumb|upright=1.1|A Welsh Mountain sheep]]
In sheep breeds lacking facial wool, the visual field is wide. In 10 sheep (Cambridge, Lleyn and Welsh Mountain breeds, which lack facial wool), the visual field ranged from 298° to 325°, averaging 313.1°, with binocular overlap ranging from 44.5° to 74°, averaging 61.7°.<ref name=Piggins1996>Piggins, D. and C. J. C. Phillips. 1996. The eye of the domesticated sheep and its implications for vision. Animal Science. 62: 301–308.</ref> In some breeds, unshorn facial wool can limit the visual field; in some individuals, this may be enough to cause "wool blindness". In 60 Merinos, visual fields ranged from 219.1° to 303.0°, averaging 269.9°, and the binocular field ranged from 8.9° to 77.7°, averaging 47.5°; 36% of the measurements were limited by wool,<ref name=Hutson1980>Hutson, G. D. 1980. Visual field, restricted vision and sheep movement in laneways. Appl. Anim. Ethol. 6: 175–187.</ref> although photographs of the experiments indicate that only limited facial wool regrowth had occurred since shearing. In addition to facial wool (in some breeds), visual field limitations can include ears and (in some breeds) horns,<ref name=Hutson1980/> so the visual field can be extended by tilting the head. Sheep eyes exhibit very low [[hyperopia]] and little [[Astigmatism (eye)|astigmatism]]. Such visual characteristics are likely to produce a well-focused retinal image of objects in both the middle and long distance.<ref name=Piggins1996/> Because sheep eyes have no [[accommodation (eye)|accommodation]], one might expect the image of very near objects to be blurred, but a rather clear near image could be provided by the [[Tapetum lucidum|tapetum]] and large retinal image of the sheep's eye, and adequate close vision may occur at muzzle length.<ref name=Piggins1996/> Sheep have good [[depth perception]] within the narrow field seen by both eyes directly in front of them, as confirmed in "visual cliff" experiments.<ref name=Hutson1980/><ref>Hargreaves, A. L. and G. D. Hutson. 1997. Handling systems for sheep. Livestock Production Science 49: 121–138.</ref>{{sfn|Simmons|Ekarius|2019|at=1. Starting with Sheep: Behavior}} Sheep are thought to have color vision, and can distinguish between a variety of colors: black, red, brown, green, yellow, and white.<ref name="Alexander and Shillito, (1978)">Alexander, G. and Shillito, E.E. (1978). Maternal responses in Merino ewes to artificially coloured lambs. Applied Animal Ethology, 4: 141–152</ref>

Sight is a vital part of sheep communication, and when grazing, they maintain visual contact with each other.<ref name="Kilgour, (1977)">Kilgour, R., (1977). Design sheep yards to suit the whims of sheep. N.Z. Farmer, 98(6): 29–31</ref> Each sheep lifts its head upwards to check the position of other sheep in the flock. This constant monitoring is probably what keeps the sheep in a flock as they move along grazing. Sheep become stressed when isolated; this stress is reduced if they are provided with a mirror, indicating that the sight of other sheep reduces stress.<ref name="Parrott, (1990)">Parrott, R.F., (1990). Physiological responses to isolation in sheep. Social Stress in Domestic Animals, Kluwer Academic Publishers, Dordrecht, Netherlands: 1990. 212 -226</ref>

Taste is the most important sense in sheep, establishing forage preferences, with sweet and sour plants being preferred and bitter plants being more commonly rejected. Touch and sight are also important in relation to specific plant characteristics, such as succulence and growth form.<ref name="Krueger, et al., (1974)">Krueger, W.C., Laycock, W.A. and Price, D.A., (1974). Relationships of taste, smell, sight and touch on forage selection. Journal of Range Management, 27(4): 258–262</ref> The ram uses his [[vomeronasal]] organ (sometimes called the Jacobson's organ) to sense the pheromones of ewes and detect when they are in [[estrus]].<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Ungerfeld | first1 = R. | last2 = Ramos | first2 = M. A. | last3 = Möller | first3 = R. | year = 2006 | title = Role of the vomeronasal organ on ram's courtship and mating behaviour and on mate choice among oestrous ewes | journal = Appl. Anim. Behav. Sci. | volume = 99 | issue = 3–4| pages = 248–252 | doi=10.1016/j.applanim.2005.10.016}}</ref> The ewe uses her vomeronasal organ for early recognition of her neonate lamb.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Booth | first1 = K. K. | last2 = Katz | first2 = L. S. | year = 2000 | title = Role of the vomeronasal organ in neonatal offspring recognitions in sheep | journal = Biol. Reprod. | volume = 63 | issue = 3| pages = 353–358 | doi = 10.1095/biolreprod63.3.953 | pmid = 10952943 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

==Reproduction==
{{Main|Domestic sheep reproduction}}
[[File:Sheep in Yorkshire Dales2.jpg|thumb|upright=1.1|4-week-old lambs in the Yorkshire Dales]]
[[File:Emerging lamb cropped.jpg|thumb|upright=1.1|The second of twins being born]]
Sheep follow a similar [[Reproduction|reproductive]] strategy to other herd animals. A group of ewes is generally mated by a single ram, who has either been chosen by a breeder or, in [[feral]] populations, has established dominance through physical contest with other rams.{{sfn|Wooster|2005|pp=103-110}} Most sheep are [[seasonal breeder]]s, although some are able to breed year-round. Ewes generally reach sexual maturity at six to eight months old, and rams generally at four to six months.{{sfn|Wooster|2005|pp=112-113}} However, there are exceptions. For example, Finnsheep ewe lambs may reach puberty as early as 3 to 4 months, and Merino ewes sometimes reach puberty at 18 to 20 months.<ref>Jainudeen, M. R. et al. 2000, "Sheep and goats". In: Hafez, E. S. E. and B. Hafez (eds.) Reproduction in farm animals. 7th ed. Lippincott, Williams and Wilkins. pp. 172–181.</ref> Ewes have [[estrus]] cycles wherein they are in heat for around 30 hours on average every 17 days, although individual ewes can vary anywhere in a range of 12&ndash;48 hours. Ewes exhibit few external signs of being in heat; the best signal is that they will follow rams around, then stand still to be mounted.  This has led to the use of "teaser rams" (vasectomized or castrated rams) by shepherds to detect which ewes are still unmated and need more time with the mating ram, or to be culled.{{sfn|SPH8|2015|pp=1005, 1012}}{{sfn|Ensminger|2002|p=83}}{{sfn|Wooster|2005|p=111}}

In feral sheep, mature rams live in all-male bands most of the year, but join female flocks during the autumn breeding season, commonly known as the [[Rut (mammalian reproduction)|rut]].  High-ranking rams engage in violent head-on clashes and flank-butting to defend estrous ewes from competing males. These contests reduce their forage intake and can leave adult males vulnerable to winter starvation, resulting in a skewed adult sex ratio the next spring.<ref>{{cite book |last=Clutton-Brock |first=Tim H. |author-link=Tim Clutton-Brock|chapter=Population Dynamics in Soay Sheep |title=Soay Sheep: Dynamics and Selection in an Island Population |publisher=Cambridge University Press |date=2003 |pages=64–70 }}</ref>

After mating, sheep have a [[gestation]] period of about five months, and normal labor takes one to three hours.{{sfn|Wooster|2005|pp=71, 124}}  Most breeds produce single or twin lambs, with the occasional line producing triplets or more.{{sfn|Simmons|Ekarius|2019|at=2. Breeding and Breeds: Individual Breeds}}<ref name="quints">{{cite news |title=Quintuplet birth takes sheep breeder by surprise |url=http://www.praguemonitor.com/en/258/czech_business/17581/ |work=Prague Daily Monitor |publisher=Czech News Agency |date= 24 January 2008 |access-date=25 January 2008 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20080129030117/http://www.praguemonitor.com/en/258/czech_business/17581/| archive-date = 29 January 2008}}</ref> During or soon after labor, ewes and lambs may be confined to small [[Glossary of sheep husbandry|lambing jugs]], small pens designed to aid both careful observation of ewes and to cement the bond between them and their lambs.{{sfn|Smith|Aseltine|Kennedy|1997|pp=31-32}}{{sfn|Brown|Meadowcroft|1989|p=115}}{{sfn|Wooster|2005|pp=122-123}}

[[File:Lamb first steps (edited).jpg|thumb|right|upright=1.1|A lamb's first steps]]

Ovine [[obstetrics]] can be problematic. By selectively breeding ewes that produce multiple offspring with higher birth weights for generations, sheep producers have inadvertently caused some domestic sheep to have difficulty lambing compared to their wild brethren. It is in a sheep raiser's financial interest to intervene and assist such difficult lambing to save the ewe and her lamb, but this has reduced the influence of [[natural selection]] on encouraging easier and safer lambing, favoring instead higher peak productivity.{{sfn|Budiansky|1999|pp=122–23}}<ref name="celi-russel-pregnancy">{{cite book |last1=Celi |first1=Pietro |last2=Bush |first2=Russel |chapter=10. Pregnancy, lambing and survival |editor-last=Cottle |editor-first=David J. |title=International Sheep and Wool Handbook |date=2010 |publisher=Nottingham University Press |isbn=978-1-904761-86-0 |pages=223–249 }}</ref> In the case of problems, humans present at lambing can assist the ewe by extracting or repositioning lambs.{{sfn|Wooster|2005|pp=125-128}} After the birth, ewes ideally break the [[amniotic sac]] (if it is not broken during labor), and begin licking clean the lamb.{{sfn|Wooster|2005|pp=118-119}}  Most lambs will begin standing within an hour of birth.{{sfn|Wooster|2005|pp=118-119}} In normal situations, lambs nurse after standing, receiving vital [[colostrum]] milk. Lambs that either fail to nurse or are rejected by the ewe require help to survive, such as bottle-feeding or fostering by another ewe.{{sfn|Smith|Aseltine|Kennedy|1997|pp=110-111}}

After lambs are several weeks old, [[Glossary of sheep husbandry|lamb marking]], [[Glossary of sheep husbandry|ear tagging]], [[Docking (animal)|docking]], and [[castrating]] are carried out.{{sfn|Wooster|2005|pp=145-147}} Vaccinations are usually applied in this period as well. Ear tags with numbers are attached, or ear marks are applied, for ease of later identification of sheep. Tail docking is commonly done 24&ndash;48 hours after birth (to avoid interference with maternal bonding and consumption of colostrum) and not later than one week after birth, to minimize pain, stress, recovery time and complications.<ref>MAFF (UK) 2000. Sheep: codes of recommendations for the welfare of livestock. Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food, London.</ref><ref>Canadian Veterinary Medical Association. Position Statement, March 1996.</ref> Castration of male lambs was once done promptly during the first week of life in 20th century practice, but now usually happens around three or four weeks of age.<ref name="spencer-1937">{{cite book |last=Spencer |first=James Burns |title=Sheep Husbandry in Canada |url=https://publications.gc.ca/collections/collection_2016/aac-aafc/agrhist/A12-8-30-1937-eng.pdf |publisher=[[Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada|Canadian Department of Agriculture]] |date=1937 |edition=8th |pages=69–70 }}</ref>{{sfn|Simmons|Ekarius|2009|pp=258–259}}<ref name="abbott-2018">{{cite book |last=Abbott |first=Kym |title=The Practice of Sheep Veterinary Medicine |url=https://www.adelaide.edu.au/press/system/files/media/documents/2019-04/uap-sheep-medicine-ebook.pdf |publisher=University of Adelaide Press |date=2018 |pages=564–565 }}</ref> The first course of vaccinations (commonly anti-clostridial) is commonly given at an age of about 10 to 12 weeks; i.e. when the concentration of maternal antibodies passively acquired via colostrum is expected to have fallen low enough to permit development of active immunity.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.drugs.com/vet/covexin-8-can.html|title=Covexin 8 (Canada) for Animal Use|website=Drugs.com|access-date=14 April 2014|archive-date=15 April 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140415072810/http://www.drugs.com/vet/covexin-8-can.html|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>Tizard, I. R. 2000. Veterinary Immunology: An Introduction. 6th ed. Saunders.</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=de la Rosa |first1=Cristina |last2=Hogue |first2=Doug |last3=Thonney |first3=Michael L. |year=1997 |title=Vaccination schedules to raise antibody concentrations against epsilon-toxin of Clostridium perfringens in ewes and their triplet lambs |journal=Journal of Animal Science |volume=75|issue=9|pages=2328–2334|doi=10.2527/1997.7592328x|pmid=9303449}}</ref> Ewes are often revaccinated annually 3 to 4 weeks before lambing, to provide high antibody concentrations in colostrum during the first several hours after lambing.<ref name="kimberling-1988">{{cite book |last=Kimberling |first=Cleon V. |date=1988 |title=Jensen and Swift's Diseases of Sheep |edition=3rd |publisher=Lea & Febiger|isbn=0-8121-1099-4 |pages=83, 116, 173–175}}</ref> Ram lambs that will either be slaughtered or separated from ewes before sexual maturity are not usually castrated.{{sfn|Simmons|Ekarius|2009|pp=308–309}}{{sfn|Ensminger|2002|pp=397–398}}{{sfn|Brown|Meadowcroft|1989|pp=183–185}}  [[Mulesing]] is a controversial practice now on the decline that scars a sheep's hindquarters in order to reduce the risk of flystrike and require less frequent crutching.<!-- Where still permitted, it is done from 2 to 8 weeks of age. -->  Objections to all these procedures have been raised by animal rights groups, but farmers defend them by saying they save money and are necessary for sheep health.<ref name="bell-management">{{cite book |last=Bell |first=Kevin |chapter=17. Sheep Management |editor-last=Cottle |editor-first=David J. |title=International Sheep and Wool Handbook |date=2010 |publisher=Nottingham University Press |isbn=978-1-904761-86-0 |pages=408–409 }}</ref>{{sfn|Armstrong|2016|pp=128–129}}

Sheep are the only species of mammal except for humans which exhibit [[Homosexual behavior in sheep|exclusive homosexual behavior]].<ref name="Poiani2010">{{cite book| first1 = Aldo | last1 = Poiani | first2 = A. F. | last2 = Dixson |title=Animal Homosexuality: A Biosocial Perspective|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=EftT_1bsPOAC&pg=PA179|date=2010|publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]]|page=179|quote=This makes O. aries (ram) only the second mammal known, apart from humans, capable of displaying exclusive homosexuality.|isbn=9781139490382}}</ref><ref name="levay" /><ref name="Roselli2011">{{cite journal |author1=Roselli CE |author2=Reddy RC |author3=Kaufman KR |title=The development of male-oriented behavior in rams |journal=[[Frontiers in Neuroendocrinology]] |publisher=[[Elsevier]]|date=2011 |volume=32 |issue=2 |pages=164–9 |doi=10.1016/j.yfrne.2010.12.007 |pmid=21215767|pmc=3085551 }}</ref> About 10% of rams refuse to mate with ewes but readily mate with other rams,<ref name="levay">{{cite book |title=Gay, Straight, and The Reason Why: The Science of Sexual Orientation|last=Levay| first=Simon |year=2017| url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-J6kDAAAQBAJ |via=[[Google Books]]|edition=2nd |url-access=limited |publisher=[[Oxford University Press]]|pages=38, 119|isbn=978-0-19-029737-4 }}</ref> and thirty percent of all rams demonstrate at least some homosexual behavior.<ref name="merck-vet-manual">{{cite book|last=Scrivener |first=C. J. |year=2005 |chapter-url=https://archive.org/details/merckveterinarym09edunse/page/1312/mode/1up |via=[[Internet Archive]] |page=1312 |chapter=Social Behavior and Behavioral Problems | title= Merck Manual of Veterinary Medicine| publisher=[[Merck & Co.]]|edition=9th |isbn=978-0-911910-50-6 |chapter-url-access=limited}}</ref><ref name="roselli-stormshak-2009">{{cite journal | vauthors = Roselli CE, Stormshak F | title = Prenatal programming of sexual partner preference: the ram model | journal = [[Journal of Neuroendocrinology]] |publisher=[[Wiley-Blackwell]]| volume = 21 | issue = 4 | pages = 359–64 | date = March 2009 | pmid = 19207819 | pmc = 2668810 | doi = 10.1111/j.1365-2826.2009.01828.x }}</ref> Additionally, a small number of females that were accompanied by a male fetus ''in utero'' (i.e. as [[Twins#Dizygotic (fraternal) twins|fraternal twins]]) are [[freemartin]]s (female animals that are behaviorally masculine and lack functioning [[Ovary|ovaries]]).<ref name="freemartin-sheep">{{multiref2|{{cite journal |last=Padula |first=A. M. |year=2005 |title=The freemartin syndrome: an update |journal=Animal Reproduction Science |volume=87 |issue=1–2 |pages=93–109 |doi=10.1016/j.anireprosci.2004.09.008 |pmid=15885443 }}|{{cite journal |last=Parkinson |first=T. J. |display-authors=etal |date=2001 |title=Inter-relationships among gonadotrophins, reproductive steroids and inhibin in freemartin ewes |journal=Reproduction |volume=122 |issue=3 |pages=397–409 |doi=10.1530/rep.0.1220397 |pmid=11597305 |doi-access=free }}|{{cite journal |last1=Smith |first1=K. C. |display-authors=etal |year=2003 |title=Morphological, histological and histochemical studies of the gonads of ovine freemartin |journal=Veterinary Record |volume=152 |issue=6 |pages=164–169 |doi=10.1136/vr.152.6.164 |pmid=12622286 |s2cid=21340132 }} }}</ref>

==Health==
[[File:Scrapie testing.jpg|thumb|upright=1.1|A veterinarian draws blood to test for resistance to [[scrapie]]]]
Sheep may fall victim to poisons, [[List of infectious sheep and goat diseases|infectious diseases]], and physical injuries. As a prey species, sheep try to hide signs of illness, to prevent being targeted by predators.  This can cause unobservant shepherds to miss signs of a sheep in need.{{sfn|Wooster|2005|p=171}} However, some signs of ill health are obvious, with sick sheep eating little, lying down excessively, and being generally listless.{{sfn|Wooster|2005|p=187}} 

Throughout history, much of the money and labor of sheep husbandry has aimed to prevent sheep ailments. Historically, shepherds often created remedies by experimentation on the farm. In some developed countries, including the United States, sheep lack the economic importance for drug companies to perform expensive clinical trials required to approve more than a relatively limited number of drugs for ovine use.{{sfn|Smith|Aseltine|Kennedy|1997|pp=95-96}} Extra-label drug use in sheep production is permitted in many jurisdictions, subject to certain restrictions.{{NoteTag|In the United States, for example, regulations governing extra-label drug use in animals are found in 21 CFR (Code of Federal Regulations) Part 530.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.accessdata.fda.gov/scripts/cdrh/cfdocs/cfCFR/CFRSearch.cfm?CFRPart=530&show |title=CFR – Code of Federal Regulations Title 21 |website=Accessdata.fda.gov |date=7 November 1996 |access-date=14 April 2014 |archive-date=15 April 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140415080612/http://www.accessdata.fda.gov/scripts/cdrh/cfdocs/cfCFR/CFRSearch.cfm?CFRPart=530&show |url-status=dead }}</ref>}} In the 20th and 21st centuries, a minority of sheep owners have turned to alternative treatments such as [[homeopathy]] and [[herbalism]] to treat sheep veterinary problems.{{sfn|Simmons|Ekarius|2019|at=7. General Health Considerations: Alternative Health Practices}} The effectiveness of alternative veterinary medicine has been met with skepticism by agricultural scientists.<ref>{{cite journal|author1=Paolo Bellavite |author2=Riccardo Ortolani |author3=Anita Conforti |name-list-style=amp |date=June 2006 |title=Immunology and Homeopathy. Experimental Studies on Animal Models |journal=Evidence-Based Complementary and Alternative Medicine |volume=3 |issue=2 |pages=171–86 |pmid=16786046|doi=10.1093/ecam/nel016|pmc=1475939}}</ref>  Certified [[organic farming]] with sheep requires eschewing certain medications, resulting in some shepherds recommending keeping two flocks &ndash; the lucky and healthy sheep who aren't immediately treated and stay in the organic flock, while any sheep needing anti-parasite drugs or [[antibiotics]] are moved into a standard flock.{{sfn|Wooster|2005|pp=208-210}}

Many breeders take a variety of [[Preventive medicine|preventive measures]] to ward off problems. Regulating sheep intermixing can check the spread of disease from flock to flock. This can mean verifying sheep health before they are transferred or purchased, and [[Quarantine|quarantining]] new sheep for two or three weeks. Good nutrition and good sanitation also greatly improve sheep health.{{sfn|Simmons|Ekarius|2019|at=7. General Health Considerations: Healthy Strategies}}  Avoiding poisons is  important; common poisons sheep can encounter are [[pesticide]] sprays, inorganic [[fertilizer]], [[motor oil]], and radiator coolant containing ethylene glycol.{{sfn|Simmons|Ekarius|2019|at=6. Feeds and Feeding: Types of Feed}}  

Reducing stress in sheep is also important for their health. Restraint, isolation, loud noises, novel situations, pain, heat, extreme cold, fatigue and other stressors can lead to secretion of cortisol, a stress hormone, in amounts that may indicate welfare problems.<ref>Grandin, T. (ed.). 2007. Livestock handling and transport. 3rd Ed. CABI, Wallingford, UK. 386 pp.</ref><ref name="Gregory, N. G 1998">Gregory, N. G. 1998. Animal welfare and meat science. CABI, Wallingford, UK. 298 pp.</ref><ref>Houpt, K. A. 2004. Behavioral physiology. In: Reece, W. O. (ed.). Dukes' physiology of domestic animals. 12th Ed. Cornell Univ. Press, Ithaca, New York. pp. 952–961.</ref><ref name="Moberg, G. P 2000. pp. 1-21">Moberg, G. P. and J. A. Mench. 2000. The biology of animal stress: basic principles and implications for welfare. CABI, Wallingford, UK. pp. 1–21.</ref> Excessive stress can compromise the immune system.<ref name="Moberg, G. P 2000. pp. 1-21"/> "Shipping fever" (pneumonic mannheimiosis, formerly called pasteurellosis) is a disease of particular concern, that can occur as a result of stress, notably during transport and (or) handling.<ref name="plummer-respiratory">{{cite book |last1=Plummer |first1=Paul J. |last2=Plummer |first2=Cassandra L. |last3=Still |first3=Kelly M. |chapter=7. Diseases of the Respiratory System |editor1-last=Pugh |editor1-first=David G. |editor2-last=Baird |editor2-first=A. Nickie |title=Sheep and Goat Medicine |edition=2nd |date=2012 |publisher=Saunders |isbn=978-1-4377-2353-3 |page=135 }}</ref><ref>Brogden, K. A., H. D. Lehmjuhl, R. C. Cutlip. 1998. Pasteurella haemolytica complicated respiratory infections in sheep and goats. Vet. Res. 29: 233–254.</ref><ref name="kimberling-1988" /> Pain, fear and several other stressors can cause secretion of epinephrine (adrenaline). Considerable epinephrine secretion in the final days before slaughter can adversely affect meat quality (by causing glycogenolysis, removing the substrate for normal post-slaughter acidification of meat) and result in meat becoming more susceptible to colonization by spoilage bacteria.<ref name="Gregory, N. G 1998"/>  

[[File:Sheep with orf.jpg|thumb|right|upright=1.1|A sheep infected with [[Orf (disease)|orf]], a disease transmittable to humans through skin contact]]

Both external and internal [[parasite]]s are the most prevalent malady in sheep, and can reduce their productivity or outright kill them.  To deal with this, common forms of preventive medication for sheep are [[vaccination]]s and a variety of medicinal treatments.{{sfn|Simmons|Ekarius|2019|at=7. General Health Considerations: Causes of Illness in Sheep}} Worms are the most common internal parasites, including [[Nematode|roundworm]]s, [[Moniezia expansa|tapeworm]]s, [[Fasciola hepatica|liver fluke]]s, and others. They are ingested during grazing, incubate within the sheep, and are expelled through the digestive system, beginning the cycle again. Worms can cause [[diarrhea]] (scouring) in mild cases, and death in severe cases. Oral anti-parasitic medicines, known as [[Deworming|drenches]], are given to a flock to treat worms, sometimes after worm eggs in the feces has been counted to assess infestation levels. Afterwards, sheep may be moved to a new pasture to avoid ingesting the same parasites.{{sfn|Brown|Meadowcroft|1989|pp=81–84}} External sheep parasites include [[Bovicola ovis|lice]], [[Melophagus ovinus|sheep keds]], [[Oestrus ovis|nose bot flies]], [[Psorergates ovis|sheep itch mites]], and [[maggot]]s. Keds are blood-sucking parasites that cause general malnutrition and decreased productivity, but are not fatal. Maggots are those of the [[bot fly]] and the [[blow-fly]], commonly ''[[Common green bottle fly|Lucilia sericata]]'' or its relative ''L. cuprina''. Fly maggots cause the extremely destructive condition of [[flystrike]]. Flies lay their eggs in wounds or wet, manure-soiled wool; when the maggots hatch they burrow into a sheep's flesh, eventually causing death if untreated. In addition to other treatments, [[crutching]] (shearing wool from a sheep's rump) is a common preventive method. Some countries allow [[mulesing]], a practice that involves stripping away the skin on the rump to prevent fly-strike, normally performed when the sheep is a lamb.<ref name="DPI SOP">{{cite web |url = http://www.dpi.nsw.gov.au/agriculture/livestock/animal-welfare/general/other/livestock/sop/sheep/mulesing
|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20070906155137/http://www.dpi.nsw.gov.au/agriculture/livestock/animal-welfare/general/other/livestock/sop/sheep/mulesing
|archive-date = 6 September 2007
|title = Standard Operating Procedures – sheep Mulesing
|website = New South Wales Department of Primary Industries
|access-date = 1 March 2008}}</ref><ref name="Model Code">{{cite book
|url = http://www.publish.csiro.au/nid/22/pid/5389.htm
|format = PDF
|title = Model Code of Practice for the Welfare of Animals: The Sheep
|edition = 2nd
|series = Primary Industries Report Series 89
|pages = 17–23
|publisher = [[CSIRO]] Publishing
|author = Primary Industries Ministerial Council
|year = 2006
|access-date = 1 March 2008
|isbn = 978-0-643-09357-7
|archive-date = 29 August 2016
|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20160829214844/http://www.publish.csiro.au/nid/22/pid/5389.htm
|url-status = live
}}</ref>  Nose bots are fly larvae that inhabit a sheep's [[Paranasal sinus|sinuses]], causing breathing difficulties and discomfort. Common signs are a discharge from the nasal passage, sneezing, and frantic movement such as head shaking. External parasites may be controlled through the use of [[Glossary of sheep husbandry|backliners]], sprays, or immersive [[sheep dip]]s.{{sfn|Simmons|Ekarius|2019|at=7. General Health Considerations: Parasites}}<ref name="besier-health">{{cite book |last1=Besier |first1=Brown |last2=Jacobson |first2=Caroline |last3=Woodgate |first3=Rob |last4=Bell |first4=Kevin |chapter=20. Sheep Health |editor-last=Cottle |editor-first=David J. |title=International Sheep and Wool Handbook |date=2010 |publisher=Nottingham University Press |isbn=978-1-904761-86-0 |pages=471–486 }}</ref>

[[File:Huda Ram.jpg|thumb|upright=1.1|An [[Uda sheep|Uda]] ram, Nigeria]]
A wide array of bacterial and viral diseases affect sheep. Diseases of the hoof, such as [[foot rot]] and foot scald may occur, and are treated with footbaths and other remedies. [[Foot rot]] is present in over 97% of flocks in the UK.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/fawc-opinion-on-sheep-lameness|title=FAWC opinion on sheep lameness|website=gov.uk|access-date=4 June 2019|archive-date=4 June 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190604045854/https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/fawc-opinion-on-sheep-lameness|url-status=live}}</ref> These painful conditions cause lameness and hinder feeding. Ovine [[Johne's disease]] is a chronic, incurable wasting disease in which infected sheep lose weight despite eating normally, and usually die. Sheep are usually infected when young, but often show no signs until they are several years old.<ref name="besier-health" />{{sfn|Ensminger|2002|pp=184–185}}{{sfn|Simmons|Ekarius|2019|at=7. General Health Considerations: Other Disorders of Sheep}} [[Bluetongue disease]] is an insect-borne illness causing fever and inflammation of the [[mucous membrane]]s. [[Ovine rinderpest]] (or ''peste des petits ruminants'') is a highly contagious and often fatal [[virus|viral]] disease affecting sheep and goats. Sheep may also be affected by primary<ref>{{cite journal |author1=Jane C. Quinn |author2=Yuchi Chen |author3=Belinda Hackney|author4=Muhammad Shoaib Tufail|author5=Panayiotis Loukopoulos |title=Acute-onset high-morbidity primary photosensitisation in sheep associated with consumption of the Casbah and Mauro cultivars of the pasture legume biserrula |journal=BMC Veterinary Research |volume=14 |issue=1 |pages=11 |year=2018 |doi=10.1186/s12917-017-1318-7|pmid=29325550 |pmc=5765607 |doi-access=free }}</ref> or secondary photosensitization. [[Tetanus]] can also afflict sheep through wounds from [[Sheep shearing|shearing]], [[Docking (animal)|docking]], [[castration]], or vaccination. The organism also can be introduced into the reproductive tract by unsanitary humans who assist ewes during lambing.<ref name="mathis-ross-2005">{{Cite web |url=https://pubs.nmsu.edu/_circulars/CR604.pdf |first1=Clay P. |last1=Mathis |first2=Tim |last2=Ross |date=January 2005 |title=Sheep Production and Management |publisher=New Mexico State University College of Agriculture and Home Economics }}</ref><ref name="besier-health" />

[[Scrapie]] is a fatal [[prion]] disease of the nervous system of sheep and goats, with an incubation period measured in years.{{sfn|Ensminger|2002|pp=188–189}}<ref name="greenlee-scrapie">{{cite journal |last=Greenlee |first=Justin J. |title=Review: Update on Classical and Atypical Scrapie in Sheep and Goats |journal=Veterinary Pathology |volume=56 |issue=1 |pages=6–16 |date=2019 |doi=10.1177/0300985818794247 |pmid=30200819}}</ref> [[Foot-and-mouth disease]] (FMD) is a highly contagious viral disease of cloven-hoofed livestock that causes fever and blisters on the mouth and feet; it is often mild in sheep, who can spread it without showing obvious signs. The [[2001 United Kingdom foot-and-mouth outbreak|2001 outbreak in the United Kingdom]], one of the largest on record, led to the culling of about six million animals, 4.9 million of them sheep.<ref name="reilly-musculoskeletal">{{cite book |last1=Reilly |first1=Laura K. |last2=Baird |first2=A. Nickie |last3=Pugh |first3=David G. |chapter=11. Diseases of the Musculoskeletal System |editor1-last=Pugh |editor1-first=David G. |editor2-last=Baird |editor2-first=A. Nickie |title=Sheep and Goat Medicine |edition=2nd |date=2012 |publisher=Saunders |isbn=978-1-4377-2353-3 |page=307 }}</ref><ref name="sellick-rgs-fmd">{{cite web |last=Sellick |first=Jessica |title=Foot and Mouth Disease (FMD) |url=https://www.rgs.org/schools/resources-for-schools/foot-and-mouth-disease-fmd |publisher=[[Royal Geographical Society]] |access-date=27 October 2026}}</ref>

A few sheep diseases are transmissible to humans. [[Orf (animal disease)|Orf]] (also known as scabby mouth or contagious ecthyma) is a viral skin disease that can spread via skin contact.<ref name="besier-health" /> [[Anthrax]] usually kills sheep within an hour of symptoms appearing, and people can catch it from handling infected animals or their wool and hides.{{sfn|Ensminger|2002|pp=175–176}} Enzootic abortion, caused by ''[[Chlamydia abortus]]'', can spread to human women and cause miscarriage, so pregnant women are advised to stay away from lambing ewes.<ref name="gov-scot-lambing">{{cite web |title=Pregnant women in lambing season: advice |url=https://www.gov.scot/publications/pregnant-women-lambing-season-advice/pages/chlamydia/ |publisher=Scottish Government |date=8 January 2015 |access-date=27 October 2026}}</ref>  

Of the 600,300 sheep lost to the US economy in 2004, 37.3% were lost to predators, while 26.5% were lost to some form of disease. Poisoning accounted for 1.7% of non-productive deaths.<ref name="usda-nass-2005"/>

When all else fails, veterinarians can perform a [[necropsy]] on a dead sheep's carcass.  While it is obviously too late to save that sheep, this can aid in understanding the cause of death, and if there is a broader threat to the flock.{{sfn|Simmons|Ekarius|2019|at=7. General Health Considerations: Healthy Strategies}}

===Predators===
{{Main|Domestic sheep predation}}
[[File:Coyotekilling.jpg|thumb|upright=1.1|A lamb being attacked by [[coyote]]s with a bite to the throat]]

Other than parasites and disease, [[predation]] is a threat to sheep and the profitability of sheep raising. Sheep have little ability to defend themselves, compared with other species kept as livestock. Even if sheep survive an attack, they may die from their injuries or simply from panic.{{sfn|Simmons|Ekarius|2019|at=5. Protecting against Predators: Managing for Predators}} However, the impact of predation varies dramatically with region. In Africa, Australia, the Americas, and parts of Europe and Asia predators are a serious problem. In the United States, for instance, over one third of sheep deaths in 2004 were caused by predation.<ref name="usda-nass-2005" /> Some nations avoid this; predators are largely not a concern in [[New Zealand]].<ref>{{cite journal |last=Shelton |first=Maurice |date=2004 |title=Predation and Livestock Production: Perspective and Overview |journal=Sheep & Goat Research Journal |volume=19 |pages=2–5}}</ref>  Worldwide, [[Canidae|canids]]—including the domestic dog—are responsible for most sheep deaths.<ref>{{cite news |title=Sheep mauled by wild dogs |url=http://www.tweeddailynews.com.au/news/apn-sheep-mauled-by-wild/145009/ |work=Tweed Daily News |date=18 January 2008 |access-date=21 January 2008 |archive-date=24 April 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160424020849/http://www.tweeddailynews.com.au/news/apn-sheep-mauled-by-wild/145009/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite news |first=Gareth |last=Lewis |title=Sheep worrying leads to warning from farmers |url=http://www.dailyecho.co.uk/debusiness/news/display.var.1980009.0.sheep_worrying_leads_to_warning_from_farmers.php |work=The Daily Echo |date= 21 January 2008 |access-date=21 January 2008|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210119031549/https://www.dailyecho.co.uk/business/1980009.sheep-worrying-leads-to-warning-from-farmers/ | archive-date=19 January 2021|url-status=live|quote=In total dog attacks cost the industry more than £2m a year Mr Wyeth says thousands of sheep and cattle die as a result of injuries caused by dogs every year. His warning comes at a time when ewes are in lamb and likely to abort if chased by dogs. }}</ref><ref name="macdonald-canids">{{cite book |title=The Biology and Conservation of Wild Canids |last=Macdonald |first=David Whyte |author2=Claudio Sillero-Zubiri |year=2004 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-851555-5 }}</ref> Other animals that occasionally prey on sheep include felines, bears, birds of prey, ravens, and [[feral pig]]s.<ref name="usda-nass-2005">{{cite web |date=6 May 2005 |title=Sheep and Goats Death Loss |publisher=[[National Agricultural Statistics Service]] |website=usda.library.cornell.edu |url=https://esmis.nal.usda.gov/sites/default/release-files/hh63sv88v/xk81jp327/9g54xm03j/sgdl-05-06-2005.pdf |access-date=22 January 2019 |archive-date=22 January 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190122144925/https://downloads.usda.library.cornell.edu/usda-esmis/files/hh63sv88v/xk81jp327/9g54xm03j/sgdl-05-06-2005.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref>{{sfn|Simmons|Ekarius|2019|at=5. Protecting against Predators: Managing for Predators}}

Sheep producers have used a wide variety of measures to combat predation. Pre-modern shepherds used their own presence, [[livestock guardian dog]]s, and protective structures such as barns and fences.{{sfn|Wooster|2005|pp=79-93}}  These older techniques have been adjusted; [[Electric fence|electric fencing]] began to be used in the 20th century in addition to regular fences, but is less effective on sheep (naturally insulated by their wool from electricity) than on cattle.<ref name="hanrahan-structures">{{cite book |last=Hanrahan |first=P. D. |chapter=21. Farm Structures |editor-last=Cottle |editor-first=David J. |title=International Sheep and Wool Handbook |date=2010 |publisher=Nottingham University Press |isbn=978-1-904761-86-0 |pages=489-505 }}</ref>  Another recent adjustment has been penning sheep at night for sheep who normally externally graze.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Breck |first1=Stewart W. |last2=Vorster |first2=Anthony G. |last3=Evangelista |first3=Paul |last4=Krebs |first4=Cameron |last5=Elzinga |first5=Glenn |last6=Elzinga |first6=Caryl |last7=Grandin |first7=Temple |author-link7=Temple Grandin |last8=Salerno |first8=Jonathan |title=Transitory night penning of sheep and cattle for predation protection: Costs, benefits, and challenges |journal=Rangelands |volume=48 |issue=1 |year=2026 |pages=15–22 |doi=10.1016/j.rala.2025.11.004|doi-access=free }}</ref>  Modern shepherds use guns, [[Animal trapping|traps]], and poisons to kill predators,{{sfn|Simmons|Ekarius|2019|at=5. Protecting against Predators: Managing for Predators}} causing significant decreases in predator populations. In the wake of the environmental and conservation movements, the use of these methods now usually falls under the purview of specially designated government agencies in most developed countries.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.aphis.usda.gov/wildlife_damage/nwrc/downloads/effects_on_predators.pdf |title=Effects of Wildlife Services on Predator Populations |date=October 2001 |publisher=Wildlife Services |website=www.aphis.usda.gov |access-date=14 August 2016 |archive-date=20 December 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161220132947/https://www.aphis.usda.gov/wildlife_damage/nwrc/downloads/effects_on_predators.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref>

The 1970s saw a resurgence in the use of livestock guardian dogs and the development of new methods of predator control by sheep producers, many of them non-lethal.<!-- NOTE Needs a source. --> [[Donkey]]s and [[guard llama]]s have been used on similar principles as livestock guardian dogs.{{sfn|Simmons|Ekarius|2019|at=5. Protecting against Predators: Managing for Predators}} Multi-species pasturing, usually with larger livestock such as cattle or horses, may help to deter predators, even if such species do not actively guard sheep.{{sfn|Ensminger|2002|pp=917-920}}  In addition to animal guardians, contemporary sheep operations may use non-lethal predator deterrents such as motion-activated lights and loud alarms, although light seems to be much more effective than noise.{{sfn|Ensminger|2002|pp=914-915}}

== Economic importance ==

{{Main|Agricultural economics}}
