|first3=Aaron A. |last4=Hairsine |first4=Peter B. |last5=Bartley |first5=Rebeca |last6=Baker |first6=Brett |title=Grazing impacts on gully dynamics indicate approaches for gully erosion control in northeast Australia |date=5 January 2018 |journal=[[Earth Surface Processes and Landforms]] |doi=10.1002/esp.4339 |volume=43 |issue=8 |pages=1711–25 |bibcode=2018ESPL...43.1711W |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/322344231 |access-date=27 March 2026 }}</ref> which often results in ground compaction.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Sharrow |first=Steven H. |title=Soil compaction by grazing livestock in silvopastures as evidenced by changes in soil physical properties |date=4 July 2007 |journal=Agroforestry Systems |doi=10.1007/s10457-007-9083-4 |volume=71 |issue=3 |pages=215–23 |bibcode=2007AgrSy..71..215S |url=https://z-library.sk/book/gjGeyaGmOW |access-date=27 March 2026 }}</ref> Because the soil is exposed, it loses the ability to absorb excess water, and erosion can develop in susceptible areas.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://agriculture.vic.gov.au/farm-management/soil/erosion/gully-erosion |title=Gully erosion |website=[[Agriculture Victoria]] |date=4 June 2020 |access-date=27 March 2026 }}</ref>

=== Rivers and streams{{Anchor|gully erosion|ephemeral gully erosion}} ===
{{further|topic=water's erosive ability|Hydraulic action}}
[[File:Dobbingstone Burn - geograph.org.uk - 1291882.jpg|thumb|Dobbingstone Burn, Scotland—This photo illustrates two different types of erosion affecting the same place. Valley erosion is occurring due to the flow of the stream, and the boulders and stones (and much of the soil) that are lying on the edges are [[glacial till]] that was left behind as [[ice age]] glaciers flowed over the terrain.]]
''Valley'' or ''stream erosion'' occurs with continued [[water flow]] along a linear feature. The erosion is both [[Downcutting|downward]], deepening the [[valley]], and [[headward erosion|headward]], extending the valley into the hillside, creating [[Head cut (stream geomorphology)|head cuts]] and steep banks. In the earliest stage of [[stream]] erosion, the erosive activity is dominantly vertical, the valleys have a typical '''V''' cross-section and the stream gradient is relatively steep.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Tucker |first1=Gregory E. |last2=Whipple |first2=Kelin X. |title=Topographic outcomes predicted by stream erosion models: sensitivity analysis and intermodel comparison |date=September 2002 |journal= Journal of Geophysical Research: Solid Earth|doi=10.1029/2001JB000162 |volume=107 |issue=B9 |article-number=2179 |bibcode=2002JGRB..107.2179T |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/215614578 |access-date=20 April 2026 }}</ref> When some [[base level]] is reached, the erosive activity switches to lateral erosion, which widens the valley floor and creates a narrow [[floodplain]]. The stream gradient becomes nearly flat, and lateral deposition of [[sediment]]s becomes important as the stream [[meander]]s across the valley floor. In all stages of stream erosion, by far the most erosion occurs during times of [[flood]], when more and faster-moving water is available to carry a larger [[sediment load]].<ref>{{cite web |last=Panchuk |first=Karla |title=Stream erosion and deposition |website=[[LibreTexts]] Geosciences |date=24 April 2023 |url=https://geo.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Geology/Physical_Geology_(Panchuk)/14%3A_Streams_and_Floods/14.03%3A_Stream_Erosion_and_Deposition |access-date=30 March 2026 }}</ref> In such processes, it is not the water alone that erodes: suspended [[abrasive]] particles, [[pebble]]s and [[boulder]]s can also act erosively as they traverse a [[Erosion surface|surface]], in a process known as ''traction''.<ref>{{cite web |last=Ritter |first=Michael |title=Geologic work of streams |website=The Physical Environment: an Introduction to Physical Geography |date=6 May 2012 |url=https://www.thephysicalenvironment.com/Book/fluvial_systems/geologic_work_of_streams.html |access-date=30 March 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120506040721/http://www4.uwsp.edu/geo/faculty/ritter/geog101/textbook/fluvial_systems/geologic_work_of_streams.html |archive-date=6 May 2012 |url-status=live }}</ref>

''Bank erosion'' is the wearing away of the banks of a [[stream]] or [[river]]. This is distinguished from changes on the bed of the [[watercourse]], which is referred to as ''scour''. Erosion and [[River bank failure|changes in the form of river banks]] may be measured by inserting metal rods into the bank and marking the position of the bank surface along the rods at different times.<ref>{{cite book |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=_PJHw-hSKGgC&pg=PA113 |title=Stream hydrology: an introduction for ecologists |last1=Gordon |first1=Nancy D. |last2=McMahon |first2=Thomas A. |last3=Finlayson |first3=Brian L. |last4=Gippel |first4=Christopher J. |last5=Nathan |first5=Rory J. |chapter=Erosion and scour |page=113 |isbn=978-0-470-84357-4 |date=1 June 2004 |publisher=[[John Wiley and Sons]] |location=Hoboken, New Jersey |edition=2nd |access-date=30 March 2026 }}</ref>

''Thermal erosion'' is the result of [[melting]] and weakening [[permafrost]] due to moving water.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://nsidc.org/learn/cryosphere-glossary/thermal-erosion |title=Thermal erosion |website=[[National Snow and Ice Data Center|NSIDC]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101218124656/http://nsidc.org/cgi-bin/words/word.pl?thermal%20erosion |archive-date=18 December 2010 |url-status=live |access-date=30 March 2026 }}</ref> It can occur both along rivers and at the coast. Rapid [[river channel migration]] observed in the [[Lena River]] of [[Siberia]] is due to [[Fluvio-thermal erosion|thermal erosion]], as these portions of the banks are composed of permafrost-cemented non-cohesive materials.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1002/esp.592 |title=Fluvial thermal erosion investigations along a rapidly eroding river bank: application to the Lena River (central Siberia) |date=November 2003 |last1=Costard |first1=François |last2=Dupeyrat |first2=Laure |last3=Gautier |first3=Emmanuèle |last4=Carey-Gailhardis |first4=Évelyne |journal=[[Earth Surface Processes and Landforms]] |volume=28 |issue=12 |pages=1349–59 |bibcode=2003ESPL...28.1349C |s2cid=131318239 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/227701165 |access-date=30 March 2026 }}</ref> Much of this erosion occurs as the weakened banks fail in large [[Slump (geology)|slump]]s.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1016/j.coldregions.2012.07.007 |title=Development and thermal regime of a thaw slump in the Qinghai-Tibet plateau |date=December 2012 |last1=Niu |first1=Fujun |last2=Luo |first2=Jing |last3=Lin |first3=Zhanju |last4=Ma |first4=Wei |last5=Lu |first5=JiaHao |journal=Cold Regions Science and Technology |volume=83–84 |issue=42 |pages=131–8 |bibcode=2012CRST...83..131N |url=https://z-library.sk/book/zOoLrxpeRQ |access-date=30 March 2026 }}</ref> Thermal erosion also affects the [[Arctic]] coast, where wave action and near-shore temperatures combine to undercut permafrost [[cliff|bluffs]] along the [[shoreline]] and cause them to fail. Annual erosion rates along a {{convert|100|km|mi|abbr=off|adj=on}} segment of the Beaufort Sea shoreline averaged {{convert|5.6|m|ft|abbr=off}} per year from 1955 to 2002.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Jones |first1=Benjamin M. |last2=Hinkel |first2=Kenneth M. |last3=Arp |first3=Christopher D. |last4=Eisner |first4=Wendy R. |date=December 2008 |title=Modern erosion rates and loss of coastal features and sites, Beaufort Sea Coastline, Alaska |journal=[[Arctic (journal)|Arctic]] |volume=61 |issue=4 |pages=361–72 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/42766295 |doi=10.14430/arctic44 |bibcode=2008Arcti..61..361J |hdl=10535/5534 |hdl-access=free |access-date=30 March 2026 }}</ref>

=== Floods ===

At extremely high flows, [[Kolk (vortex)|kolk]]s, or [[vortex|vortices]] are formed by large volumes of rapidly rushing water. Kolks cause extreme local erosion, plucking [[bedrock]] and creating [[pothole]]-type geographical features called [[rock-cut basin]]s. Examples can be seen in the [[flood]] regions result from glacial [[Lake Missoula]], which created the [[channeled scablands]] in the [[Columbia River drainage basin|Columbia Basin]] region of eastern [[Washington (state)|Washington]].<ref>{{cite journal |last=Bretz |first=J. Harlen |date=September 1969 |title=The Lake Missoula floods and the channeled scabland |journal=[[The Journal of Geology]] |volume=77 |issue=5 |pages=505–43 |url=https://z-library.sk/book/zOoDkZ9kRQ |doi=10.1086/627452 |bibcode=1969JG.....77..505B |access-date=30 March 2026 }}</ref>

=== Wind erosion ===
[[File:Im Salar de Uyuni.jpg|thumb|[[Árbol de Piedra]], a rock formation in the [[Altiplano]], [[Bolivia]], sculpted by wind erosion]]
{{main|Aeolian processes}}
Wind erosion is a major [[geomorphological]] force, especially in [[arid]] and [[Semi-arid climate|semi-arid]] regions. It is also a major source of land degradation, evaporation, desertification, harmful airborne dust, and crop damage—especially after being increased far above natural rates by human activities such as [[deforestation]], [[urbanization]], and [[agriculture]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Zheng |first=Xiaojing |title=Mechanics of wind-blown sand movements |chapter=Wind erosion |publisher=[[Springer Science+Business Media]] |location=Dordrecht, The Netherlands |year=2009 |isbn=978-3-540-88253-4 |pages=7–8 |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=R6kYrbA3XSAC&pg=PA7 |access-date=30 March 2026 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Cornelis |first= Wim S. |chapter=Hydroclimatology of wind erosion in arid and semi-arid environments |editor-last1=D'Odorico |editor-first1=Paolo |editor-last2=Porporato |editor-first2=Amilcare |title=Dryland ecohydrology |publisher=[[Springer Science+Business Media]] |location=Dordrecht, The Netherlands |year=2006 |isbn=978-1-4020-4261-4 |page=141 |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=rUsUPZbFHK8C&pg=PA141 |access-date=30 March 2026 }}</ref>

Wind erosion is of two primary varieties: ''[[Aeolian processes#Wind erosion|deflation]]'', where the wind picks up and carries away loose particles; and ''[[Abrasion (geology)|abrasion]]'', where surfaces are worn down as they are struck by airborne particles carried by wind. Deflation is divided into three categories: (1) ''[[Downhill creep|surface creep]]'', where larger, heavier particles slide or roll along the ground; (2) ''[[Saltation (geology)|saltation]]'', where particles are lifted a short height into the air, and bounce and saltate across the surface of the soil; and (3) ''[[Suspension (chemistry)|suspension]]'', where very small and light particles are lifted into the air by the wind, and are often carried for long distances (e.g. [[Saharan dust]]). Saltation is responsible for the majority (50–70%) of wind erosion, followed by suspension (30–40%), and then surface creep (5–25%).<ref>{{cite book |last1=Blanco-Canqui |first1=Humberto |last2=Lal |first2=Rattan |chapter=Wind erosion |editor-last1=Blanco-Canqui |editor-first1=Humberto |editor-last2=Lal |editor-first2=Rattan |title=Principles of soil conservation and management |publisher=[[Springer Science+Business Media|Springer Science+Business]] |location=Dordrecht, The Netherlands |isbn=978-1-4020-8709-7 |pages=56–57 |year=2008 |doi=10.1007/978-1-4020-8709-7_1 |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Wj3690PbDY0C&pg=PA56 |access-date=31 March 2026 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Balba |first=A. Monem |chapter=Wind erosion |title=Management of problem soils in arid ecosystems |publisher=[[CRC Press]] |location=Boca Raton, Florida |year=1995 |isbn=978-0-87371-811-0 |page=214 |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=uS62XNzDZDsC&pg=PA214 |access-date=31 March 2026 }}</ref> [[Silt]]y soils (e.g. [[loess]]) tend to be the most affected by wind erosion; silt particles are relatively easily detached and carried away.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Jefferson |first1=Ian F. |last2=Smalley |first2=Ian J. |url=https://infosys.ars.usda.gov/WindErosion/symposium/proceedings/jefferso.pdf |title=Saltating sand erodes metastable loess: events in the impact zone |website=[[United States Department of Agriculture]] |access-date=31 March 2026 |archive-date=27 December 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161227024025/https://infosys.ars.usda.gov/WindErosion/symposium/proceedings/jefferso.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref>

Wind erosion is much more severe in arid areas and during times of drought. For example, in the [[Great Plains]], it is estimated that soil loss due to wind erosion can be as much as 6100 times greater in drought years than in wet years.<ref>{{cite book |last=Wiggs |first=Giles F. S. |chapter=Geomorphological hazards in drylands |editor-last=Thomas |editor-first=David S. G. |title=Arid zone geomorphology: process, form and change in drylands |publisher=[[John Wiley & Sons]] |location=Hoboken, New Jersey |year=2011 |isbn=978-0-470-71076-0 |doi=10.1002/9780470710777.ch23 |page=588 |chapter-url=https://z-library.sk/book/ZjKlKpQPv0 |access-date=31 March 2026 }}</ref>

=== Mass movement ===
[[File:NegevWadi2009.JPG|thumb|Wadi in Makhtesh Ramon, Israel, showing gravity collapse erosion on its banks]]
''[[Mass wasting|Mass movement]]'' is the downward and outward movement of rock and sediments on a sloped surface, mainly due to the force of [[gravity]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Van Beek |first1=Rens |last2=Cammeraat |first2=Erik |last3=Andreu |first3=Vicente |last4=Mickovski |first4=Slobodan B. |last5=Dorren |first5=Luuk |chapter=Hillside processes: mass wasting, slope stability, and erosion |editor-last1=Norris |editor-first1=Joanne E. |editor-last2=Stokes |editor-first2=Alexia |editor-last3=Mickovski |editor-first3=Slobodan B. |editor-last4=Cammeraat |editor-first4=Erik |editor-last5=Van Beek |editor-first5=Rens |editor-last6=Nicoll |editor-first6=Bruce C. |editor-last7=Achim |editor-first7=Alexis |title=Slope stability and erosion control: ecotechnological solutions |publisher=[[Springer Science+Business Media]] |year=2008 |page=20 |isbn=978-1-4020-6675-7 |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=YWPcffxM_A0C&pg=PA20 |access-date=31 March 2026 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Gray |first1=Donald H. |last2=Sotir |first2=Robbin B. |chapter=Surficial erosion and mass movement |title=Biotechnical and soil bioengineering slope stabilization: a practical guide for erosion control |editor-last1=Gray |editor-first1=Donald H. |editor-last2=Sotir |editor-first2=Robbin B. |publisher=[[John Wiley & Sons]] |location=Hoboken, New Jersey |year=1996 |isbn=978-0-471-04978-4 |page=20 |chapter-url=https://archive.org/details/gray-sotir-1996 |access-date=31 March 2026 }}</ref>

Mass movement is an important part of the erosional process, and is often the first stage in the breakdown and transport of [[Weathering|weathered]] materials in mountainous areas.<ref>{{cite book |last=Nichols |first=Gary |title=Sedimentology and stratigraphy |publisher=[[John Wiley & Sons]] |location=Hoboken, New Jersey |year=2009 |edition=2nd |isbn=978-1-4051-9379-5 |page=93 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=zl4L7WqXvogC&pg=PA93 |access-date=31 March 2026 }}</ref> It moves material from higher elevations to lower elevations where other eroding agents such as [[stream]]s and [[glacier]]s can then pick up the material and move it to even lower elevations. Mass-movement processes are always occurring continuously on all slopes; some mass-movement processes act very slowly; others occur very suddenly, often with disastrous results. Any perceptible [[Downslope creep|downslope]] movement of rock or sediment is often referred to in general terms as a [[landslide]]. However, landslides can be classified in a much more detailed way that reflects the mechanisms responsible for the movement and the velocity at which the movement occurs. One of the visible topographical manifestations of a very slow form of such activity is a [[scree]] slope.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Sun |first1=Wenyi |last2=Shao |first2=Quanqin |last3=Liu |first3=Jiyuan |last4=Zhai |first4=Jun |date=October 2014 |title=Assessing the effects of land use and topography on soil erosion on the Loess Plateau in China |journal=Catena |language=en |volume=121 |pages=151–63 |doi=10.1016/j.catena.2014.05.009 |bibcode=2014Caten.121..151S |issn=0341-8162 |url=https://z-library.sk/book/2R2rKdAqRG |access-date=31 March 2026 }}</ref>

''[[Slump (geology)|Slumping]]'' happens on steep hillsides, occurring along distinct [[Fracture (geology)|fracture]] zones, often within materials like [[clay]] that, once released, may move quite rapidly downhill. They will often show a spoon-shaped [[isostatic depression]], in which the material has begun to slide downhill. In some cases, the slump is caused by water beneath the slope weakening it. In many cases it is simply the result of poor engineering along [[highway]]s where it is a regular occurrence.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Van den Berg |first1=Jan |last2=Van de Wal |first2=Roderick S. W. |last3=Milne |first3=Glenn A. |last4=Oerlemans |first4=Johannes |date=31 May 2008 |title=Effect of isostasy on dynamical ice sheet modeling: a case study for Eurasia |journal=  Journal of Geophysical Research: Solid Earth|language=en |volume=113 |issue=B5 |article-number=B05412 |doi=10.1029/2007JB004994 |bibcode=2008JGRB..113.5412V |issn=0148-0227 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

''Surface creep'' is the slow movement of soil and rock debris by [[gravity]] which is usually not perceptible except through extended observation.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1002/2016JB013394 |title=Surface creep on the North Anatolian Fault at Ismetpasa, Turkey, 1944–2016 |date=30 September 2016 |last1=Bilham |first1=Roger |last2=Ozener |first2=Haluk |last3=Mencin |first3=David |last4=Dogru |first4=Asli |last5=Ergintav |first5=Semih |last6=Çakir |first6=Ziyadin |last7=Aytun |first7=Alkut |last8=Aktug |first8=Bahadir |last9=Yilmaz |first9=Onur |last10=Johnson |first10=Wade |last11=Mattioli |first11=Glen |journal=  Journal of Geophysical Research: Solid Earth|volume=121 |issue=10 |pages=7409–31 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2016JGRB..121.7409B }}</ref> However, the term can also describe the rolling of dislodged soil particles {{convert|0.5|to|1.0|mm|abbr=on|2}} in diameter by wind along the soil surface.<ref>{{cite book |title=Soils and their environment |last1=Hassett |first1=John J. |last2=Banwart |first2=Wayne L. |publisher=[[Prentice Hall]] |location=Hoboken, New Jersey |year=1992 |isbn=9780134840499 |page=163 |url=https://archive.org/details/bwb_O9-ABU-798/page/162/mode/2up |access-date=31 March 2026 }}</ref>

=== Tillage erosion ===
[[File:Eroded hilltops.jpg|thumb|Eroded hilltops due to tillage erosion]]
[[Tillage erosion]] occurs in [[cultivated field]]s due to the movement of soil by [[tillage]].<ref name="Van Oost2006">{{cite journal |last1=Van Oost |first1=Kristof |last2=Govers |first2=Gerard |last3=De Alba |first3=Saturnio |last4=Quine |first4=Timothy Andrew |date=August 2006 |title=Tillage erosion: a review of controlling factors and implications for soil quality |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/233426051 |journal=[[Progress in Physical Geography]] |language=en |volume=30 |issue=4 |pages=443–66 |doi=10.1191/0309133306pp487ra |bibcode=2006PrPG...30..443V |issn=0309-1333 |access-date=31 March 2026 }}</ref> There is growing evidence that tillage erosion is a major soil erosion process in agricultural land, surpassing water and wind erosion in many fields all around the world, especially on sloping and hilly lands.<ref name="Van Oost2006"/> Eroded hilltops are actually caused by tillage erosion as water erosion mainly causes [[soil loss]]es in the midslope and lowerslope segments of a slope, not the hilltops.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Wang |first1=Yong |last2=Zhang |first2=Jianhui |last3=Zhang |first3=Z. H. |last4=Jia |first4=Lizhi  |date=1 May 2016 |title=Impact of tillage erosion on water erosion in a hilly landscape |url=https://z-library.sk/book/Bj46ZpBmO3 |journal=[[Science of the Total Environment]] |language=en |volume=551–552 |issue=6 |pages=522–32 |doi=10.1016/j.scitotenv.2016.02.045 |pmid=26896581 |bibcode=2016ScTEn.551..522W |issn=1879-1026 |access-date=31 March 2026 }}</ref> Tillage erosion results in [[soil degradation]], which can lead to significant reduction in [[crop yield]] and, therefore, economic losses for the farm.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1073/pnas.1922375118 |title=The extent of soil loss across the US Corn Belt |date=15 February 2021 |last1=Thaler |first1=Ivan A. |last2=Larsen |first2=Isaac J. |last3=Yu |first3=Qian |journal=[[PNAS]] |volume=118 |issue=8 |article-number=e1922375118 |doi-access=free |pmid=33593895 |pmc=7923383 |bibcode=2021PNAS..11822375T }}</ref>
[[File:Tillage erosion in field with diversion terraces.jpg|thumb|Tillage erosion in field with diversion terraces]]

== Factors affecting soil erosion ==

=== Climate ===

The [[Quantity|amount]] and [[Intensity mapping|intensity]] of [[rainfall|precipitation]] is the main [[Climate|climatic factor]] [[governing]] soil erosion by water. The [[Relationship science|relationship]] is particularly strong if heavy rainfall occurs at times when, or in locations where, the soil's surface is not well protected by [[vegetation]]. This might be during periods when [[agriculture|agricultural activities]] leave the soil bare,<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1016/j.agee.2020.107047 |title=Agricultural land use and management weaken the soil erosion induced by extreme rainstorms |date=1 October 2020 |last1=Han |first1=Jianqiao |last2=Ge |first2=Wenyan |last3=Hei |first3=Zhe |last4=Cong |first4=Chenyu |last5=Ma |first5=Chunling |last6=Xie |first6=Mengxia |last7=Liu |first7=Baoyuan |last8=Feng |first8=Wei |last9=Wang |first9=Fei |last10=Jiao |first10=Juying |journal=[[Agriculture, Ecosystems & Environment]] |volume=301 |article-number=107047 |bibcode=2020AgEE..30107047H |url=https://z-library.sk/book/wRNg0r90j9 |access-date=31 March 2026 }}</ref> or in [[Semi-arid climate|semi-arid]] regions where vegetation is naturally sparse.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1111/1365-2664.13597 |title=Trade-off between vegetation type, soil erosion control and surface water in global semi-arid regions: a meta-analysis |date=May 2020 |last1=Wu |first1=Gao-Lin |last2=Liu |first2=Yi-Fan |last3=Cui |first3=Zeng |last4=Liu |first4=Yu |last5=Shi |first5=Zhi-Hua |last6=Yin |first6=Rui |last7=Kardol |first7=Paul |journal=[[Journal of Applied Ecology]] |volume=57 |issue=5 |pages=875–85 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2020JApEc..57..875W }}</ref> [[Wind erosion]] requires strong winds, particularly during times of drought when vegetation is sparse and soil is dry (and so is more erodible).<ref>{{cite book |last1=Zobeck |first1=Ted M. |last2=Van Pelt |first2=R. Scott |chapter=Wind erosion |title=Soil management: building a stable base for agriculture |editor-last1=Hatfield |editor-first1=Jerry L. |editor-last2=Sauer |editor-first2=Thomas J. |publisher=[[American Society of Agronomy]] and [[Soil Science Society of America]] |location=Madison, Wisconsin |date=25 April 2011 |isbn=9780891181958 |doi=10.2136/2011.soilmanagement.c14 |pages=209–27 |chapter-url=https://digitalcommons.unl.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2414&context=usdaarsfacpub |access-date=1 April 2026 }}</ref> Other climatic factors such as average [[temperature]] and temperature range may also affect erosion, via their effects on [[vegetation]] and soil properties.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1016/j.ecolmodel.2006.04.019 |title=Modeling vegetation coverage and soil erosion in the Loess Plateau Area of China |date=15 September 2006 |last1=Zhou |first1=Z. C. |last2=Shangguan |first2=Z. P. |last3=Zhao |first3=Duli |journal=[[Ecological Modelling]] |volume=198 |issue=1–2 |pages=263–8 |bibcode=2006EcMod.198..263Z |url=https://www.academia.edu/74244539 |access-date=1 April 2026 }}</ref> In general, given similar vegetation and [[ecosystem]]s, areas with more [[precipitation]] (especially high-intensity [[rainfall]]), more wind, or more [[storm]]s are expected to have more erosion.<ref>{{cite web |title=Raindrops keep falling: understanding and managing water erosion |last1=Bingner |first1=Ron |last2=Wells |first2=Robert |url=https://www.ars.usda.gov/oc/utm/raindrops-keep-falling-understanding-and-managing-water-erosion |date=1 October 2025 |access-date=1 April 2026 |website=www.ars.usda.gov }}</ref>

In some areas of the world (e.g. the [[Midwestern United States]] and the [[Amazon rainforest|Amazon Rainforest]]), rainfall intensity is the primary determinant of erosivity, with higher intensity rainfall generally resulting in more soil erosion by water.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1016/j.catena.2026.109853 |title=Spatiotemporal analysis of rainfall erosivity in Oklahoma |date=April 2026 |last1=Chen |first1=Mangting |last2=Schussler |first2=Jaime Catherine |last3=Mishra |first3=Deb |journal=Catena |volume=265 |article-number=109853 |bibcode=2026Caten.26509853C |url=https://archive.org/details/chen-et-al.-2026 |access-date=1 April 2026 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1007/s40808-019-00697-6 |title=Modeling of the spatial and temporal dynamics of erosivity in the Amazon |date=5 December 2019 |last1=dos Santos Silva |first1=Danielle Sebastiana |last2=Cavalcante Blanco |first2=Claudio José |last3=dos Santos |first3=Cláudio Sebastião Jr |last4=Dias Martins |first4=Wanleysson Larry |journal=Modeling Earth Systems and Environment |volume=6 |issue=3 |pages=513–23 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/337768278 |access-date=1 April 2026 }}</ref> The size and velocity of [[rain drop]]s is also an important factor. Larger and higher-velocity rain drops have greater [[kinetic energy]], and thus their impact will displace soil particles by larger distances than smaller, slower-moving rain drops.<ref name="Blanco2008">{{cite book |last1=Blanco |first1=Humberto |last2=Lal |first2=Rattan |chapter=Water erosion |title=Principles of soil conservation and management |editor-last1=Blanco |editor-first1=Humberto |editor-last2=Lal |editor-first2=Rattan |publisher=[[Springer Science+Business Media]] |location=Dordrecht, The Netherlands |date=16 September 2008 |isbn=978-90-481-8529-0 |doi=10.1007/978-1-4020-8709-7_2 |pages=29–31 |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Wj3690PbDY0C&pg=PA29 |access-date=1 April 2026 }}</ref>

In other regions of the world (e.g. [[western Europe]]), [[Runoff (hydrology)|runoff]] and erosion result from relatively low intensities of [[Precipitation types#Stratiform|stratiform rainfall]] falling onto previously saturated soil. In such situations, rainfall amount rather than intensity is the main factor determining the severity of soil erosion by water.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Boardman |first1=John |last2=Poesen |first2=Jean |chapter=Soil erosion in Europe: major processes, causes and consequences |title=Soil erosion in Europe |editor-last1=Boardman |editor-first1=John |editor-last2=Poesen |editor-first2=Jean |publisher=[[John Wiley & Sons]] |location=Hoboken, New Jersey |date=22 September 2006 |isbn=9780470859209 |doi=10.1002/0470859202.ch36 |pages=477–87 |chapter-url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/229956244 |access-date=1 April 2026 }}</ref>

=== Soil structure and composition ===
[[File:Dead Sea Coastal Erosion March 2012.JPG|thumb|Erosional gully in unconsolidated [[Dead Sea]] (Israel) sediments along the southwestern shore. This gully was excavated by floods from the [[Judean Mountains]] in less than a year.]]
The [[Texture (geology)|texture]], [[moisture]], and [[Compaction (geology)|compaction]] of soil are all major factors in determining the erosivity of rainfall. Sediments containing more [[clay mineral]]s tend to be more resistant to erosion than those with [[sand]] or [[silt]], because the clay helps bind soil particles together.<ref>{{cite book |last=Mirsal |first=Ibrahim A. |chapter=Soil degradation |title=Soil pollution: origin, monitoring and remediation |edition=2nd |publisher=[[Springer-Verlag]] |location=Berlin, Germany |year=2008 |isbn=978-3-540-70775-2 |page=100 |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Lr5bMTxom0IC&pg=PA100 |access-date=1 April 2026 }}</ref> Soil containing high levels of [[Soil organic matter|organic matter]] are often more resistant to erosion, because the organic materials coagulate [[Soil Colloids|soil colloids]] and create a stronger, more stable soil structure.<ref name="Blanco2008"/> The amount of water present in the soil before the precipitation also plays an important role, because it sets limits on the amount of water that can be absorbed by the soil (and hence prevented from flowing on the surface as erosive [[Runoff (hydrology)|runoff]]). Wet, saturated soils will not be able to absorb as much rainwater, leading to higher levels of surface runoff and thus higher erosivity for a given volume of rainfall.<ref name="Blanco2008"/><ref>{{cite book |last=Torri |first=Dino |chapter=Slope, aspect and surface storage |editor-last=Agassi |editor-first=Menachem |title=Soil erosion, conservation, and rehabilitation |publisher=[[CRC Press]] |location=Boca Raton, Florida |year=1996 |isbn=978-0-8247-8984-8 |page=95 |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-AqdSMDSUIgC&pg=PA95 |access-date=1 April 2026 }}</ref> [[Soil compaction (agriculture)|Soil compaction]] also affects the [[Permeability of soils|permeability]] of the soil to water, and hence the amount of water that flows away as runoff. More compacted soils will have a larger amount of surface runoff than less compacted soils.<ref name="Blanco2008"/>

=== Vegetative cover ===
{{See also|Vegetation and slope stability}}
[[Vegetation]] acts as an interface between the [[Atmosphere of Earth|atmosphere]] and the [[soil]]. It increases the [[Permeability (Earth sciences)|permeability]] of the [[soil]] to [[rain]]water, thus decreasing [[Runoff (hydrology)|runoff]].<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1051/agro:2007062 |title=Soil-erosion and runoff prevention by plant covers: a review |date=March 2008 |last1=Durán Zuazo |first1=Víctor Hugo |last2=Rodríguez Pleguezuelo |first2=Carmen Rocío |journal=[[Agronomy for Sustainable Development]] |volume=28 |issue=1 |pages=65–86 |bibcode=2008AgSD...28...65D |url=https://hal.science/hal-00886458/document |access-date=1 April 2026 }}</ref> It shelters the soil from [[wind]]s, which results in decreased [[wind erosion]],<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1029/2007JF000758 |title=A new model of wind erosion in the presence of vegetation |date=June 2008 |last=Okin |first=Gregory S. |journal= Journal of Geophysical Research: Earth Surface|volume=113 |issue=F2 |article-number=F02S10 |bibcode=2008JGRF..113.2S10O |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/248805022 |access-date=1 April 2026 }}</ref> as well as advantageous changes in [[microclimate]].<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1007/s11442-022-1948-y |title=Effects of vegetation restoration on local microclimate on the Loess Plateau |date=28 January 2022 |last1=Wang |first1=Chenxi |last2=Liang |first2=Wei |last3=Yan |first3=Jianwu |last4=Jin |first4=Zhao |last5=Zhang |first5=Weibin |last6=Li |first6=Xiaofei |journal=Journal of Geographical Sciences |volume=32 |issue=2 |pages=291–316 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2022JGSci..32..291W }}</ref> The [[root]]s of the [[plant]]s bind the [[soil]] together, and [[interweave]] with other roots, forming a more [[solid]] [[mass]] that is less susceptible to both [[water]]<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1191/0309133305pp443ra |title=Impact of plant roots on the resistance of soils to erosion by water: a review |date=June 2005 |last1=Gyssels |first1=G. |last2=Poesen |first2=J. |last3=Bochet |first3=Esther |last4=Li |first4=Yong |journal=[[Progress in Physical Geography: Earth and Environment]] |volume=29 |issue=2 |pages=189–217 |bibcode=2005PrPG...29..189G |url=https://z-library.sk/book/VOw3wdJJO3 |access-date=1 April 2026 }}</ref> and [[Aeolian processes|wind erosion]].<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1177/030913339301700104 |title=The protective role of sparse vegetation in wind erosion |date=March 1993 |last1=Wolfe |first1=Stephen A. |last2=Nickling |first2=William G. |journal=[[Progress in Physical Geography: Earth and Environment]] |volume=17 |issue=1 |pages=50–68 |bibcode=1993PrPG...17...50W |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/249822989 |access-date=1 April 2026 }}</ref> The removal of [[vegetation]] increases the rate of [[Erosion|surface erosion]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Styczen |first1=Merete E. |last2=Morgan |first2=Roy P. C. |chapter=Engineering properties of vegetation |editor-last1=Morgan |editor-first1= Roy P. C. |editor-last2=Rickson |editor-first2=R. Jane |title=Slope stabilization and erosion control: a bioengineering approach |publisher=[[Taylor & Francis]] |location=Abingdon-on-Thames, United Kingdom |year=1995 |isbn=978-0-419-15630-7 |chapter-url=https://archive.org/details/styczen-morgan-1995 |pages=4–60 |access-date=1 April 2026 }}</ref>

=== Topography ===

The [[topography]] of the [[land]] determines the [[velocity]] at which [[surface runoff]] will flow, which in turn determines the [[Erosion|erosivity]] of the runoff. Longer, steeper slopes (especially those without adequate vegetative cover) are more susceptible to very high rates of erosion during heavy rains than shorter, less steep slopes.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1016/j.catena.2017.10.013 |title=Effects of topographic factors on runoff and soil loss in Southwest China |date=January 2018 |last1=Zhang |first1=Xingqi |last2=Hu |first2=Maochuan |last3=Guo |first3=Xinya |last4=Yang |first4=Hong |last5=Zhang |first5=Zhenke |last6=Zhank |first6=Keli |journal=Catena |volume=160 |pages=394–402 |bibcode=2018Caten.160..394Z |url=https://z-library.sk/book/8jmLANPwRZ |access-date=2 April 2026 }}</ref> Steeper terrain is also more prone to [[mudslide]]s, [[landslide]]s, and other forms of [[Gravity|gravitational]] erosion processes.<ref>{{cite book |last=Whisenant |first=Steve G. |chapter=Terrestrial systems |editor-last1=Perrow |editor-first1=Michael R. |editor-last2=Davy |editor-first2=Anthony J. |title=Handbook of ecological restoration, Volume 1, Principles of restoration |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]] |location= Cambdridge, United Kingdom |year=2008 |isbn=978-0-521-04983-2 |doi=10.1017/CBO9780511549984.008 |page=89 |chapter-url=https://z-library.sk/book/Bj4VKKMyO3 |access-date=2 April 2026 }}</ref><ref name="Blanco2008"/><ref>{{cite book |last1=Wainwright |first1=John |last2=Brazier |first2=Richard E. |chapter=Slope systems |editor-last=Thomas |editor-first=David S. G. |title=Arid zone geomorphology: process, form and change in drylands |pages=209–33 |publisher=[[John Wiley & Sons]] |location=Hoboken New Jersey |edition=3rd |year=2011 |isbn=978-0-470-71076-0 |chapter-url=https://z-library.sk/book/0OZdAxd1jd |doi=10.1002/9780470710777.ch10 |access-date=2 April 2026 }}</ref>

== Human activities that aid soil erosion ==

=== Agricultural practices ===
{{see also|agricultural pollution|overgrazing}}
[[File:Soil erosion at Hill Farm - geograph.org.uk - 1287527.jpg|thumb|Tilled farmland such as this is very susceptible to erosion from rainfall, due to the destruction of vegetative cover and the loosening of the soil during plowing.]]
Unsustainable [[agricultural practice]]s increase rates of erosion by one to two [[Order of magnitude|orders of magnitude]] over the natural rate and far exceed replacement by soil production.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Montgomery |first1=David R. |title=Soil erosion and agricultural sustainability |journal=[[PNAS]] |date=8 August 2007 |volume=104 |issue=33 |pages=13268–72 |doi=10.1073/pnas.0611508104 |pmid=17686990 |pmc=1948917 |bibcode=2007PNAS..10413268M |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Wuepper |first1=David |last2=Borrelli |first2=Pasquale |last3=Finger |first3=Robert |date=January 2020 |title=Countries and the global rate of soil erosion |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/337698100 |journal=[[Nature Sustainability]] |language=en |volume=3 |issue=1 |pages=51–5 |doi=10.1038/s41893-019-0438-4 |s2cid=208539010 |issn=2398-9629 |access-date=2 April 2026 }}</ref> The [[tillage]] of [[agricultural land]]s, which breaks up soil into finer particles, is one of the primary factors. The problem has been exacerbated in modern times, due to mechanized agricultural equipment that allows for [[deep plowing]], which severely increases the amount of soil that is available for transport by water erosion. Others include [[monocropping]], farming on steep slopes, [[pesticide]] and [[chemical fertilizer]] usage (which kill [[Soil biology|organism]]s that bind soil together), row-cropping, and the use of [[surface irrigation]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Blanco-Canqui |first1=Humberto |last2=Lal |first2=Rattan |chapter=Tillage erosion |editor-last1=Blanco-Canqui |editor-first1=Humberto |editor-last2=Lal |editor-first2=Rattan |title=Principles of soil conservation and management |publisher=[[Springer Science+Business Media|Springer Science+Business]] |location=Dordrecht, The Netherlands |isbn=978-1-4020-8709-7 |page=109 |year=2008 |doi=10.1007/978-1-4020-8709-7_5 |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Wj3690PbDY0C&pg=PA109 |access-date=2 April 2026 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Lobb |first=D. A. |chapter=Soil movement by tillage and other agricultural activities |doi=10.1016/B978-008045405-4.00832-6 |editor-last=Jørgensen |editor-first=Sven Erik |title=Applications in ecological engineering |publisher=[[Academic Press]] |location=Cambridge, Massachusetts |page=247 |year=2009 |isbn=978-0-444-53448-4 |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=aRKO6ZazC8UC&pg=PA247 |access-date=2 April 2026 }}</ref> A complex overall situation with respect to defining nutrient losses from soils, could arise as a result of the size selective nature of soil erosion events.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1016/j.jhydrol.2011.06.010 |title=Flow-driven soil erosion processes and the size selectivity of sediment |date=18 August 2011 |last1=Asadi |first1=Hossein |last2=Moussavi |first2=Ali |last3=Ghadiri |first3=Hossein |last4=Rose |first4=Calvin W. |journal=[[Journal of Hydrology]] |volume=406 |issue=1–2 |pages=73–81 |bibcode=2011JHyd..406...73A |url=https://www.academia.edu/68216520 |access-date=2 April 2026 |hdl=10072/42591 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> Loss of total [[phosphorus]], for instance, in the finer eroded fraction is greater relative to the whole soil.<ref>{{cite journal |title=Bioavailable phosphorus in fine-sized sediments transported from agricultural fields |last1=Poirier |first1=Simon-Claude |last2=Whalen |first2=Joann K. |last3=Michaud |first3=Aubert R. |date=January 2012 |volume=76 |issue=1 |pages=258–67 |doi=10.2136/sssaj2010.0441 |journal=[[Soil Science Society of America Journal]] |bibcode=2012SSASJ..76..258P |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/259559160 |access-date=2 April 2026 }}</ref> Extrapolating this evidence to predict subsequent behaviour within receiving aquatic systems, the reason is that this more easily transported material may support a lower solution P concentration compared to coarser sized fractions.<ref>{{cite journal |title=Phosphorus loss in overfertilized soils: the selective P partitioning and redistribution between particle size separates |last1=Scalenghe |first1=Riccardo |last2=Edwards |first2=Anthony C. |last3=Barberis |first3=Elisabetta |date=July 2007 |volume=27 |issue=11 |pages=72–80 |doi=10.1016/j.eja.2007.02.002 |journal=European Journal of Agronomy |bibcode=2007EuJAg..27...72S |url=https://z-library.sk/book/NOV4MMB0jk |access-date=2 April 2026 }}</ref> Tillage also increases wind erosion rates, by dehydrating the soil and breaking it up into smaller particles that can be picked up by the wind.<ref>{{cite journal |title=Tillage affects soil aggregation parameters linked with wind erosion |last1=Hevia |first1=Graciela G. |last2=Mendez |first2=Mariano |last3=Buschiazzo |first3=Daniel E. |date=15 June 2007 |volume=140 |issue=1–2 |pages=90–6 |doi=10.1016/j.geoderma.2007.03.001 |journal=Geoderma |bibcode=2007Geode.140...90H |url=https://z-library.sk/book/VOwPd750R3 |access-date=2 April 2026 |hdl=11336/81757 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> Exacerbating this is the fact that most of the trees are generally removed from agricultural fields, allowing winds to have long, open runs to travel over at higher speeds.<ref>{{cite book |last=Whitford |first=Walter G. |chapter=Wind and water processes |title=Ecology of desert systems |editor-last=Whitford |editor-first=Walter G. |publisher=[[Academic Press]] |location=San Diego, California |year=2002 |isbn=978-0-12-747261-4 |page=65 |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=OZ4hZbXS8IcC&pg=PA65 |access-date=2 April 2026 }}</ref> Heavy [[grazing]] reduces [[vegetative cover]] and causes severe [[Soil compaction (agriculture)|soil compaction]], both of which increase erosion rates.<ref>{{cite book |last=Imeson |first=Anton |chapter=Human impact on degradation processes |title=Desertification, land degradation and sustainability |publisher=[[John Wiley & Sons]] |location=Hoboken, New Jersey |editor-last=Imeson |editor-first=Anton |doi=10.1002/9781119977759.ch5 |year=2012 |isbn=978-1-119-97776-6 |page=165 |chapter-url=https://archive.org/details/imeson-et-al.-2012 |access-date=3 April 2026 }}</ref>

=== Deforestation ===
[[File:BURNED CLEAR-CUT AREA OF OLYMPIC NATIONAL TIMBERLAND WASHINGTON. NEAR OLYMPIC NATIONAL PARK - NARA - 555088.tif|thumb|In this [[clearcut]], almost all of the vegetation has been stripped from the surface of steep slopes, in an area with very heavy rains. Severe erosion occurs in cases such as this, causing stream [[sedimentation]] and the loss of nutrient-rich [[topsoil]].]]
In an undisturbed [[forest]], the mineral soil is protected by a layer of [[leaf litter]] and [[humus]] that covers the [[forest floor]]. These two layers form a protective mat over the soil that absorbs the impact of rain drops. They are [[porosity|porous]] and highly [[Permeability (Earth sciences)|permeable]] to rainfall, and allow rainwater to slow [[percolate]] into the soil below, instead of flowing over the surface as [[surface runoff|runoff]].<ref name="Sands2005">{{cite book |last=Sands |first=Roger |chapter=The environmental value of forests |title=Forestry in a global context |publisher=[[CABI Publishing]] |location=Wallingford, United Kingdom |editor-last=Sands |editor-first=Roger |year=2005 |isbn=978-0-85199-089-7 |pages=74–75 |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=UO1DAI60IQEC&pg=PA74 |access-date=3 April 2026 }}</ref> The [[root]]s of trees and forest plants and the [[Mycelium|mycelia]] of forest [[Fungus|fungi]] also play a major role in binding soil particles together, preventing them from being washed away.<ref>{{cite book |title=Vegetation root system, soil erosion and ecohydrology system: a review |date=September 2015 |last1=Liu |first1=Bing |last2=Xie |first2=Gang |last3=Zhang |first3=Xiaoming |last4=Zhao |first4=Yang |last5=Yin |first5=Xiaolin |last6=Cheng |first6=Chen |doi=10.2991/ifeesm-15.2015.52 |isbn=978-94-6252-117-9 |url=https://www.atlantis-press.com/proceedings/ifeesm-15/25841098 |access-date=3 April 2026 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1073/pnas.60.2.497 |title=The biological and mechanical role of soil fungi |date=15 June 1968 |last1=Went |first1=F. W. |last2=Stark |first2=N. |journal=[[PNAS]] |volume=60 |issue=2 |pages=497–504 |doi-access=free |pmid=16591652 |pmc=225075 |bibcode=1968PNAS...60..497W }}</ref> The vegetative cover acts to reduce the [[velocity]] of the [[raindrop]]s that strike the foliage and stems before hitting the ground, reducing their [[kinetic energy]]. However it is the forest floor, more than the canopy, that prevents surface erosion. The [[terminal velocity]] of rain drops is reached in about {{convert|8|m|ft|abbr=off}}. Because forest canopies are usually higher than this, rain drops can often regain terminal velocity even after striking the canopy. However, the [[intact forest landscape|intact forest]] floor, with its layers of leaf litter and organic matter (see [[humus form]]), is still able to absorb the impact of the rainfall.<ref>{{cite book |last=Goudie |first=Andrew |chapter=The human impact on the soil |title=The human impact on the natural environment |publisher=[[MIT Press]] |location=Cambridge, Massachusetts |year=2000 |isbn=978-0-262-57138-8 |editor-last=Goudie |editor-first=Andrew |page=188 |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=r8l-DMj3XTgC&pg=PA188 |access-date=3 April 2026 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Stuart |first1=Gordon W. |last2=Edwards |first2=Pamela J. |title=Concepts about forests and water |journal=Northern Journal of Applied Forestry |volume=23 |issue=1 |pages=11–9 |date=March 2006 |url=https://www.academia.edu/66653214 |doi=10.1093/njaf/23.1.11 |access-date=3 April 2026 }}</ref>

[[Deforestation]] causes increased erosion rates due to exposure of [[mineral]] [[soil]] by removing the humus and litter layers from the soil surface, removing the vegetative cover that binds soil together, and causing heavy [[soil compaction]] from logging equipment. Once trees have been removed by fire or logging, infiltration rates become high and erosion low to the degree the forest floor remains intact. Severe fires can lead to significant further erosion if followed by heavy rainfall.<ref>{{cite book |last=Goudie |first=Andrew |chapter=The human impact on the soil |title=The human impact on the natural environment |publisher=[[MIT Press]] |location=Cambridge, Massachusetts |year=2000 |isbn=978-0-262-57138-8 |editor-last=Goudie |editor-first=Andrew |page=196 |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=r8l-DMj3XTgC&pg=PA196 |access-date=3 April 2026 }}</ref>

Globally one of the largest contributors to erosive soil loss is the [[Slash-and-burn agriculture|slash-and-burn]] treatment of [[tropical]] [[forest]]s.<ref>{{cite web |title=Shifting cultivation |author=FAO Staff |website=[[Food and Agriculture Organization|FAO]] |location=Rome, Italy |year=1957 |url=https://www.fao.org/4/x5382e/x5382e03.htm |access-date=3 April 2026 }}</ref> For example, on the [[Madagascar]] high central [[plateau]], comprising approximately ten percent of that country's land area, virtually the entire landscape is sterile of [[vegetation]], with [[gully]] erosive [[furrow]]s typically in excess of {{convert|50|m|ft}} deep and {{convert|1|km|mi|abbr=off|1}} wide.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1016/j.agee.2006.07.012 |title=Influence of slash-and-burn farming practices on fallow succession and land degradation in the rainforest region of Madagascar |date=March 2007 |last1=Styger |first1=Erika |last2=Rakotondramasy |first2=Harivelo M. |last3=Pfeffer |first3=Max J. |last4=Fernandes |first4=Erick C. M. |last5=Bates |first5=David M. |journal=[[Agriculture, Ecosystems & Environment]] |volume=119 |issue=3–4 |pages=257–69 |bibcode=2007AgEE..119..257S |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/223833849 |access-date=3 April 2026 }}</ref> [[Shifting cultivation]] (also called [[swidden]] cultivation) is a traditional farming system which sometimes incorporates the [[slash and burn]] method in some regions of the world. This degrades the soil and causes the soil to become less and less fertile.<ref>{{cite thesis |title=Shifting cultivation in the upland secondary forests of the Philippines: biodiversity and carbon stock assessment, and ecosystem services trade-offs in land-use decisions |publisher=[[University of Queensland]] Library |location=Brisbane, Australia |last=Mukul |first=Sharif Ahmed |year=2016 |doi=10.14264/uql.2016.222 |url=https://espace.library.uq.edu.au/view/UQ:384780 |access-date=3 April 2026 |url-access=subscription }}</ref> However, there is a debate about what is the worst practice in the [[tropics]]: slash-and-burn [[sustainable agriculture]], with fast recovery of the [[secondary forest]] after a few years of soft [[subsistence agriculture]],<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1590/S1981-81222013000300013 |title=The impacts of shifting cultivation on tropical forest soil: a review |date=December 2013 |last1=Ribeiro Filho |first1=Alexandre Antunes |last2=Adams |first2=Cristina |last3=Sereni Murrieta |first3=Rui Sergio |journal=Boletim do Museu Paraense Emílio Goeldi, Ciências Humanas |volume=8 |issue=3 |pages=693–727 |url=https://www.scielo.br/j/bgoeldi/a/Y9jrKvTfVhr75RpKVjLPqFH/?lang=en |access-date=3 April 2026 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1016/0167-8809(94)00531-I |title=The ecological sustainability of slash-and-burn agriculture |date=February 1995 |last1=Kleinman |first1=Peter J. A. |last2=Pimentel |first2=David |last3=Bryant |first3=Ray B. |journal=[[Agriculture, Ecosystems & Environment]] |volume=52 |issue=2–3 |pages=235–49 |bibcode=1995AgEE...52..235K |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/222346055 |access-date=3 April 2026 |doi-access=free }}</ref> or permanent [[pasture]]s and [[cash crop]]s after conventional [[logging]], with [[soil degradation]] (e.g. [[lateritization]] and [[Soil compaction (agriculture)|soil compaction]], respectively) preventing any hope of forest and [[soil regeneration]]?<ref>{{cite journal |title=Lateritic soils |date=November 1964 |last=McNeil |first=Mary |journal=[[Scientific American]] |volume=211 |issue=5 |pages=96–106 |doi=10.1038/scientificamerican1164-96 |bibcode=1964SciAm.211e..96M |url=https://os.pennds.org/archaeobib_filestore/pdf_articles/ScientificAmerican/1964_211_5_McNeil.pdf |access-date=6 April 2026 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1016/j.still.2002.12.001 |title=Temporal variation of soil compaction and deterioration of soil quality in pasture areas of Colombian Amazonia |date=January 2004 |last1=Martı́nez |first1=L. Joel |last2=Zinck |first2=Joseph Alfred |journal=Soil and Tillage Research |volume=75 |issue=1 |pages=3–18 |bibcode=2004STilR..75....3M |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/223786633 |access-date=6 April 2026 }}</ref> It has been shown in Brazil that along a complete cycle of [[Slash-and-burn agriculture|slash-and-burn]] cultivation (including forest regrowth) [[Runoff (hydrology)|runoff]] and [[soil loss]] decrease [[Exponential decay|exponentially]] from the burned phase of [[Shifting cultivation|shifting]] to the early stages of [[secondary forest]], exhibiting patterns similar to those of a forested area after just 4–5 years of regeneration.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1016/j.agee.2013.01.008 |title=Slash-and-burn agriculture: establishing scenarios of runoff and soil loss for a five-year cycle |date=15 March 2013 |last=Lopes Thomaz |first=Edivaldo |journal=[[Agriculture, Ecosystems & Environment]] |volume=168 |pages=1–6 |bibcode=2013AgEE..168....1T |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/257015496 |access-date=3 April 2026 }}</ref> Another Brazilian study showed that a fallow period of 15 years after a crop cycle of slash-and-burn agriculture can restore the original soil conditions.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1002/jsfa.10123 |title=Long fallows allow soil regeneration in slash-and-burn agriculture |date=3 November 2019 |last1=Gonçalves Lintemani |first1=Mariane |last2=Loss |first2=Arcângelo |last3=Sepulveda Mendes |first3=Camilo |last4=Celso Fantini |first4=Alfredo |journal=[[Journal of the Science of Food and Agriculture]] |volume=100 |issue=3 |pages=1142–54 |pmid=31680261 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/337009509 |access-date=3 April 2026 }}</ref>

=== Roads and human impact ===
[[File:Erosion pollution.jpg|thumb|Erosion polluted the Kasoa highway after downpour in Ghana.]]
[[Human impact on the environment|Human Impact]] has major effects on erosion processes, first by denuding the land of [[vegetative cover]], altering [[Drainage system (geomorphology)|drainage]] patterns, and [[Soil compaction (agriculture)|compacting]] the soil during construction, and next by covering the land in an impermeable layer of [[Asphalt concrete|asphalt]] or [[concrete]] that increases the amount of [[surface runoff]] and increases surface wind speeds.<ref>{{cite book |last=Nîr |first=Dov |title=Man, a geomorphological agent: an introduction to anthropic geomorphology |publisher=[[Springer Science+Business Media]] |location=Dordrecht, The Netherlands |year=1983 |isbn=978-90-277-1401-5 |pages=121–122 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=3HSCQvZ7U2kC&pg=PA121 |access-date=6 April 2026 }}</ref> Much of the sediment carried in runoff from [[urban area]]s (especially roads) is highly contaminated with [[fuel]], [[Petroleum|oil]], and other chemicals.<ref>{{cite book |last=Randhir |first=Timothy O. |title=Watershed management: issues and approaches |publisher=[[IWA Publishing]] |location=London, United Kingdom |year=2007 |isbn=978-1-84339-109-8 |page=56 |url=https://archive.org/details/watershedmanagem0000rand/page/56/mode/2up |access-date=6 April 2026 }}</ref> This increased runoff, in addition to [[erosion| eroding]] and [[land degradation|degrading]] the land that it flows over, also causes major disruption to surrounding watersheds by altering the volume and rate of water that flows through them, and filling them with [[chemical pollution|chemically polluted]] [[sedimentation]]. The increased flow of water through local waterways also causes a large increase in the rate of bank erosion.<ref>{{cite book |last=James |first=William |chapter=Channel and habitat change downstream of urbanization |editor-last=Herricks |editor-first=Edwin E. |title=Stormwater runoff and receiving systems: impact, monitoring, and assessment |publisher=[[CRC Press]] |location=Boca Raton, Florida |year=1995 |isbn=978-1-56670-159-4 |page=105 |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=X0xt9HZbyToC&pg=PA105 |access-date=6 April 2026 }}</ref>

=== Climate change ===
{{see also|Land degradation}}
The warmer atmospheric temperatures observed over the past decades are expected to lead to a more vigorous [[hydrological cycle]], including more extreme [[rainfall]] events.<ref>{{cite web |author=Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) |year=1995 |title=IPCC Second assessment synthesis of scientific-technical information relevant to interpreting Article 2 of the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change |page=5 |url=https://archive.ipcc.ch/pdf/climate-changes-1995/ipcc-2nd-assessment/2nd-assessment-en.pdf |access-date=6 April 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130309040926/http://www.ipcc.ch/pdf/climate-changes-1995/2nd-assessment-synthesis.pdf |archive-date=9 March 2013 |url-status=live |website=[[Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change|IPCC]] }}</ref> The [[rise in sea levels]] that has occurred as a result of climate change has also greatly increased [[coastal erosion]] rates.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Bicknell |first1=Jane |last2=Dodman |first2=David |last3=Satterthwaite |first3=David |title=Adapting cities to climate change: understanding and addressing the development challenges |publisher=[[Earthscan]] |year=2009 |isbn=978-1-84407-745-8 |page=114 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=77Kmhw6sVOMC&pg=PA114 |access-date=6 April 2026 }}</ref><ref>For an overview of other human activities that have increased [[coastal erosion]] rates, see: {{cite book |last=Goudie |first=Andrew |chapter=Accelerated coastal erosion |editor-last=Goudie |editor-first=Andrew |title=The human impact on the natural environment |publisher=[[MIT Press]] |location=Cambridge, Massachusetts |year=2000 |isbn=978-0-262-57138-8 |page=311 |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=r8l-DMj3XTgC&pg=PA311 |access-date=6 April 2026 }}</ref>
[[File:Ghana Flooding 2.jpg|thumb|Most part of [[Accra]] mostly flooded during rainy season, causing environmental crisis in [[Ghana]]]]
Studies on soil erosion suggest that increased [[rainfall]] amounts and intensities will lead to greater rates of soil erosion. Thus, if rainfall amounts and intensities increase in many parts of the world as expected, erosion will also increase, unless amelioration measures are taken. Soil erosion rates are expected to change in response to changes in climate for a variety of reasons. The most direct is the change in the erosive power of rainfall. Other reasons include: a) changes in [[plant canopy]] caused by shifts in plant [[Productivity (ecology)|biomass production]] associated with [[moisture]] regime; b) changes in [[plant litter|litter]] cover on the ground caused by changes in both plant residue [[decomposition]] rates driven by temperature and moisture dependent soil [[microbial activity]] as well as plant biomass production rates; c) changes in soil moisture due to shifting precipitation regimes and [[evapotranspiration]] rates, which changes [[Infiltration (hydrology)|infiltration]] and [[Runoff (hydrology)|runoff]] ratios; d) soil [[erodibility]] changes due to decrease in [[soil organic matter]] concentrations in soils that lead to a [[soil structure]] that is more susceptible to erosion and increased runoff due to increased [[soil surface sealing]] and crusting; e) a shift of winter precipitation from non-erosive snow to erosive rainfall due to increasing winter temperatures; f) [[melting]] of [[permafrost]], which induces an erodible soil state from a previously non-erodible one; and g) shifts in [[land use]] made necessary to accommodate new climatic regimes.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Klik |first1=Andreas |last2=Eitzinger |first2=Josef |date=30 March 2010 |title=Impact of climate change on soil erosion and the efficiency of soil conservation practices in Austria |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/231829005 |journal=[[The Journal of Agricultural Science]] |language=en |volume=148 |issue=5 |pages=529–41 |doi=10.1017/S0021859610000158|bibcode=2010EGUGA..12.5412K |s2cid=86550618 |issn=0021-8596 |access-date=6 April 2026 }}</ref>

Studies by Pruski and Nearing indicated that, other factors such as land use unconsidered, it is reasonable to expect approximately a 1.7% change in soil erosion for each 1% change in total precipitation under climate change.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Pruski |first1=Fernando F. |last2=Nearing |first2=Mark A. |year=2002 |title=Runoff and soil loss responses to changes in precipitation: a computer simulation study |journal=[[Journal of Soil and Water Conservation]] |volume=57 |issue=1 |pages=7–16 |doi=10.1080/00224561.2002.12457413 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/43258594 |access-date=6 April 2026 }}</ref> Studies performed at the onset of the 21st century predicted increases of rainfall erosivity over the 21st century by 17% in the [[United States]],<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Nearing |first1=Mark A. |last2=Pruski |first2=Fernando F. |last3=O'Neal |first3=Michael R. |year=2004 |title=Expected climate change impacts on soil erosion rates: a review |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/43258785 |journal=[[Journal of Soil and Water Conservation]] |language=en |volume=59 |issue=1 |pages=43–50 |doi=10.1080/00224561.2004.12435709 |issn=0022-4561 |access-date=6 April 2026 }}</ref> by 18% in Europe,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Panagos |first1=Panos |last2=Ballabio |first2=Cristiano |last3=Meusburger |first3=Katrin |last4=Spinoni |first4=Jonathan |last5=Alewell |first5=Christine |last6=Borrelli |first6=Pasquale |title=Towards estimates of future rainfall erosivity in Europe based on REDES and WorldClim datasets |journal=[[Journal of Hydrology]] |volume=548 |pages=251–62 |doi=10.1016/j.jhydrol.2017.03.006 |pmid=28649140 |pmc=5473165 |date=May 2017 |bibcode=2017JHyd..548..251P |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/314276384 |access-date=7 April 2026 }}</ref> and globally 30 to 66%.<ref name="Borrelli2020">{{cite journal |last1=Borrelli |first1=Pasquale |last2=Robinson |first2=David A. |last3=Panagos |first3=Panos |last4=Lugato |first4=Emanuele |last5=Yang |first5=Jae E. |last6=Alewell |first6=Christine |last7=Wuepper |first7=David |last8=Montanarella |first8=Luca |last9=Ballabio |first9=Cristiano |date=8 September 2020 |title=Land use and climate change impacts on global soil erosion by water (2015-2070) |journal=[[Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America]] |language=en |volume=117 |issue=36 |pages=21994–22001 |doi=10.1073/pnas.2001403117 |issn=0027-8424 |pmid=32839306 |pmc=7486701 |bibcode=2020PNAS..11721994B |doi-access=free }}</ref>

== Global environmental effects ==
[[File:Runoff and filtersoxx.ogv|left|thumb|468x468px]]
[[File:Water erosion map.jpg|thumb|325px|World map indicating areas that are vulnerable to high rates of water erosion]]
[[File:Rano Raraku quarry.jpg|thumb|During the 17th and 18th centuries, [[Easter Island]] experienced severe erosion due to [[deforestation]] and unsustainable agricultural practices. The resulting loss of topsoil ultimately led to ecological collapse, causing mass [[starvation]] and the complete disintegration of the Easter Island civilization of [[Rapa Nui people]].<ref>{{cite web |last=Dangerfield |first=Whitney |title=The mystery of Easter Island |website=[[Smithsonian (magazine)|Smithsonian Magazine]] |date=1 April 2007 |url=https://www.smithsonianmag.com/travel/the-mystery-of-easter-island-151285298/ |access-date=7 April 2026 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Chamberlain |first=Thomas |chapter=Islands in time |title=Dirt: the erosion of civilizations |publisher=[[University of California Press]] |location=Berkeley, California |editor-last=Montgomery |editor-first=David R. |date=14 May 2007 |edition=1st |isbn=978-0-520-25806-8 |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=HSu8r15-nnoC&pg=PA217 |access-date=7 April 2026 }}</ref>]]

Due to the severity of its ecological effects, and the scale on which it is occurring, [[erosion]] constitutes one of the most significant global [[environmental problem]]s we face today.<ref name="Toy2002"/>

=== Land degradation ===

Water and wind erosion are now the two primary causes of [[land degradation]]; combined, they are responsible for 84% of degraded acreage.<ref name="Blanco-Canqui2008"/>

Each year, about 75 billion tons of soil is eroded from the land, a rate that is about 13–40 times as fast as the natural rate of erosion.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Durán Zuazo |first1=Victor Hugo |last2=Rodríguez Pleguezuelo |first2=Carmen Rocio |chapter=Soil erosion and runoff prevention by plant covers: a review |editor-last1=Lichtfouse |editor-first1=Eric |editor-last2=Navarrete |editor-first2=Mireille |editor-last3=Debaeke |editor-first3=Philippe |editor-last4=Souchère |editor-first4=Véronique |editor-last5=Alberola |editor-first5=Caroline |title=Sustainable agriculture |publisher=[[Springer Science+Business Media]] |location=Dordrecht, The Netherlands |year=2009 |isbn=978-90-481-2665-1 |page=785 |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7cP-2jIIO2wC&pg=PA785 |access-date=7 April 2026 }}</ref> Approximately 40% of the world's [[agricultural land]] is seriously degraded.<ref>{{cite news |last=Sample |first=Ian |title=Global food crisis looms as climate change and population growth strip fertile land |work=[[The Guardian]] |date=30 August 2007 |url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2007/aug/31/climatechange.food |access-date=7 April 2026 }}</ref> According to the [[United Nations]], an area of fertile soil the size of [[Ukraine]] is lost every year because of [[drought]], [[deforestation]] and [[climate change]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Smith |first1=Kate |last2=Edwards |first2=Rob |title=2008: the year of global food crisis |work=[[The Herald (Scotland)]] |date=8 March 2008 |url=https://www.heraldscotland.com/news/12767615.2008__The_year_of_global_food_crisis/ |access-date=7 April 2026 }}</ref> In [[Africa]], if current trends of [[soil degradation]] continue, the continent might be able to feed just 25% of its population by 2025, according to [[United Nations University|UNU]]'s Ghana-based Institute for Natural Resources in Africa.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://news.mongabay.com/2006/1214-unu.html |website=news.mongabay.com |title=Africa may be able to feed only 25% of its population by 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061216080905/http://news.mongabay.com/2006/1214-unu.html |archive-date=16 December 2006 |date=14 December 2006 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

Recent [[Simulation|modeling]] developments have quantified rainfall erosivity at global scale using high [[temporal resolution]] (<30 min) and high fidelity rainfall recordings. An extensive global [[data collection]] effort produced the Global Rainfall Erosivity Database (GloREDa) which includes rainfall erosivity for 3,625 stations and covers 63 countries. This first ever Global Rainfall Erosivity Database was used to develop a global erosivity map at 30 arc-seconds(~1 km) based on sophisticated [[Geostatistics|geostatistical]] process.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Panagos |first1=Panos |last2=Borrelli |first2=Pasquale |last3=Meusburger |first3=Katrin |last4=Yu |first4=Bofu |last5=Klik |first5=Andreas |last6=Lim |first6=Kyoung Jae |last7=Yang |first7=Jae E. |last8=Ni |first8=Jinren |last9=Miao |first9=Chiyuan |last10=Chattopadhyay |first10=Nabansu |last11=Sadeghi |first11=Seyed Hamidreza |last12=Hazbavi |first12=Zeinab |last13=Zabihi |first13=Mosen |last14=Larionov |first14=Gennady A. |last15=Krasnov |first15=Sergey F. |last16=Gorobets |first16=Andrey V. |last17=Levi |first17=Yoav |last18=Erpul |first18=Gunay |last19=Birkel |first19=Christian |last20=Hoyos |first20=Natalia |last21=Naipal |first21=Victoria |last22=Oliveira |first22=Paulo Tarso S. |last23=Bonilla |first23=Carlos A. |last24=Meddi |first24=Mohamed |last25=Nel |first25=Werner |last26=Al Dashti |first26=Hassan |last27=Boni |first27=Martino |last28=Diodato |first28=Mazzareno |last29=Van Oost |first29=Kristof |last30=Nearing |first30=Mark |last31=Ballabio |first31=Cristiano |date=23 June 2017 |title=Global rainfall erosivity assessment based on high-temporal resolution rainfall records |journal=[[Scientific Reports]] |language=en |volume=7 |issue=1 |article-number=4175 |doi=10.1038/s41598-017-04282-8 |pmid=28646132 |pmc=5482877 |issn=2045-2322 |bibcode=2017NatSR...7.4175P |doi-access=free }}</ref> According to a new study published in [[Nature Communications]], almost 36 billion tons of soil is lost every year due to water, and deforestation and other changes in land use make the problem worse. The study investigates global soil erosion dynamics by means of [[high-resolution]] spatially distributed [[modelling]] (c. 250 × 250 m cell size). The [[Geostatistics|geo-statistical]] approach allows, for the first time, the thorough incorporation into a global soil erosion model of [[land use]] and changes in land use, the extent, types, spatial distribution of global [[cropland]]s and the effects of different regional [[cropping system]]s.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Borrelli |first1=Pasquale |last2=Robinson |first2=David A. |last3=Fleischer |first3=Larissa R. |last4=Lugato |first4=Emanuele |last5=Ballabio |first5=Cristiano |last6=Alewell |first6=Christine |last7=Meusburger |first7=Katrin |last8=Modugno |first8=Sirio |last9=Schütt |first9=Brigitta |last10=Ferro |first10=Vito |last11=Bagarello |first11=Vincenzo |last12=Van Oost |first12=Kristof |last13=Montanarella |first13=Luca |last14=Panagos |first14=Panos |date=8 December 2017 |title=An assessment of the global impact of 21st century land use change on soil erosion |journal=[[Nature Communications]] |language=en |volume=8 |issue=1 |article-number=2013 |doi=10.1038/s41467-017-02142-7 |pmid=29222506 |pmc=5722879 |issn=2041-1723 |bibcode=2017NatCo...8.2013B |doi-access=free }}</ref>

The loss of [[soil fertility]] due to erosion is further problematic because the response is often to apply chemical [[fertilizer]]s, which leads to further water and [[soil pollution]], rather than to allow the land to regenerate.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Potter |first1=Kenneth W. |last2=Douglas |first2=Jamie C. |last3=Brick |first3=Edmund M. |chapter=Impacts of agriculture on aquatic ecosystems in the humid United States |editor-last1=DeFries |editor-first1=Ruth S. |editor-last2=Asner |editor-first2=Gregory P. |editor-last3=Houghton |editor-first3=Richard A. |title=Ecosystems and land use change |publisher=[[American Geophysical Union]] |location=Washington, District of Columbia |year=2004 |isbn=978-0-87590-418-4 |page=34 |chapter-url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/259662005 |access-date=7 April 2026 }}</ref>

=== Sedimentation of aquatic ecosystems ===

Soil erosion (especially from agricultural activity) is considered to be the leading global cause of diffuse [[water pollution]], due to the effects of the excess [[sediment]]s flowing into the world's [[waterway]]s. The sediments themselves act as [[pollutant]]s, as well as being carriers for other pollutants, such as attached [[pesticide]] molecules or [[heavy metals]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Da Cunha |first=L. V. |chapter=Sustainable development of water resources |editor-last1=Bau |editor-first1=João |editor-last2=Lobo Ferreira |editor-first2=J. P. |editor-last3=Henriques |editor-first3=José Duarte |editor-last4=de Oliveira Raposo |editor-first4=José |title=Integrated approaches to water pollution problems |publisher=[[Taylor & Francis]] |location=Abingdon-on-Thames, United Kingdom |year=1991 |isbn=978-1-85166-659-1 |pages=12–13 |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=79ztZNhaNvMC&pg=PA12 |access-date=7 April 2026 }}</ref>

The effect of increased [[Sediment load|sediments load]]s on [[aquatic ecosystem]]s can be catastrophic. [[Silt]] can smother the [[spawning bed]]s of fish, by filling in the space between [[gravel]] on the [[stream bed]].<ref>{{cite journal |last=Lisle |first=Thomas E. |title=Sediment transport and resulting deposition in spawning gravels, north coastal California |journal=[[Water Resources Research]] |volume=25 |issue=6 |pages=1303–19 |doi=10.1029/WR025i006p01303 |date=June 1989 |bibcode=1989WRR....25.1303L |url=https://z-library.sk/book/8vll1WZave |access-date=7 April 2026 }}</ref> It also reduces their [[food supply]], and causes major [[Respiratory system|respiratory]] issues for them as sediment enters their [[gills]].<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1002/hyp.7940 |title=The impacts of fine sediment on riverine fish |date=30 May 2011 |last1=Kemp |first1=Paul |last2=Sear |first2=David |last3=Collins |first3=Adrian |last4=Naden |first4=Pamela |last5=Jones |first5=Iwan |journal=Hydrological Processes |volume=25 |issue=11 |pages=1800–21 |bibcode=2011HyPr...25.1800K |url=https://www.academia.edu/29073245 |access-date=7 April 2026 }}</ref> The [[biodiversity]] of aquatic [[plant]] and [[Algae|algal]] life is reduced,<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1002/rra.1486 |title=The relationship between fine sediment and macrophytes in rivers |date=September 2012 |last1=Jones |first1=John Iwan |last2=Collins |first2=Adrian L. |last3=Naden |first3=Pamela S. |last4=Sear |first4=David A. |journal=River Research and Applications |volume=28 |issue=7 |pages=1006–18 |bibcode=2012RivRA..28.1006J |url=https://www.academia.edu/144496647 |access-date=7 April 2026 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1016/j.scitotenv.2009.06.049 |title=Effects of sediment deposition on periphytic biomass, photosynthetic activity and algal community structure |date=15 October 2009 |last1=Izagirre |first1=Oihana |last2=Serra |first2=Alexandra |last3=Guasch |first3=Helena |last4=Elosegi |first4=Arturo |journal=[[Science of the Total Environment]] |volume=407 |issue=21 |pages=5694–700 |pmid=19666189 |bibcode=2009ScTEn.407.5694I |url=https://z-library.sk/book/ZjKxxK6Xv0 |access-date=7 April 2026 }}</ref> and invertebrates are also unable to survive and reproduce.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1002/rra.1516 |title=The impact of fine sediment on macro-invertebrates |date=October 2012 |last1=Jones |first1=John Iwan |last2=Murphy |first2=J. F. |last3=Collins |first3=Adrian L. |last4=Sear |first4=David A. |last5=Naden |first5=Pamela S. |last6=Armitage |first6=Patrick Desmond |journal=River Research and Applications |volume=28 |issue=8 |pages=1055–71 |bibcode=2012RivRA..28.1055J |url=https://www.academia.edu/54725356 |access-date=7 April 2026 }}</ref> While the [[sedimentation]] event itself might be relatively short-lived, the ecological disruption caused by the [[mass die-off]] often persists long into the future.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1016/S0022-0981(02)00495-1 |title=Photophysiological stress in scleractinian corals in response to short-term sedimentation |date=26 February 2003 |last1=Philipp |first1=Eva |last2=Fabricius |first2=Katharina |journal=[[Journal of Experimental Marine Biology and Ecology]] |volume=287 |issue=1 |pages=57–78 |bibcode=2003JEMBE.287...57P |url=https://www.academia.edu/120938904 |access-date=7 April 2026 }}</ref>

Until measures taken in the 1980s for soil erosion control, one of the most serious and long-running [[water erosion]] problems worldwide was in the [[People's Republic of China]], on the middle reaches of the [[Yellow River]]<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1016/j.catena.2021.105330 |title=Response of sediment discharge to soil erosion control in the middle reaches of the Yellow River |date=August 2021 |last1=Zhao |first1=Yang |last2=Hu |first2=Chunhong |last3=Zhang |first3=Xiaoming |last4=Lv |first4=Xizhi |last5=Yin |first5=Xiaolin |last6=Wang |first6=Zhaoyan |journal=Catena |volume=203 |article-number=105330 |bibcode=2021Caten.20305330Z |url=https://archive.org/details/zhao-et-al.-2021 |access-date=7 April 2026 }}</ref> and the upper reaches of the [[Yangtze River]].<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1080/0143116021000056028 |title=A data fusion approach for soil erosion monitoring in the Upper Yangtze River Basin of China based on Universal Soil Loss Equation (USLE) model |date=27 May 2010 |last1=Ma |first1=J. W. |last2=Xue |first2=Yong |last3=Ma |first3=C. F. |last4=Wang |first4=Z. G. |journal=[[International Journal of Remote Sensing]] |volume=24 |issue=23 |pages=4777–89 |url=https://z-library.sk/book/7vbaKrXMjY |access-date=7 April 2026 }}</ref> From the [[Yellow River]], over 1.6&nbsp;billion tons of sediment flows into the ocean each year, originating primarily from water erosion in the [[Loess Plateau]] region of the northwest.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1007/s13131-015-0619-6 |title=Sediment discharge of the Yellow River, China: past, present and future. A synthesis |date=18 February 2015 |last=Ren |first=Mei’e |journal=Acta Oceanologica Sinica |volume=34 |issue=2 |pages=1–8 |bibcode=2015AcOSn..34....1R |url=https://z-library.sk/book/Zjd8D8r5jW |access-date=7 April 2026 }}</ref>

=== Airborne dust pollution ===

Soil particles picked up during wind erosion of soil are a major source of [[air pollution]], in the form of [[airborne particulates]] called [[dust]]. These airborne soil particles are often contaminated with toxic chemicals such as [[pesticide]]s or [[petroleum]] fuels, posing ecological and public health hazards when they later land, or are inhaled/ingested.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Majewski |first1=Michael S. |last2=Capel |first2=Paul D. |title=Pesticides in the atmosphere: distribution, trends, and governing factors |publisher=[[CRC Press]] |location=Boca Raton, Florida |year=1996 |isbn=978-1-57504-004-2 |page=121 |url=https://z-library.sk/book/V8vlwbq8je |access-date=7 April 2026 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |author=[[ScienceDaily|Science Daily]] |date=14 July 1999 |url=https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/1999/07/990714073433.htm |title=African dust called a major factor affecting Southeast U.S. air quality |access-date=7 April 2026 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Nowell |first1=Lisa H. |last2=Capel |first2=Paul D. |last3=Dileanis |first3=Peter D. |title=Pesticides in stream sediment and aquatic biota: distribution, trends, and governing factors |publisher=[[CRC Press]] |location=Boca Raton, Florida |year=1999 |isbn=978-1-56670-469-4 |page=199 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=UzpDTEO3ZVcC&pg=PA199 |access-date=7 April 2026 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Shao |first=Yaping |chapter=Wind-erosion and wind-erosion research |title=Physics and modelling of wind erosion |editor-last=Shao |editor-first=Yaping |publisher=[[Springer Science+Business Media]] |location=Dordrecht, The Netherlands |year=2008 |edition=2nd |isbn=978-1-4020-8894-0 |page=3 |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=XSwwVeraxjcC&pg=PA3 |access-date=7 April 2026 }}</ref>

Dust from erosion acts to suppress rainfall and changes the [[sky]] color from blue to white, which leads to an increase in red sunsets.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Meng |first=Yihang |date=24 July 2024 |url=https://www.e3s-conferences.org/articles/e3sconf/abs/2024/83/e3sconf_epec2024_03010/e3sconf_epec2024_03010.html |publisher=[[EDP Sciences]] |title=Effect of air pollution on the colour of the sky |journal=E3S Web of Conferences |volume=553 |page=03010 |doi=10.1051/e3sconf/202455303010 |bibcode=2024E3SWC.55303010M |access-date=7 April 2026 |doi-access=free }}</ref> Dust events have been linked to a decline in the health of [[coral reef]]s across the [[Caribbean]] and [[Florida]], primarily since the 1970s.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Shinn |first1=Eugene A. |last2=Smith |first2=Garriet W. |last3=Prospero |first3=Joseph M. |last4=Betzer |first4=Peter |last5=Hayes |first5=Marshall L. |last6=Garrison |first6=Virginia |last7=Barber |first7=Richard T. |date=1 October 2000 |title=African dust and the demise of Caribbean coral reefs |journal=[[Geophysical Research Letters]] |language=en |volume=27 |issue=19 |pages=3029–32 |doi=10.1029/2000GL011599 |issn=1944-8007 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2000GeoRL..27.3029S }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Muhs |first1=Daniel R. |last2=Budahn |first2=James R. |last3=Prospero |first3=Joseph M. |last4=Carey |first4=Steven N. |date=June 2007 |title=Geochemical evidence for African dust inputs to soils of western Atlantic islands: Barbados, the Bahamas, and Florida |journal= Journal of Geophysical Research: Earth Surface|language=en |volume=112 |issue=F2 |article-number=F02009 |doi=10.1029/2005JF000445 |issn=2169-9011 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2007JGRF..112.2009M }}</ref> Similar dust [[Plume (fluid dynamics)|plume]]s originate in the [[Gobi desert]], which combined with pollutants, spread large distances downwind, or eastward, into North America.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bishop |first1=James K. B. |last2=Davis |first2=Russ E. |last3=Sherman |first3=Jeffrey T. |date=25 October 2002 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/11063287 |title=Robotic observations of dust storm enhancement of carbon biomass in the North Pacific |journal=[[Science (journal)|Science]] |volume=298 |issue=5594 |pages=817–21 |doi=10.1126/science.1074961 |pmid=12399588 |bibcode=2002Sci...298..817B |access-date=9 April 2026 }}</ref>

== Monitoring, measuring and modelling soil erosion ==
{{See also|Erosion prediction}}
Monitoring and [[Simulation|modeling]] of [[erosion]] processes can help people better understand the [[Soil erosion#Factors affecting soil erosion|causes of soil erosion]], make predictions of erosion [[Scenario planning|under a range of possible conditions]], and plan the implementation of [[Soil erosion#Prevention and remediation|preventative and restorative strategies for erosion]]. However, the complexity of erosion processes and the number of scientific disciplines that must be considered to understand and model them (e.g. [[climatology]], [[hydrology]], [[geology]], [[soil science]], [[agriculture]], [[chemistry]], [[physics]], etc.) makes accurate modelling challenging.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Evans |first=Robert |title=Assessment and monitoring of accelerated water erosion of cultivated land: when will reality be acknowledged?
