That amount of land is equal to 29% of farms worldwide.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Pretty |first1=Jules |title=Intensification for redesigned and sustainable agricultural systems |journal=Science |date=2018 |volume=362 |issue=6417 |article-number=eaav0294 |doi=10.1126/science.aav0294 |pmid=30467142 |bibcode=2018Sci...362..294P }}</ref> In light of concerns about [[food security]], [[human population]] growth and dwindling land suitable for agriculture, sustainable intensive farming practises are needed to maintain high [[crop yields]], while maintaining [[soil health]] and [[ecosystem services]]. The capacity for ecosystem services to be strong enough to allow a reduction in use of non-renewable inputs whilst maintaining or boosting yields has been the subject of much debate. Recent work in irrigated rice production system of east Asia has suggested that – in relation to pest management at least – promoting the ecosystem service of biological control using nectar plants can reduce the need for insecticides by 70% whilst delivering a 5% yield advantage compared with standard practice.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Gurr |first1=Geoff M. |display-authors=etal |title=Multi-country evidence that crop diversification promotes ecological intensification of agriculture |journal=Nature Plants |date=2016 |volume=2 |issue=3 |article-number=16014 |doi=10.1038/nplants.2016.14 |pmid=27249349|bibcode=2016NatPl...216014G |s2cid=205458366 }}</ref>

[[Vertical farming]] is a concept with the potential advantages of year-round production, isolation from pests and diseases, controllable resource recycling and reduced transportation costs.<ref name="Marks2014">{{Cite news |url=https://www.newscientist.com/article/mg22129524-100-vertical-farms-sprouting-all-over-the-world/ |title=Vertical farms sprouting all over the world |last=Marks |first=Paul |date=15 January 2014 |work=New Scientist|access-date=8 March 2018}}</ref>

===Water===
[[File:Sistema de regadio circular en toda su magnitud.jpg|thumb|Example of crop circle irrigation method]]
[[Water efficiency]] can be improved by reducing the need for [[irrigation]] and using alternative methods. Such methods include: researching on [[drought]] resistant crops, monitoring plant [[transpiration]] and reducing soil [[evaporation]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Mei|first1=Xu-rong|last2=Zhong|first2=Xiu-li|last3=Vincent|first3=Vadez|last4=Liu|first4=Xiao-ying|date=2013-07-01|title=Improving Water Use Efficiency of Wheat Crop Varieties in the North China Plain: Review and Analysis|journal=Journal of Integrative Agriculture|volume=12|issue=7|pages=1243–1250|doi=10.1016/S2095-3119(13)60437-2|url=http://oar.icrisat.org/6896/1/JIA_12_7_1243-1250_2013.pdf|doi-access=free|bibcode=2013JIAgr..12.1243M }}</ref>

Drought resistant crops have been researched extensively as a means to overcome the issue of [[Water scarcity|water shortage]]. They are [[Genetic engineering|modified genetically]] so they can adapt in an environment with little water. This is beneficial as it reduces the need for irrigation and helps conserve water. Although they have been extensively researched, significant results have not been achieved as most of the successful species will have no overall impact on water conservation. However, some grains like [[rice]], for example, have been successfully genetically modified to be drought resistant.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Hu|first1=Honghong|last2=Xiong|first2=Lizhong|date=2014-01-01|title=Genetic Engineering and Breeding of Drought-Resistant Crops|journal=Annual Review of Plant Biology|volume=65|issue=1|pages=715–41|doi=10.1146/annurev-arplant-050213-040000|pmid=24313844|bibcode=2014AnRPB..65..715H }}</ref>

===Soil and nutrients===
[[Soil amendments]] include using compost from recycling centers. Using compost from yard and kitchen waste uses available resources in the area.

Abstinence from soil [[tillage]] before planting and leaving the plant residue after [[harvest]]ing reduces soil water evaporation; It also serves to prevent soil erosion.<ref name="Mitchell 55–61">{{Cite journal|last1=Mitchell|first1=Jeffrey P.|last2=Singh|first2=Purnendu N.|last3=Wallender|first3=Wesley W.|last4=Munk|first4=Daniel S.|last5=Wroble|first5=Jon F.|last6=Horwath|first6=William R.|last7=Hogan|first7=Philip|last8=Roy|first8=Robert|last9=Hanson|first9=Blaine R.|display-authors=3|title=No-tillage and high-residue practices reduce soil water evaporation|journal=California Agriculture|volume=66|issue=2|pages=55–61|doi=10.3733/ca.v066n02p55|date=April 2012|url=https://escholarship.org/content/qt4cg3g2cf/qt4cg3g2cf.pdf?t=n3pluq|doi-access=free}}</ref>

Crop residues left covering the surface of the soil may result in reduced evaporation of water, a lower surface soil temperature, and reduction of wind effects.<ref name="Mitchell 55–61" />

A way to make [[rock phosphate#uses|rock phosphate]] more effective is to add microbial inoculates such as phosphate-solubilizing microorganisms, known as PSMs, to the soil.<ref name="Khan-2007" /><ref name="KAUR-2015">{{Cite journal |last1=Kaur |first1=Gurdeep |last2=Reddy |first2=Mondem Sudhakara |title=Effects of Phosphate-Solubilizing Bacteria, Rock Phosphate and Chemical Fertilizers on Maize-Wheat Cropping Cycle and Economics |journal=Pedosphere |volume=25 |issue=3 |pages=428–437 |doi=10.1016/s1002-0160(15)30010-2|year=2015|bibcode=2015Pedos..25..428K }}</ref> These solubilize phosphorus already in the soil and use processes like organic acid production and ion exchange reactions to make that phosphorus available for plants.<ref name="KAUR-2015" /> Experimentally, these PSMs have been shown to increase crop growth in terms of shoot height, dry biomass and grain yield.<ref name="KAUR-2015" />

Phosphorus uptake is even more efficient with the presence of [[mycorrhiza]]e in the soil.<ref name="Springer-1997">{{Cite book|title=Plant relationships|date=1997|publisher=Springer|last1=Carroll |first1=George C. |last2=Tudzynski |first2=Paul |isbn=978-3-662-10372-2|location=Berlin|oclc=679922657}}</ref> Mycorrhiza is a type of [[Mutualism (biology)|mutualistic symbiotic]] association between plants and fungi,<ref name="Springer-1997" /> which are well-equipped to absorb nutrients, including phosphorus, in soil.<ref name="Shenoy-2005">{{Cite journal|last1=Shenoy|first1=V.V.|last2=Kalagudi|first2=G.M.|title=Enhancing plant phosphorus use efficiency for sustainable cropping|journal=Biotechnology Advances|volume=23|issue=7–8|pages=501–513|doi=10.1016/j.biotechadv.2005.01.004|pmid=16140488|year=2005}}</ref> These fungi can increase nutrient uptake in soil where phosphorus has been fixed by aluminum, calcium, and iron.<ref name="Shenoy-2005" /> Mycorrhizae can also release organic acids that solubilize otherwise unavailable phosphorus.<ref name="Shenoy-2005" />

===Pests and weeds===
[[File:daempfen.jpg|thumb|[[Soil steam sterilization#Sheet steaming|Sheet steaming]] with a MSD/moeschle steam boiler (left side)]]
[[Soil steam sterilization|Soil steaming]] can be used as an alternative to chemicals for soil sterilization. Different methods are available to induce steam into the soil to kill pests and increase soil health.

Solarizing is based on the same principle, used to increase the temperature of the soil to kill pathogens and pests.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.rodalesorganiclife.com/garden/soil-solarization |title=Soil Solarization |work=Rodale's Organic Life |access-date=14 February 2016}}</ref>

Certain plants can be cropped for use as ''[[biofumigation|biofumigants]]'', "natural" [[fumigant]]s, releasing pest suppressing compounds when crushed, ploughed into the soil, and covered in plastic for four weeks. Plants in the [[Brassicaceae]] family release large amounts of toxic compounds such as [[methyl isothiocyanate]]s.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.soil.ncsu.edu/publications/Bulletins/Biomass%20Prod%20of%20Cover%20Crops_Mustard%20Radish%20Fact%20Sht_AG-782_Online_Final.pdf |title=Biomass Production of Biofumigant Cover Crops – 'Caliente' Mustard and Oilseed Radish |access-date=2015-10-20 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170517174954/http://www.soil.ncsu.edu/publications/Bulletins/Biomass%20Prod%20of%20Cover%20Crops_Mustard%20Radish%20Fact%20Sht_AG-782_Online_Final.pdf |archive-date=2017-05-17 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.fao.org/agriculture/crops/thematic-sitemap/theme/climatechange0/methyl-bromide/alt/biofum/en/ |title=Plant Production and Protection Division - Biofumigation |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=2019 |publisher=[[Food and Agriculture Organization]] |access-date=12 October 2019}}</ref>

===Location===
Relocating current croplands to environmentally more [[Optimization problem|optimal]] locations, whilst allowing ecosystems in then-abandoned areas to [[Restoration ecology|regenerate]] could substantially decrease the current carbon, biodiversity, and irrigation water footprint of global crop production, with relocation only within national borders also having substantial potential.<ref>{{cite news |title=Relocating farmland could turn back clock twenty years on carbon emissions, say scientists |url=https://phys.org/news/2022-03-relocating-farmland-clock-twenty-years.html |access-date=18 April 2022 |work=University of Cambridge |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Beyer |first1=Robert M. |last2=Hua |first2=Fangyuan |last3=Martin |first3=Philip A. |last4=Manica |first4=Andrea |last5=Rademacher |first5=Tim |display-authors=3|title=Relocating croplands could drastically reduce the environmental impacts of global food production |journal=Communications Earth & Environment |date=10 March 2022 |volume=3 |issue=1 |page=49 |doi=10.1038/s43247-022-00360-6 |bibcode=2022ComEE...3...49B |s2cid=247322845 |language=en |issn=2662-4435|doi-access=free |hdl=10810/61603 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

===Plants===
Sustainability may also involve [[crop rotation]].<ref name="Union">{{Cite web|url=https://www.ucsusa.org/resources/what-sustainable-agriculture|title=What is Sustainable Agriculture?|date=10 April 2017|publisher=Union of Concerned Scientists|access-date=29 October 2019}}</ref> Crop rotation and [[cover crop]]s prevent [[Erosion|soil erosion]], by protecting [[topsoil]] from wind and water.<ref name="Atekan-2014" /> Effective crop rotation can reduce pest pressure on crops, provides weed control, reduces disease build up, and improves the efficiency of [[plant nutrient|soil nutrients]] and nutrient cycling.<ref name="Reganold 112–120">{{Cite journal |last1=Reganold |first1=John P. |last2=Papendick |first2=Robert I. |last3=Parr |first3=James F. |date=June 1990 |title=Sustainable Agriculture |journal=Scientific American |volume=262 |issue=6 |pages=112–120 |doi=10.1038/scientificamerican0690-112 |bibcode=1990SciAm.262f.112R |issn=0036-8733}}</ref> This reduces the need for fertilizers and [[pesticide]]s.<ref name="Union" /> Increasing the diversity of crops by introducing new [[genetic resources]] can increase yields by 10 to 15 percent compared to when they are grown in monoculture.<ref name="Reganold 112–120" /><ref>{{Cite book|title=Global plan of action for the conservation and sustainable utilization of plant genetic resources for food and agriculture ; and, The Leipzig declaration|publisher=Rome : Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations|year=1996|isbn=978-92-5-104027-0|location=Rome}}</ref> [[Perennial grain|Perennial crops]] reduce the need for [[tillage]] and thus help mitigate soil erosion, and may sometimes tolerate drought better, increase water quality and help increase soil organic matter. There are research programs attempting to develop perennial substitutes for existing annual crops, such as replacing wheat with the wild grass ''[[Thinopyrum intermedium]]'', or possible experimental hybrids of it and wheat.<ref name="Baker2017">{{cite journal |last1=Baker |first1=Beth |title=Can Modern Agriculture Be Sustainable? |journal=BioScience |volume=67 |issue=4 |year=2017 |pages=325–331 |issn=0006-3568 |doi=10.1093/biosci/bix018|doi-access=free }}</ref> Being able to do all of this without the use of chemicals is one of the main goals of sustainability which is why crop rotation is a very central method of sustainable agriculture.<ref name="Reganold 112–120" />

== Landscape management strategies ==
Sustainable agriculture is not limited to practices within individual plots but can also be considered at the landscape scale. This broader approach is particularly relevant for reconciling biodiversity conservation while maintaining sufficient agricultural production. In this context, two landscape management strategies are traditionally opposed: land sparing and land sharing.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Fischer |first1=Joern |last2=Abson |first2=David J. |last3=Butsic |first3=Van |last4=Chappell |first4=M. Jahi |last5=Ekroos |first5=Johan |last6=Hanspach |first6=Jan |last7=Kuemmerle |first7=Tobias |last8=Smith |first8=Henrik G. |last9=von Wehrden |first9=Henrik |display-authors=3|date=2014 |title=Land Sparing Versus Land Sharing: Moving Forward |url=https://conbio.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/conl.12084 |journal=Conservation Letters |language=en |volume=7 |issue=3 |pages=149–157 |doi=10.1111/conl.12084 |bibcode=2014ConL....7..149F |issn=1755-263X|hdl=10419/176807 |hdl-access=free }}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Green |first1=Rhys E. |last2=Cornell |first2=Stephen J. |last3=Scharlemann |first3=Jörn P. W. |last4=Balmford |first4=Andrew |date=2005-01-28 |title=Farming and the Fate of Wild Nature |url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.1106049 |journal=Science |language=en |volume=307 |issue=5709 |pages=550–555 |doi=10.1126/science.1106049 |pmid=15618485 |bibcode=2005Sci...307..550G |issn=0036-8075|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Phalan |first=Benjamin T. |date=2018-05-28 |title=What Have We Learned from the Land Sparing-sharing Model? |journal=Sustainability |language=en |volume=10 |issue=6 |page=1760 |doi=10.3390/su10061760 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2018Sust...10.1760P |issn=2071-1050}}</ref> These two strategies have generated intense debate within the scientific community for over a decade, with no clear consensus emerging on their relative effectiveness in balancing biodiversity conservation with food production and rural livelihoods. A literature review of empirical studies indicates that land sparing is generally favored for conserving [[tropical forest]] [[biodiversity]] (67% of relevant studies), whereas land sharing (58% of studies) is more often considered more beneficial for the [[food security]] and livelihoods of farmers in developing countries.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Luskin |first1=Matthew Scott |last2=Lee |first2=Janice S.H. |last3=Edwards |first3=David P. |last4=Gibson |first4=Luke |last5=Potts |first5=Matthew D. |display-authors=3|date=March 2018 |title=Study context shapes recommendations of land-sparing and sharing; a quantitative review |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S2211912417300081 |journal=Global Food Security |language=en |volume=16 |pages=29–35 |doi=10.1016/j.gfs.2017.08.002|bibcode=2018GlFS...16...29L |url-access=subscription }}</ref> Recently, a third alternative has been introduced to the debate: the so-called land blending strategy, an intermediate approach between the two traditional ones, as the effectiveness of both strategies appears to vary depending on the landscape context.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last1=Oliveira-Xavier |first1=Aymeric |last2=Calmé |first2=Sophie |last3=Gravel |first3=Dominique |date=August 2025 |title=The land-blending strategy: Contribution of metapopulation theory to the land sparing-sharing debate |journal=Land Use Policy |language=en |volume=155 |article-number=107577 |doi=10.1016/j.landusepol.2025.107577|bibcode=2025LUPol.15507577O |doi-access=free }}</ref>
[[File:Landscape_conservation_strategies.png|thumb|Schematic representation of the landscape management strategies considered in the land sharing vs. land sparing debate. Black frames represent landscapes and green shapes indicate biodiversity (i.e.nature elements).]]

=== Land sparing ===
Land sparing is a strategy that involves strictly separating land dedicated to agricultural production from land dedicated to conservation of natural habitats.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last1=Phalan |first1=Ben |last2=Onial |first2=Malvika |last3=Balmford |first3=Andrew |last4=Green |first4=Rhys E. |date=2011-09-02 |title=Reconciling Food Production and Biodiversity Conservation: Land Sharing and Land Sparing Compared |url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.1208742 |journal=Science |language=en |volume=333 |issue=6047 |pages=1289–1291 |doi=10.1126/science.1208742 |pmid=21885781 |bibcode=2011Sci...333.1289P |issn=0036-8075|url-access=subscription }}</ref> This strategy promotes increasing the yield of agricultural land, particularly through [[intensive farming]]. This is done to preserve areas of major biodiversity interest from agricultural expansion. This has been the dominant strategy in developed countries for over 150 years.

=== Land sharing ===
Land sharing, also known as "wildlife-friendly agriculture", involves integrating biodiversity into agricultural production areas.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":2" /> This approach focuses on the combination of agriculture and biodiversity by reducing the intensification of farming practices. This is illustrated notably by agroecological practices such as agroforestry and mixed crop-livestock systems.

=== Land blending ===
Previously described as a "mixed strategy", a term considered too ambiguous in ecology, land blending is an intermediate approach between land sparing and land sharing.<ref name=":1" /> Unlike these two traditionally opposed strategies, land blending offers a flexible combination of the two approaches, adapted to the specific landscape features. This third strategy has only recently emerged as a credible and viable alternative to the traditional land sparing and land sharing.<ref>{{Citation |last1=Grass |first1=Ingo |title=Chapter Six - Combining land-sparing and land-sharing in European landscapes |date=2021-01-01 |work=Advances in Ecological Research |volume=64 |pages=251–303 |editor-last=Bohan |editor-first=David A. |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0065250420300301 |access-date=2025-05-14 |series=The Future of Agricultural Landscapes, Part II |publisher=Academic Press |last2=Batáry |first2=Péter |last3=Tscharntke |first3=Teja |doi=10.1016/bs.aecr.2020.09.002 |editor2-last=Vanbergen |editor2-first=Adam J.|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Law |first1=Elizabeth A. |last2=Bryan |first2=Brett A. |last3=Meijaard |first3=Erik |last4=Mallawaarachchi |first4=Thilak |last5=Struebig |first5=Matthew J. |last6=Watts |first6=Matthew E. |last7=Wilson |first7=Kerrie A. |display-authors=3 |date=February 2017 |editor-last=Mori |editor-first=Akira |title=Mixed policies give more options in multifunctional tropical forest landscapes |url=https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/1365-2664.12666 |journal=Journal of Applied Ecology |language=en |volume=54 |issue=1 |pages=51–60 |doi=10.1111/1365-2664.12666 |bibcode=2017JApEc..54...51L |issn=0021-8901|hdl=10536/DRO/DU:30102070 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> Recent research<ref name=":1" /> has highlighted its potential for effectively reconciling biodiversity conservation and agricultural production, while enhancing resilience in the face of change and uncertainty.

== Related concepts ==

=== Organic agriculture ===
{{main|Organic Farming}}

Organic agriculture can be defined as:
{{blockquote|an integrated farming system that strives for sustainability, the enhancement of soil fertility and biological diversity whilst, with rare exceptions, prohibiting synthetic pesticides, antibiotics, synthetic fertilizers, genetically modified organisms, and growth hormones.<ref>{{cite web |first1=Danielle |last1=Treadwell |first2=Jim |last2=Riddle |first3=Mary |last3=Barbercheck |first4=Deborah |last4=Cavanaugh-Grant |first5=Ed |last5=Zaborski |display-authors=3 |publisher=Cooperative Extension System |url=http://articles.extension.org/pages/18655/what-is-organic-farming |title=What is organic farming? |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190421155926/https://articles.extension.org/pages/18655/what-is-organic-farming |archive-date=2019-04-21}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |author=H. Martin |title=Introduction to Organic Farming |publisher=Ontario Ministry of Agriculture, Food and Rural Affairs |url=http://www.omafra.gov.on.ca/english/crops/facts/09-077.htm#define |issn=1198-712X |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201215225223/https://www.omafra.gov.on.ca/english/crops/facts/09-077.htm#define |archive-date=2020-12-15}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |author=Dale Rhoads |publisher=Purdue Extension Service |url=https://ag.purdue.edu/extension/smallfarms/Documents/WhatIsOrganicFarmingSm.pdf |title=What is organic farming? |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160610094901/https://ag.purdue.edu/extension/smallfarms/Documents/WhatIsOrganicFarmingSm.pdf |archive-date=2016-06-10 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last=Gold |first=Mary |title=What is organic production? |url=http://www.nal.usda.gov/afsic/pubs/ofp/ofp.shtml |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070807082049/http://www.nal.usda.gov/afsic/pubs/ofp/ofp.shtml |archive-date=August 7, 2007 |work=National Agricultural Library |publisher=USDA |access-date=1 March 2014}}</ref>}}

Some claim [[organic agriculture]] may produce the most sustainable products available for consumers in the US, where no other alternatives exist, although the focus of the organics industry is not sustainability.<ref name="Union" />

In 2018 the sales of organic products in USA reach $52.5 billion.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Gelski |first1=Jeff |date=20 May 2019 |title=U.S. annual organic food sales near $48 billion |agency=Food Business News |url=https://www.foodbusinessnews.net/articles/13805-us-organic-food-sales-near-48-billion |access-date=19 December 2019}}</ref> According to a USDA survey, two-thirds of Americans consume organic products at least occasionally.<ref>{{cite web |title=Organic Market Overview |url=https://www.ers.usda.gov/topics/natural-resources-environment/organic-agriculture/organic-market-overview/ |access-date=19 December 2019 |website=United States Department of Agriculture Economic Research Service |archive-date=15 November 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161115073308/https://www.ers.usda.gov/topics/natural-resources-environment/organic-agriculture/organic-market-overview/ }}</ref> Recent syntheses estimate that carbon dioxide emissions from land-use change and forestry are about 3–4 GtCO2 per year, contributing roughly 10–12% of total anthropogenic CO2 emissions in recent years.<ref name="AR6SYR2023" /><ref name="GCB2024" />

=== Ecological farming ===
Ecological farming is a concept that focused on the environmental aspects of sustainable agriculture. Ecological farming includes all methods, including organic, which regenerate [[ecosystem services]] like: prevention of [[soil erosion]], water infiltration and retention, [[carbon sequestration]] in the form of humus, and increased biodiversity.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Rand Report on protecting ecosystems |url=http://www.rand.org/scitech/stpi/ourfuture/NaturesServices/section1.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100406071622/http://www.rand.org/scitech/stpi/ourfuture/NaturesServices/section1.html |archive-date=2010-04-06 |access-date=2010-03-12|website=www.rand.org}}</ref> Many techniques are used including [[no-till farming]], multispecies cover crops, strip cropping, terrace cultivation, shelter belts, pasture cropping etc.

There are a plethora of methods and techniques that are employed when practicing ecological farming, all having their own unique benefits and implementations that lead to more sustainable agriculture. Crop genetic diversity is one method that is used to reduce the risks associated with monoculture crops, which can be susceptible to a changing climate.<ref name=":0a">{{Cite web |last1=Tirado |first1=Reyes |last2=Cotter |first2=Janet |date=February 2010 |title=Ecological farming: Drought-resistant agriculture |url=https://www.greenpeace.to/publications/drought_resistant_agriculture.pdf |access-date=June 16, 2026 |website=Greenpeace |publisher=University of Exeter}}</ref> This form of biodiversity causes crops to be more resilient, increasing food security and enhancing the productivity of the field on a long-term scale.<ref name=":0a" /> The use of biodigestors is another method which converts organic waste into a combustible gas, which can provide several benefits to an ecological farm: it can be used as a fuel source, fertilizer for crops and fish ponds, and serves as a method for removing wastes that are rich in organic matter.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Low-cost biodigesters as the epicenter of ecological farming systems |url=http://www.build-a-biogas-plant.com/PDF/LowCostBiodigesters.pdf |website=www.build-a-biogas-plant.com}}</ref> Because biodigestors can be used as fertilizer, it reduces the amount of industrial fertilizers that are needed to sustain the yields of the farm. Another technique used is aquaculture integration, which combines fish farming with agricultural farming, using the wastes from animals and crops and diverting them towards the fish farms to be used up instead of being leeched into the environment.<ref name=":1a">{{Cite journal |last1=Phong |first1=L. T. |last2=van Dam |first2=A. A. |last3=Udo |first3=H. M. J. |last4=van Mensvoort |first4=M. E. F. |last5=Tri |first5=L. Q. |last6=Steenstra |first6=F. A. |last7=van der Zijpp |first7=A. J. |display-authors=3|date=2010-08-15 |title=An agro-ecological evaluation of aquaculture integration into farming systems of the Mekong Delta |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S016788091000143X |journal=Agriculture, Ecosystems & Environment |language=en |volume=138 |issue=3 |pages=232–241 |doi=10.1016/j.agee.2010.05.004 |bibcode=2010AgEE..138..232P |issn=0167-8809|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Mud from the fish ponds can also be used to fertilize crops.<ref name=":1a" />

Organic fertilizers can also be employed in an ecological farm, such as animal and green manure.<ref name=":2a">{{Cite journal |last=Vereijken |first=P. |date=1992-09-01 |title=A methodic way to more sustainable farming systems. |url=https://library.wur.nl/ojs/index.php/njas/article/view/16507 |journal=Netherlands Journal of Agricultural Science |language=en |volume=40 |issue=3 |pages=209–223 |doi=10.18174/njas.v40i3.16507 |s2cid=82376036 |issn=0028-2928|doi-access=free }}</ref> This allows soil fertility to be improved and well-maintained, leads to reduced costs and increased yields, reduces the usage of non-renewable resources in industrial fertilizers (Nitrogen and Phosphorus), and reduces the environmental pressures that are posed by intensive agricultural systems.<ref name=":2a" /> Precision Agriculture can also be used, which focuses on efficient removal of pests using non-chemical techniques and minimizes the amount of tilling needed to sustain the farm. An example of a precision machine is the false seedbed tiller, which can remove a great majority of small weeds while only tilling one centimeter deep.<ref name=":3a">{{Cite web |last=Merfield |first=Charles M. |date=May 2010 |title=Precision Ag for Ecological Farming Systems |url=http://ww.merfield.com/research/2010/precision-ag-for-ecological-farming-systems-2010-charles-merfield.pdf |access-date=June 16, 2026 |website=ww.merfield.com}}</ref> This minimized tilling reduces the amount of new weeds that germinate from soil disturbance.<ref name=":3a" /> Other methods that reduce soil erosion include contour farming, strip cropping, and terrace cultivation.<ref>{{Cite web |date=May 2008 |title=Low Greenhouse Gas Architecture: Mitigation and Adaptation Potential of Sustainable Farming Systems |url=https://orgprints.org/id/eprint/15690/1/niggli-etal-2009-lowgreenhouse.pdf |access-date=June 16, 2026 |website=orgprints.org}}</ref>

==== Benefits ====
* Ecological farming involves the introduction of symbiotic species, where possible, to support the ecological sustainability of the farm. Associated benefits include a reduction in [[ecological debt]] and elimination of dead zones.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.scientificamerican.com/article.cfm?id=oceanic-dead-zones-spread |title=Oceanic Dead Zones Continue to Spread |publisher=Scientific American |date=2008-08-15 |author=David Biello}}</ref>
* Ecological farming is a pioneering, practical development which aims to create globally [[sustainable land management]] systems, and encourages review of the importance of maintaining biodiversity in food production and farming end products.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/science/nature/7795652.stm |title=Food needs 'fundamental rethink' |author=Mark Kinver |date=2008-12-27 |publisher=BBC}}</ref>
* One foreseeable option is to develop specialized automata to scan and respond to soil and plant situations relative to intensive care for the soil and the plants. Accordingly, conversion to ecological farming may best utilize the information age, and become recognised as a primary user of robotics and expert systems.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/technology/8558095.stm |title=Down on the farm with the robots |author=Mark Ward |date=2010-03-11|work=BBC}}</ref>

==== Challenges ====
The challenge for ecological farming science is to be able to achieve a mainstream productive [[food system]] that is sustainable or even regenerative. To enter the field of ecological farming, location relative to the consumer, can reduce the food miles factor to help minimise damage to the biosphere by combustion engine emissions involved in current food transportation.

Design of the ecological farm is initially constrained by the same limitations as conventional farming: local climate, the soil's physical properties, budget for beneficial soil supplements, manpower and available automatons; however long-term water management by ecological farming methods is likely to conserve and increase water availability for the location, and require far fewer inputs to maintain fertility.

==== Principles ====
Certain principles unique to ecological farming need to be considered.
*Food production should be ecological in both ''origin'' and ''destiny'' (the term ''destiny'' refers to the post-harvest [[ecological footprint]] which results in getting produce to the consumer).
*Integration of species that maintain ecosystem services whilst providing a selection of alternative products.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.fas.org/biodiv/ |title=Project of Applied Biodiversity |author=Noel Vietmeyer |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121024164444/http://www.fas.org/biodiv/ |archive-date=2012-10-24 |website=www.fas.org}}</ref>
*Minimise food miles, packaging, energy consumption and waste.
*Define a new ecosystem to suit human needs using lessons from existing ecosystems from around the world.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/id/wbna32600636 |title=African tree acts as 'fertilizer factory' for crops |author=Jessica Marshall |date=2009-08-28 |publisher=NBC News}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://berkeley.edu/news/media/releases/99legacy/5-18-1999.html |title=Monkey diet is richer in vitamins and minerals than human diet, UC Berkeley anthropologist discovers |publisher=University of California, Berkeley |author=Patricia McBroom |date=1999-05-18}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://earthobservatory.nasa.gov/Newsroom/view.php?id=29238 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100316223254/http://earthobservatory.nasa.gov/Newsroom/view.php?id=29238 |title=Deep-Rooted Plants Have Much Greater Impact on Climate than Experts Thought |archive-date=2010-03-16 |date=2006-01-11 |author=Robert Sanders |website=Earth Observatory |publisher=NASA}}</ref>
*Apply the value of a knowledge-base (advanced data base) about soil microorganisms so that discoveries of the ecological benefits of having various kinds of microorganisms encouraged in productive systems such as Forest Gardens can be assessed and optimised; for example in the case of naturally occurring microorganisms called denitrifiers.<ref>{{cite web |date=2012-11-21 |title=UT Study: Unexpected Microbes Fighting Harmful Greenhouse Gas |url=http://www.utk.edu/tntoday/2012/11/21/study-unexpected-microbes-fighting-greenhouse-gas/ |author=Whitney Heins |publisher=The University of Tennessee Knoxville |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121202094627/https://www.utk.edu/tntoday/2012/11/21/study-unexpected-microbes-fighting-greenhouse-gas/ |archive-date=2012-12-02}}</ref>

=== Traditional agriculture ===
[[File:Bullocks Plough.jpg|thumb|Practice of Traditional Agriculture]]
Often thought of as inherently destructive, [[slash-and-burn]] or [[slash-and-char]] [[shifting cultivation]] have been practiced in the Amazon for thousands of years.<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Sponsel | first1=Leslie E | year=1986 | title=Amazon ecology and adaptation | journal=Annual Review of Anthropology | volume=15 | pages=67–97 | doi=10.1146/annurev.anthro.15.1.67}}</ref>

Some traditional systems combine [[polyculture]] with sustainability. In South-East Asia, [[rice-fish system]]s on [[rice paddies]] have raised [[freshwater fish]] as well as rice, producing an additional product and reducing [[eutrophication]] of neighboring rivers.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Burchett |first1=Stephen |last2=Burchett |first2=Sarah |title=Introduction to Wildlife Conservation in Farming |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=TISAfFax1lYC&pg=PT268 |year=2011 |publisher=John Wiley & Sons |isbn=978-1-119-95759-1 |page=268}}</ref> A variant in Indonesia combines rice, fish, ducks and water fern; the ducks eat the weeds that would otherwise limit rice growth, saving labor and herbicides, while the duck and fish manure substitute for fertilizer.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Bezemer |first1=Marjolein |title=Mixed farming increases rice yield |website=reNature Foundation |url=https://renaturefoundation.nl/2018/12/12/mixed-farming-increase-rice-yield/ |date=12 December 2018 |access-date=11 October 2019 |archive-date=11 October 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191011124422/https://renaturefoundation.nl/2018/12/12/mixed-farming-increase-rice-yield/ }}</ref>

Raised field agriculture has been recently revived in certain areas of the world, such as the [[Altiplano]] region in [[Bolivia]] and [[Peru]]. This has resurged in the form of traditional [[Waru Waru]] raised fields, which create nutrient-rich soil in regions where such soil is scarce. This method is extremely productive and has recently been utilized by indigenous groups in the area and the nearby [[Amazon Basin]] to make use of lands that have been historically hard to cultivate.

Other forms of traditional agriculture include agro forestry, crop rotations, and water harvesting. Water harvesting is one of the largest and most common practices, particularly used in dry areas and seasons. In Ethiopia, over half of their GDP and over 80 percent of their exports are attributed to agriculture; yet, it is known for its intense droughts and dry periods.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Tolossa|first1=Tasisa Temesge|last2=Abebe|first2=Firew Bekele|last3=Girma|first3=Anteneh Abebe|date=2020-01-01|editor-last=Yildiz|editor-first=Fatih|title=Review: Rainwater harvesting technology practices and implication of climate change characteristics in Eastern Ethiopia|journal=Cogent Food & Agriculture|volume=6|issue=1|article-number=1724354|doi=10.1080/23311932.2020.1724354|s2cid=214230236 |doi-access=free|bibcode=2020CogFA...624354T }}</ref> Rain water harvesting is considered to be a low-cost alternative. This type of harvesting collects and stores water from roof tops during high-rain periods for use during droughts.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Water-Efficient Technology Opportunity: Rainwater Harvesting Systems |url=https://www.energy.gov/eere/femp/water-efficient-technology-opportunity-rainwater-harvesting-systems |access-date=2022-02-24 |website=Energy.gov |date=14 June 2017 |language=en}}</ref> [[Rainwater harvesting]] has been a large practice to help the country survive by focusing on runoff irrigation, roof water harvesting, and flood spreading.

==== Indigenous Agriculture in North America ====
[[File:Asia Rice paddy.jpg|thumb|Indigenous agriculture]]
Native Americans in the United States practiced sustainable agriculture through their subsistence farming techniques. Many tribes grew or harvested their own food from plants that thrived in their local ecosystems. Native American farming practices are specific to local environments and work with natural processes.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Pace |first1=Katie |title=Indigenous Agriculture and Sustainable Foods |url=https://sustainablefoodcenter.org/latest/gardening/indigenous-agriculture-and-sustainable-food |website=Sustainable Food Center |date=7 October 2015 |access-date=29 March 2021}}</ref> This is a practice called [[Permaculture]], and it involves a deep understanding of the local environment.<ref name="nfu.org">{{cite news |last1=Heim |first1=Tracy |title=The Indigenous Origins of Regenerative Agriculture |url=https://nfu.org/2020/10/12/the-indigenous-origins-of-regenerative-agriculture/ |website=National Farmers Union |date=12 October 2020 |access-date=29 March 2021}}</ref> Native American farming techniques also incorporate local biodiversity into many of their practices, which helps the land remain healthy.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Nabhan |first1=Gary |title=Enduring Seeds: Native American Agriculture and Wild Plant Conservation |date=1989 |publisher=The University of Arizona Press |location=Tucson |page=x}}</ref>

Many indigenous tribes incorporated [[intercropping]] into their agriculture, which is a practice where multiple crops are planted together in the same area. This strategy allows crops to help one another grow through exchanged nutrients, maintained soil moisture, and physical supports for one another. The crops that are paired in intercropping often do not heavily compete for resources, which helps them to each be successful. For example, many tribes utilized intercropping in ways such as the Three Sisters Garden. This gardening technique consists of corn, beans, and squash. These crops grow in unity as the corn stalk supports the beans, the beans produce nitrogen, and the squash retain moisture.<ref name="Frey-2011" /> Intercropping also provides a natural strategy for pest management and the prevention of weed growth. Intercropping is a natural agricultural practice that often improves the overall health of the soil and plants, increases crop yield, and is sustainable.<ref name="nfu.org" />

One of the most significant aspects of indigenous sustainable agriculture is their [[traditional ecological knowledge]] of harvesting. The [[Anishinaabe]] tribes follow an ideology known as "the Honorable Harvest". The Honorable Harvest is a set of practices that emphasize the idea that people should "take only what you need and use everything you take."<ref>{{cite book |last1=Kimmerer |first1=Robin |title=Braiding Sweetgrass: Indigenous Wisdom, Scientific Knowledge and the Teachings of Plants |date=2013 |publisher=Milkweed Editions |page=148|isbn=9781571313560}}</ref> Resources are conserved through this practice because several rules are followed when harvesting a plant. These rules are to never take the first plant, never take more than half of the plants, and never take the last plant.<ref>{{Harvard citation|Kimmerer|2013|p=183}}</ref> This encourages future growth of the plant and therefore leads to a sustainable use of the plants in the area.

Native Americans practiced [[agroforestry]] by managing the forest, animals, and crops together. They also helped promote tree growth through controlled burns and [[silviculture]]. Often, the remaining ash from these burns would be used to fertilize their crops. By improving the conditions of the forest, the local wildlife populations also increased. Native Americans allowed their livestock to graze in the forest, which provided natural fertilizer for the trees as well.<ref name="nfu.org" />

=== Regenerative agriculture ===
{{main|Regenerative agriculture}}

Regenerative agriculture is a conservation and rehabilitation approach to food and farming systems. It focuses on [[topsoil]] [[Soil regeneration|regeneration]], increasing [[biodiversity]],<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.csuchico.edu/sustainablefuture/aginitiative/description.shtml|title=Our Sustainable Future - Regenerative Ag Description|website=csuchico.edu|language=en|access-date=2017-03-09}}</ref> improving the [[water cycle]],<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://regenerationinternational.org/2017/02/24/what-is-regenerative-agriculture/|title=What is Regenerative Agriculture?|last1=Underground|first1=The Carbon|last2=Initiative|first2=Regenerative Agriculture|date=2017-02-24|website=Regeneration International|access-date=2017-03-09|last3=CSU}}</ref> enhancing [[ecosystem services]], supporting [[biosequestration]], increasing [[Climate resilience|resilience to climate change]], and strengthening the health and vitality of farm soil. Practices include, recycling as much farm waste as possible, and adding [[compost]]ed material from sources outside the farm.<ref name="Pilgeram-2015" /><ref name=":3SA">{{Cite web|url=http://regenerativeagriculturefoundation.org/regenerative-agriculture/|title=Regenerative Agriculture |publisher=Regenerative Agriculture Foundation|website=regenerativeagriculturefoundation.org|language=en-US|access-date=2017-03-09}}</ref><ref name="Atekan-2014" /><ref name=":4SA">{{Cite web|url=https://us.organicindia.com/our-stories/regenerative-agriculture|title=Regenerative Organic Agriculture |publisher=Organic India |website=us.organicindia.com|language=en|access-date=2017-03-09|archive-date=2016-03-13|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160313113750/https://us.organicindia.com/our-stories/regenerative-agriculture}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Schreefel |first1=L. |last2=Schulte |first2=R. P. O. |last3=de Boer |first3=I. J. M. |last4=Schrijver |first4=A. Pas |last5=van Zanten |first5=H. H. E. |display-authors=3|date=2020-09-01 |title=Regenerative agriculture – the soil is the base |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2211912420300584 |journal=Global Food Security |volume=26 |article-number=100404 |doi=10.1016/j.gfs.2020.100404 |bibcode=2020GlFS...2600404S |issn=2211-9124}}</ref> In recent years this regenerative approach to agriculture has been gaining momentum across food system actors such as farmers and industries.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Schreefel |first1=Loekie |last2=Steenman |first2=Emile |last3=Adler |first3=Fabian |last4=Buffara |first4=Ricardo |last5=Freundt |first5=Stephan |last6=DeClerck |first6=Fabrice |last7=Duncan |first7=Jessica |last8=Giller |first8=Ken E. |last9=Koster |first9=Howard |last10=van Zanten |first10=Hannah H. E. |display-authors=3|date=2025-11-05 |title=Beyond the buzz: analyzing actors promoting regenerative agriculture in Europe |journal=npj Sustainable Agriculture |language=en |volume=3 |issue=1 |page=59 |doi=10.1038/s44264-025-00100-1  |doi-access=free|bibcode=2025npjSA...3...59S |issn=2731-9202}}</ref>

=== Alternative methods ===
==== Permaculture ====
{{excerpt|Permaculture}}

==== Polyculture ====
{{further|Polyculture}}
There is limited evidence [[polyculture]] may contribute to sustainable agriculture. A meta-analysis of a number of polycrop studies found that predator insect biodiversity was higher at comparable yields than conventional in certain [[intercropping|two-crop system]]s with a single [[cash crop]] combined with a cover crop.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Iverson |first1=Aaron L. |last2=Marín |first2=Linda E. |last3=Ennis |first3=Katherine K. |last4=Gonthier |first4=David J. |last5=Connor-Barrie |first5=Benjamin T.|last6=Remfert |first6=Jane L. |last7=Cardinale |first7=Bradley J. |last8=Perfecto |first8=Ivette |display-authors=3|date=2014 |title=REVIEW: Do polycultures promote win-wins or trade-offs in agricultural ecosystem services? A meta-analysis |journal=Journal of Applied Ecology |volume=51 |issue=6 |pages=1593–1602 |doi=10.1111/1365-2664.12334|doi-access=free |bibcode=2014JApEc..51.1593I |hdl=2027.42/109639 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

One approach to sustainability is to develop polyculture systems using [[perennial crop]] varieties. Such varieties are being developed for rice, wheat, sorghum, barley, and sunflowers. If these can be combined in polyculture with a leguminous cover crop such as alfalfa, fixation of nitrogen will be added to the system, reducing the need for fertilizer and pesticides.<ref name="Baker2017" />

==== Local small-scale agriculture ====
The use of available city space (e.g., [[rooftop gardens]], [[community gardens]], [[garden sharing]], [[organopónicos]], and other forms of [[urban agriculture]]) may be able to contribute to sustainability.<ref>{{Cite book |title=Continuous Productive Urban Landscapes: Designing Urban Agriculture for Sustainable Cities |date=2005 |publisher=Taylor & Francis |editor1=Viljoen, Andre|editor2=Howe, Joe |isbn=978-1-136-41432-9 |oclc=742299840}}</ref> Some consider "[[guerrilla gardening]]" an example of sustainability in action<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Crane |first1=Annie |last2=Viswanathan |first2=Leela |last3=Whitelaw |first3=Graham |title=Sustainability through intervention: a case study of guerrilla gardening in Kingston, Ontario |journal=Local Environment |date=January 2013 |volume=18 |issue=1 |pages=71–90 |doi=10.1080/13549839.2012.716413 |bibcode=2013LoEnv..18...71C |s2cid=144854053 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/263719489}}</ref> – in some cases seeds of edible plants have been sown in local rural areas.<ref>{{cite news |title=Incredible edible: Guerrilla gardeners are planting veg for the masses |url=https://www.independent.co.uk/property/gardening/incredible-edible-guerrilla-gardeners-are-planting-veg-for-the-masses-in-west-yorkshire-8657717.html |access-date=26 April 2022 |work=The Independent |date=13 June 2013 |language=en}}</ref>

==== Hydroponics or soil-less culture ====
Hydroponics is an alternative to agriculture that creates the ideal environment with water for optimal growth without using a dormant medium. This innovative farming technique produces higher crop yields without compromising soil health. The most significant drawback of this sustainable farming technique is the cost associated with development.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Nalwade |first1=Rahul |last2=Mote |first2=Tushar |title=2017 International Conference on Trends in Electronics and Informatics (ICEI) |chapter=Hydroponics farming |date=May 2017 |chapter-url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1109/icoei.2017.8300782 |pages=645–650 |publisher=IEEE |doi=10.1109/icoei.2017.8300782|isbn=978-1-5090-4257-9 |s2cid=44978740 }}</ref>

==Standards ==
[[File:Contour buffer strips NRCS.jpg|thumb]]
Certification systems are important to the agriculture community and to consumers as these standards determine the sustainability of produce. Numerous [[sustainability standards and certification]] systems exist, including [[organic certification]], [[Rainforest Alliance]], [[Fairtrade certification|Fair Trade]], [[UTZ Certified]], [[GLOBALG.A.P|GlobalGAP]], Bird Friendly, and the Common Code for the Coffee Community (4C).<ref name="SAI" /> These standards specify rules that producers, manufacturers and traders need to follow so that the things they do, make, or grow do not hurt people and the environment.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Voluntary Sustainability Standards |publisher=UNCTAD |url=https://unctad.org/topic/trade-analysis/voluntary-sustainability-standards |access-date=2026-02-10 |language=en-US}}</ref> These standards are also known as Voluntary Sustainability Standards (VSS) that are private standards that require products to meet specific economic, social or [[environmental sustainability]] metrics. The requirements can refer to product quality or attributes, but also to production and processing methods, as well as transportation.

VSS are mostly designed and marketed by non-governmental organizations (NGOs) or private firms and they are adopted by actors up and down the value chain, from farmers to retailers. Certifications and labels are used to signal the successful implementation of a VSS. According to the ITC standards map the mostly covered products by standards are agricultural products.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Sustainability Map |url=https://www.standardsmap.org/standards?q=eyJzZWxlY3RlZENsaWVudCI6Ik5PIEFGRklMSUFUSU9OIn0= |access-date=2021-03-03 |website=www.standardsmap.org}}</ref> Around 500 VSS today apply to key exports of many developing countries, such as coffee, tea, bananas, cocoa, palm oil, timber, cotton, and organic agri-foods.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Fostering Green Exports through Voluntary Sustainability Standards in Developing Countries |publisher=UNCTAD |url=https://unctad.org/project/fostering-green-exports-through-voluntary-sustainability-standards-developing-countries |access-date=2021-03-03 |website=unctad.org}}</ref> VSS are found to reduce eutrophication, water use, greenhouse gas emissions, and natural ecosystem conversion.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Smith |first1=W. K. |last2=Nelson |first2=E. |last3=Johnson |first3=J. A. |last4=Polasky |first4=S. |last5=Milder |first5=J. C. |last6=Gerber |first6=J. S. |last7=West |first7=P. C. |last8=Siebert |first8=S. |last9=Brauman |first9=K. A. |last10=Carlson |first10=K. M. |last11=Arbuthnot |first11=M. |display-authors=3|date=2019-02-05 |title=Voluntary sustainability standards could significantly reduce detrimental impacts of global agriculture |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |language=en |volume=116 |issue=6 |pages=2130–2137 |bibcode=2019PNAS..116.2130S |doi=10.1073/pnas.1707812116 |issn=0027-8424 |pmc=6369756 |pmid=30670643 |doi-access=free}}</ref> And thus are considered as a potential tool for sustainable agriculture.

The [[United States Department of Agriculture|USDA]] produces an organic label that is supported by nationalized standards of farmers and facilities. The steps for certification consist of creating an organic system plan, which determines how produce will be tilled, grazed, harvested, stored, and transported. This plan also manages and monitors the substances used around the produce, the maintenance needed to protect the produce, and any nonorganic products that may come in contact with the produce. The organic system plan is then reviewed and inspected by the USDA certifying agent. Once the certification is granted, the produce receives an approval sticker from the USDA and the produce is distributed across the U.S. In order to hold farmers accountable and ensure that Americans are receiving organic produce, these inspections are done at least once a year.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Ferguson |first=James J. |date=1969-12-31 |title=USDA Organic Certification: Who Should Be Certified? |journal=EDIS |volume=2004 |issue=4 |doi=10.32473/edis-hs210-2004 |issn=2576-0009|doi-access=free }}</ref> This is just one example of sustainable certification systems through produce maintenance.

== Policy ==
[[File:Delaware Valley University - Roth Center for Sustainable Agriculture, Montgomery County, Pennsylvania.jpg|thumb|Delaware Valley University's "Roth Center for Sustainable Agriculture", located in Montgomery County, Pennsylvania.]]

Sustainable agriculture is a topic in international policy concerning its potential to reduce environmental risks. In 2011, the Commission on Sustainable Agriculture and Climate Change, as part of its recommendations for policymakers on achieving food security in the face of climate change, urged that sustainable agriculture must be integrated into national and international policy.<ref name="cgiar">{{cite web |url=http://ccafs.cgiar.org/sites/default/files/assets/docs/climate_food_commission-spm-nov2011.pdf |title=Achieving food security in the face of climate change: Summary for policymakers from the Commission on Sustainable Agriculture and Climate Change |publisher=CGIAR Research Program on Climate Change, Agriculture and Food Security (CCAFS) |date=November 2011}}</ref>

The Commission stressed that increasing weather variability and climate shocks will negatively affect agricultural yields, necessitating early action to drive change in agricultural production systems towards increasing resilience.<ref name="cgiar" /> It also called for dramatically increased investments in sustainable agriculture in the next decade, including in national research and development budgets, [[land rehabilitation]], economic incentives, and infrastructure improvement.<ref name="cgiar" />

=== At the global level ===
During [[2021 United Nations Climate Change Conference]], 45 countries pledged to give more than 4 billion dollars for transition to sustainable agriculture. The organization "Slow Food" expressed concern about the effectivity of the spendings, as they concentrate on technological solutions and reforestation en place of "a holistic agroecology that transforms food from a mass-produced commodity into part of a sustainable system that works within natural boundaries."<ref>{{cite news |last1=Rosane |first1=Olivia |title=45 Countries Pledge Over $4 Billion to Support Sustainable Agriculture, But Is It Enough? |url=https://www.ecowatch.com/cop26-sustainable-agriculture-2655521091.html |access-date=11 November 2021 |agency=Ecowatch |date=8 November 2021}}</ref>

Additionally, the Summit consisted of negotiations that led to heavily reducing CO<sub>2</sub> emissions, becoming carbon neutral, ending deforestation and reliance on coal, and limiting methane emissions.<ref name="bookSur">{{Cite book |date=2021-11-16 |doi=10.52487/49704 |s2cid=247960201 |doi-access=free |title=Surveillance of the impact of COP26 on COVID-19 infections in Scotland - Preliminary report 16 November 2021 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Pacini |first1=Andrea |last2=Rossini |first2=Stefano |title=Day 1 Mon, November 15, 2021 |date=2021-12-09 |chapter=Tackling the Methane Quandary: Curbing Emissions from Control Valves |chapter-url=https://onepetro.org/SPEADIP/proceedings/21ADIP/1-21ADIP/D011S020R004/473916 |publisher=SPE |article-number=D011S020R004 |doi=10.2118/207337-MS}}</ref>

In November, the Climate Action Tracker reported that global efforts are on track to for a 2.7&nbsp;°C temperature increase with current policies, finding that the current targets will not meet global needs as coal and natural gas consumption are primarily responsible for the gap in progress.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Geiges |first1=Andreas |last2=Fyson |first2=Claire |last3=Hans |first3=Frederic |last4=Jeffery |first4=Louise |last5=Mooldijk |first5=Silke |last6=Gidden |first6=Matthew |last7=Ramapope |first7=Deborah |last8=Hare |first8=Bill |last9=Stockwell |first9=Claire |display-authors=3|date=2021-03-04 |title=Implications of current net zero targets for long-term emissions pathways and warming levels |journal=EGU General Assembly Conference Abstracts|doi=10.5194/egusphere-egu21-11018 |bibcode=2021EGUGA..2311018G |s2cid=237960433 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="bookSur" /> Since, like-minded developing countries, like those in Africa,<ref>{{cite web |author=Chris Hoy |date=2016-02-09 |title=Can developing countries afford the SDGs? |website=Devpolicy Blog |publisher=Development Policy Centre, Australian National University |url=https://devpolicy.org/can-developing-countries-afford-the-sdgs-20160209/}}</ref> asked for an addendum to the agreement that removed the obligation for developing countries to meet the same requirements of wealthy nations.<ref>{{Cite web |title=World's Poorest Nations Left Behind in Reaching Sustainable Development Goals, Delegates Stress as Second Committee Begins General Debate|url=https://press.un.org/en/2018/gaef3495.doc.htm |access-date=2026-06-21 |website=United Nations|date=2018-10-08 |language=en}}</ref>

=== European Union ===
{{Further|European Green Deal}}
In May 2020 the European Union published a program, named "From Farm to Fork" for making its agriculture more sustainable. In the official page of the program [[From Farm to Fork]] is cited [[Frans Timmermans]] the Executive Vice-President of the European Commission, saying that:

{{blockquote|The coronavirus crisis has shown how vulnerable we all are, and how important it is to restore the balance between human activity and nature. At the heart of the Green Deal the Biodiversity and Farm to Fork strategies point to a new and better balance of nature, food systems, and biodiversity; to protect our people's health and well-being, and at the same time to increase the EU's competitiveness and resilience. These strategies are a crucial part of the great transition we are embarking upon.<ref name="Farm to Fork"/>}}

The program includes the next targets:
 
* Making 25% of EU agriculture organic, by 2030.
* Reduce by 50% the use of [[pesticide]]s by 2030.
* Reduce the use of [[fertilizer]]s by 20% by 2030.
* Reduce [[nutrient loss]] by at least 50%.
* Reduce the use of [[antimicrobials in agriculture]] and [[antimicrobials in aquaculture]] by 50% by 2030.
* Create sustainable food labeling.
* Reduce [[food waste]] by 50% by 2030.
* Dedicate to R&I related to the issue €10 billion.<ref name="Farm to Fork">{{cite web |title=From Farm to Fork |url=https://ec.europa.eu/info/strategy/priorities-2019-2024/european-green-deal/actions-being-taken-eu/farm-fork_en |website=European Commission website |publisher=European Union |access-date=26 May 2020}} [[File:CC-BY icon.svg|50px]] Text was copied from this source, which is available under a [https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License].</ref>

=== United States ===
'''Policies from 1930 to 2000'''

The [[New Deal]] implemented policies and programs that promoted sustainable agriculture. Under the Agriculture Adjustment Act of 1933, it provided farmers payments to create a supply management regime that capped production of important crops.<ref name="Carlisle-2019a">{{Cite journal|last1=Carlisle|first1=Liz|last2=Montenegro de Wit|first2=Maywa|last3=DeLonge|first3=Marcia S.|last4=Iles|first4=Alastair|last5=Calo|first5=Adam|last6=Getz|first6=Christy|last7=Ory|first7=Joanna|last8=Munden-Dixon|first8=Katherine|last9=Galt|first9=Ryan|last10=Melone|first10=Brett|last11=Knox|first11=Reggie|display-authors=3|date=2019-11-01|title=Transitioning to Sustainable Agriculture Requires Growing and Sustaining an Ecologically Skilled Workforce|journal=Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems|volume=3|article-number=96|doi=10.3389/fsufs.2019.00096|issn=2571-581X|doi-access=free|bibcode=2019FrSFS...3...96C }}</ref><ref name="Shaffer-2017">{{Citation|last=Shaffer|first=Timothy J.|chapter=Thinking beyond food and fiber|date=2017-08-17|title=The Intersection of Food and Public Health|pages=307–326|location=New York|publisher=Routledge|doi=10.1201/9781315153094-21|doi-broken-date=9 June 2026 |isbn=978-1-4987-5895-6}}</ref><ref name="Carlisle-2019b">{{Cite journal|last1=Carlisle|first1=Liz|last2=de Wit|first2=Maywa Montenegro|last3=DeLonge|first3=Marcia S.|last4=Calo|first4=Adam|last5=Getz|first5=Christy|last6=Ory|first6=Joanna|last7=Munden-Dixon|first7=Katherine|last8=Galt|first8=Ryan|last9=Melone|first9=Brett|last10=Knox|first10=Reggie|last11=Iles|first11=Alastair|display-authors=3|date=2019-01-01|editor-last=Kapuscinski|editor-first=Anne R.|editor2-last=Méndez|editor2-first=Ernesto|title=Securing the future of US agriculture: The case for investing in new entry sustainable farmers|journal=Elementa: Science of the Anthropocene|language=en|volume=7|article-number=17|doi=10.1525/elementa.356|s2cid=190434574|issn=2325-1026|doi-access=free|bibcode=2019EleSA...7...17C }}</ref> This allowed farmers to focus on growing food and not competing in the market based system. The [[New Deal]] also provided a monetary incentive for farmers that left some of their fields unsown or ungrazed to order to improve the soil conditions.<ref name="Carlisle-2019a" /> The Cooperative Extension Service was also established that set up sharing funding responsibilities amongst the [[United States Department of Agriculture|USDA]], land-grant universities, and local communities.<ref name="Shaffer-2017" />

The 1950s to 1990s was when the government switched its stance on agriculture policy which halted sustainable agriculture. The [[Agricultural Act of 1954]] passed which supported farmers with flexible price supports, but only to commodity programs.<ref name="USDA-SCS?-1977">{{Cite book|title=Forestry summary report / [prepared by U.S. Department of Agriculture Soil Conservation Service, Economic Research Service, Forest Service, in cooperation with Montana Department of Natural Resources and Conservation]|chapter=Forestry summary report |date=1977|publisher=USDA-SCS?|location=Portland, Or.?|doi=10.5962/bhl.title.27205}}</ref> The [[Food and Agriculture Act of 1965|Food and Agricultural Act of 1965]] had new income support payments and continued supply controls but reduced priced supports.<ref name="USDA-SCS?-1977" /> [[Agriculture and Consumer Protection Act of 1973]] removed price supports and instead introduced target prices and deficiency payments.<ref name="USDA-SCS?-1977" /> It continued to promote commodity crops by lowering interest rates. [[Food Security Act of 1985]] continued commodity loan programs.<ref name="Carlisle-2019b" /><ref name="USDA-SCS?-1977" /> These policies incentivized profit over sustainability because the US government was promoting farms to maximize their production output instead of placing checks.<ref name="USDA-SCS?-1977" /> This meant that farms were being turned into food factories as they became bigger in size and grew more [[Cash crop|commodity crops]] like corn, wheat, and cotton. From 1900 to 2002, the number of farms in the US decreased significantly while the average size of a farm went up after 1950.<ref name="USDA-SCS?-1977" /><ref name="Carlisle-2019b" /> The U.S was almost annually setting new records in crop-production and labor efficiency for 40 years after WWII.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Reganold |first1=John P. |last2=Papendick |first2=Robert I. |last3=Parr |first3=James F. |date=1990 |title=Sustainable Agriculture |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/24996835 |journal=Scientific American |volume=262 |issue=6 |pages=112–121 |doi=10.1038/scientificamerican0690-112 |jstor=24996835 |bibcode=1990SciAm.262f.112R |issn=0036-8733}}</ref>

'''Current policies'''

In the United States, the federal [[Natural Resources Conservation Service]] ([[USDA]]) provides technical and financial assistance for those interested in pursuing natural resource conservation along with production agriculture. With programs like [[Sustainable Agriculture Research and Education|SARE]] and China-UK [[Sustainable Agriculture Innovation Network|SAIN]] to help promote research on sustainable agriculture practices and a framework for agriculture and climate change respectively.

'''Future policies'''

Currently, there are policies on the table that could move the US agriculture system into a more sustainable direction with the [[Green New Deal]]. This policy promotes decentralizing agrarian governance by breaking up large commodity farms that were created in the 1950s to 1980s.<ref name="Carlisle-2019a" /> Decentralized governance within the farming community would allow for more adaptive management at local levels to help focus on [[climate change mitigation]], [[food security]], and landscape-scale ecological stewardship.<ref name="Carlisle-2019a" /> The [[Green New Deal]] would invest in public infrastructure to support farmers transition from industrial food regime and acquire [[Agroecology|agroecological]] skills.<ref name="Carlisle-2019a" /> Just like in the [[New Deal]], it would invest in [[cooperative]]s and commons to share and redistribute resources like land, food, equipment, research facilities, personnel, and training programs.<ref name="Carlisle-2019a" /> All of these policies and programs would break down barriers that have prevented sustainable farmers and agriculture from taking place in the United States.<ref name="Carlisle-2019b" />

=== Current movements in the U.S. ===
In the United States there has been a movement with key advocates like Leah Penniman for sustainable agriculture. Leah Penniman has been a science teacher, farmer, writer, and Co-Founder of Soul Fire Farm.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |title=Leah Penniman Farms for Food and Land Justice |url=https://www.earthisland.org/journal/index.php/magazine/entry/leah-penniman-farms-for-food-and-land-justice/ |access-date=2026-04-09 |website=Earth Island Journal}}</ref> Soul Fire Farm uses regenerative agriculture and many of the techniques invented by George Washington Carver.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Karas |first=Sheryl |date=2026 |title=Leah Penniman's Inspirational Keynote Address at the This Way to Sustainability Conference |url=https://www.csuchico.edu/regenerativeagriculture/blog/leah-penniman.shtml |access-date=April 19, 2026 |website=Center for Regenerative Agriculture and Resilient Systems (California State University, Chico)}}</ref> Penniman wrote the book ''Farming While Black: Soul Fire Farm's Practical Guide to Liberation on the Land'' which guides African-heritage farmers on Afro-Indigenous sustainable farming practices while highlighting their historical contributions to sustainable agriculture as well. The community farm built by Penniman is also a training center whose goal is to end racism in agriculture.<ref name=":3" />

Like Penniman, Dr. Monica M. White has been advocating for the use of more sustainable agriculture.  Her focus has been on the expansion of urban agriculture and how it's more sustainable in a [[food desert]], such as Detroit.  Members of the community in Detroit, referred to as D-Town, offer workshops about healthy food choices, composting, and "the importance of sustainable agriculture."<ref>{{Cite journal |last=White |first=Monica M. |date=2010 |title=Shouldering Responsibility for the Delivery of Human Rights: A Case Study of the D-Town Farmers of Detroit |url=https://monicamariewhite.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/10/Shouldering_Responsibility_for_the_Deliv.pdf |journal=Race/Ethnicity: Multicultural Global Contexts}}</ref>

=== Asia ===

==== China ====
In 2016, the [[Chinese government]] adopted a plan to reduce China's meat consumption by 50%, for achieving more sustainable and healthy food system.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Matthew |first1=Bossons |title=New Meat: Is China Ready for a Plant-Based Future? |url=https://www.thatsmags.com/shanghai/post/31101/china-meets-new-meat-is-the-prc-ready-for-a-plant-based-future |access-date=21 June 2020 |website=That's}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Milman |first1=Oliver |last2=Leavenworth |first2=Stuart |date=20 June 2016 |title=China's plan to cut meat consumption by 50% cheered by climate campaigners |agency=The Guardian |url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2016/jun/20/chinas-meat-consumption-climate-change |access-date=21 June 2020}}</ref>

In 2019, the National Basic Research Program or [[Program 973]] funded research into Science and Technology Backyard (STB). STBs are hubs often created in rural areas with significant rates of [[Smallholding|small-scale farming]] that combine knowledge of traditional practices with new innovations and technology implementation. The purpose of this program was to invest in sustainable farming throughout the country and increase food production while achieving few negative environmental effects. The program was ultimately proven to be successful, and the study found that the merging of traditional practices and appropriate technology was instrumental in higher crop yields.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Jiao |first1=Xiao-qiang |last2=Zhang |first2=Hong-yan |last3=Ma |first3=Wen-qi |last4=Wang |first4=Chong |last5=Li |first5=Xiao-lin |last6=Zhang |first6=Fu-suo |display-authors=3|date=2019 |title=Science and Technology Backyard: A novel approach to empower smallholder farmers for sustainable intensification of agriculture in China |journal=Journal of Integrative Agriculture |volume=18 |issue=8 |pages=1657–1666 |doi=10.1016/S2095-3119(19)62592-X |bibcode=2019JIAgr..18.1657J |issn=2095-3119|doi-access=free }}</ref>

==== India ====
In collaboration with the Food and Land Use Coalition (FOLU), CEEW (council for energy, environment and water), has given an overview of the current state of sustainable agriculture practices and systems (SAPSs) in India.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2021-04-16 |title=Sustainable Agriculture in India 2021 |url=https://www.ceew.in/publications/sustainable-agriculture-india |access-date=2022-06-09 |website=CEEW |language=en}}</ref> India is aiming to scale-up SAPs, through policymakers, administrators, philanthropists, and other which represent a vital alternative to conventional, input-intensive agriculture. In idea these efforts identify 16 SAPSs{{snd}}including agroforestry, crop rotation, rainwater harvesting, organic farming and natural farming{{snd}}using agroecology as an investigative lens. In a conclusive understanding it is realised that sustainable agriculture is far from mainstream in India. Further proposals for several measures for promoting SAPSs, including restructured government support and rigorous evidence generation for benefits and implementation of sustainable farming are ongoing progress in Indian Agriculture.

An example of initiatives in India towards exploring the world of sustainable farming has been set by the [[Sowgood foundation]] which is a nonprofit founded by educator Pragati Chaswal.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Delhi-based SowGood Foundation fosters a green thumb |url=https://www.newindianexpress.com/cities/delhi/2021/oct/17/delhi-basedsowgood-foundation-fosters-agreen-thumb-2372266.html |access-date=2022-06-09 |website=The New Indian Express|date=17 October 2021 }}</ref> It started by teaching primary school children about sustainable farming by helping them farm on small farm strips in suburban farmhouses and gardens. Today many government and private schools in Delhi, India have adopted the sowgood foundation curriculum for sustainable farming for their students.

=== Other countries ===

==== Israel ====
In 2012, the Israeli Ministry of Agriculture found itself at the height of the Israeli commitment to sustainable agriculture policy. A large factor of this policy was funding programs that made sustainable agriculture accessible to smaller Palestinian-Arab communities. The program was meant to create biodiversity, train farmers in sustainable agriculture methods, and hold regular meetings for agriculture stakeholders.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Gutkowski |first=Natalia |date=August 2018 |title=Governing Through Timescape: Israeli Sustainable Agriculture Policy and the Palestinian-Arab Citizens |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/identifier/S002074381800079X/type/journal_article |journal=International Journal of Middle East Studies |language=en |volume=50 |issue=3 |pages=471–492 |doi=10.1017/S002074381800079X |issn=0020-7438 |s2cid=165180859|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

== History ==
In 1907, the American author [[Franklin Hiram King|Franklin H. King]] discussed in his book ''Farmers of Forty Centuries'' the advantages of sustainable agriculture and warned that such practices would be vital to farming in the future.<ref>{{cite book|last1=King|first1=Franklin H.|url=http://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/5350|title=Farmers of forty centuries|date=2004|access-date=20 February 2016}}</ref> The phrase 'sustainable agriculture' was reportedly coined by the Australian [[agronomist]] [[Gordon McClymont]].<ref>{{cite web|author=Rural Science Graduates Association|year=2002|title={{sic |In Memo |rium |hide=y |expected=In Memoriam}} - Former Staff and Students of Rural Science at UNE|url=http://agbu.une.edu.au/~aaabg/rsga/im.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130606220152/http://agbu.une.edu.au/~aaabg/rsga/im.html|archive-date=6 June 2013|access-date=21 October 2012|publisher=[[University of New England (Australia)|University of New England]]}}</ref> The term became popular in the late 1980s.<ref name="Frey-2011">{{Cite book |last=Frey |first=Darrell |title=Bioshelter market garden: a permaculture farm |date=2011 |publisher=New Society Publishers |isbn=978-0-86571-678-0 |location=Gabriola Island, BC |oclc=601130383}}</ref> There was an international symposium on sustainability in horticulture by the International Society of Horticultural Science at the International Horticultural Congress in Toronto in 2002.<ref>{{cite journal |url=http://www.actahort.org/books/638/638_65.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180601204508/http://www.actahort.org/books/638/638_65.htm|archive-date=2018-06-01 |vauthors= Bertschinger L, Anderson JD, de Groot N, Granatstein D, Habib R, Mullinix K, Neilsen D, Pomares García F, Weibel FP, Zinati G |display-authors=3|date=2004 |title=Conclusions from the 1st Symposium on Sustainability in Horticulture and a Declaration for the 21st Century. In: Proc. XXVI IHC – Sustainability of Horticultural Systems |journal=Acta Hort |issue=638 |publisher=ISHS |pages=509–512 |doi=10.17660/ActaHortic.2004.638.65 |access-date=2009-03-16}}</ref> At the following conference at Seoul in 2006, the principles were discussed further.<ref>{{cite journal |author=Lal, R. |year=2008 |title=Sustainable Horticulture and Resource Management. In: Proc. XXVII IHC-S11 Sustainability through Integrated and Organic Horticulture. |editor=R.K. Prange and S.D. Bishop |journal=Acta Hort |issue=767 |publisher=ISHS |pages=19–44 |doi=10.17660/ActaHortic.2008.767.1 }}</ref>

This potential future inability to feed the world's population has been a concern since the English political economist [[Thomas Robert Malthus|Thomas Malthus]] in the early 1800s, but has become increasingly important recently.<ref name="Ehrlich">{{cite journal |jstor=2938383 |title=Food Security, Population and Environment |last1=Ehrlich |first1=Paul R. |last2=Ehrlich |first2=Anne H. |last3=Daily |first3=Gretchen C. |journal=Population and Development Review |date=1993 |volume=19 |issue=1 |pages=1–32 |doi=10.2307/2938383 }}</ref> Starting at the very end of the twentieth and early twenty-first centuries, this issue became widely discussed in the U.S. because of growing anxieties of a rapidly increasing global population. [[Agriculture]] has long been the biggest industry worldwide and requires significant land, water, and labor inputs. At the turn of the twenty-first century, experts questioned the industry's ability to keep up with population growth.<ref name="Singh-2017" /> This debate led to concerns over global [[Food security|food insecurity]] and "solving hunger".<ref name="rieff"/><ref name="AR6SYR2023">{{cite report |title=AR6 Synthesis Report: Climate Change 2023 |publisher=Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) |date=2023-03-20 |url=https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/syr/ |type=Synthesis Report |quote=AFOLU (including deforestation) remains a significant source of net CO2 emissions; recent assessments place its share at roughly one-tenth of total anthropogenic CO2 emissions. }}</ref><ref name="GCB2024">{{cite journal |title=Global Carbon Budget 2024 |journal=Earth System Science Data |year=2024 |doi=10.5194/essd-2024-XXX |doi-broken-date=9 June 2026 |doi-access=free |url=https://globalcarbonbudget.org/ |quote=CO2 emissions from land-use change are estimated at ~3–4 GtCO2 yr−1, corresponding to about 10–12% of total fossil and land-use CO2 emissions in recent years. }}</ref>
